Department of Lands and Survey Report-Accuracy
WEDNESDAY, 16 AUGUST 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
DEPARTMENT OF LANDS AND SURVEY REPORT-ACCURACY
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): A point of order, Mr Speaker. A few days ago I had
cause to draw the attention of the Minister of Maori Affairs to an error in a departmental
report that had been furnished and tabled, and the House was asked to agree to a motion
that it be printed. Today I draw the attention of the Minister of Lands to the fact that an
error appears in the report of the Department of Lands and Survey, which the House
resolved should be printed. On page 42 of the report there is an error in the totals given in
the summary of land development. I am sure it is not your wish, Mr Speaker, or the wish of
any other member, that figures of tremendous public interest should remain in error, and I'
suggest that you consider reminding the Government that it is absolutely essential that
reports furnished to the House-which is asked to approve their printing—should be as
accurate as possible.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): If the honourable member for Northern Maori
can give me details of the error, I shall make sure that the House is informed of it. However,
as a former Minister, the member knows very well that the proof reading of the details in the
report is done by departmental officials. Nevertheless, I shall check the error he mentioned.
Mr SPEAKER: I am not really sure that this is a proper point of order, because it is on a
matter that does not involve me. Certainly, a motion was put before the House that the
report be printed, but nothing in the motion suggests that the report must be accurate or
otherwise, although one would assume it should be correct. Possibly, a happier solution to
this type of error, when it is found, would be simply to take it up with the Minister
concerned. Certainly, the House is involved, but I believe it would be more appropriate for
the Minister to acquaint members of the correction to be made.
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Road Cartage Limit-Extension
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), on behalf of Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to
the Minister of Transport: Has he read the report in the Southland Times of 4 August of the
statement made at a seminar in Napier by a senior economist with the Ministry of Transport:
"I see a gradual lengthening of the 150 kilometre limit", and can he indicate when the
Government proposes accordingly to extend the 150 kilometre limit?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Acting Minister of Transport): Yes, I have seen the report in the
Southland Times referred to by the honourable member. The predictions by the senior
economist in the ministry at the seminar in Napier were his own and did not purport to
represent the views of either his department or the Government. This was made clear at the
time, but was not reported by the Southland Times. The 1978 Budget included a statement
that future steps in the transport field would include a review of the transport licensing
system and a decision on the next stage of extending competition between road and rail.
There is no question at present of the limit being extended.
Mr Hunt: The Minister has said that the gradual lengthening of the 150 km limit forms
no part of the Government's policy. Does the use of the word "gradual" imply exactly that
meaning?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The recent review was a major one, and the first for a long time.
No responsible Government would change things again without giving the new system a fair
trial.
Hon. M. Rata: What steps has the Minister taken to ensure that the public is acquainted
with the fact that the statement is the personal view of the officer concerned?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I am not interested. I have yet to find two economists who think
alike.

16 August
Questions for Oral Answer
Energy Use for Public Buildings
2. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) to the Minister of Energy: What form of energy is at
present being recommended for use in new hospitals, schools, and public buildings; and, if it
is oil, how do the source availability and cost compare with those for electricity?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Energy.
"No form of energy is at present being recommended for use in new hospitals, schools, and
public buildings. However the interdepartmental committee on the heating of public
buildings, which decides on the fuel usage of new Government buildings, gives preference to
natural gas and coal. In practice, for cost reasons, oil is not normally selected when
indigenous fuels are available unless it is being used on an interim basis pending the
availability of natural gas. Likewise, electricity is usually too expensive for all but the
smallest heating loads of intermittent duration".
Mr Cooper: Are any public buildings heated by solar heating?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I believe there is a move towards incorporating solar heating as
part of the heating component in buildings. In the Lake County hospital in the member's
own electorate there is a proposal for the joint use of coal and solar heating.
Health-Free Medicines
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen an article in the New
Zealand Herald of 5 August 1978 in which the Executive Director of the Pharmaceutical
Manufacturers Association, Mr R. W. Martin, is reported to have said that “cutting back on
the number of drugs would mean that people would no longer be able to expect the advanced
medical standards now available in New Zealand", and that the Government "is moving
away from the concept of free medicine", and, if so, does he propose to cut back in this way.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Yes, I have seen the article. It is not proposed to
cut back in this way.
Mr Hunt: In view of the announcement made last night by the Australian Minister of
Finance that the Medibank system in Australia is to be abolished, can the Minister give an
absolute assurance that similar proposals, which would include cutting back the amounts
allocated for free prescriptions, will not be permitted?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I have not seen the announcement referred to. We have never had a
system in this country similar to the Australian one. Our medical programme will continue as
at present in accordance with announced National Party policy.
Mr Malcolm: Can the Minister confirm that at times a variety of similar drugs with
different brand names and different prices, but with the same performance, are on the
market and the department does its best to encourage the use of the lower-priced product
that is of equal quality?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes; one of the main weapons in our arsenal for controlling the price
of drugs is that, when a drug comes out under a variety of brand names, the cheapest but not
the least efficient is put on the free list. Therefore if a doctor prescribes a drug by using its
generic name rather than its brand name he will ensure that his patients receive the drug on
the free list. Even if a doctor prescribes a drug not on the free list--because a patient has
confidence in it under its brand name-he can approach the department and the drug can be
issued free.
Mr Hunt: Has the Minister a proposal to provide a system whereby the generic name of
drugs is automatically made available on the packages so that a doctor can inform his
patient?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The Opposition spokesman on health does not understand the
position very clearly. Under the Food and Drugs Act, drugs are labelled correctly in regard
to their contents and makeup. The thing that causes confusion is that doctors are not always
up to date on whether a drug is on the free list. I recently looked at the problem and found
that it would cost $22,000 a year for printing and postage to keep all doctors strictly up to
date each time a change was made. So we now send copies of the list to the medical officers
of health in each district, and if a doctor has any doubts he has only to ring up the medical
officer of health to obtain the correct brand name or to find out whether the drug is on the
free list.

Questions for Oral Answer
Chatsfield-West Harbour Subdivision
4. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Housing: How many sections
have been offered to the public by ballot or tender in the Chatsfield-West Harbour
subdivison?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Three hundred sections have been
offered to the public.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: How many sections have been offered in the West Harbour portion
of the subdivision, and how much response has there been for stage I?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: As the honourable gentleman knows, the West Harbour land
is being offered in a number of stages. For stage I, 17 sections have so far been offered for
sale to the public, 9 by ballot and 8 by tender. For the 8 offered by tender only 3 tenders were
received, and as none was acceptable the sections were retained by the corporation.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: By how much has the Government raised the price of sections since
1975? Is the figure $3,000 or $4,000?
Mr SPEAKER: That is really beyond the scope of the question.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not have that information with me. If the honourable
gentleman would like it I am sure he is capable of putting down his own question.
Air Fares, Auckland - Dunedin
5. Mr KIRK (Sydenham), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the
Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services: How many hours did a man on the
average ordinary-time weekly wage have to work to pay for the cost of an air fare between
Auckland and Dunedin in November 1975 and in August 1978?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Acting Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
Based on earnings before tax, in November 1975 a man had to work 23.6 hours, and in
August 1978 he has to work only 20 hours. On earnings after tax, in November 1975 a man
had to work 28.7 hours, and in August 1978 he has to work only 26.2 hours. Those figures
show that a person is obviously better off today then he was in 1975.
Mr Kirk: How will those computations be affected by the 12 percent increase in air fares
that is being sought now?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: If the honourable member submits a question when the amount
of the increase has been decided, I am sure the Minister will be happy to give him the
answer.
Mr. D. M. J. Jones: What will be the effect on air fares in the event of a foreign
exchange levy being imposed for the purchase of new aircraft overseas?
Mr SPEAKER: That is a hypothetical question, which may not be asked or answered.
Coromandel Gymnasium
6. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Education: When will the proposed
multipurpose gymnasium for Coromandel be approved, and when is construction likely to
commence?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Education. "My department is now preparing a submission recommending a grant to
enable the acceptance of the lowest tender for the construction of the Coromandel general
purpose hall. Subject to my approval, construction should begin shortly".
Mr Schultz: In view of the delay that has taken place, and in the event of any further
delay, will the local community be expected to provide further funds?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: From my reading of the supplementary information I
understand that the difficulties have been ironed out. I cannot see any question of
supplementary funds being considered, but I advise the honourable member to check that
out with the Minister.
Mr Hunt: Will the Minister concede that if there are further delays the cost will
obviously rise, and will he concede also that the question asked by the member for
Coromandel is a perfectly valid one? Will the Government make up the difference so that
the local community will not have to undertake an enormous fund-raising effort to pay for
the Government's delay.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I hesitate to contradict the member, but the delays have
been caused by differences of opinion over construction and tendering. As I understand it.

Wheaten Cornflour-Price Increase
7. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER
(Mt. Albert), to the Minister of Trade and Industry: How does he explain the fact that,
under the supervision of his department, the price of wheaten cornflour has moved from 6.2c
per 100 grams in November 1975 to 21.3c per 100 grams in August 1978—an increase of over
300 percent?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry): I
reply on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Industry. "The general retail price of a 1lb
packet of cornflour in November 1975 was 50c. This was equivalent to 44c for 400g. The
present retail price is generally 88c for a 400g packet. This represents an increase of 100
percent, not 300 percent. The principal reason for this increase is that flour, from which
cornflour is made, which had remained priced at $112 a tonne from June 1972 to March
1976, is now priced at $235 a tonne—an increase of 110 percent".
Mr Bruce Barclay: Why has the price of flour increased by that amount when the price
of wheat, from which flour is made, has increased by only 25 percent since 1975?
Mr ALLEN: The price of flour was subject to a subsidy for 4 years during the Labour
Government's term, which meant that the price was kept down artificially. When the
subsidies were removed the price increased to a more realistic level.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is it correct that Labour's 1975 Budget stated that subsidies would be
reduced at the end of 1975?
Mr ALLEN: I understand that to be so.
“Golden Age” Air Fare Concessions
8. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the
Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services: When were the "Golden Age" air
fare concessions introduced by New Zealand's national airline, and what was the number of
bookings made under this scheme in 1977?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Acting Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
"Golden Age" fare concessions were introduced on 1 July 1972, and in 1977 the number of
journeys made totalled 79 085.
Miss Dewe: What are the actual "Golden Age" air fare concessions?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The concession is a 30 percent discount on published fares, which
applies to any flights on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, excluding flights
on public holidays.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it correct that the Government, since introducing national
superannuation, has reduced the number of people who can take advantage of these
concessions by eliminating the concession available to people under the age of 65?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: On the contrary, under national superannuation retired people
have been given financial independence and are now receiving a benefit equivalent to or
better than the wage earned by many people. I am sure national superannuitants will be
delighted to be able to pay the full fare.
Taxation
9. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: What is the current tax payable by a single-income married couple earning $140
a week, with (a) 1 child (b) 2 children, and (c) 3 children?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department):
The tax payable depends on the ages of the children. If one of the children is under the age of
5 years the taxpayer would qualify for the spouse rebate and the young-family rebate.
Therefore, the current PAYE tax would be $24.57 a week. If there were no children under 5
years of age, the current PAYE tax would be $33.57 a week. In addition, if one of the
children was under the age of 10 there would be an entitlement to the single-income family
rebate of $208 a year or $4 a week, which would be allowed in an end-of-year assessment.

Questions for Oral Answer
These figures will be substantially affected by the proposed changes set out in the Bills
before the House.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Could the Minister explain why a man who earns $140 a week and
has one child pays the same tax as a man who earns $140 a week and has three children,
although the children are in the same age group?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am not sure what the honourable member is getting at. He
asked a question about a specific situation. If he wants to argue with the amount paid, that is
fine, but the tax tables are fair and reasonable.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is it correct that single-income and young-family rebates amounting
to about $14 a week were introduced by the National Government, not the Labour
Government during its term of office?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes. Of course, we have been over this in the House. The
reason for the assistance at the young family level is that the highest demand is made on the
family when the children are young. I do not think that was the point the member for
Manukau was trying to make, because he has consistently overlooked it.
Rhodesia-Removal of Sanctions
10. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: In view of recent
statements by the United States and Great Britain about the possibility of their removing
sanctions against Rhodesia, is he prepared to make a similar statement on behalf of the New
Zealand Government?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Foreign Affairs. "The statements to which the honourable member refers were not made by
the British or American Governments. It is, therefore, not the intention of the New Zealand
Government to make a similar statement".
Mr Malcolm: Is it within the terms of the United Nations Charter for New Zealand to
make any such statement unilaterally?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The sanctions were imposed following a decision of the
Security Council in 1968 that was mandatory in terms of the United Nations Charter on all
member Governments. The New Zealand Government does not have the right to lift
sanctions until a further decision is taken by the Security Council.
Mr Prebble: Is it not correct that both the United States Government and the British
Government have recently officially indicated that they will not lift sanctions against
Rhodesia?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: As I said in my original reply, the statements to which the
honourable member refers were not made by the British or American Governments.
Overseas Students-Political Activities
11. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Immigration: For how long has New
Zealand imposed restrictions on political activities of private overseas students?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): As far as I can ascertain, restrictions were
first imposed on private overseas students on 21 June 1974, when the Labour Government
Minister of Immigration obtained from the New Zealand University Students Association a
written undertaking, which stated, inter alia, "We are aware of your concern regarding the
political activities of Mr Isaacs during his period in New Zealand. As we agreed during the
interview with you, NZUSA will advise Mr Isaacs of your concern and will not encourage
him to take any active political role in this country".
Mr Marshall: Can the Minister give any evidence that there is a written statement from
any previous Minister-from a Minister, not to a Minister-imposing such restrictions as are
now proposed to be imposed on the South African students coming to this country?
Hon. T. F. GILL: To a large extent a Minister's papers are his own. The member
probably ought to be posing his question in private to the previous Minister of Immigration.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Is it not a fact that the matter arose because a condition of the

Area School Teachers-Salaries
13. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Can he explain why
a teacher training an evening class in an area school is paid at a considerably lower hourly
rate than if the school had retained its district high school status?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Education. "Secondary teachers at district high schools were paid on an overtime basis for
taking evening classes in terms of the secondary teachers salary determination. Teachers at
area schools are paid in terms of the area schools salary determination, under which there is
no provision for the payment of overtime. All teachers taking evening classes in area schools
are paid the specified rates for technical and continuation classes".
Mr Prebble: Does the Government plan to alter the present scale for teachers taking
evening classes in area schools, who are secondary school teachers who have taken up
appointments at area schools, and can the Minister say why they are paid at a lower rate?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I believe that is a matter for negotiation. Any person taking
a position in an area school under the new conditions would know the determination under
which he or she was working.

belong to the NZEI, and because the possibility of an agreement between those
organisations is pretty slight, who negotiates on behalf of the teachers in area schools?
Mr SPEAKER: That question has been answered in the House at least once this session.
I must point out that a question cannot be asked again during the same session. I will allow
the Minister to answer if he can.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: My understanding—and I can supplement it—is that the
PPTA is responsible, and that a working party is being set up to consider the matter.

Farm Workers' Award
17. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Labour: Has the
increase in the farm workers' award led to an increase in the amount paid by farmers to farm
workers under the special work scheme, and, if so, by how much?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Farmers employing farm workers under the
farm employment scheme are, like all other people employing labour, legally obliged to pay
at least the minimum rate specified in the appropriate award made under the Agricultural
Workers Act. If the amount previously paid was less than the new minimum rate, the farmer
is required to increase the farm worker's pay. If the new wage payable to a farm worker
employed under the farm employment scheme falls between $120 and $150 a week there will
be an increase in the subsidy paid by the Department of Labour to the farmer.
Mr Bruce Barclay: What is the increase in the subsidy to be paid by the department?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The questioner asks for an answer in dollars and cents.
Obviously, I cannot give that, as I would have to get the breakdown for the individuals on
the farms, and whether they were being paid award wages. The most significant figure I
have-which surprised me--and I am sure would surprise the member-is that 42 percent of
those on the scheme are under the age of 18.
Motor Cycle Injury Statistics
18. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden), to the
Minister of Labour: Will he advise the House, from the Accident Compensation
Commission's actuarial statistics of motor-cycle related injuries, what percentage is caused
by motor-cycle driver fault and what percentage is caused by other road users?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The accident compensation scheme
abolishes consideration of fault. Accordingly, the Accident Compensation Commission does
not collect statistics from which fault can be attributed to those involved in accidents, nor
would it be administratively possible to do so. Having regard to the disputes that used to be
involved in the establishment of fault, the commission does not accept as reliable any
estimates or opinions given at the present day on percentages of blame attributable to
different classes of persons or vehicles involved in accidents.
Mr Prebble: As Parliament has placed an obligation on the Accident Compensation
Commission to reduce accidents, can the Minister say whether it is doing any research into
the cause of the high number of motor cycle accidents, and which section is at fault-the

Overseas Students-Public Speaking
19. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Immigration: Does he intend to
inform private overseas students how many people constitute a public meeting so that the
students will be able to conform to the Government ruling on public speaking while they are
in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): No, I do not intend to inform private
overseas students what constitutes public meetings. The restriction imposed by the
Government applies only to students sponsored from within New Zealand, and is a
restriction only on taking part in political activities, including political speech making. As I
said in answer to a question on 9 August, defining political speech making is similar to
defining disorderly conduct. Each case must be considered according to the circumstances
prevailing at that particular place and time.

which asked the Minister, "Does he intend to inform private overseas students how many
people constitute a public meeting. . . .?"
Hon. M. Rata: In the Minister's answer he said-
Mr SPEAKER: I have considered the Minister's answer. The honourable member is
now asking the Minister if he will explain the reasons for adopting a certain policy. That
question is not related specifically to the original question. Perhaps the honourable member
could try again.
Hon. M. Rata: Can the Minister explain the requirement he has imposed upon overseas
students-including a ban on political speech making-which involves the principle of free
speech?
Mr SPEAKER: That is as remote from the original question as the first supplementary
question. If the honourable member wants to ask such a question there is no reason why he
should not do so on a different occasion.

9.
Hospitals Closed
(28/7/78)
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Health: Would he list
occasions since the coming into force of the Hospitals Act 1957 on which, under
section 55 of the Act, Ministers of Health have granted consent to the closing of
any institution (as defined in section 2 of the Act) or have consented to the
estricting of any forms of care, treatment, or relief in or from any such institution;
and in the process of so doing would he give the following information: (a) the
name of the hospital board, (b) the address and name of the institution, (c) the
type of the institution, and (d) the reasons for closing the institution or restricting
care, treatment, or relief?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Many of the closures of hospital
board institutions since 1957 have been of small maternity hospitals. These have
all been closed for much the same reasons, or combination of reasons: under-
utilisation, caused in the main by more mothers preferring to be delivered in the
larger obstetric hospitals where all facilities are available in the event of a sudden
emergency; the very real difficulties in finding qualified midwives to work in
institutions where the small number of births means that their skills are not being
fully used; the high cost of running institutions that for large parts of the year
may be unoccupied; and, in more recent years, a reluctance on the part of some
doctors to undertake deliveries in these small hospitals, as the undergraduate
training course for doctors does not provide the same experience in obstetrics as
previously. The maternity hospitals that have been closed, or hospitals where
maternity facilities have ceased, are as follows:

Marinoto Home, Dunedin-Otago Hospital Board; this was used as a convales-

Malvern geriatric ward-Ashburton Hospital Board; the board found that it
had an oversupply of this type of accommodation.
Huntsbury Children's Home, Christchurch-North Canterbury Hospital Board;
the home had been used for children who had been exposed to, but had not
contracted, tuberculosis, and it was found that fewer and fewer children were
using the home.
Cornwall Hospital-Auckland Hospital Board; this hospital was remnants of a
large World War II military hospital built on reserve land that the Auckland
Hospital Board was allowed to use until it had built suitable alternative
accommodation.
Central Park Hospital, Wellington-Wellington Hospital Board; the hospital,
used for geriatric patients, was in a very run-down condition, and because
of the high expense of required renovations it was decided to close the hospital
and transfer patients to other institutions.

Solar Water Heaters
(1/8/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Can he give
the average cost of a solar water heater, the cost of installing it (a) in a new house,
and (b) in an existing house; what is the estimated kWh equivalent during daylight
hours of the average solar heater (sun above horizon) in either Auckland or
Wellington, and by how much does this fall short of the electrical needs of the
average household; or, in other words, how much additional electrical power would
be needed for water heating in the average home when a reasonably efficient solar
heater is installed?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The average cost of a solar
water heater installed depends on several factors such as the type of system, the
number of collector panels or cylinders, and the amount of plumbing required.
In a new house the cost of an average-sized system would be between $600 and
$800 For an existing house the cost would be about $100 more. The average

household consumption of electricity for water heating is 4000 kWh per year. An
effectively operated solar unit can, in a favourable location, save up to half this
electricity. In this case 2000 kWh of electricity a year would be needed for water
heating.

Papanui High School-Accommodation
(2/8/78)
17.
Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St. Albans) to the Minister of Education:
What plans has the department for relieving the pupil pressure at Papanui High
School, and when will the present situation of pupil accommodation in temporary
rooms be overcome?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: My department has
recently discussed with the Papanui High School Board alternative proposals to
improve the accommodation at Papanui High School. If roll projections, following
receipt of the 1 July 1978 primary school roll returns, show that a new school at
Redwood is still required, then initial planning and the preparation of costs based
on standard documents for the new school will be completed and the temporary
rooms at Papanui High School will be resited and upgraded to provide a more
suitable teaching environment until the new school is ready. If roll forecasts
clearly indicate that a new secondary school is not required it is proposed to
arrange the provision of additional permanent accommodation at Papanui High
School.
18.
Belfast Primary School-Staff Improvements
(2/8/78)
Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St. Albans) to the Minister of Education:
What plans has the department to improve staffing and provide remedial reading
at Belfast Primary School?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Belfast School has
been fully staffed to entitlement throughout 1978. At the end of term 1 the roll
grew to the extent that the staffing entitlement rose by 0.3 of a teacher. The
principal decided to form a new class by combining this 0.3 with the existing
part-time component of 0.6 of a teacher, which had been used during the first
term for remedial reading work in the School. This action was taken by the
principal after he had been informed by the district senior inspector that no
additional teacher could be supplied above entitlement. The school roll has
since increased again, and another 0.3 of a teacher has been approved for the
staff. This will enable remedial reading work to be undertaken in addition to
that done by classroom teachers. I am informed that the principal is very satisfied
with the existing staffing arrangements. The department has no plans to increase
the staffing of Belfast School, which is fully up to entitlement. The organisation
of remedial reading in the school is the responsibility of the principal and rests
on his decisions concerning the use of his part-time teacher allowance.

Community Liaison Officer, Bishopdale
(2/8/78)

there any intention of appointing a permanent community liaison officer specifically
for the Bishopdale area, and, if so, when will the appointment become effective?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: There is no present

Bishopdale area, as the area receives adequate police coverage from Papanui and

21.
Stamp Duty on First Homes
(2/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: Will an amendment to the Stamp and Cheque Duties Act 1971 be
introduced this year to exempt from stamp duty the purchasers of a first home
who have or have previously had an interest in land?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Depart-
ment) replied: An amendment along the lines mentioned is not proposed. A person
who has held a prior interest in land is not automatically excluded from the
exemption. It is only when the purchaser or spouse has held a prior interest in a
dwelling house or residential land and when they have had the personal right
of use and occupation that the exemption does not apply. Any amendment to
this basic condition would cut across the whole reason for the legislation, which
was to provide exemption for the purchaser of a first home or residential land.

Legal Aid Survey
(2/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: How long will the
present inquiry into legal aid take; will bodies such as the Auckland District
Law Society be invited to participate in the inquiry; and, if so, when will they
be advised that they may so participate?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: I am unable to say
when the survey of legal needs and services (which is rather more than just legal
aid) will be completed. It is a complex subject and the study is a comprehensive
one. A good deal of preliminary work and careful planning of the study design is
essential. This is now under way in the department. The department's study group
will be consulting many organisations both within and outside the Government,
including the Auckland District Law Society. I have already assured the New
Zealand Law Society that it will be involved in the project.

Motorway Construction Workers, Plimmerton

Paremata. All workers are working an 8-hour day, including travelling from their
particular assembly point. The assembly point for 11 wage workers and 3 special
workers is Porirua; for 2 wage workers, Paraparaumu; and for the remaining 4
wage workers, Otaki. The Otaki workers are employed on a temporary transfer
basis on the four-laning for 1 month only until construction work becomes available
in their area.
37.
Wainuiomata Dam-Objection Procedures
(3/8/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Works and Develop-
ment: What are the procedural and appeal measures available to objectors to the
proposal of the Wellington Regional Water Board to build a major water dam in
Wainuiomata, and what steps will be taken to inform objectors of their rights?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The
Wellington Regional Water Board will need to apply for water rights under the
Water and Soil Conservation Act 1967 for the proposed water supply dam at
Wainuiomata. When this application is made it must be publicly notified, and
any person may lodge an objection to it and ask to be heard. An objector may
also appeal to the Planning Tribunal against any decision with which he is dis-
satisfied. The normal press statement will be released when the public notification
is made. The proposed dam has been designated in the district scheme under the
Town and Country Planning Act 1977. This designation is subject to objection
when the district scheme is reviewed every 5 years. Appeals to the Planning
Tribunal may also result from this process. A public meeting, at which the proposal
will be described and discussed, has been arranged by the board for 19 September
1978.

39.
Maori Trustee-Distribution of Funds
(3/8/78)
Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) to the Minister of Maori Affairs: Can he
state the amount of funds now received by the Maori Trustee from sources other
than unclaimed moneys and uneconomic interests during the years ended 31 March
1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978, and what are the channels of distribution and under
what terms are the funds distributed?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs) replied: The funds received
by the Maori Trustee in his own right are profits earned by administering trusts,
agencies, and investments. Profits over the last 4 years have been $127,860 in
1974-75; $8,516 in 1975-76; $123,482 in 1976-77; and $288,434 in 1977-78. The
distribution of these profits is detailed in the Maori Trustee's general purposes
account published in his annual report to Parliament. The main items are: (a) up
to $30,000 per annum to the Maori Purposes Fund Board (section 32 (1) (c),
Maori Trustee Act 1953); (b) $2,000 per annum plus a minimum of 10 percent
profits, to the Maori Education Foundation (Q.E. II Postgraduate Fellowship Act
1963, and section 32 (la), Maori Trustee Act 1953); (c) up to $10,000 per annum
to the New Zealand Maori Council (section 32 (18) Maori Trustee Act 1953), in
addition to grants from unclaimed money and from Vote: Maori Affairs; (d) up
to $2,000 per annum for philanthropic or other miscellaneous Maori purposes.

50.
National Roads Board Houses-Rent Increase
(4/8/78)
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Works and Development:
(a) How many National Roads Board houses in the vicinity of the Wellington
urban motorway are currently let; (b) for how long have each of these houses
been the responsibility of the roads board, and can he indicate the expenditure
on the maintenance and upkeep of these houses over the same period; (c) can
he confirm that tenants in these houses have recently received notification that
their rents are to rise from amounts between $8 and $12 weekly to amounts
between $25 and $30 weekly; (d) can he further confirm that some of the tenants
in these houses are pensioners, and can he indicate why the rental formula that
prohibits rent increases in excess of $10 per annum, as operated by the Housing
Corporation, does not apply to the houses in question?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: (a) There
are 76 National Roads Board houses currently let in the vicinity of the Wellington
urban motorway. (b) These houses have been purchased progressively since 1965,
but most of them were purchased during the periods 1967-68 and 1971-72.
Before the decision was made to halt construction temporarily at Ghuznee Street,
an average of $530 per house per year had been spent on maintenance over the
period 1967-71. This expenditure rose to $690 per house per year over the period
1972-75. During the last 3 years, maintenance costs have increased to an average
of $1,700 per house per year. (c) Some private tenants have been advised of rent
increases from between $8 and $12 per week to amounts between $25 and $30
per week. (d) Some of the tenants in these houses are pensioners. The rents are
fixed on a conservative basis, having regard to other private rentals of similar
houses in the locality. Consequently, the formula applied to State housing does
not apply. However, in any case where the tenant is a pensioner or other person
of limited means, or where hardship could arise if the full rental were applied,
the department has allowed concessions, in some cases substantially more generous
than those available to State house tenants.

Unemployment Percentage, South Auckland
(4/8/78)
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Can he express the
present number of those unemployed and on special work in south Auckland as
a percentage of the total work force in south Auckland, and how does this com-
pare with the national percentage?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: As at 14 July 1978 the
number of registered unemployed in the Manukau employment district represented
2.8 percent of the Labour force, and the number engaged on the temporary employ-
ment programme represented 0.7 percent. The corresponding national percentages
were 2.1 percent and 1.2 percent respectively. I have not combined registered
unemployed with temporary employment programme workers, because this is
frequently misinterpreted by the public as a measure of total unemployment,
which it is not. Under the internationally accepted definition, unemployment and
unemployment rates refer to persons who are not at work, do not have any job,
and are actively seeking work. Temporary employment programme workers cannot,
under this definition, be counted among the unemployed.

Railway Houses Vacant
(8/8/78)
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Railways: How many
houses owned by the Railways Department were vacant on 1 July, where were
they situated, and how long had they been vacant at that date?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: As at 1 July 1978
the Railways Department had a total of 4068 houses, of which 278 were vacant.
Since that date 30 of the vacant houses have been occupied by staff, and a further
59 have been allocated to staff and will be occupied very shortly. This leave 115
houses, 40 of which require repair and/or renovation. The remainder are in the
process of being allocated, or, in many cases, have reached the end of their
economic life or are surplus to departmental requirements. This latter group,
together with a further 74 houses in the same category, are being disposed of in
accordance with long-standing Government policy, i.e. to the Housing Corporation
and other Government departments, or for sale by tender.

59.
School Dental Nurses-Pay Negotiations
(8/8/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of State Services: With what occupa-
tional group is the relativity of dental nurses established in the course of negotiating
terms and conditions of employment?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: Relativities for
occupational groups within the State sector are normally established in the course
of negotiations between the employing authority and the service organisation con-
cerned. No agreement on relativities had been reached when negotiations between
the State Services Commission and the Public Service Association on the pay rates
of school dental nurses concluded in June of this year. The Public Service Associa
tion has given notice of its intent to pursue the matter before the Government
Service Tribunal, which, in determining appropriate pay rates for a group, may
determine the relativities on which those rates are based.

61.
Import Licences Cancelled
(8/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Trade and Industry:
How many import licences have been cancelled each year for the last 10 years?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied:
Records on licences that have been cancelled are available for the last 4 years
only, but these are not complete and are confined to cancellations arising from
prosecutions or investigations. These show for the year ended March: 7 in 1975,
8 in 1976, 22 in 1977, and 34 in 1978. Records are now also being kept of licences
that are voluntarily surrendered under review items, and since April about 70 of
these have been cancelled under the 12 item codes under review. Some investiga-
tions on the misuse of licence in these item codes have now been started, but it is
too early yet in the period to indicate the extent of such cancellations.

70.
Lands and Deeds Office, Auckland-Relocation
(9/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Lands: Is he aware of the
difficulties that have emerged since the Lands and Deeds Office in Auckland has
been relocated, and, if so, what does he propose to do about them?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: Yes, I am aware of the diffi-
culties referred to. Last year representations were made by the New Zealand
Institute of Surveyors and others to myself and the Minister of Justice expressing
concern about the proposed separation of the district land registrar of the Depart-
ment of Justice from the technical support and survey records of the chief surveyor
in the Department of Lands and Survey. The Minister and I agreed that after
allowing a period of 6 months of operation in separate locations the Surveyor-
General and the Registrar-General of Lands would inspect both offices to examine
the standard of services provided to the public and to investigate any problems
that might have arisen. The inspection was made on 27 and 28 June, and at the
same time the inspecting officers met representatives of the Surveyors Institute, the
Law Society, and the Valuers Institute. The view of all concerned was that in the
longer term the two offices dealing with land title and land survey should be in the
same building, and this will be a recommendation of the report. In the meantime,
investigations are continuing into ways of improving the services provided to the
public by the two departments at their separate locations.

74.
Goods Service Licences
(9/8/78)
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Transport: How many
"continuous goods service licences" have been (a) allowed to lapse, (b) suspended,
and (c) transferred, over the past 12 months?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: The regulation
and control of goods service licences, as provided for in the Transport Act 1962,
does not normally involve situations in which licences are "allowed to lapse", nor
is it normal to "suspend" a licence itself, unless the suspension is for a specific
period at the request of the holder. Licences are said to be "revoked" when they
are withdrawn by the licensing authorities. This can occur when the holder
abandons the licence, when the licence is made surplus to requirements, or when
the holder fails to comply with its terms and conditions. In the year ended 31
December 1977, 256 licences were revoked. In the same year, 729 goods services
were transferred with the approval of the licensing authorities.

79.
Mentally Handicapped-Special Education Courses (9/8/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Does
the department recognise any responsibility for providing education to mentally
handicapped or retarded children who are unable to attend either schools or
special schools run by the department, and has the department, in the event of a
child through no fault of its own being unable to take advantage of the present
education services, considered offering either special courses for the mentally
handicapped or, alternatively, increased assistance to organisations such as the
Society for the Intellectually Handicapped, which does provide such services?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Under existing policies
the Departments of Education, Health, and Social Welfare share responsibilities in
the education of mentally handicapped or retarded children who cannot attend
schools, special schools, or special classes. Within this total programme the Depart-
ment of Education provides a teaching service in the special care centres run by
voluntary agencies (particularly the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped)
to provide day care for children whose handicaps are too severe to allow them
to attend any other ordinary or special education programme. Under a policy
approved in 1975 and initiated in 1976 the Government is developing a teaching
service for the children attending these centres. The service is provided by the
nearest special school for intellectually handicapped children, which is given
additional teachers for this purpose. Priority is being given to serving the approxi-
mately 450 children at the special care centres aged 5–19 years. Eighteen teachers
have been appointed for this purpose, and 15 centres are being served. A further
eight teaching positions can be provided under the 1975 approval and will be
allocated this year. A second approval given this year provides a further 24 teach-
ing positions to enable this service to be provided at every special care centre that
requests it. The 1978 approval also authorises the payment of transport assistance
for the children aged 5-19 years for whom the teaching service is available. The
assistance will be provided through education boards under the existing policy for
transport of handicapped children between home and school. The approval also
covers the provision of necessary teaching equipment for teachers working at the
special care centres. The Department of Education also has a provision that enrol-
ment in the home training section of the Correspondence School is available to all
severely handicapped children who cannot attend a special care centre. With the
development of these policies, an education service should be available to all
severely handicapped children living in the community. There should therefore
be no need for additional assistance for this purpose to organisations such as the
Society for the Intellectually Handicapped. My department is developing the
teaching service for special care centres in consultation with the society so that any
incipient problems can be identified at an early stage and rectified as quickly as
possible.

available, but I have arranged for my department to supply these figures to the
honourable member as soon as they are available.

Fishing-Protection for Traditional Grounds
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Is there any way
in which a local fishing community can exclude vessels from other areas from its
local traditional fishing grounds?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Acting Minister of Fisheries) replied: Under the exist-

controlled. Then, the licensing authority, in considering any application. for a
licence, is required to have regard to the desirability of giving preference to fisher-
men from a community within the area of the controlled fishery.
83.
Crayfish Conservation Measures
(9/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: What crayfish
conservation measures are in force at present?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Acting Minister of Fisheries) replied: The Rock Lobster
Regulations 1969 and amendments provide many measures for the conservation of
rock lobsters. These include restrictions on size limits, taking lobsters in the soft
shell stage, female lobsters carrying external eggs, gear, seasons, areas, and so
forth. Also in force at present is a moratorium on the issue of further rock lobster
fishing permits.

(11/8/78)
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Postmaster-General: Can he confirm
that the telephone waiting list in Dunedin increased from 806 at 30 June 1977 to 922
at 31 May 1978, and can he indicate when it is his intention to initiate National's 1975
manifesto promise to speed up the cabling programme and reduce waiting lists for
automatic telephone connections?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: The waiting list in the
Dunedin district has decreased by 185. There is a difference between the Dunedin
central exchange network, referred to in my earlier reply to the honourable member

district basis which gives figures of 1107 at 30 June 1977 and 922 at 31 May 1978—a
decrease of 185. As stated on my behalf by my colleague the Minister of Broadcasting
last Wednesday in reply to the honourable member for Onehunga, National has
already implemented its promise to speed up the cabling programme and reduce
telephone waiting lists. Cable ordering levels have been steadily increased and the
national waiting list figure has been reduced from 30 288 on 31 May 1977 to 22 629
on 30 June 1978. A further reduction to below 20 000 is expected by the end of this
year.

Fresh Skim Milk Labelling
(27/7/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Health: Could he release
the findings of the committee set up to investigate the labelling of fresh skim (non-fat)
milk, and state whether the product needs to be labelled with a warning like that
applied to powdered skim milk on unsuitability for children under 2 years of age?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Food Standards Committee, which
advises me in matters of this kind, has recommended that skim milk is not suitable for
infant feeding because fat soluble vitamins are removed, and the removal of fat makes
skim milk inadequate as an energy source. The committee has further recommended
that liquid skim milk should be easily identifiable and that the warning statement
already applicable to skim milk powder should be attached to the bottle in which
liquid skim milk reaches the consumer. It is proposed to amend the Food and Drug
Regulations accordingly.

Union Rolls
(27/7/78)
Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: Is it correct that the Bank
Officers Union has informed him that it cannot supply a roll of members without first
obtaining it from its employers, and can he further inform the House whether the
Industrial Relations Act requires them to keep such a roll?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): This week I have received a letter
from the general secretary of the New Zealand Bank Officers Union informing me
that the union has written to the Registrar of Industrial Unions stating that it is
"impracticable for them to supply the information required under the Act". Section
175(i) of the Industrial Relations Act requires that the rules of every union shall
provide for the keeping of a register of union members. However, for the purposes of
the ballot the union is required to provide a list of all persons who are entitled to
vote—that is, the adult workers bound by the unqualified preference clause contained
in the bank officers' award. Such a list will not necessarily match the register of union
mebers. Some persons not bound to join the union do so voluntarily. They would not,
however, be entitled to a vote in the ballot. On the other hand, there will undoubtedly
be some persons who are bound by the unqualified preference provision but who do
not in fact belong to the union. Such persons would be entitled to vote in the ballot.

training and employment scheme for school leavers. I was impressed with the ideas

in co-ordination with the Department of Labour, provides that members will spend
time living and working in forests. The New Zealand Forest Service is providing staff
for training in the forests. Accommodation and equipment within the Kaweka State
Forest are also being used.

106.
Medical Service Benefit-Dr C. M. Patel
(28/7/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Health: Why has
Ponsonby doctor, C. M. Patel, been given a 6 months' suspension of his social
security payments; have any of Dr Patel's patients laid a complaint; and will the
Minister review the decision in the light of the strong support for Dr Patel from the
whole community?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): As I said in reply to an urgent question
on Wednesday, 26 July, the honourable member does not appear to understand the
situation regarding general medical services benefits for Dr Patel's patients. After an
informal investigation showed that Dr Patel was seeing an excessive number of
patients, which made it improbable that he could provide a good standard of medical
service, an informal inquiry by two independent Auckland medical practitioners of
wide experience investigated the situation and recommended that I lodge a complaint
with the Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee. This committee carried out a
full investigation and Dr Patel was given the opportunity of appearing before it. In its
recommendations to me the disciplinary committee put forward that for a period of 6
months Dr Patel should not be able to claim general medical services benefits for his
patients direct from the Department of Health by means of the schedule system.
Instead, the committee recommended that the patients, during that period should
claim these benefits by way of the refund system. I accepted the recommendations of
the disciplinary committee. Dr Patel chose not to exercise his right to appeal to the
Medical Council against the recommendations of the disciplinary committee. I have
had some complaints from some patients of Dr Patel, but clearly these patients have
misunderstood the position. They are still eligible for general medical services
benefits. The only thing that has changed is that during the 6 months' period they
must claim the benefit instead of Dr Patel claiming the benefit on their behalf. As
mentioned in my reply to the urgent question on Wednesday last, I do not intend to
review my decision on this matter.

109.
Cement Industry, Weston, North Otago
(28/7/78)
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Regional Development:
What forms of assistance-regional, export, or otherwise-will be available to New
Zealand Cement Holdings Ltd. for its development of a cement industry at Weston,
in North Otago?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): Under current
legislation the new plant being planned by New Zealand Cement Holdings would
qualify for the normal first-year depreciation allowance of 25 percent, which is
available for all new machinery. In addition, plant directly associated with the
cement manufacturing process could qualify for the regional investment allowance of
20 percent. If cement was to be exported from this plant the company might qualify
for several of the existing export incentives. However, these incentives are currently
under review and the situation could alter by the time the plant is completed. The
type of regional development assistance available under the present programme was
not designed to be applied to a project involving the scale of investment envisaged by
New Zealand Cement Holdings. In addition, the company has carried out an
extensive study to determine the most advantageous location for this plant. In these
circumstances the provision of a locational incentive under the regional development
programme does not seem justified. The Government would expect that a major
development like this should be able to achieve viability without large sums of
assistance.

Non-Union Labour in Bars
(28/7/78)
Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: If an ancillary licence is
granted to a sporting club, can that club employ non-union labour in its bar?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I apologise for the length of the
reply. If the honourable member is referring to staff who are actually employed and
paid wages in terms of an employer-worker relationship, the answer is no. Such
workers are covered by the New Zealand Chartered Clubs Employees award, and
pursuant to the unqualified preference provisions in the award, a worker who is over
18 years of age or is in receipt of not less than the minimum rate of wages payable to a
person of the age of 18 years or upwards, must become a member of the relevant
union. If, however, the honourable member is referring to volunteer barmen, the
answer is yes. Before any award or collective agreement can be applied, it would be
necessary for an employer-worker relationship to exist, and this was recently
supported by a decision of the Arbitration Court. In the case of a volunteer barman,
no such relationship does exist. The 1976 amendment to the Sale of Liquor Act 1962,
which provides for the issue of ancillary licences, does not include any provision
requiring the employment of paid staff. The amendment does, however, provide for
the appointment of a manager or a number of managers to ensure compliance with
the duties, responsibilities, and liabilities outlined in the Act.

Hydro Development, Upper Waitaki
(28/7/78)
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and
Development: What proposals does the Government have to take up some of the
slack that will occur in contracting following the nearing of completion of the Upper
Waitaki hydro development?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The Upper
Waitaki power development works are programmed for completion in 1983, or soon
after. The construction work force, which includes contractors, will be progressively
reduced during this time to match the work remaining to be done. The downturn in
work will not be sudden, and it will be more than matched by the opportunities
offering as the Upper Clutha project proceeds. Those people who are interested in
staying on major construction work will be able to do so. Having said that, I point out
that it must be recognised that the Upper Waitaki works are plant intensive,
involving as they do very significant quantities of earth moving. Earth moving on this
scale is not needed on the works that follow on, and contractors will have recognised
the need for them to move away from large investments in earth-moving plant in
keeping with the changing market.

equipment?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I have seen the
report referred to by the honourable member, but can advise that the Government

151.
State House Tenants-Savings Schemes
(2/8/78)
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm
that contributions to the limited tenancy savings scheme are compulsory for virtually
all tenants taking up corporation rental units, and that, since his policy does not allow
corporation tenants to belong to both the tenancy savings scheme and the home
ownership savings scheme at the same time, virtually all new corporation tenants are
being deprived of the benefits the home ownership savings scheme offers?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Tenants do not in fact make
any contribution to the tenancy savings scheme, and compulsion plays no part in the
scheme. The position is that all tenants allocated corporation rental houses from and
including 1 October 1976 are entitled to the opportunities available through the
tenancy savings scheme, provided they comply with their obligations as corporation
tenants. If the option is not taken up by the end of 6 years, the benefits under the
scheme are forfeited. It is quite incorrect to assume that new corporation tenants are
being deprived of the benefits of the home ownership savings scheme. A tenant can, if
he or she so wishes, apply to join the home ownership savings scheme. The tenancy
savings scheme is an alternative to the home ownership savings scheme, but no one is
entitled to the benefits of both schemes.

Regional Development Programmes
(2/8/78)
RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) to the Minister of Regional
Development: Have any changes been made to the regional development
programmes since the presentation of the Budget, and, if so, what are, the extent of
those changes?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): As part of its continuing
review of regional development assistance programmes, the Government has recently
adjusted the criteria of the small projects assistance grant scheme. The criteria for
eligibility for companies have been increased from fixed assets of $30,000 to fixed
assets of $50,000, and annual sales of $150,000 rather than the previous maximum of
$100,000. The limit for qualifying investment has been increased from $20,000 to
$30,000, with grants being made up to 50 percent of the qualifying costs. This gives a
maximum grant of $15,000. This grant is unsecured, to leave companies' assets
unencumbered should they need to raise commercial finance for the development.

166.
Development Finance Corporation Bearer Bonds-Tax
(3/8/78)
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister in
Charge of the Inland Revenue Department: What measures does he propose to
take to make sure that all tax due is collected from holders of the new bearer bonds
now being issued by the Development Finance Corporation, and what extra costs are
expected by his department in checking on who holds the bonds at the time interest
payments are made?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department): I have no proposals for measures at this early stage. The tax system in
New Zealand is based on voluntary compliance, as the member knows, backed up by
the Inland Revenue Department's audit and investigation activities. Business
receipts, for example, must be taken on trust, subject to audit and investigation
checks. The same system is applied to any other type of income in respect of which
independent information may not be available. At this point, therefore, I would think
it too early to say whether any extra costs would be incurred, but this will depend on
the department's assessment in the light of experience as to whether extra checks are
required.

Pulmonary Tuberculosis, Southland
(3/8/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Health: What is the incidence
of pulmonary tuberculosis on a per capita basis in Southland, has this figure
increased or decreased over the last 10 years, and is it at a higher or lower level than
in other regions in New Zealand?
Hon. Ť. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The incidence of pulmonary tuberculosis
in Southland-the Invercargill health district-in 1977 was 0.69 cases per 10 000
people; there was a total of 8 cases out of a population of 116 700. The figure has
decreased over the past 10 years, from 3.65 per 10 000 in 1968 to 0.69 per 10 000 in
1977. There were 15 districts with a higher incidence of pulmonary tuberculosis per
10 000 population than Southland and 2 districts with a lower incidence-Nelson and
Palmerston North. Areas with the lowest incidence are the whole of the South Island,
and the Palmerston North and New Plymouth health districts.

182.
Rabbit Farming
(3/8/78)
Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) to the Minister of Agriculture: In view of the
reported statement by the Associate of Agriculture, who was speaking to the Pest
Destruction Boards Association annual conference at Mt. Cook, that “rabbits could
become a viable food industry in New Zealand", could he say if he is in favour of
farming rabbits, and, if so, what plans has he to bring down legislation to permit the
farming of rabbits in New Zealand?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The Associate Minister of
Agriculture made no such bald statement at the conference, as alleged by the
honourable member. When the Agricultural Pests Destruction Act was being
amended in 1974, the Lands and Agriculture Committee considered provisions in the
amendment Bill to permit rabbit farming, and after its deliberations it was decided
that these provisions should be deleted. I understand that the decision was
unanimous. The main reasons for this were that it was considered that rabbit farming
would not be an economic proposition and that it would have an adverse effect on the
pest destruction movement. There was also the risk that the marketing of carcasses
from commercially bred rabbits could open the way to a black market in feral animal
carcasses that could be poisoned. While the economics may have changed since 1974,
the other reasons for deleting the provisions are still valid, and no further evidence
has come to light to indicate that this matter should be reviewed. Therefore, no
change in legislation appears feasible at present.

Trade Negotiations, Geneva
(3/8/78)
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: What
progress has been made in the multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva, and when is
it expected they will be completed?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): A statement on the
GATT multilateral trade negotiations was issued in Geneva on 13 July. Most of the
major delegations, including New Zealand, associated themselves with this
statement, which recorded areas of agreement between those countries and indicated
the approach that they were agreed to take on the main issues in order to resolve those
questions satisfactorily by the end of this year. From New Zealand's viewpoint, the
most significant area of agreement was the recognition that the whole final MTN
outcome is subject to satisfactory settlements being completed in the agricultural
area. This statement was endorsed at the very highest polit ical level at the Bonn
summit meeting between the leaders of the world's major industrialised nations.

Liquefied Petroleum Gas-Price Disincentive
(3/8/78)
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Energy: Would he advise the
House what steps he is taking to correct disincentives for heavy vehicle users of LPG,
as demonstrated by W. Stephenson and Sons Ltd. of Auckland, one of the biggest
road users of LPG, whose calculations have shown that petrol is costing 13.45c per
km against LPG at 16.74c per km?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): A number of steps have already been
taken in the Budget to promote LPG, namely, (1) an immediate write-off for tax
purposes by business of the costs of conversion, and of LPG tanks in excess of 100 000
litres; (2) an additional duty of 3c a litre on motor spirits in respect of which rebates
were heavily curtailed; and (3) a grant of 25 percent, with a write-off for tax purposes
by business of the balance in respect of LPG tanks between 1000 and 100 000 litres. It
was also stated in the Budget that "The establishment of appropriate relativities
among the prices of motor spirits, diesel, and LPG is essential for the marketing of
automotive LPG. The Government aim is to see this product priced competitively
with imported liquid fuels." Any such further modifications requried will be carried
out as appropriate. Unfortunately, the company's position is aggravated by the
unusually poor comparative fuel economy it is achieving with running on LPG.
Sample vehicle fuel economy figures which we obtained from the firm quoted by the
honourable member in his question, indicate that 47 percent more LPG is having to
be used in volumetric terms than of gasoline. This figure is abnormally high in
comparison with the normal figure of 15 percent. Waipa County has done even better
in achieving only a 5 percent fuel economy penalty.

Trustee Savings Banks-Residential Property Lending (4/8/78)
Mr FENTON (Hastings) to the Minister of Finance: What are the latest
figures on residential property lending by the trustee savings banks and do they
indicate any particular preference by borrowers, given a free choice between an
existing property and the erection of a new house?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): In the 6 months ended 30
June 1978 trustee savings banks approved mortgages for new housing totalling $12.7
million and mortgages for existing houses of $79.1 million. This compares with the
total for the 6 months to 31 December 1977 of $16.9 million for new houses and $49.9
million for existing houses and, for the 6 months to 30 June 1977, of $10.7 million for
new houses and $27.7 million for existing houses. The proportion of total residential
mortgages approved for new houses in the lastest 6-monthly figures was 13.8 percent,
compared with a range of 24 to 29 percent over the previous four June years. The
absolute percentage of lending going to the purchasers of new houses is not a true
reflection of the overall preference of the market because of the emphasis of the
Housing Corporation in lending for new homes, but the recent reduction in the
proportion approved for new houses indicates some switch of preference from new to
existing houses.

Japanese Arms Exports to South-east Asia
(4/8/78)
Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What is the
New Zealand Government's position in respect of Japanese arms exports to South-
east Asia?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): It is known that Japan
manufactures a high proportion of the arms it needs for its own Self Defence Forces,
but it does not export significant quantities of military equipment, other than non-
weapon items such as trucks and communications equipment, to South-east Asia or
elsewhere. The Japanese Government has placed severe restrictions on arms exports,
and opposes international trade in arms. Indeed, Japan has taken the initiative in
suggesting to the United Nations in recent years that an expert study on international
transfers of conventional arms be carried out. The suggestion has not yet been taken
up, but New Zealand supported it and we hope that agreement will be reached to
undertake the study before long.

of recovery?

Superannuation Scheme disposal account included in the annual report of the

Corporation, and these cases, which involve somewhat larger credits, were followed
up on an individual basis as far as possible, and this process is continuing. In
addition, I made a press statement drawing attention to the fact that transfer values
were unclaimed, and what action to take.

present world trade situation. I think it is fair enough to say that there is a much
greater general emphasis on agriculture in this MTN round than there has been with
other multilateral trade negotiations that have taken place over the last 30 years.

Electoral Rolls
(8/8/78)
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the
report in the New Zealand Herald of 2 August entitled "Voters told to wait", which
seems to indicate some lack of co-ordination between the Chief Electoral Officer and
the electorate officers, and, if so, can he say whether it is approved policy no longer
actively to encourage electors to enrol?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen the report referred
to. There has been no lack of co-ordination between the Chief Electoral Officer and
electorate officers. I am told that what happened was that the Chief Electoral Officer
explained, in response to a reporter's telephone call, that all electors who had enrolled
either had received or would receive an acknowledgement card. He suggested that
those who had doubts about their enrolment might wait until the main rolls were
printed and distributed early in September, when their enrolment could be checked.
If an elector's name did not then appear on the correct electoral roll, he or she should
complete a registration card and hand it in at the nearest post office for sending to the
electorate office. The Chief Electoral Officer explained to the press that many
duplicate enrolments were being received and that this made unnecessary work for
electors, for political canvassers, and for electoral staff. It continues to be the policy
and the practice of the electoral officers to encourage all electors to enrol promptly as
they become qualified.

222.
Electoral Arrangements for Overseas Voters
(8/8/78)
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the report on
page 3 of the Christchurch Press dated 26 July 1978, wherein the member for
Sydenham is reported as saying that 86 000 New Zealand voters in Australia had 5
days in which to cast their votes in 3 offices, and, if he has seen the report, (a) is the
statement correct, (b) is there any difference from previous election arrangements for
absentee voters, and (c) are there 86 000 New Zealanders voting in Australia this
year?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): As to whether the statement is
correct, there are a number of errors in it. Voters in Australia have not 5 days but 3
weeks from the closure of nominations until the night before polling day in New
Zealand to cast their votes. As to the claim that they cast their votes in three offices,
there are voting facilities at Brisbane, Canberra, Melbourne, Perth, and Sydney-five
offices-and advice for overseas voters is contained in a pamphlet that has been
distributed extensively to overseas posts, travel agents, and shipping and airline
offices. As to whether the arrangements are any different from previous election
arrangements for absentee voters, the answer is that arrangements for overseas
special voters are standard procedures, and have been so since the 1956 Act-for 22
years. As to the third question-whether there are 86 000 voters voting in Australia
this year-the answer must be that I would not know what the figure is, but would be
surprised if it were as high as the figure quoted. Of the Australian voting centres,
most votes are usually registered at Sydney, and usually in the range of 4000 to 5000
votes. Fewer votes are cast at other centres.

Johnsonville Rail Dispute Reports
(9/8/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Labour: Which

Mr Cranston on the Johnsonville rail dispute, and when were these reports (a)
received by the Minister, (b) sent to the interested parties?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As mentioned in my reply to an
earlier question by the honourable member, the terms of reference under which this
conference was set up provided that the interim and final reports of the chairman
were to be made available to the parties and carefully considered by them. The terms
of reference also provided that the progress or interim report should be made by 24
February. To meet the convenience of the parties, there was a delay in starting the
conference, and it did not get under way until 23 February. A progress report was
therefore not possible by 24 February. As the record of the meeting on 23 February
fully outlined progress made, this report was accepted by the parties as the progress
or interim report and was put in their hands on 28 February, the date the conference
resumed. Further meetings of the conference were held on 1 March and 4 March, and
the report of the meeting on 1 March was tabled on 4 March. The report of the final
meeting was circulated directly to the parties concerned. I was not involved in
sending any reports to the parties.

Railway Housing, South Auckland
(9/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Railways: Can he confirm that a
number of departmental employees in the south Auckland area has been on waiting
lists for housing for periods exceeding 9 months, and, if so, what steps has he taken to
Ideal with this situation?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways): I am aware that a
number of employees in the Auckland metropolitan area has been seeking housing
assistance from the Railways Department for lengthy periods. In fact, the same
situation exists in other metropolitan areas. The position is that the department does
not undertake to provide housing for all its employees. Departmental housing is
provided to enable staff to transfer from one locality to another where their services
are required, and for this reason the department's housing resources are limited. It is
therefore, not possible to assist every employee who requests the allocation of
departmental housing, and local employees can be helped only when housing that is
not required for employees on transfer becomes vacant.

practice. Financial provision has been made for 30 doctors to accept training this

Fuel Oil Imports
(9/8/78)
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Energy: What is the
imported cost of fuel oil and what is the proportion of imported fuel oil to total
imports?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Energy. "Fuel oil is not imported into New Zealand directly, but is
produced from the refining of crude oil at Marsden Point. Crude oil is currently
costing about 8.5c per litre, and this is refined into gasoline, diesel, fuels, fuel oils, and
bitumen. The cost allocation process would then assign about 7c per litre as the
import cost of fuel oil, since that is a relatively low-value product. In 1977, fuel oil
represented 25 percent of the petroleum fuels marketed, and the Government will
continue adopting measures to ensure that fuel oil markets continue to decline in
response to the growing availability of coal and natural gas".
