Telephone List-Christchurch
(9/8/78)
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Postmaster-General:
Can he confirm that the Christchurch waiting list for people wanting telephone
connections has increased from 3485 as at 6 May 1976 to 4177 as at 31 May, and can
he advise when he intends to start implementing National's 1975 manifesto promise
to speed up the cabling programme and reduce waiting lists for automatic telephone
connections?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): The waiting list for telephones
in the Christchurch district stood at 3485 on 30 April 1976, rose to a peak of 5595 on
30 September 1977, and then decreased to 4177 on 31 May 1978. The figure continues
to decrease as corrective actions take effect, and was 4082 at the end of June 1978. As
I have already stated in answer to another recent question, National has implemented
its 1975 election promise. Cable ordering levels have increased annually, and waiting
lists are being reduced from a peak of 30 000 in mid-May 1977 to we hope, under
20 000 by the end of this year.

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to
questions, I move, That the House do now adjourn. I wish to refer to questions 8, 44, 57, and
142, which all relate to south Auckland and its associated problems. In particular, I want to
discuss the problems associated with the recent rapid growth that has taken place in
Manurewa, and to refer to a recent report on a research survey on recreation and leisure
time in the Manurewa area printed by the Manukau City Council. The survey showed some
alarming problems that need to be tackled urgently. The report pointed out that within the
Manurewa border is the new high-density subdivision of Rowandale, in which most of the
families are young and loaded with mortgage repayments.
In this area, broadly defined as Homai in the census, the report states that there are
nearly 3000 young people aged between 5 and 14 years, nearly 20 percent of whom are
Maoris. The report points out that another similar area is Manurewa South. Another point
of interest in the report related to the use of amenities in the area. In particular, the report
pointed out that well over half the people in the lounge bar of the local pub were young
people below the age of 20. Referring to the Southmall shopping centre, the report makes it
clear that there is a particular problem in the group aged between 7 and 14 years. It states
that the young people in that age group have surplus energy, and tend to run wild in the area,
some in shop-lifting gangs. I have had shopkeepers in Southmall telephone me to discuss this
problem.
The report adds that the majority in this age group are interested in organised activity,
without which they could become potential troublemakers, resulting in fighting and name
calling. Those responsible for preparing the report attempted to gauge the attitude of young
people to civic amenities. I believe their comments are of real significance and should be
noted by members. The report stated: "Attitude of youth to civic amenities-We could
determine no real cohesive feeling towards civic amenities. . . . Another thing is that most of
the popular set-ups are without the shadow of Government or council attached to them.
People, especially young people, think of the council as a tax set-up, a disciplinary
authoritative body, and do not associate it with what is ‘cool', and what can cater for their
social needs. That is why a set-up like Te Puke - Otara, constructed for the people by the
people, admittedly with Government and council backing, was so attractive."
The report makes 19 recommendations, and I would like to read the final one: "All the
above"-the other 18 recommendations-"could be incorporated into the Manurewa
community centre formed along the lines of Te Puke - Otara, so it is planned and built by
people, and then organised and run by them." The report went on to state that in Manurewa
there are groups of young people who have the energy and the inclination to work towards
their own set-up, like Te Puke - Otara, and that they would prefer to make the actual
arrangements themselves rather than have them made completely by the council, or by the
Government. I believe that the Government should allow young people in areas such as
Manurewa, where there is rapid growth, and in other areas, to undertake some of these
projects on their own.

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I address myself to questions 125, 141 and 192, all of
which deal with union amalgamations. I agree with the member for Whangarei that the
figure of 106 unions, mentioned in a report in the Northern Advocate is, strictly speaking,
incorrect. The correct figure is 293 if all the tiddley-winking unions in the country are
considered. Contrary to the impression given by the member for Whangarei, the party which
I have the privilege to lead has for years advocated amalgamation of unions. In 1974, we
published what was considered to be a major paper recommending that amongst other
things. There is a very urgent need for a substantial reduction in the number of unions.
I was most gratified to see the Federation of Labour move in that direction, and also
that the Minister of Labour appreciated the federation's move. It is important to achieve a
substantial reduction in the excessive number of horizontal and occupational unions,
because the present position means that a disturbance in one place can spread all over the
country. We need a much smaller number of horizontal or occupational unions, linked to a
national organisation such as the Federation of Labour, which should be charged with the
job of negotiating minimum standards. We also need vertical industrial councils at each
major work site, uniting all the workers, regardless of occupation. That is especially needed
in the freezing industry. The whole question of union amalgamation ought to be tied to the
question of worker shareholding in industry. The two can be and ought to be, related. As I
stated the other night, the usual method that is suggested for achieving worker shareholding
in industry-that it be achieved on the basis of the retained profits in industry-will no
longer work, because the retained profits in industry are simply insufficient to enable worker
shareholding to move off the ground by that method.
Worker shareholding in major industries could be achieved by extending overdraft
principles that now apply to industries, such as the dairy industry, with low-interest Reserve
Bank loans being advanced to workers for share purchase in major industries. The initial
dividends in the early years of shareholding could be used for loan repayments, or for loan
cancellations. Thus, a painless method would be used for the acquisition of shares, and a
much needed infusion of equity capital into some of our major industries would be achieved.
The linkage between worker shareholding and union amalgamation could be achieved by the
privilege of low-interest loans being made available for shareholding, conditional upon
workers in the major industries, particularly the freezing industry, agreeing to the
establishment of industrial councils, uniting all workers on sites.
Mr Malcolm: You mean, coercion by the Government?
Mr BEETHAM: No. It would be, in effect, a policy of offering incentives. Pardon me if
I am mistaken, but I was under the belief that this was something about which the National
Party had some philosophy.

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be

Mr LANGE (Mangere): During the Committee stage the Minister in charge of the Bill
was asked whether "personal chattels" included works of art, antique furniture, and other
items of use or adornment that could have spectacular value. The Minister was inclined to
agree that those items were included in the definition of "personal chattels", and it was
claimed that that definition had been inserted by a previous Labour Government. The fact
is, of course, that the definition of "personal chattels" was inserted by an amendment to the
Act in 1970, when the National Government was in office.
I want to record the fact that the Government is seeking to enhance the rights of people
of considerable means, who have the ability during their lifetime to spend their wealth on
items of very considerable value-on masterpieces of painting, antique furniture, and other
items beyond the grasp of most people. They purchase these for pecunious reasons, simply
as a hedge against death duties-not because they appreciate art or have any of the
sophistication necessary to understand a McCahon.
When the Minister introduced the Bill he was certainly not at pains to point out that the
House was being asked to agree to a provision that would enable those people with
considerable means to avoid the liability of paying a just amount of death duty. The
Opposition has no quarrel at all with removing exemption from personal chattels, or those
that are reasonably needed as an incident to the lives of the people who formerly used them,
but it does object to the suggestion that, before their death, people can load their houses
with paintings, elephants' feet, works of art, and Persian carpets-the sort of splendour one
is accustomed to see in the houses of people who make substantial contributions to the
National Party in the Egmont electorate-and thereby render themselves immune from that
particular form of death duty. The Bill raises a point of principle that should be disclosed. I
emphasise that no Labour Government has been in'any way responsible for the definition of
"personal chattels". It is indeed an absurdity that the gates have been opened and the
antique market is rising in anticipation of the passing of this Bill.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I should like to endorse and further advance the remarks made by
the member for Mangere.
Hon. H. C. Templeton: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I merely make the point that
there was no discussion on this issue in the Committee stage, although it was referred to in
the second reading debate. I am perfectly happy to debate it, so long as the House
understands that point; and I thought I should draw it to your attention.
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members should understand that the purpose of a third
reading debate is not simply to traverse what took place in the Committee of the Whole
House; that is merely one of the purposes of the third reading. It also gives members an
opportunity to give a Bill final consideration or final examination. A Bill may emerge from
the Committee of the Whole House with or without amendment, and in many cases it is
different from the Bill introduced. In many cases, too, a Bill being read for the third time is
different from the measure that was given a second reading. Members debate the Bill they
have in their hands at the time. In fact, in this case the Bill has not been amended since it was
introduced, but the third reading gives members an opportunity to debate the principles
incorporated in it. Speeches may not be as wide as is permitted in a second reading, but they
may cover more than the matters raised in the Committee of the Whole House.
Dr WALL: Thank you for your ruling, Mr Speaker; it was most timely. The Bill
introduces an entirely new principle to which the Opposition is totally opposed. No one
objects to the fact that certain people acquire wealth by their own efforts, their own
circumstances, and their own industry, and no one objects to them passing their wealth on to
their successors. However, in New Zealand it has been traditionally felt that wealth
aggregated by certain families should not be passed on from generation to generation
without restriction. In other parts of the world that practice has, over the centuries,
produced an inequitable distribution of wealth, which, untaxed and undiminished, has been
handed down from one generation to the next. At about the turn of the century the evil of
that process became so apparent in New Zealand that steps were taken to limit the
aggregation of wealth by that method, and land tax was imposed.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The honourable member is going outside the scope of what is
permitted in a third reading debate. Perhaps I may be able to help him. In a third reading

This year the Government will take more from each member of the labour force than

but in its 3 years it expects to collect $1.66 in income tax for every dollar that the Labour
Government collected. In all forms of taxation the Government will have collected $1.73 for

inflation, which would be a relevant and relative method of monitoring the indecency of the
increases.
During the last 3 years the labour force has hardly changed, and the total population has
increased only slightly, which means that the average tax paid by every member of the labour
force and the average tax paid on a per capita basis have risen-even allowing for inflation,
and despite what the Government might say to the contrary. I challenge Government

among the many minions of the master-to dispute that statement. The Government's so-

with teenagers.
I shall now point out another four giant-size anomalies in the Bills. The first is that a
married man earning $150 a week, with four teenage children, will pay $14 more a week than
a married man with a non-earning wife and a child under the age of five years. I ask the
Minister what sort of thinking went into creating such an anomaly. The answer is clearly
none at all. The Government obviously did not think its tax package through. It is a botch,
unlike the well considered tax proposals announced by the Labour Party. Cabinet Ministers,
in the upper income bracket, obviously do not know what it means to live on the average
wage and bring up a family.
Let me help them with a few basic facts. It is indisputable that teenage children cost at
least as much to feed as adults. Figures produced by Otago University show that the basic
weekly food bill for an adolescent boy is $9.50, if you have the time to purchase selectively,
which so many do not; nor do they have the private transport. I suggest that that is a minimal
estimate. A 1-year-old costs $3 a week to feed, $6 less than it costs for an adolescent boy.
That means that a married man with four teenage children will pay $51.25 each week on
food, and a married man with a 1-year-old child will pay $18.75, a difference of $32.50 a
week on food bills only. The teenage children will cost more to clothe than the 1-year-old,
making teenage children more expensive still. Despite all those obvious realities, the
Government has decided that a married man with teenage children will pay $14 a week more
in tax. That is incredible, some would say it is insanity, and certainly it is economic
ineptitude, and ill-considered blundering.
The Government has claimed that, when the children are older, the wife can go to work,
but with massive unemployment most of them could not get a job, no matter how hard they
tried. Those who do get work discover that their earnings are taxed at rip-off rates because of
the phasing out of rebates. A married woman with a young child will discover that the
effective tax on her income between $10 and $42 a week is 39.5c in the dollar. That is a rip-
off rate, and that is the second giant-sized anomaly to which I want to refer the ludicrously
high rate of tax on such a low income, paid by a wife who is forced to work part time because
of economic duress.
The third giant-sized anomaly is the position of the widow, which is even worse. A
widow with four teenage children will pay $17 a week more tax than a man with a non-
earning wife and a child under the age of 5. How can that be justified? It is unjust, and it
should be changed. The fourth giant-sized anomaly occurs when a marriage breaks up and a
husband separates from his wife and children, and moves into a flat. He then has to struggle
with a hefty maintenance bill as well as the costs involved in two residences-and any
member for Southern Maori can talk with a certain authority on the cost of simultaneously
maintaining two residences. His difficult financial situation is made worse by taking away the
two family rebates. It means that the man's tax bill upon separation, goes up $14 a week, just

is a drop of 0.1 percent! In the coming year-the year of these great tax cuts-income tax

I want to mention briefly the export incentive allowances, an important proposal in the
1978 Budget. It allows people who have increased exports to claim a tax reduction as a credit
at a maximum rate of 45c in the dollar, to be paid in the same manner as the normal tax
refund. This is an important proposal, implementing the Government's policy to streamline
and make more effective the export incentive allowance schemes. In the early stages of
export, some companies are not making a profit and have been unable to claim tax rebates.
The present proposal would allow people, when they start to export, to claim tax incentives
as a rebate paid in cash, which will help their cash flow in the early stages of their export
market development.

Fishing Industry Board Amendment Bill
THURSDAY, 17 AUGUST 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
FISHING INDUSTRY BOARD AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That the Fishing Industry Board
Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill provides for the reconstitution of the Fishing
Industry Board established in 1963, and for a new fish levy to be paid by fishermen. Also, it
alters the name of the board to the New Zealand Fishing Industry Board to make it clear
which board is being referred to in overseas communications.
The reconstituted board should bring a more direct involvement of the catching,
processing, and exporting sectors of the fishing industry on the board. The present board
consists of a chairman and three others recommended by the Minister; one representative
from each of the fish catching, wholesaling and processing, and retailing sectors; and the
Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries in a non-voting capacity. The proposed board
will consist of a chairman and one other appointed by the Minister; one nominee from the
Federation of Commercial Fishermen; one from the Sharefishermen's Association; two from
the Seafood Processors Association; one representative appointed by the Minister to
represent the fish retailers; and the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries. All eight
members will have voting rights.
The proposed reconstitution of the board has been recommended by a fishing industry
review group that was set up in August 1976 to make recommendations on the institutional
structure that would best serve the needs of the developing fishing industry. The review
group concluded that the paramount concern was to have an authoritative industry body that
could present a strong and single voice on all major issues, be representative of the industry
and play a major role in shaping the industry of the future and further developing its export
potential. The review group considered many suggestions and concluded that the most
effective and practical method of achieving this would be to reconstitute the Fishing Industry
Board to bring greater involvement of the industry on the board and make a wider viewpoint
available.
The review group consisted of Messrs Corner, Chairman of the Fishing Industry Board,
Hufflet, from Sealord, Mills, from Sandford, Hazard, from Jaybel Nichimo, Kenton, who, at
that stage, was the President of the Federation of Commercial Fishermen, Donald, from
Wrightson NMA, and Dr Johns, who was the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries.
I wish to draw attention to to the composition of that group, because I believe that they were
able to put forward a view representative of the aspirations of the industry. It was thus a very
representative group whose recommendations for changes in the composition of the board
are implemented by the Bill.
It is also proposed to insert a new section 14A to impose a new levy on fish, payable only
by fishermen, which will be payable to an organisation or organisations representing
fishermen, as directed by the Minister, to provide finance for the administration costs of
these organisations. This will be in addition to the levy currently payable by fishermen,
wholesalers, and retailers, and used to fund the Fishing Industry Board. A levy such as this
would be similar to the levy collected for Federated Farmers to finance their activities. The
objective is quite simple. It is to ensure that the funds of the organisations representing
fishermen are adequate for the task being thrust upon them. The exact rate of the levy and
the organisations to whom it would be paid will be set by regulations.
Other amendments are included at the request of the Fishing Industry Board to make it
clear that the present levy under the Fish Levy Regulations 1976 is payable on all fish caught
by New Zealand fishing craft within the exclusive economic zone, even if they are not landed
in New Zealand. It will also clarify that this levy is payable only once if a fisherman
wholesales his own fish. There was some slight doubt in that area before.
I believe the proposals to reconstitute the Fishing Industry Board will receive
widespread support from the fishing industry, as will the proposed levy, which has been
asked for by the organisations involved. The Bill reaffirms the Government's commitment to


## p. 2731 (#127) ###########################################

17 August
2731
Fishing Industry Board Amendment Bill
the fishing industry by restructuring the board that represents it. The industry's own voice
will be more clearly represented on the board and in the deliberations it enters into and the
submissions it makes to the Government. The Bill will ensure that commercial fishermen
and the Sharefishermen's Association have sufficient finance to perform their task
adequately and thus ensure the continued growth of this valuable New Zealand industry.

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): When referring to clause 9, the member

determines that that should be the course of action.
Because the fish retailers do not have a strong central organisation to nominate a
representative for the board, the wording in the Bill is designed to allow the Minister to
appoint a representative who he feels will adequately represent the retailing sector. As is
common in many Acts of a similar nature, the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries
has the responsibility of representing consumers, as do other direct nominees of the
Government. They have a broad responsibility on such bodies as the Fishing Industry Board.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Central would be about 30 percent short of eligible voters"-is even less capable of

Trade Union Amalgamation
20. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Labour: To what extent have efforts
been made by the Federation of Labour, the Government, or other interested parties to
amalgamate New Zealand's plethora of unions?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. "The Federation of Labour has drawn up 10 industrial groups for affiliated unions
to be organised into. I understand that these are still the subject of discussion between the
Federation of Labour and affiliated unions. It has yet to be seen whether these discussions
result in a genuine amalgamation of unions. The most potentially fruitful means of achieving
amalgamation is through the composite agreement procedure in the Industrial Relations
Act. This enables two or more unions within an industry to join together and formulate a
common set of claims. The coming together in negotiations in this way represents a
significant first step towards eventual amalgamation. The composite agreement procedure is
being increasingly used by unions in certain industries, and I am hopeful that it will
eventually be used by the parties in the freezing industry."

International Year of the Child-National Commission
23. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Social Welfare: What progress has
been made to date by New Zealand's National Commission for the International Year of the
Child, established in October 1977, how is it serviced, and how many Government
departments are involved?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): In addition to funding the
administration of the national commission, the Department of Social Welfare has: (1)
seconded an executive officer to the national commission's secretariat; (2) commissioned a
feature film, to be produced for showing on television during 1979, intended to provoke
parents, especially hard-to-reach parents, to think about the quality of their interaction with
their children; (3) helped set up regional theme committees throughout New Zealand in
initiate discussion, research, and constructive action programmes on a neighbourhood level.
A different theme is to be brought to public attention each month, and should concentrate
interest in specific areas-for example, health, learning, the law, and parenthood. All social
service departments are involved in providing information and resource material to the
executive, the secretariat, and the theme committees. The aim is to involve as much of the
community as possible in some aspect of the international year. A full-time co-ordinator is
currently organising and stimulating discussion on the international year programmes on a
regional basis.
Dr Shearer: As the United Nations may announce an International Year of the
Disabled, are the disabled to be considered in one of these monthly projects?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I do not have that information with me, but a different theme is
taken each month. I am sure that children, irrespective of whether or not they are disabled,
will be considered.
Health Standards of Children, South Auckland
24. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Health: What action is being taken to
check health standards of children in the south and south-east Auckland area, and what steps
are being taken towards parental involvement?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): On 20 December 1977, a contract was signed
between the Department of Health and the Plunket Society whereby the society assumed
responsibility for the health surveillance of infants and pre-school children in the south
Auckland health district, allowing the department's public health nurses to concentrate their
efforts on the health of school-age children. In May 1978, a pilot scheme, using a number of
schools in the south and south-east Auckland area, was implemented in order to extend
school health services. The scheme involves the public health nurse being attached to one or
two primary schools with a total school population in the region of 800, and includes the
screening of all new entrants. The nurse also carries out her usual public health duties in a
small area around the school, encompassing as far as possible the homes of those children
attending school. A further pilot scheme is in operation in two south Auckland primary
schools that share the services of a public health nurse on a full-time basis.
Mr Downie: Is there any policy or plan whereby the parent-teacher association of a
school can be included in the health scheme?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I do not see any possibility of making parent-teacher associations
have responsibility for health, but the liaison is very good and representations have been
made to me from time to time about what should be done. Associations have been good
enough to write acknowledging their pleasure at what has been done.

Maori Affairs Bill
MAORI AFFAIRS BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): I move, That the Maori Affairs Bill
be introduced. This is basically a consolidation of the existing law. It is some 25 years since
the last consolidation and the Bill is desirable for the convenience of all. I assure the House
that no significant changes are proposed in the Bill. Some minor housekeeping amendments
have been made. All are fully detailed in the explanatory notes appended to the Bill; they
are all reasonably insignificant and could not be considered controversial. Upon introduction
the Bill will be referred to the Maori Affairs Committee to enable interested people to
express their views, and I will suggest then that that committee should be open to the news
media.
At this stage I intend to go briefly through only the clauses that introduce something
completely new to the existing law. In total, there are 526 clauses. Clause 3 (2) (d) provides
that Maori freehold land that is the subject of a contract of sale will continue to be defined as
Maori freehold land until the transfer is actually registered in the Land Transfer Office. The
existing law provides for the land to become general land once the transfer document has
been signed. Clause 39 is a new provision. It provides for the Registrar of the Maori Land
Court to have a formal seal. The registrar has statutory authority to make certain orders, and
it is desirable that he should have a seal to complete those orders formally.
Clause 43 (2) precludes judges of the Maori Land Court from issuing procedural
directives, known as practice notes, in respect of applications to be dealt with
administratively by the Registrar of the Maori Land Court. Such applications are not heard
by the courts. Clause 55 (4) gives local authorities the right to be heard on any application to
the court for a freehold order or partition order when it is intended to include in the new title
any area of accretion. Clause 83 gives the Maori Land Court power to make an order
charging the real or personal property of any person who receives financial aid from the
Maori Land Court special aid fund. The present law makes no provision for such a charge.
Clause 91 introduces two new provisions: subclause (1) allows the Registrar of the
Maori Land Court to make minor amendment to registrars' orders to accord with the true
nature of the application that gave rise to the order. Subclause (3) is intended to permit any
person affected by a registrar's order to apply to the registrar for a review of that order. The
registrar will be permitted under subclause (4) to cancel or amend the order, subject to the
written consent of all persons who would be affected by the amendment.
Clauses 93 to 96 inclusive increase fines which may be imposed by a judge of the Maori
Land Court. The details are: clause 93 increases the fine for contempt of court from $40 to
$200; clause 94 increases the fine for failing to comply with an injunction imposed by the
court from $100 to $200; clause 95 increases the fine for wilfully insulting a judge of the
Court from $20 to $200; clause 96 increases the fine for obstructing an officer of the court
from $40 to $100.
Clause 140 is an interpretation clause introducing and defining the expression "relevant
date". This refers to 1 April 1968, the date on which the Maori Affairs Amendment Act 1967
came into force. The date is relevant because it altered provisions relating to the succession
of Maori land interests of a person who died on or after 1 April 1968, the essential
differences being that the land interest formed part of the owner's estate and was vested in
an administrator. Clause 140 does not change this; it merely introduces the term "relevant
date" as a matter of convenience.
Clause 166 provides for an appeal to be made to the Maori Appellate Court against an
order made by the registrar in terms of either clause 164 or 165. Clause 164 allows orders
vesting the land interests of a deceased person in an administrator. It is not a new provision,
but has been in operation since April 1968. Clause 165 permits registrars to make orders
vesting land interests from an administrator to the person beneficially entitled. The provision
was introduced by section 20 of the Maori Purposes Act 1976. It is not anticipated that the
proposed clause 166 will be used to any great extent. However, as the existing law provides
no appeal forum in respect of registrars' orders, it is desirable that the present proposal
should be included.
Clause 234 (2) (d) is a new provision, which makes it clear that the proceeds of the
alienation of land owned by a Maori incorporation need to be paid to the Maori Trustee.
Clause 236 (3) dispenses with the need for leases of Maori freehold land owned by an
incorporation to be produced to the registrar of the court. As the Maori Trustee is not


## p. 2759 (#155) ###########################################

2759
Maori Affairs Bill
concerned with collection of the rent under a lease granted by an incorporation, production
to the registrar is unnecessary. Clause 248 (3) precludes a recording officer-a departmental
officer responsible for conducting formal meetings of owners-from accepting appointment
as proxy for an owner. The recording officer is required to advise those at the meeting on
procedural matters and on the options open to the owners. If he were also acting as a proxy
for an owner this could involve a conflict of duties.
Clause 283 (4) is a minor amendment of a purely machinery nature to define the term
"land value" as having the same meaning as the now obsolete term "unimproved value".
Clause 284 (6) is a minor procedural amendment to ensure that the Valuer-General receives
early notice of any objection lodged against a valuation completed for the purposes of

Clause 318 proposes to increase from $2,000 to $5,000 the value of shares in a Maori
incorporation that can be transferred to those beneficially entitled without its having to go to
the sometimes unwarranted expense of obtaining a formal grant of administration. Clause
347 increases the fines payable by a Maori incorporation or one of its officers for certain
offences; for example, the failure to supply accounts. The increases are from $20 to $50 for
the initial offence and from $5 to $10 for each day the offence continues. Clause 376 (6)

Act, except that subsections 4 and 5 are deleted. The effect of this is that the responsibility
for nominating and paying a surveyor now lies squarely with the owner of the land, and the
chief surveyor is no longer concerned that the surveyor's costs are guaranteed before
authorising the survey.

WAR PENSIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister in Charge of War Pensions): I move, That
the War Pensions Amendment Bill be introduced. This is mainly a machinery Bill validating
increases in the rates of war pensions payable to ex-servicemen and their dependants. The
rates of income-tested war pensions—that is, war veterans' allowances, war service pensions,
and war economic pensions—are increased every 6 months in accordance with movements in
the consumer price index. These pensions have been increased on two occasions in 1978, in
January and again in July. The Bill validates both increases in clauses 5 and 7.
Non-income-tested pensions, such as war disablement pensions and war widows'
pensions, are reviewed annually as at 1 April and increased in line with movements in the
consumer price index during the year ended 31 March. This procedure is in accordance with
a longstanding agreement with the New Zealand Returned Services Association. The
increases from 1 April 1976 are validated in clause 6 of the Bill.
The new income test for social welfare beneficaries legislated for in the Social Security
Amendment Bill is extended to income-tested war pensioners in clause 9 of the Bill. The new
income test is to be introduced from 18 October 1978, and from that date the allowable
income will increase from $17 to $25 a week. This will be combined with a significant
relaxation of the rates of abatement for excess income. Details of the new income test are
given on page 2 of the explanatory notes to the Bill. Clause 8 validates the increase in the
rate of additional pension payments for dependent children from 26 July 1978. From that
date the additional amount payable for the third and subsequent children of war widows is
increased from $1.25 to $2 a week. The additional amount payable for the second and
subsequent dependent children of married couple pensioners is also increased from $1.25 to
$2 a week.
Later this year the system of payment of war pensions is to be changed. At present,
payments are made at 4-weekly intervals by posted payment orders. The frequency of
payment is to be changed to fortnightly, and, in addition, provision is to be made for war
pensioners to receive payments directly credited to a savings or bank account. Clauses 2 and
3 amend the principal Act to allow for this new payment system.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Introduction
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That the Social Security
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. This Bill makes a number of important changes in the
Social Security Act and is further evidence of the Government's concern to promote the
social well-being of New Zealanders.
It was announced in the Budget that legislation would be introduced this year to provide
for the payment of a non-taxable allowance of $8 a week to the parents of seriously
physically or mentally handicapped children. Clauses 4 and 9 of the Bill legislate for this
allowance, which has been welcomed by all parents caring for a seriously handicapped child.
The allowance is the first positive recognition by the State of the emotional and financial
strain on the family caring for a handicapped child.
In the Budget it was announced also that, as promised in the Government's 1975
election manifesto, the income test for income-tested social security beneficiaries is to be
relaxed. The new income test is legislated for in clauses 5 and 29, and will be introduced in
October 1978. The allowable income is increased to $1,300 a year, or $25 a week. At present
the allowable income is $21 a week for widows and domestic purposes beneficiaries with
dependent children, and $17 a week for all other beneficiaries. At the present time income
over the allowable income and up to $25 a week reduces the benefit by $1 for each complete
$2. Income over $25 a week reduces the benefit by $3 for each complete $4. These provisions
have been significantly relaxed, and from October income over the new allowable income of
$25 a week and up to $40 a week will reduce the benefit by 40c for each complete dollar.
Income over $40 a week will reduce the benefit by 80c for each complete dollar. These new
provisions will give beneficiaries an incentive to help themselves by supplementing their
benefit income, as will clause 31, which provides for up to $20 a week of a solo parent's or
widow's earnings to be exempted as income if she is incurring child care costs.
Clauses 26 and 27 validate the increase in social security benefits in January and July
1978. As members are aware, since taking office the Government's policy has been to
increase the rates of social security benefits every 6 months in accordance with movements in
the consumer price index. The January and July increases were in accordance with this policy
and have ensured that the incomes of beneficiaries have kept pace with increases in the cost
of living.
In its 1975 election manifesto the Government undertook to find a better system of
payment of benefits than the present one of sending cheques by mail. An investigation has
led to a decision to introduce in October 1978 a new system of payment of national
superannuation under which those superannuitants who do not receive payment directly to a
trading bank or trustee savings bank will be issued with a payment book enabling them to
collect their instalments at any branch of the Post Office. This system, which is far more
satisfactory than sending payments through the mail, will eventually be extended to other
categories of social security benefits and beneficiaries. A concentrated publicity campaign
has been carried out by the department to explain the new system to superannuitants.
Clauses 22 and 23 of the Bill provide the necessary legislative authority for the new payment
system.
The national superannuation scheme of course, becomes fully operative from 31 August
1978. From that date married couples will receive 80 percent of the average ordinary-time
weekly wage, and single superannuitants will receive 60 percent of the married-couple rate.
From 31 August 1978 the increase in net payments for married couples after tax will be
$14.16 a week, bringing the net rate of their national superannuation to $91.30. The increase
for single superannuitants after tax will be $7.82 a week, bringing their net rate to $53.76 a
week. If the former age benefit had been retained, the rates of that benefit would now have
been $77.28 for married couples instead of $91.30, and $46.37 for single persons instead of
$53.76 a week.

Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
As previously announced, the Government considers that, when fully operative, the
national superannuation scheme will provide all superannuitants with a realistic retirement
income, obviating any necessity for special supplements such as telephone and television
concessions and additional benefits. Clauses 13, 15, 18, and 19 of the Bill clarify the

Finally, I should like to refer briefly to clauses 11, 12, and 16. Clauses 11 and 12 make it
clear that it is not the purpose of the social security scheme to support persons on strike. This
has been the long-established policy of successive Governments, and the amendment makes
it clear that a striker will not qualify for a benefit even if the strike is unresolved within 6
weeks.
Clause 16 deals with a de facto marriage relationship for social security benefit
purposes. A recent Supreme Court judgment highlighted the inadequacies of the present
wording of section 63 of the principal Act in this regard, and clause 16 makes it clear that the
Social Security Commission can regard as married for benefit purposes any person who has
entered into a relationship of the nature of a marriage.

Questions for Oral Answer
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Inflation
1. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Statistics: Can he explain why
there has not been a decline of 7 percent in the New Zealand inflation rate, in view of the
answer he gave to a written question by the member for Hutt on 15 August, in which he
indicated that import price rises in 1975 led eventually to an approximate increase in the
consumer price index of 9.7 percent, while the corresponding figures for 1976 and 1977 were
2.6 percent and 2.7 percent respectively?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Statistics): In his written reply referred to,
the Minister of Statistics provided estimates of the contribution to the increases in the
consumer price index that could be expected from rises in import prices during each year
from 1973 to 1977. There is nothing in the answer to suggest that the consumer price index
should decline, nor that the rate of increase should decline as a result. Import prices are one
of many factors that influence the consumer price index, and, whilst import prices have risen
less steeply since 1975, internal factors have tended to enlarge their contribution to increases
in the consumer price index.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: As the Minister said that internal factors have increased, can it be
taken from his answer that he admits that internal inflation is now about 3.5 to 4 percent
higher than it was in 1975?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: All I am saying is that, when lined up against import prices,
other factors have to be taken into account when measuring the causes of internal inflation. I
am sure the member knows that if there was a statistical method by which one could measure
the lag to gauge the effect of import prices on internal inflation, I would give it to him.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Inasmuch as the Minister mentioned the lag between import
prices and the domestic price index, is it not a fact that inflation in the first half of this year
was at an annual rate of little over 9 percent, and in 1975 was at an annual rate of 15.7
percent-a difference of 6.5 percent, which is very close to the 7 percent mentioned in the
question?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I find nothing wrong with the Prime Minister's reasoning.

of seminars under the auspices of either the ministry or a body working with the ministry
over the next few months. I hope to have one or two this side of the end of the year.

Overseas Students-Public Speaking
4. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Immigration: Does he intend to restrict

by Rotary and the American Field Service is quite different from that of people on southern

number of countries, and are fully reciprocal. The young people who travel to New Zealand,
and from here to other countries, under these schemes are required to comply with
internationally agreed rules and conditions applied to the scholarships by the organising
bodies. The Government does not intend to intervene in those arrangements".

break the conditions under which they are admitted to the country, then I hope that their
visas will be withdrawn.

he wishes.

Domestic Violence Bill
DOMESTIC VIOLENCE BILL
Introduction
Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Domestic
Violence Bill. The Bill deals with a largely hidden phenomenon in our society, but a
phenomenon which, like alcoholism, affects people in all walks of life—namely, violence in
the home between husband and wife. Because society has historically regarded a man's
home as his castle, and what he does in his home as his own business, the law has not
interfered in what goes on in a marriage, unless absolutely necessary. The result of this has
led to the situation, at best illogical and at worst tragic, whereby a non-molestation order
forbidding either spouse to molest the other can be obtained only when the marriage has
ceased to exist and a separation order has been made.
The Bill could be said simply to extend the present law about non-molestation orders,
but it differs in two important ways. The Bill is modelled on British legislation, and is
presented to Parliament to remedy a failure in the law and to provide a starting point for
legislation to deal with violence in the home. The Bill is innovative in two areas. It will allow
the spouse in a marriage, or in a de facto marriage, to apply to a magistrate's court for an
injunction restraining the other party from molesting the applicant or causing bodily harm to
either the applicant or the children of the marriage. In cases in which the other party has
already caused bodily harm to the applicant the magistrate may attach a power of arrest to
the injunction. The present law provides for either spouse-and it is generally the woman-
to apply for a non-molestation order after the marriage has collapsed, and after a separation
order has been applied for. If she is struggling to hold her marriage together and to bring up
the children, she has no way of preventing violence from her spouse, apart from having him
arrested for assault. Few wives are willing to opt for that remedy.
The Bill will allow the wife to gain an injunction to prevent violence within the
marriage. It will give the police the power to arrest, without warrant, any person who breaks
an injunction. The person must be kept in custody before being brought before a magistrate
within 24 hours of arrest. This will provide a speedy method of removing from the
matrimonial home any spouse who threatens violence, and will ensure that the person
cannot be released on bail pending the case's being dealt with by the court.
The other innovation in the Bill is the provision whereby an injunction can be obtained
to exclude the spouse from the matrimonial home. That would mean that a woman and her
children would not be turned out of their home by a drunken, violent husband and father.
That circumstance has led to a series of women's refuge centres being set up in Whanganei,
Christchurch, and Dunedin. The refuge centres for women are doing a magnificent job by
providing places to which desperate women and children may flee. Violence against women
is not confined to the few places where refuge centres have been established. While an
injunction would not bar either spouse permanently from the matrimonial home, it would
provide a breathing space, or a cooling-off period, in which each person could think again. It
would give women a chance to find somewhere to go, on a long-term basis, without having to
flee with children in the middle of the night. Under the Bill it will be up to the police to
decide whether the injunction has been breached seriously enough to warrant an arrest being
made.
I want to mention the role of the police in domestic disputes, and to make a suggestion.
It is often pointed out that it is the police who come at the crunch point of domestic disputes.
They are required to act in many capacities-from referees to marriage guidance
counsellors—and often represent the only social agency to which desperate women can turn.
Not only are they called upon to demonstrate tact, maturity, and judgment, but they can also
find themselves in a situation where an ongoing relationship with the family is called for and
where specialist training would be of help. I would suggest that the police could consider the
establishment of a domestic section with specialist squads similar to the youth aid section.
Such a section could incorporate the following features: personnel with a vocation for
this kind of work, special training for personnel, an equal number of female members and
male members, and a low-key conciliation approach. The functions could include assembling
files on families with a history of difficulties, and establishing an ongoing liaison with them;
domestic education; liaising with other agencies, including the Social Welfare Department,
the Department of Maori Affairs, court conciliation services, other marriage guidance
counsellors, and child welfare officers, and referring families to those services when
necessary. The section could also attend to calls relating to molestation, and keep records of
all injunctions and non-molestation orders made by local courts.
The potential for such a section is enormous, and in public relations could only do


## p. 2786 (#182) ###########################################

2786
18 August
Domestic Violence Bill
significant good for both the public and the police. The public could deal with sympathetic
personnel experienced in dealing with domestic difficulties, and that could mean less
involvement for those members of the police force whose preference lay in other areas. The
Bill is a start, and I intend to move that it be referred to a select committee. I have no doubt
that it will be said that the Bill does not go far enough, and I tend to agree that in its present
form it is not perfect. Certainly, it does not cover rape in marriage, nor does it make
counselling or psychiatric treatment mandatory. I know that many people consider they are
necessary.
The Bill provides a sound basis, and could be used as a first step in our efforts to
recognise and correct the very real problems of violence in the home. Its referral to a select
committee will enable interested parties to make submissions and, perhaps, bring up matters
that could be improved. If we really care about family life, then this Bill should be accepted
by every member of Parliament.
Debate interrupted.
MINISTERIAL STATEMENT-CURRENCY TRADING
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): With the leave of the House, I wish to
make a ministerial statement on a matter raised by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition. I
was not in the House when he raised the matter of the Reserve Bank's suspension of
quotations in certain currencies this morning. He was apparently unaware that the Reserve
Bank had issued a statement setting out the details and the reasons for it. Quotations of the
United States dollar are still being made, although there are difficulties with other currencies
because of the erratic movement of the United States dollar in the last day or two, and the
consequential movement of other currencies, either in sympathy or as a result. The matter is
purely technical and has no relevance whatever to the continuing value of the New Zealand
dollar. There is certainly no proposal to make any formal change in the value of the New
Zealand dollar. As I said, the difficulty is purely technical, and is caused by the rapid and
somewhat confusing movement of the United States dollar. Inevitably there will be some
disruption in the short term, but I hope that matters will clarify over the weekend. The most
important thing for me to say is that there is no reason for anyone to suspect that the value of
the New Zealand dollar is involved.
Hon. W. W. Freer (Mt. Albert): I wonder if I might crave the indulgence of the House
to speak and to ask the Prime Minister a question relating to his statement.
Mr SPEAKER: Is it the pleasure of the House that leave be granted the honourable
member for Mt. Albert to make a statement, and to ask the Prime Minister a question?
There appears to be no objection.
Hon. W. W. FREER: First, on behalf of Opposition members, may I say how much we
appreciate the Prime Minister's clarifying the situation. The Deputy Prime Minister was
unaware of the issue when it was raised, but the promptness of the Prime Minister in making
a statement is appreciated. Will normal trading conditions prevail on Monday?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I certainly expect that they will. At the
time the statement was issued by the Reserve Bank it was not clear whether we would have
the Australian rates later on today. We usually get them about midday. I am not sure
whether we have received the rates, or whether we will be able to quote them later. I
certainly expect the matter to have settled down by Monday. It is purely a result of the
movement of the United States dollar-which went in two considerably different directions
in one day—and the difficulty that other currencies have had in catching up. For purely
technical reasons, we have been unable to say this morning whether the Australian dollar
will be quoted this afternoon. I am informed that at the moment it is impossible to get a line
between New Zealand and Australia. Apparently, there is some considerable excitement.
However, I expect it to be short term and of no great consequence to New Zealand currency
transactions. I should be astonished if it was not tidied up by Monday.

violence, and assures her that her concern is widely shared. In fact, the National Party has

matter for common concern that the law should deal adequately with the problem of
domestic violence. I make the observation, that will be reflected in the Government's Bill on
matrimonial proceedings when it is introduced, after the Royal Commission on the Courts
has reported at the end of this month-and that is holding things up at the moment-that
legal protection from abuse stems from the general criminal law. The member will
appreciate that. There is little point in duplicating legal protection by providing orders to
restrain a respondent from doing what it is unlawful for him to do. That is why the present
law on non-molestation orders is framed in the way it is. There is no point in duplicating the
law.
Nevertheless, in our working papers on the Government's proposed Matrimonial
Proceedings Bill, we have recognised that the best means of securing some improvement
may be to devise a speedy and simple procedure so that a violent husband can be temporarily
excluded from the matrimonial home, particularly when the law enforcement agencies-
principally the police-are reluctant to intervene in domestic disputes. The court could be
empowered to make an ex parte order, giving exclusive possession temporarily to the
applicant spouse, when the respondent has used violence against an applicant or a child of

What we have before us now is, frankly, a steal from British legislation-the Domestic
Violence and Matrimonial Proceedings Act 1976. It is a straight take from that, with the
exception that it omits the final provision in that Act, which deals with a residential or
property situation, because Britain does not have our joint family home legislation, nor do
we have anything that strictly parallels Britain's Matrimonial Homes Act. For that reason it
was thought desirable to leave out that aspect, but in considering it the committee might very
well add it. It proceeds on a line of remedy that would be novel in New Zealand, and indeed
was novel in Britain when it was introduced.
I am not quite sure whether I heard the Minister correctly, when he asked whether it
was desirable to duplicate the criminal law in what is proposed here, saying it was available
under criminal law, or whether he referred to that aspect of the Government Bill. I do not
believe that the law relating to assault is sufficient. In all events, there is a need for
something that would not require the high standard of proof needed in criminal cases, and in
considering whether there should be an injunction under this legislation a magistrate would
not be required to satisfy himself with the high standard of proof needed in a criminal case.
What is envisaged here is an injunction that really runs counter to the whole practice of
injuction as a remedy in the British courts, which traditionally do not meddle with the
private affairs of people. The court will not seek to enjoin that which it cannot effectively
enforce. Here it goes perilously close to the first instance, but it has been done in Britain,
and seems to be operating successfully there, although I am bound to add that some county
court judges appear to have more enthusiasm for it than others. But, over the whole
spectrum, it seems to fill a badly wanted need, of dealing with a position that requires an
urgent remedy. As the member in charge of the Bill said, the only available remedy now-
namely, the non-molestation order-is available only after the parties have separated and
after a separation order has been made, because a non-molestation order can be issued only
after the couple possess a separation order.

Police Amendment Bill
TUESDAY, 22 AUGUST 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
POLICE AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police): I move, That the Police
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill contains amendments that are designed to deal with
administrative, disciplinary, penal, and wage fixing procedures. It has 16 clauses. Clause 1
relates to the short title. Clause 2 is an interpretative provision which defines certain terms in
the amending Bill. Clause 3 enables a temporary member of the police, who may not satisfy
physical or other requirements, to be appointed permanently. In the main, this provision will
be used for members who are radio technicians, or in similar positions. Clause 4 provides for
the appointment of a successful appellant to the rank to which the appeal relates. The
Minister or the commissioner is given a discretionary power to cancel the original
recommendation. Clause 5 empowers the commissioner to vary or rescind a decision
concerning the suspension of a member pending the hearing of a charge. Clause 6 increases
the maximum penalties that may be imposed on members found guilty of breaches of duty.
Clause 7 provides for the publication of the Police Gazette and extends the protection
previously afforded to the Police Gazette to other publications relating to crime.
Clauses 8 to 16 amend the existing provisions of the principal Act to bring wage fixing
procedures for members into line with those prescribed for the public sector by the State
Services Conditions of Employment Act 1977. In particular, the amendments give effect to
the 12-month rule and the reconstitution of the police staff tribunal.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): Have the provisions of the Bill been discussed
with the New Zealand Police Association and the Police Officers Guild, and are those
organisations in general agreement with the proposals? Has there been any examination of
the stress placed on the police in the course of duty, and if so will the proposals vary the
terms of employment and working conditions to take account of that stress?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police): The terms of the Bill have been
discussed with the Police Officers Guild and the New Zealand Police Association. The guild
did not express any doubt about the provisions, but the association expressed doubt about
clause 6. The member may have noted that clause 6 updates the quantum of the fines. The
original Act was passed in 1958, and the proposed increases in the penalties from $100 to
$300, from $50 to $150, and from $40 to $120 are only reasonable in the light of the inflation
of the past 20 years. The member also asked about the stress survey. It has not been
completed. Obviously the result would be taken into account in negotiations.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): A small portion of the Bill deals with disciplinary
charges and other aspects of police behaviour. This has been considered in various parts of
the world, and has been the subject of a number of reports. It hardly needs to be said that the
public has great confidence in the Police Department and the manner in which its officers
conduct themselves. When there is any fall from the high level expected of them and adhered
to by them in general terms, the matter is always promptly inquired into. The manner in
which it ought to be inquired into has been questioned in a number of parts of the world,
largely because of incidents that fortunately have not occurred here. I refer to events in
Hong Kong, in the Metropolitan Police in London, and in one or two other places. As a
result, there has been some pressure for reviewing disciplinary tribunals by ensuring that
they are not kept internally orientated, but have some representation from the general
public.
I remember that when Mr Sharp was the commissioner he seemed to favour views of
that kind. In what I do not think was a private conversation, he intimated to me that he
would like representation on tribunals from outside the police when inquiries were set up. It
is known that he did promulgate some regulations for the police in difficult circumstances. I
shall not elaborate on this at great length.


## p. 2792 (#188) ###########################################

2792
22 August
Police Amendment Bill
I take the opportunity to ask the Minister whether consideration has been given to such
reports as have been made by the Australian Law Reform Commission, which were
generally well received by various police forces in Australia, although I do not believe any of
them have been fully acted on, for a review of the manner in which disciplinary inquiries are
carried out, and whether he is satisfied that not only-to use the old cliche—justice is done in
these matters, but justice is seen to be done to the satisfaction of the public.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police): The matter raised by the member
for Henderson is of great interest to the Commissioner of Police, and any studies done in
comparable jurisdictions are of interest. The existing law allows for an outside judicial
officer to be brought into police domestic matters. The member would know that a
magistrate can be called in to preside over any inquiry or action contemplated in respect of
disciplinary proceedings within the police. He would also know that when members of the
police offend against the general criminal law the due process of law in the criminal
jurisdiction is followed. There is no protection for the police from the grasp of criminal law.
The Bill does not go into those wider areas. I am assured that the commissioner will study
with interest any reports produced in Australia, Canada, or any comparable jurisdiction.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): Without having had an opportunity to examine the Bill in
detail, I ask the Minister whether it provides for any extra emolument for members of the
police who are moved into the community as liaison officers, where their work is not merely
during the period of duty, but extends to attending meetings of community groups and being
involved in school and other activities, which means that they work far longer hours than
they are paid for. In many cases, because they reside in the district, they are called upon
outside working hours to be the "man on the spot".
Secondly, does any provision in the Bill cover the recent situation that arose after the
determination of the Chief Judge of the High Court of the Cook Islands, as announced in the
House, when certain New Zealand police officers were sworn in as officers under that court's
jurisdiction? I do not raise any exception to that as the matter has yet to be examined, but it
seems to me that it would be appropriate for this legislation to provide for a similar situation.
Were those officers paid by the Cook Islands authorities, or did they continue to receive
remuneration from the New Zealand police authorities? What exactly was their status?
Perhaps the Minister could consider providing legislation to cover such a situation.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police): In reply to the latter question
raised by the member for Mangere, before the second reading I shall find out who was
responsible for paying the New Zealand policemen sworn in in the Cook Islands. The other
question related to the extra work policemen and women do for the community. Although a
timebook has not been kept for those extra duties, a percentage of ordinary salary has been
built in for many years, and was already available when I was Minister of Police from 1969 to
1972. That provision was agreed upon in ordinary negotiations between the police and their
employer, the commissioner.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): I thank the Minister for his information about
discussions with police organisations. I was aware of the association's doubt about some of
the provisions in clause 6. As those provisions increase the maximum penalties for breaches
of duty, does the Minister propose to increase such penalties in all other legislation to take
account of changes in the value of money? If so, when will those amendments come before
Parliament?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police): Earlier this year I instructed the
Department of Justice, when drafting the Police Offences Act—which when it is introduced
will be known as the Summary Offences Act-to update all the penalties because they are
becoming out of date. It is ridiculous to have an alternative penalty of 3 months'
imprisonment or $200. That might have made sense years ago when the legislation was first
passed, because $200 might well have been what a man could earn in 3 months. Today, he
could earn $1,000, $1,500, or more. Under the Crimes Act the Supreme Court is not limited
in the amount of a fine it might impose. However, generally speaking—and that was how the
member put his question-where monetary penalties are imposed they are being updated
when statutes are amended or drafted, so that they have meaning in 1978.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Pensioners-Subsidised Housing
1. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister
of Housing: Has he read the report in the Dominion of 17 August 1978 on the cutoff point for
pensioners' assets above which they are no longer eligible for subsidised pensioner housing,
and, if so, what steps is he proposing to take to raise the figure or provide some other form of
relief?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Yes, I have read the statement. The
asset limitation applicable to the Government's subsidised pensioner housing scheme was
increased from $5,000 to $7,500 as recently as the 1977 Budget. I am not proposing a further
increase in the meantime. The honourable member should be aware that a recent sampling
by the Housing Corporation of metropolitan local authority waiting lists disclosed that more
than 50 percent of applicants had realisable assets of less than $2,000. With that area of need
disclosed I consider it is unrealistic to widen the eligibility criteria. The honourable member
should also know that the Housing Corporation is funded to assist local authorities and other
sponsoring organisations in providing owner-occupier and tenant-contribution flats for
elderly home owners with assets over $7,500.
Mr T. J. Young: Will the Minister accept a deputation from the Lower Hutt City
Corporation about the anomalies it has pointed out?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I have already received a deputation from the Lower Hutt
City Corporation. Indeed, the article appeared as a result of that deputation. I think the
answer was given to the deputation. I repeat what I said in the earlier part of my answer—
that as long as a need exists for pensioner housing within the qualifications of assets of
$7,500, I do not think there is a need to change that at this stage.

Rope Imports from Korea
7. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the
Minister of Trade and Industry: What volume of low-cost Korean ropes has been imported
into New Zealand, as reported in the New Zealand Herald of 15 August, and why was this
importation, which adversely affected local manufacture, permitted?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): Import licences
were granted for $25,000 worth of a special type of Korean rope for crayfishing. The
identical rope is not made in New Zealand, and the purpose of the licences was to give some
interim assistance to fishermen and to allow time for a similar rope to be made in New
Zealand. The New Zealand Herald article refers to Donaghy's position. As these imports are
estimated at approximately 0.9 percent of the company's total value of rope production, the
assumption in the question that the imports adversely affect that production is not well
founded.
Mr Marshall: Does the Minister know how long it will be before that particular type of
rope is produced in New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: No, but I have had discussions with Donaghy's
recently and have visited their plant. I have discussions also with the fishermen from time to
time. No final decision has been made on whether what I would call genuine token licences
will be issued to the fishermen. I should like to see New Zealand producing all its rope
requirements, but from time to time industries do make representations, and for
comparative and competitive purposes, at the request of fishermen, we allowed an
importation that represents less than 1 percent of Donaghy's total rope production.
Richard Walls: Can the Minister confirm that some of the token licences issued were in
fact given to the manufacturers?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, and that is done from time to time. If it is
possible, if the manufacturer is genuinely a manufacturer wholesaler, and if the licences are
given because of representations by their clients and other New Zealand industries, we
endeavour to provide some of the licences to the manufacturer as a wholesaler, as well as to
other wholesalers.

Consumer Price Index
9. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Statistics: Does the consumer
price index provide a statistical series roughly comparable with the similar price indexes in
the United Kingdom, Australia, the United States, Japan, and West Germany, and, if so,


## p. 2796 (#192) ###########################################

2796
22 August
Questions for Oral Answer
can he advise the House of the most recent annual percentage increase for each country,
including New Zealand?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Statistics): Although the consumer price
indexes of New Zealand, Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan, and
West Germany are all based on the general recommendations of the United Nations
International Labour Organisation, there are differences of a conceptual and coverage
nature when the indexes are compared with each other. They differ particularly in respect of
the statistical formulae used to calculate them, the geographic and household coverage in the
weighting pattern, and the range and treatment of the goods and services covered.
Consequently, although international comparisons can be made, these must be treated as
approximations. Increases for the latest 12-monthly periods available are as follows: Japan,
3.5 percent; West Germany, 2.1 percent--for the year ended May 1978; United Kingdom,
7.4 percent; Australia, 7.9 percent; United States, 7.4 percent; New Zealand, 12.2 percent-
for the year ended June 1978. Because of the factors referred to, I emphasise that these
comparisons have definite limitations.

## p. 2797 (#193) ###########################################

Questions for Oral Answer
the union to supply the registrar with a roll containing the correct names and addresses of
persons entitled to vote. The persons who are entitled to vote are those who are bound by

knowledge that not every person bound by an unqualified preference clause is a member of
the union. In this respect the Bank Officers Union would not be able to supply a complete
roll from its register of members only.

Hydro Projects-Employment Opportunities
14. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Energy: Do small hydro
programmes offer employment opportunities in the regions in which they are located, and
can he give an indication of present and prospective job opportunities arising from those
projects?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): There are three distinct stages to small hydro
development—an initial assessment of potential schemes, detailed investigation of the most
promising sites, and actual construction. Virtually no local labour is required for initial
assessment. Detailed investigation may involve extensive site drilling, construction of roads
for access, and other engineering activities that should involve local firms. Power station and
transmission line construction would require both unskilled and skilled labour, and civil and
other types of contracts. Construction work is controlled by the local supply authority, which
decides on the extent to which local resources are used.
Mr Schultz: The Minister has given an outline of the work involved in the investigation.
Could he enlarge on the second part-what employment will arise from the contracts that
are let?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I cannot give details for the whole country, but I have here two
examples of labour content. The Dillmans project on the West Coast employed 100 people
at the peak of the development, in addition to power board staff, and the Lloyd Mandeno
scheme near Tauranga currently involves 85 or 90 contractor's staff; at the peak of last
summer the number was about 100. That was in addition to 65 or 70 power board staff.
Those are general figures, but give an indication that some scores of workers are involved in
some of the small projects.

Australian Budget-Effect on NZ Goods
21. Mr LANGE (Mangere) on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the

in the Australian Budget in so far as they affect the import of New Zealand manufactured
goods into Australia?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The information

that confirmation has been received that the additional duty will not be applied to goods of

from third countries.

APPROPRIATION BILL-ESTIMATES
In Committee
New Zealand Post Office
Further consideration of vote, Post Office, $450,170,000.
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) said that the National Party had published two similar
advertisements of considerable political concern-one in the Sunday Express, New
Plymouth, on 2 July, and the other in the Taranaki Herald on 28 June. The advertisement
had claimed that Spotswood was getting the new long-awaited telephone exchange, thanks
to the efforts of the National member of Parliament, who had successfully represented the
case for it to the Postmaster-General.
The advertisements raised the serious question of pork-barrel politics. Did the
Postmaster-General and his Cabinet colleagues take action only in electorates where the
seats of National members were in jeopardy, or could everyone be assured that Government
decisions had nothing whatever to do with that? It appeared that Post Office facilities were
to be provided in those electorates that were represented by Government members.
In addition, the advertisements contained misinformation. They had claimed that only
after the establishment of the Spotswood exchange could planning proceed for the new New
Plymouth exchange, which Labour had promised in 1973 and then cancelled in 1975.
In August 1973 the Labour Cabinet works committee had approved the preparation of
sketch plans and working drawings for the building. A month later the sketch plans, which
apparently had been based on plans prepared 4 years earlier, had been found to provide
insufficient space for local requirements. Therefore negotiations had been continued and the
revised sketch plans had been sent to the district engineer for his comments in July 1975. The
district engineer had commented to Post Office Headquarters that the building would still be
too small, and Post Office Headquarters had agreed. That decision taken by the Labour
Government was not political. The building delays had occurred in June 1976, and not in
1975 when the former member for New Plymouth held the seat.
In November 1977 the Cabinet works committee had made exactly the same decision as
the Labour Government Cabinet works committee had made in August 1973 by approving
work on the plans and drawings. The Postmaster-General should advise his colleagues that it
was misleading to claim credit for something which would happen anyway, and also to claim
incorrectly that one Government had delayed building certain facilities.
Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) said that two telephone exchanges were involved.
In 1973 the former Labour member for New Plymouth had announced that his Government
would be going ahead with building a new central telephone exchange; and in the latter part
of 1975 the same Government had removed that project from the programme because it did
not have sufficient funds. The telephone exchange referred to in the advertisement was now
being built at Spotswood; it would be an integral part of the overall telephone system in New
Plymouth. Funds for the work were available because the National Government had
adjusted postal charges. If the Labour Government had continued in office no funds would
have been available. The statement in the advertisement was correct.
