Appropriation Bill-Estimates
He had great sympathy with the former Labour member for New Plymouth, Mr
Barclay, because he had had to announce something which could not go ahead because of his
Government's policies. In 1974 the Post Office had suffered a loss of $38.7 million.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the member for New Plymouth to produce evidence to
back up his claims. The Massey telephone subexchange and the Te Atatu subexchange of the
Henderson exchange had had automatic number identification systems installed, which
meant that when a subscriber made a telephone call the number from which the call was
made appeared on the board in the exchange. It would be easy to record them and to make a
charge for every call. Did the member for Waitemata believe that was a "great improvement
in the telephone system offered to Massey and Ranui residents" as the member for
Waitemata had claimed in a leaflet he had recently distributed? Any proposal by the
Government to charge for local calls would be rescinded immediately after the election of a
Labour Government.
The Postmaster-General had claimed that the Post Office had introduced a courier
system. He hoped the Postmaster-General would apologise to Parliament, because notes
supplied by Post Office officials had stated that such a system was still being considered. Had
private operators, who stood to lose their jobs if such a service were introduced, been
consulted?
Under the sinking-lid policy, 44 people a month, or 1.5 percent of the staff, were not
replaced. The Postmaster-General had said that approval had been given to the director-
general to employ 140 extra staff. However, he had not said that those 140 people were not
approved until the beginning of June, which meant, under the sinking lid policy, that for the
first 2 months 88 of the 140 people could not be employed. He congratulated the Post Office
workers at Piha and Karekare for the magnificent job they did. They worked under great
stress. Because of the lack of staff Post Office officials had to put up with abuse at the
counter.
Mr BELL (Gisborne) said that the Ruatoria exchange had been upgraded to semi-
automatic status. The board on which the numbers were carried would be extended to
reduce some of the party lines, which at present carried about 10 or 12 subscribers. Approval
for a new post office at Hicks Bay had been granted, and a new post office was being built at
Te Hapara. The improvement in telephone services in his electorate had been made possible
by the improved profitability of the Post Office. The free calling service had been extended
to 96 percent of subscribers compared with 93 percent in 1975, and about 95 percent of
subscribers now enjoyed the services of automatic exchanges compared with 92 percent 2
years ago.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked why equipment that would enable a charge to
be made for every call had been installed at the Massey and Te Atatu subexchanges of the
Henderson exchange. Any organisation running a monopoly service could make a profit if it
increased its charges by more than 100 percent. Through increased charges, Post Office
revenue had been increased by $176 million in the last 2 years, representing an 80 percent
rise, yet the profit had been only $39 million. Where had the rest of the $176 million gone?
Since February 1976 surface letter charges had jumped 150 percent from 4c to 10c;
airmail letter charges had jumped 140 percent from 5c to 12c; telephone rentals had
increased by almost 100 percent from $61.60 in 1975 to $120.50; reconnection fees for
telephones had jumped 300 percent from $15 to $50; and the cost of telephone connections
had gone from $30 to $55. People could no longer afford to have a telephone. Postal services
had been slashed back in every direction-more than 60 rural post offices had been closed
and an additional 43, many of them rural, had been placed on restricted hours; clearances of
suburban post boxes had been cut back.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) said that a replacement exchange for
Wanganui, at a cost of $4,559,000, had been approved on 30 March 1977 and that a major
extension to the Porirua exchange, at a cost of $2,394,000, had been approved in June 1977,
and was now under construction. Transportable telephone exchanges would give the districts
that benefited a telephone exchange service about 2 years earlier than would otherwise have
been the case. They would be installed in areas such as Torbay, Browns Bay, Howick,
Albany, Beachlands, Greenhithe, Belmont, Rolleston, Cromwell, Massey, Wiri,
Beckenham, Burwood, and Ravensbourne, none of which were in marginal electorates. The
Spotswood exchange had been approved on 16 December 1977 at a cost of $1,132,000.
There was no substance in the suggestion that the Government had been pork-barrelling
with the Post Office. A recent statement by the member for New Plymouth had indicated

The Post Office had been accused of installing automatic number identification for local

had closed. Post offices had also been closed during Labour's term in office. Opposition

waiting lists would be lower at the end of this year than they had been at any time during the
past 5 years. It had been said that post offices had local charging equipment and that more
had been ordered. No such equipment had been ordered and none was available. Opposition
members had said that the Government had "siphoned off" $64.9 million into the
Consolidated Account. Such payments had also taken place during Labour's term in office.
By innuendo, Opposition members had indicated that there was something sinister about
paying in interest on borrowings and Post Office Savings Bank profits.
The former Labour Government had run a pilot study in Christchurch and had halved
the clearances of suburban street posting boxes there because of declining patronage. An
isolated case had been quoted of a letter posted on Friday that had not been delivered until
Monday. The Post Office delivered 2 000 000 items of mail every day, most of which was
delivered without complaint. Only a fraction of the mail went astray.
It had been said that under the next Labour Government the Post Office would be run
at a "reasonable profit". Between 1972 and 1975 the Post Office had made a loss.
Opposition members said that the $37.7 million profit was excessive. It was suggested that a
profit of $5 million would be considered more reasonable. When applied to the need for
expenditure on capital works of about $80 million for 1978 and $289 million for wages,
excluding the supplementaries, where would the balance come from? He gave an assurance
that he had not taken a proposal about local call charges to Cabinet, and the Prime
Minister's statement on the subject after the Cabinet meeting had been the end of the
matter. The National Government had greatly reduced the waiting lists, which had reached a
peak of 30 000 by mid-1977. By the end of 1978 the waiting list should be reduced to below
20 000, the lowest figure in 5 years. The Post Office had converted 28 manual telephone
exchanges to automatic, and 66 new automatic exchanges had been installed, increasing the
percentage of subscribers on automatic exchanges to 93. Subscriber toll dialling had been
introduced and was available to 42 percent of subscribers. There had been an expansion of
free-calling areas and 95 percent of subscribers now had free calling to a city.
The Government had nothing to be ashamed of in its administration of the Post Office.
It had been through the most difficult phase in its history, due to mismanagement by the
former Labour Government. When posterity viewed the administration of the portfolio
during the past 3 years it would not rate it too badly.

Appropriation Bill-Estimates
The National Government in its first year had slashed the Recreation and Sport item
from the $5.1 million of 1975 to $3.5 million. For the second year of the National
Government it was again $3.5 million. The figure for the current year was just over $4
million, but when inflation was taken into account it was still $3 million less in real money
terms than the amount allocated by the Labour Government in 1975.
The National Government and the Minister seemed to have intentionally lost the whole
field of recreation and sport. Why had the name been removed? Where was the money for
recreation and sport? It seemed to have been gobbled up in the new item of community and
recreation development. The Council for Recreation and Sport was upset about that, and
about what had been happening under the present Minister. The development in that field
had changed since the time of the Labour Government; the grant to local bodies per
individual had been slashed from $1 to 50c. The Government had increased it to 75c for
individuals this year and had said it would possibly increase it to $1 next year. That is the
never-never system. New Zealand's Commonwealth Games athletes had got to Canada,
mostly on their own merit, with no support and no finance from the Government.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) said that in its first year of office the
National Government had found the economy in such a mess that it had to cut the recreation
and sport grant by over $1 million. That had been a difficult decision, but it had to be done to
get the economy straight.
In the estimates, $4.26 million had been provided, and in the meantime a grant of
$100,000 had been given for the world rowing championships. The Lotteries Board of
Control had decided to give $600,000 to establish a community development fund. Only that
afternoon a fund of $700,000 had been created to replace the regional recreation and sport
scheme created by the Labour Government. The total amount to be granted to recreation
and sports clubs throughout the country would be more than $5 million.
Last year the Government had given 50c a head of the population to local authorities for
recreation and sport. Now, under community and recreation development, that 50c had
been increased to 75c a head. The words "community development” had been added so that
local authorities could use the money as they saw fit. Next year, the Government would
increase the amount to $1 per head of the population, and the amount would be included in
the estimates under community and recreation development.
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) said that in 1976-77 the estimates allocated $3.55 million to
recreation and sport. The Labour Government had allocated 70c per head of population, but
the National Government had cut the figure to 50c, although in 1975 the Under-Secretary to
Minister of Recreation and Sport had said before the election that, although he was not
prepared to commit the National Government to any figure, he promised that it would at
least match the allocation made by the Labour Government that year. However, in the
National Government's first allocation the amount had been decreased by $1.4 million,
although the Labour Government had allocated $5,155,000. The National Government's
allocation had been $3.5 million.
Hon. D. A. Highet: No one denies that.
Mr ROGERS said that temporary measures had become permanent under the present
Government. Although the Government had been prepared to allocate $10,000 a year to
keep somebody in a security jail, $8,500 a year to keep somebody in borstal, or $8,000 a year
to keep a female in a medium security prison, it was not prepared to spend money on the
youth and future of New Zealand. The Government had made promises which it had
broken.

WEDNESDAY, 23 AUGUST 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
PRIVILEGE
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
want to raise what I consider is a serious breach of privilege by the member for New
Plymouth. The member has been advised that the matter would be raised. I raise the matter
under Standing Order 428. Under Standing Order 430 a prima facie case of breach of
privilege is established. Privilege has been breached on three counts in a story that appears in
today's Dominion. The article reveals that the Petitions Committee wrongfully delegated its
responsibility to hear evidence to a body not appointed by Parliament, and I refer to the
Government caucus. The opening paragraph of the article reads: "A committee verdict on
the Repeal abortion petition was approved in advance by the Government caucus. This was
disclosed last night by the petitions committee chairman Mr A. P. D. Friedlander (Govt,
New Plymouth).”
The second point is about pressure being brought to bear on members of the committee.
The newspaper article states: "He", the member for New Plymouth, "agreed pressure had
been placed on committee members by other Government MPs and Ministers."
The third point is that the decision and the deliberations of the committee were
disclosed prematurely. In support of this point I refer to the article, which states:
"Conceding in an interview that the committee decision had been left to caucus, Mr
Friedlander said: 'Fortunately, the caucus recommendation was the one I recommended to
caucus.'
Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, our major authority, is fairly precise on those
three counts. Contempt in general is dealt with on page 136: “It may be stated generally that
any act or omission which obstructs or impedes either House of Parliament in the
performance of its functions, or which obstructs or impedes any member or officer of such
House in the discharge of his duty, or which has a tendency, directly or indirectly, to produce
such results may be treated as a contempt even though there is no precedent of the offence."
On the matter of premature publication Erskine May states on page 146: "Premature
publication or disclosure of a committee's proceedings or evidence. By the ancient custom of
Parliament 'no act done at any committee should be divulged before the same be reported to
the House.'" That matter is dealt with in more detail.
Other matters in Erskine May are relevant. The paragraphs on page 150 headed
"Attempted intimidation of members" refer to pressure being brought to bear. This clearly
applies to the chairman of the committee, who made a public disclosure in one direction and
in a statement to the press said that during deliberations on a conscience issue he had voted
in another direction. The petitioners had every right to expect that the committee would
hear evidence and that the committee would deliberate on the basis of the evidence. They
expected that the committee would produce findings on the basis of the evidence presented.
The suggestion in the newspaper report was to the contrary. The committee's decision was
made by a body other than the committee, and it was not in possession of the petitioners'
evidence. There is, on the three grounds I have advanced, a clear case of breach of privilege.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Mr Speaker, the case put forward by the
Leader of the Opposition is utter nonsense. You have sat in a caucus for many years and
know what happens about the deliberations of select committees. Discussions in both
Labour and National caucuses have taken place since time immemorial.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: You wouldn't be admitted to ours.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I do not want to hear interjections from any honourable
member. We are discussing a question of privilege. Privilege is probably one of the most
important matters that can be discussed by members about their own business or the
business of people outside Parliament. There will be no interjections during a discussion of
this nature while I am presiding. I hope that is abundantly clear to all members. If it is not, I
will invite the members to leave the Chamber.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I clearly recall an incident that you, Mr Speaker, may also


## p. 2819 (#215) ###########################################

23 August
2819
Privilege
recall, because I believe you were a member of the select committee deliberating the
amendments to the Electoral Act during the Labour Government's term in office. It was
decided to make certain amendments to the Act. Labour members said they had been
talking about the amendments in caucus and that caucus would not go along with them. The
Labour members had to reverse their views and put forward different amendments. I am
sure members who were on that select committee will remember that case, which is only one
of many.
Members on both sides of the House know that the affairs of select committees are, by
custom, discussed in both caucuses. It is normal for a select committee, after deliberating, to
leave time before reporting so that members can consult their caucus colleagues. The matter
before the committee in this case was whether the petition be referred to the Government
for most favourable consideration, for favourable consideration, for consideration, or for no
recommendation. If the decision had been for no recommendation that would have been the
end of the matter. If a petition goes to the Government for most favourable consideration,
favourable consideration, or consideration, the Government has the duty to assess the merits
of the petition. Certainly the proposals differ.
The suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition that the Petitions Committee deals with
petitions is quite wrong. The committee refers a petition to the Government for most
favourable consideration, for favourable consideration, or for consideration. The matter is
then in the hands of the Government, which has to follow the evidence, act accordingly, and
report back to the House shortly after the commencement of the next Parliament. So, come
what may, it becomes a matter for the Government unless the recommendation has been for
no consideration. I take it that the Leader of the Opposition has not suggested that that was
the sort of decision the committee could have come to.
In brief, and without wishing to prolong the matter, it has been normal practice since
time immemorial for the caucuses of the two parties to discuss select committee matters. I
have not the slightest doubt that this petition was discussed in the Labour caucus, because
the leader of that caucus would not have been doing his job if no reference was made. It
would not surprise many people if the Leader of the Opposition publicly confessed that he
was not doing his job. However, I doubt whether he will.
Mr SPEAKER: Order!
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I realise I have transgressed, Mr Speaker. I have not the
slightest doubt that the matter was discussed. I would have expected it to be discussed in the

select committees are discussed in caucus. It has nothing whatever to do with privilege. I
think someone is probably trying to take a pot shot at the member for New Plymouth. He
will get nowhere with that.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I suppose we are bound to accept the authority of

antiquity since time immemorial, as he described it. He certainly has no right or authority
to speak for what goes on in the Labour caucus. He referred to an incident that occurred
during a hearing of an amendment to the Electoral Act. It is certainly true that the Bill, as it
then was, was discussed in our caucus. However, I can give him a categorical assurance that
the committee's proceedings were not discussed at that stage. I can give him a further
categorical assurance that the proceedings of the Petitions Committee on this petition were
not discussed in our caucus.
The Prime Minister went on to say that the Government had a duty to assess the merits
of the petition. That misconstrues the proceedings and the Government's responsibility,
which is to consider the report and the recommendation of the committee. The consideration
of the petition before the committee has come to some conclusion is no business of the
Government, and to stick its nose into the proceedings of the committee is to go far beyond
the sphere of its authority. Accordingly, I support the move made by the Leader of the
Opposition. I am bound to say that I do so with mixed feelings, because on more than one
occasion in the House I have expressed regret that the breach of privilege procedure is over-
used and can be invoked to magnify an incident, which, in essence, is of trivial consequence.
However, as this is such a crystal clear case, I not only consider that it ought to be raised, but
also that one is justified in participating.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to some general authorities derived from Erskine
May, the general principles of which are binding on us, and which we must observe.
However, the matter goes beyond that, as indicated in the clear directions of our own


## p. 2820 (#216) ###########################################

2820
23 August
Privilege
Standing Orders, which I feel obliged to read. I refer to three of them. Standing Order 366,
under the heading "Evidence, etc., not to be published or divulged", states: "The
proceedings of, or the evidence taken by, or the report of any select committee, or any
summary of such proceedings, evidence, or report shall be strictly confidential and not
published or divulged by any member of the committee or by any other person, until the
report of such committee has been presented to the House." It then goes on to state that
there is an exception when the chairman has been authorised by the committee to make a
specific publication, and so on. I shall not trouble you with the remainder of that Standing
Order.
Standing Order 367 is also relevant, and under the heading "Divulging proceedings or
evidence a breach of privilege", states: "Any person committing a breach of Standing Order
366 shall be deemed guilty of a breach of privilege, and may be dealt with by the House
accordingly." Finally, Standing Order 369, under the heading "Proof copies of evidence to
members only", states: "Proof copies of the evidence given before a select committee may
be distributed to members of the committee only." Therefore, other members of the House,
not being members of the committee, have no privilege beyond that of the ordinary
community, to whom disclosure would be an obvious breach of privilege. Equally, disclosure
to other members of the House is a breach of privilege in terms of Standing Order 367. That
is clearly what has happened.
I cite again the lead story from this morning's Dominion: "A committee verdict on the
Repeal abortion petition was approved in advance by the Government caucus. This was
disclosed last night by petitions committee chairman Mr A. P. D. Friedlander . . ." Not only
was there a disclosure before the report was submitted to the House, but quite obviously,
from the remaining passages of the report as quoted by the Leader of the Opposition, there
was a discussion, a finding, and one that was binding on the Government members of the
committee, which, as a result of their majority, determined the committee's finding.
Moreover, that determination by caucus was at odds with the convictions of the chairman, as
disclosed in earlier proceedings of the Bill with which it was concerned, because the member
for New Plymouth is recorded as voting against various amendments moved by the member
for Porirua, the member for Timaru, and the member for Franklin, which clearly disclosed
that his own predilection would have been something more than the very much less than milk
and water recommendation, the damning with faint praise recommendation, that was
brought in for consideration.

GOVERNMENT BUSINESS PRECEDENCE ON WEDNESDAYS
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That on and after 23 August 1978
Government business take precedence on Wednesdays for the remainder of the session. Today
is the sixty-first sitting day, and, apart from last year, when this motion was moved on the
sixty-fourth sitting day, and 1973, when it was moved on the sixtieth sitting day, this is the
latest it has been moved for some considerable time. In terms of the date-23 August-it
seems to be the latest for as far back as I can go. Now that the legislation is coming through
smoothly, it is appropriate to move the motion at this time so that we can proceed without
too many late sittings, and lead up to the election campaign at about the normal time.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): It is noticeable that the Prime
Minister, in moving the motion, dealt only with the position that has obtained in the past. He
referred only very fleetingly to the present position. The motion is that, beginning today,
Government business shall take precedence on Wednesdays. If the motion is accepted, it will
have the effect of cutting out the notices of motion on the Order Paper for discussion today.
Members, I think, should have a closer look at them. I shall come back to that point in a
moment.
I wish to refer first to some of the Prime Minister's statements about his intentions for
the session, particularly those he gave last Friday morning. It is obvious that there is not a
great deal of business before the House, and this is why I raise the point that it is more
important to discuss matters that concern us this year, rather than say that it was the sixtieth
day, or the sixty-first day, or the sixty-fourth day when it was moved on another occasion.
The Order Paper is not particularly bulky at this stage, apart from notices of motion, which
are the very things that will be cut out by this notice. The actual list of orders of the day is
remarkably slim. There are only 22 orders of the day at this stage, and many are entirely
non-contentious; several are through their second readings-and that applies to all but two
of those that could be considered remotely contentious.
We have a pattern that really decides the time that the House must occupy, and that is

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Deputy Leader of the Opposition
has left us uncertain about whether he supports the motion or opposes it. It seemed to me
that the whole of his speech was merely a moan that the motion might hurt private members,
the Opposition, or something like that. Let us think about what has happened so far this
session, and consider just how much of Parliament's time has been given to the concerns of
private members and how much of its time has been devoted to Government business.
Twelve private members' Bills have already been considered, and six of them have been
given the courtesy of a second reading. In all, they have been debated for well over 20 hours.
That might not sound very long when one realises that there are 24 hours in each day, but
Parliament does not sit all day. Indeed, Parliament sits for only 6 hours as Parliament in
session or in Committee of the Whole on each of 3 days-Tuesday, Wednesday, and
Thursday-and for only 4 hours on Friday. Even then, a great deal of that time is taken up
with formal business, the introduction of Government Bills, the giving of notices of motion,
the lodging of petitions, and the asking of questions for oral answer. Therefore, the time
available for debating either Government or private Bills is very much less than the 22 hours
a week for which the House sits.
I believe private members have had a great deal more time devoted to their concerns
this year, under the National Government's leadership, than they have for many years past.
If we look back we see that in 1973 the former Labour Government was generous to private
members, but not as generous as the National Government has been this year. The former
Labour Government closed private business that year after the sixtieth sitting day, and
today, as the Prime Minister has said, is the sixty-first sitting day this session. In 1974 the
former Labour Government chopped private members' business off after 56 sitting days, and

EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That the Education Amendment
Bill be introduced. The Bill contains seven clauses, makes miscellaneous changes to the
Education Act 1964, and repeals the Whangarei High Schools Act 1878. These changes are
necessary to improve present education policy and to bring various sections of the Act up to
date.
Clause 2 is a drafting change made as a consequence of the 1976 Education Amendment
Act (No. 2), and amends a cross reference in section 119 of the Act that provides for the
enrolment of a child at the Correspondence School if the regional superintendent of
education is unable to establish at a suitable school a pupil who has been suspended.
Clause 3 repeals section 129 of the Act, and substitutes new provisions. The new section
129, which relates to State primary schools, has essentially the same effect as the present
section 129(2), and provides that, to avoid overcrowding, an education board may, with the
approval of the Minister, limit enrolments at any primary school, other than an integrated
school, under its control. The differences in this provision merely delete the earlier reference
to Maori schools, and also make it clear that integrated schools are not covered by this
section. The new section 129A is intended to replace the present section 129(2) of the
Education Act 1964.
Members will know that under that section Ministers of Education have in the past been
called upon to make decisions on school enrolments in districts that have zoning
arrangements. They will also know that the only criterion that Ministers may take into
account when making decisions under section 129(2) relates to the availability of
accommodation in the school or schools whose enrolment is to be restricted. The legislation
proved reasonably adequate when secondary school rolls were rising, but now, when rolls
have stabilised and will begin to decline, the legislation is inadequate. Measures are
therefore necessary to protect programmes already commenced for pupils enrolled at
secondary schools. It is considered that the legislation should acknowledge the need to
rationalise the enrolment of pupils in areas where two or more schools would otherwise
compete for a declining number of students to protect as far as possible the study courses on
which students have embarked, while at the same time making appropriate use of the staff
and accommodation available at each school concerned.
Late in 1977 a working party, comprising representatives of the Secondary Schools
Boards Assocation, the Post-Primary Teachers Association, and officers of the Department
of Education, reviewed the present legislation, and recommended changes to meet new
circumstances. The proposed amendment to section 129 of the Education Act gives effect to
the working party's recommendations. The changes remove the present requirement to
restrict enrolment of students by ministerial decision based on the availability of
accommodation, and instead require school boards that have a common enrolment area, as
defined by the Director-General of Education, to meet and agree on an enrolment scheme
acceptable to them, but within agreed criteria and subject to the Minister's final approval.


## p. 2833 (#229) ###########################################

23 August
2833
Education Amendment Bill
Any enrolment scheme is also subject to the requirement of section 129B, which makes it
mandatory for a student to have access to a reasonably convenient school.
The proposed legislation includes adequate safeguards for the enrolment of pupils from
outside the enrolment area, including those who would occupy school hostels, and would
also meet the reasonable needs of parents who desired single-sex schools for their children
by allowing an agreed number of out-of-zone enrolments for each school when this was
necessary. The controlling authority of any school that disagrees with a proposed enrolment
scheme will be able to make its views known to the Minister. The Minister will take those
submissions into account in deciding whether to approve the scheme as recommended, or
approve it in a modified form, or decline to approve it. The proposed legislation will give full
legal authority to enrolment schemes, agreed by schools with common enrolment areas, that
are already operating successfully in many parts of the country with the full approval of the
department. It should also be emphasised that boards of governors of secondary schools
charged under the proposed legislation with determining enrolment schemes are controlled
by the elected representatives of the parents concerned. The rights of parents to appeal
against decisions on enrolment to the board of governors, the regional superintendent, or
the Minister, are not affected. The proposed amendment to section 129(2) of the Education
Act has the full support of the Secondary School Boards Association, the Post-Primary
Teachers Association, and the department.
Clause 4 is a procedural provision to permit an education board to establish more than
one appointments committee for primary appointments, as may be necessary in the
particular circumstances of each district. Clause 5 is also a procedural provision relating to
the notification of unsuccessful applicants for teaching positions. There is no provision in the
present Act to provide for increases in the value of bursaries or scholarships to be made
retrospective. Clause 6 provides that any increases may be made retrospectively by an
amendment to the appropriate regulations.
The Whangarei High School Board was constituted in accordance with the Whangarei
High Schools Act 1878, and its amendments. Clause 7 repeals that Act and the amendments,
and the board has now been reconstituted in accordance with the Education Act 1964.
Although there is nothing controversial in the Bill, it will affect many people, so I intend to
refer it to the Education Select Committee.
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): I congratulate the Minister on the speed with which he
has introduced the Bill. I heard him say only 4 hours ago that he hoped to introduce it within
the next few weeks, or perhaps a little earlier. He certainly very quickly confirmed the

given in the Bill to the problem of zoning? I ask this because often one comes across

restrictions. Is the Government considering any legislation on that matter?
The other matter that arises out of enrolment is the concern that some people have

legislation might be to diminish State school rolls. Is there anything in the Bill that would
safeguard school rolls? I suspect that there is no need to, because that is already taken care

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): A variety of questions has been asked.
The member for Wanganui asked about integrated rolls. An integrated school is not covered
by the Education Act, but by the Private Schools Conditional Integration Act, and the
integration agreement on rolls. I too am concerned about ensuring that a position does not
develop in which State schools have falling rolls, and integrated schools have either rising or
static rolls, and therefore are at an advantage compared with the State schools. That will
have to be looked at very carefully. The member will realise that the idea of integration
occurred before we ran into the problem of falling rolls. I do not expect any great difficulty,
because the matter will be covered by the review committees, and also by the conditions of
the integration agreements.
The member asked about the possibility of restricting rolls because of the size of
schools, and referred to Burnside as being typical of a very large secondary school. Burnside
was developed as a very large secondary school with the idea of establishing whether a school
of that size could be developed satisfactorily. It has been reasonably successful, but there is
no intention to develop any more. Again, with falling rolls it is likely that even those big
schools will have diminishing rolls. The Twizel primary school is an example of a very large
school that obviously will not be one for a long term, and the requirements of Twizel may
have to be examined. It may be that in a construction town of that sort it would be more
appropriate to build two primary schools, both probably temporary. The member for
Mangere asked about primary school zoning, and gave the example of a family that was
apparently split between two schools. I am concerned about that.
Mr Lange: I wrote to you about it.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes. I feel that is the sort of case over which I or the Director-
General would have a discretion. There is no need whatever to split up a family. Such
instances are rare-I think this is only the third case of which I have heard, since I have been
Minister of Education, of a family having difficulty about the school it attended. The
member for Hutt asked for a definition of overcrowding. We do not have a hard and fast
definition of overcrowding but, if one school has surplus accommodation and if there is a
greater number of pupils than can be accommodated according to the code of class room
space at another school, it is pretty obvious that one school has overcrowding and the other
has not.

I do not interpret overcrowding as being related to school grounds. Unfortunately,
some schools are well below the code for grounds. If we are able to extend the grounds—if it

include overcrowding of school grounds. The definition of overcrowding really is that there

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Gleneagles Agreement
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: How does he know
whether or not New Zealand is complying with the requirements of the Gleneagles
Agreement if, as stated on 18 August in answer to a written question, the Government's
records are not complete and it does not know what its citizens are doing overseas?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The member for Wanganui is
implying that the Government should keep the activities overseas of its citizens, even of an
individual citizen, under surveillance. I can assure him that this was never intended at the
time of the Gleneagles Agreement which specifically states that it is "for each Government
to determine, in accordance with its laws," the methods by which the commitments accepted
under the Gleneagles Agreement should be carried out. The Gleneagles Agreement requires
the Government to withhold any form of support for, and take every practical step to
discourage, contact or competition by New Zealanders with sporting organisations teams, or
sportsmen from South Africa. This the Government has done.
Mr Marshall: How can the Government implement the commitments under the
agreement without knowing what sportsmen are doing overseas?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: If the honourable member suggests that Big Brother should
watch every sportsman, I reject the proposal. Individual sportsmen, including professionals,
move about the world playing in tournaments-even in the Baltimore Open. If someone
moves from, say, Britain to Baltimore to play in the Baltimore Open, I know of no way in
which the Government can trace and follow the activities of that person. Nor, I suggest, is it
desirable that the Government should trace and follow the activities of every one of its
citizens who are overseas.
Mr Marshall: How strenuous are the Government's efforts to make sure that
individuals, as members of national sporting bodies, are aware of the Gleneagles Agreement
and its implications?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Perhaps there is a sporting organisation that plays two up
that has not yet got the message, but I do not think there is one individual in New Zealand
who is interested in sport who is not aware of the Gleneagles Agreement. Most people, I am
sure, have a fair idea of the content of the agreement. It could be possible that a yoga teacher
would attend a conference in South Africa-it is not possible to know everybody's
movements. Obviously most New Zealanders are prepared to conform to the principles of
the ageement.

Maori Community Development
6. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Maori Affairs: What changes have
been made in the field of Maori community development, and on what is the emphasis being
put at present?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): The main change in the field of
Maori community development has been the stronger emphasis on working with Maori
organisations in mobilising the resources of Maoridom. I refer here to Maori committees,
women's leagues, marae committees, and tribal councils. The priority has shifted from
working mostly with individuals and families requiring welfare help to a massive effort on
youth development in the fields of education and vocational training. Programmes have
been launched, such as those being undertaken by Howard Morrison in the schools and by
Maori community officers—and a more recent programme, approved by the Government,
called Tu Tangata, which sets up task-oriented community organisations to improve Maori
academic attainment. What is already emerging are homework centres, ideas about basic
skills centres, and a gathering wave of creative ideas for community development-from the
Maori people themselves.
Hon. M. Rata: Would the Minister indicate exactly how much he has in the estimates to
give effect to the programme?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: It is obvious that the member for Northern Maori does not
understand my reply. I do not need more people for the changes in duties of different
officers, to make them more creative; I am getting more cost-effect from the people
operating the scheme. The honourable member will have an opportunity to question the
actual figures when we come to the estimates of the Department of Maori Affairs.
Mr W. R. Austin: Has the present emphasis come about as a result of an intensive
inquiry into the Department of Maori Affairs?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Yes. In 1975-76, when I became Minister of Maori Affairs, I set
up a committee of inquiry to study the administration and the effectiveness of the
Department of Maori Affairs, because I thought, after the previous 3 years, the
department's spirit was not very high.
Taxation
7. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: What was the appropriate tax code at 31 March 1978 for the main earner of a
family, who has a child aged 3 and whose spouse earns $15 a week through part-time work?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department): The appropriate tax code would have been S + F. Assuming the main earner's
income was not too high to qualify for the young-family rebate, the code would signify
entitlement to that rebate. In addition, there would be entitlement to a partial spouse rebate
and the single-income family rebate as end-of-year allowances.

National Superannuation-Taxation
13. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland

completed, a person who has been in receipt of national superannuation for a full year and

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department): A person receiving national superannuation for a full year with no other
income may be entitled to a refund of income tax if he or she can claim exemptions or
rebates not taken into account in the PAYE tax deducted during the year. Examples of these
exemptions and rebates are: if a national superannuitant makes charitable donations, pays
life insurance premiums, pays a housekeeper if the taxpayer or the spouse is incapacitated,
or contributes to the support of a dependent relative. The exemption or rebate applicable
would depend on the amount actually paid in each case.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When I introduced the Bill I said that it would make a number of important
changes to the Social Security Act, and now that members have had an opportunity to study
it I am sure that they will agree that this is so. The Government has honoured its
undertakings to social security beneficiaries and to national superannuitants. The Bill
provides ample evidence of this, as does the Government's record over the past 3 years.
I first refer members to clause 9, which legislates for the new handicapped child's
allowance of $8 a week announced in the Budget. The allowance will be paid from 18
October 1978. The clause is now commonly referred to as "the Dr Shearer clause", because
earlier in the year the member for Hamilton East introduced a private member's Bill
recommending an allowance. The allowance is intended for the parents of a seriously
handicapped child. The definition of such a child is given on pages 4 and 5 of the Bill. The
definition has been discussed with the New Zealand Society for the Intellectually
Handicapped, the Crippled Children Society, the Advisory Council for the Community
Welfare of Disabled Persons, and with the Departments of Education and Health. All those
organisations agree with it.
To qualify for this allowance the parents or guardians must be caring for the seriously
handicapped child at home. However, provision is also made to pay the allowance to the
parents or guardians of a child who is in a home or hostel run by an approved voluntary
organisation, such as the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped, provided the parents or
guardians are required to meet a board charge and care for the child during school holidays
or weekends. Obviously there will be some marginal cases when a child's disability is not
considered to come within the definition of seriously handicapped. I want to stress that
decisions will be made in the light of all medical evidence available to the Department of
Social Welfare, and that, if the parents or guardians do not agree with the department's
decision, they will have a special right of appeal to an independent Handicapped Child's
Appeal Board, which will comprise a barrister or solicitor and two medical practitioners. It
has been estimated that about 4000 children will qualify for the allowance, at a cost of about
$1.5 million a year. As I said when I introduced the Bill, the allowance represents the first
positive recognition by the State of the emotional and financial strain on the family caring for
a handicapped child. It has been welcomed by all parents caring for a seriously handicapped
child as well as by the voluntary agencies working in this field.
Clause 29 legislates for the new income test for beneficiaries announced in the Budget.
The purpose of the test is to give beneficiaries greater incentive to help themselves by
supplementing benefit payments. Under the former income test, income up to $17 a week,
or $21 a week for widows and domestic purposes beneficiaries with dependent children, was
disregarded. Income over the allowable income and up to $25 a week reduced the benefit by
$1 for each $2, and income over $25 reduced the benefit by $3 for each $4. The new income
test provides for the allowable income to be increased to $25 a week. Income over $25 and
up to $40 will reduce the benefit by 40c for each $1, and income over $40 will reduce the
benefit by 80c for each $1.
It may be helpful if I illustrate the advantages of the new test by explaining its effect on a
widow with two children, who earns, say, $40 a week over and above her widow's benefit.
Under the former provision this widow would be entitled to an abated widow's benefit of
$64.03 a week. Under the new income test her entitlement will be $71.28 a week-an
increase of $7.25 a week. I think members will agree that this represents a considerable
8--Vol 420


## p. 2845 (#241) ###########################################

23 August
2845
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
improvement in her financial position and that the new test will give positive encouragement
to beneficiaries to supplement their benefits whenever possible, rather than relying on full
benefit plus additional benefit.
Widows and solo parents with dependent children are sometimes discouraged from
working because of the need to meet child-care costs. They find that, because their full
earnings are brought to charge against their benefit, once they have paid child-care costs and
other employment-related expenses they are only slightly better off, or even worse off, than
they would be if they relied solely on their benefit. Clause 31 proposes to improve the
position of those beneficiaries by allowing approved child-care costs of up to $20 a week to
be offset against a widow's or solo parent's earnings in the assessment of her benefit. For
example, if a widow is earning, say, $50 a week and incurring child-care costs of $20 a week,
only $30 of her earnings will be brought to charge in the assessment of her benefit. At
present, her full earnings of $50 a week are brought to charge.
When the Bill was introduced, Opposition speakers strongly criticised clause 16, which
will enable the Social Security Commission to regard as married any person who has entered
into a relationship in the nature of marriage, even though the couple are not legally married.
Under the present wording, the commission is required to establish that the couple are living
together on a domestic basis as husband and wife. Frankly, I do not understand the
Opposition's concern, particularly when it is remembered that the wording of clause 16 is
based on the definitions of "husband” and “Marriage" in sections 27A and 27c of the Act---
sections that were inserted in the principal Act during the term of the former Labour
Government. Those sections clearly set out the entitlement to a domestic purposes benefit,
and the present amendment to section 63 repeats the criteria for domestic purposes benefits.
No one, and I am sure this includes members of the Opposition, would suggest that a
party to a de facto relationship should qualify for a domestic purposes benefit. This would
mean that such couples would be treated more favourably than legally married couples. The
intention, then, is to place de facto couples in exactly the same position of benefit
entitlement as a legally married couple. There is nothing new about this; in fact, it has been
the intention ever since the introduction of the social security system. The Supreme Court
has referred in a recent judgment to the appropriateness of the words "living together on a
domestic basis", and to the lack of consistency between that provision and the definition of
"marriage" in section 27c of the Act. The honourable judge was of the view that, if the
legislation does not reflect the intention of Parliament, an amendment would be needed, and
that is the background to clause 16.
I have been asked to define what is meant by a relationship “in the nature of marriage”.
It is, I submit, not practical or advisable to lay down precise criteria for what is or is not a de
facto relationship. Circumstances can and do vary considerably, and decisions can be made
only by having regard to the particular circumstances of each case. It is not good enough to
say that the man is not supporting the woman and her children and, therefore, they are not
living as man and wife. The mere fact that the woman is receiving a domestic purposes
benefit can obviate any need for the man to contribute towards her support. The ultimate
test is whether the couple have so merged their lives that, to all intents and purposes, they
are no different from a legally married couple. Clause 16 simply makes this intention clear.
Opposition members have also criticised clause 11, which specifically precludes strikers
from receiving unemployment benefit. Again, I do not understand the Opposition's concern.
It has never been intented that the social security scheme should support strikers. The
purpose of the scheme is to provide income support for those, who through no fault of their
own, are unable to support themselves. A worker who has voluntarily withdrawn his labour
can hardly be said to be in this position.
As the Social Security Act is now worded, a grant of unemployment benefit can be
postponed for up to 6 weeks if the applicant has lost his employment by reason of a strike
either by himself, or by fellow members of his union at the same place of employment.
However, if the strike lasts longer than 6 weeks-and there have been two or three recent
examples of this-the people concerned can qualify for, and receive, an unemployment
benefit. As I have explained, this is contrary to the long established policy and intention of
successive Governments. Clause 11 makes the intention clear by specifically precluding these
persons from receiving the unemployment benefit irrespective of the length of the dispute.
I want to stress that the amendment has no application to persons who have been
suspended by their employer as a result of strike action taken by members of another union
at the same place of employment. Strike action by one union can, of course, affect the jobs


## p. 2846 (#242) ###########################################

2846
23 August
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
of members of other unions at the same work place, and an employer may find it necessary
to suspend his operations completely until a settlement is reached. Members of unions not
involved in the dispute, but who are suspended because of strike action, can apply for the
unemployment benefit in the usual way. Clause 11 does not affect the entitlement of these
persons to the benefit.
Clauses 13, 15, 17, and 18 relate to the entitlement of national superannuitants to
supplementary payments, such as telephone and television concessions, child supplements,
and so on. When the Government took office in 1975 the rates of the former age benefit
were $51.26 a week for married couples and $30.75 a week for single persons. The net rates
of national superannuation will be increased to $91.30 and $53.76 a week respectively, from
31 August 1978, when national superannuation becomes 80 percent of the average weekly
wage. This means that, from November 1975 to August 1978, married couples have received
a net increase of $40.04 a week, or about 78 percent. During the same period single people
have received an increase of $23 a week, or 75 percent. They are 75 percent better off since
the National Government took office. For comparative purposes, during the period
December 1975 to June 1978 the consumer price index increased by about 44 percent, which
is the amount by which the age benefit would have been increased if the benefit had been
retained.
These substantial increases were aimed at providing elderly people with a realistic and
dignified retirement income, thereby removing any need for handouts such as the telephone
and television concessions. Most of the superannuitants I have spoken to, or who have
written to me—and many have done so―are in full agreement with the policy. They would
much rather have a realistic basic income during their retirement than have to rely on means-
tested allowances. The Beneficiaries and Pensioners Association is also on record as having
stated that it wanted its members to have a living wage, rather than an age benefit
supplemented by means-tested allowances and concessions. This is exactly what the
Government has provided.
As I have said, when the Government took office the age benefit rates were $51.26 a
week for married couples and $30.75 a week for single persons. The policy of the former
Labour Government was to adjust these rates every 6 months, in line with increases in the
cost of living as measured by the consumer price index. If that policy had been followed, the
rates of the former age benefit would now be $77.28 a week for married couples and $46.37 a
week for single persons. Members will note that the married rate is more than $14 a week
below the net rate of national superannuation for a married couple, and that the single rate is
more than $7 a week below the single rate of national superannuation.
Opposition members are still quibbling over the withdrawal of telephone and television
concessions, the joint value of which is only about $1.65 a week. Superannuitants have had
tremendous increases in their benefits under the National Administration. It may help
Opposition members to place this matter in perspective if I tell them that, in 1975, the value
of the concessions represented 3.2 percent of the married rate of the age benefit. The value
of concessions today is only 1.8 percent of the married net rate of national superannuation,
which clearly shows how much better off beneficiaries are under the present system.
While I am speaking about the concessions I want to set the record straight about the
undertakings in the National Party's 1975 election manifesto. I do this deliberately, for the
benefit of the member for Auckland Central, who distorted what had been set out in the
manifesto when he spoke during the introduction of the Bill. There is no need for him to
shake his head, as his speech is recorded in Hansard for everyone to read. Where is the
Opposition's credibility? The member for Hutt is trying to interject. He can argue the point,
but the member for Auckland Central deliberately set out to mislead the House during the
introduction of the Bill.
I want to quote from the National Party's manifesto, which stated: "All television and
telephone concessions which are currently payable to beneficiaries will continue under
National at the same rates and to the same categories of persons and with the same income
tests as apply under Labour when we take over." The Government has followed that
undertaking to the last letter. The concessions have been continued, subject to the same
income test that applied when we took office. This income test provided for the concessions
to be payable when a superannuitant's income was below $88.20 a week if married, and
$60.80 a week if single. With the substantial increases in national superannuation rates from
31 August 1978, the income of all superannuitants will exceed those limits. Hence the action
taken in the Bill to repeal the concession provisions.

A major concern of the Crippled Children Society and the Society for the

Because of that disability needs constant care and attention; and (c) Is likely to need such
care and attention permanently or for a period exceeding 12 months. (2) In determining . . .
whether a seriously handicapped child needs constant care and attention the Commission
shall consider whether the child requires (a) From another person, frequent attention in
connection with his bodily functions; or (b) Attention and supervision substantially in excess

another person in order to avoid substantial danger to himself or others." The definitions are
the product of considerable discussion between members of the Department of Social
Welfare, the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped, and the Crippled Children
Society.

Section 27A and the others that follow were introduced when the Labour Government
inaugurated the domestic purposes benefit. Section 27A is the interpretation clause that
applies to that domestic purposes benefit, and to no other. It is for that reason that
"husband" is defined as it is, to cover a "de facto" situation as it is called-that is to say, a
settled and something more than a casual relationship that can properly be described in the
words the section uses as being a "relationship in the nature of a marriage". In other words,
that is intended to ensure that one party to a relationship, generally the wife, is not, on its
breaking up, deprived of her right to a domestic purposes benefit simply because the
relationship had not been sanctified by a marriage ceremony. That is what Labour believes,
and that is what the Labour Government did by introducing those amendments to the Social
Security Act when it did.
The Labour Government also recognised—and I make this open concession-that this
state of affairs is susceptible to manipulation because a couple could masquerade as each
being single and entirely separate, although pooling their resources, but otherwise not


## p. 2859 (#255) ###########################################

23 August
2859
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
assuming any of the responsibilities of a marriage, whether legal or de facto. It is for that
reason that section 63 of the principal Act directed the Social Security Commission in respect
of any benefit, not just a domestic purposes benefit, to have regard to whether the two
concerned were living together on a domestic basis as husband and wife. Mr Justice Barker
held that this meant living together under the same roof. With the greatest respect, I believe
that his judgment goes too far. I doubt whether those words justify as narrow an
interpretation as this, but in all events it is clear that the essential question was one of
economics, whether the two were supporting each other, or, more often, whether the man
was contributing to the support of the woman.
The words used in section 27A, the definition clause of the domestic purposes benefit
section, are concerned less with economics than with the social or moral question of whether
the people concerned physically live together as a husband and wife team. That is the test
that the commission must now adopt under the proposed new section 63—not who is
supporting whom, but who is sleeping with whom.
Let us apply that to the case that brought this matter to the attention of the Minister,
who in turn has brought it before the House tonight. In the Furmage case the Director-
General rightly stated to the appeal authority that under the authority of the old section 63,
his department had no right to restrict physical association between the two people
concerned, and that neither of them should have been asked to give undertakings, as they
were asked to give, not to stay together overnight on a regular basis. The amendment now
before the House will reverse that and impose on social welfare officers a duty to inquire into
the sexual habits and practices of each of the individuals concerned.
Hon. H. J. Walker: Read that clause again.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: I have just been reading it; I am doing my best. I know it is
hard to explain to the Minister what his own clause means. It is a Herculean task, but I will
do my best to clear out the stables. Social Welfare officers will have a duty to inquire into the
sexual practices of the couple, and if they conclude that they are such as to be of the nature
of a marriage then they will be obliged to treat the male as the "husband" of the “wife”.

Privilege-Speaker's Ruling
THURSDAY, 24 AUGUST 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
PRIVILEGE-SPEAKER'S RULING
Mr SPEAKER: Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked me to rule whether I
thought that prima facie the member for New Plymouth had committed a breach of
privilege. The Leader of the Opposition contended that, on the basis of a report that had
appeared in that morning's Dominion, privilege had been breached on three counts: first,
that the Petitions Committee had wrongfully delegated to the Government caucus its
responsibility to hear evidence; secondly, that pressure had been brought to bear on
members of the committee; and, thirdly, that the decision and the deliberations of the
committee were disclosed prematurely.
Dealing with those points in that order, I find there was no submission to indicate that
evidence had been heard by the Government caucus, or disclosed to it. Indeed, the Leader
of the Opposition himself claimed that the Government caucus was not in possession of the
petitioner's evidence. In any case, Standing Order 360 permits members of the House to
attend the proceedings of select committees, although they may take no part in them, and
must withdraw when the committee deliberates. Therefore, I think, it would be reasonable
to assume that the Standing Order would permit members to discuss those proceedings
among themselves.
The second point was that pressure had been brought to bear on members of the
committee. According to a newspaper article, the member for New Plymouth had agreed
that pressure had been applied by other Government members and Ministers. The question
then is whether that pressure was proper or improper. The Leader of the Opposition drew
my attention to Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice at pages 136 and 150. I do not consider
that those references are particularly helpful. As far as I know, there was no attempt to
intimidate, to solicit, or to molest members. I think it is stretching the meaning a little far to
suggest that this pressure obstructed or impeded members in the discharge of their duty.
Our own Speakers' Rulings on pages 79 and 80 proscribe the domination of members by
people or bodies outside Parliament. They are silent on attempts of members to exert
influence on their fellows. Obviously, so long as it is not done improperly, in the way I
referred to a moment or two ago, that is part of the normal process by which members are
persuaded to a particular point of view. I cannot uphold the Leader of the Opposition on the
first two of his three counts.
His third point was that the decision and the deliberations of the committee were
disclosed prematurely. Again, the Leader of the Opposition drew my attention to Erskine
May's Parliamentary Practice at page 146. However, we turn to May only for guidance when
our own Standing Orders are silent or unclear. In this case, Standing Order 366 is quite clear.
In essence, it states that a member of a select committee may not divulge, in full or in
summary the proceedings, the evidence, or the report, until the report has been presented to
the House. Were any of these three matters divulged to the Government caucus by the
honourable member for New Plymouth? I have already dealt with the proceedings and the
evidence, so the remaining question to be answered is, was the report, or a summary of it,
divulged to caucus, and if so, was that done in breach of the Standing Orders?
In answering those questions I do not have to decide whether or not there is a breach of
privilege. I have to decide simply whether, on the face of it, there could have been one. The
words attributed to the honourable member for New Plymouth in the newspaper leave some
doubt whether it was the report, or a summary of it, that he was discussing with caucus, or
simply the topic. If it was the latter, there is no problem. If it was the former, then it would
appear to be a breach of Standing Order 366. There is a proviso to that Standing Order
which specifies certain persons to whom the proceedings, evidence, or summary of a select
committee may be divulged confidentially, but this proviso makes no reference to any other
members, except the Speaker. Therefore, by implication it excludes the caucus.
Standing Order 368 (d), to which reference was made in opposition to the claim of a
breach of privilege, permits the chairman of a select committee, in his discretion, to refer any


## p. 2863 (#259) ###########################################

24 August
2863
Privilege-Speaker's Ruling
submission to any person for his comments for the purpose of assisting the committee in its
inquiries. This Standing Order is not, I believe, intended to allow the chairman to take the
decision or the intended report to caucus, but simply to enable him to seek advice at the
inquiry stage. Were it intended to allow matters before a select committee to be referred to
caucus, then obviously it could cover only reference to the Government caucus because the
chairman is the only member so authorised. He is invariably a member of the Government
party.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: No.
Mr SPEAKER: Almost invariably.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Yes.
Mr SPEAKER: Opposition members sometimes chair subcommittees. The Public
Expenditure Committee is usually chaired by a Government member, and in this case the
Petitions Committee was also chaired by a Government member. I have not known the
chairman to be other than a Government member.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: And Mr Speaker.
Mr SPEAKER: Yes, but in this case I am talking about the Petitions Committee.
Members drew to my attention the long-standing custom for Government and Opposition
members of select committees to refer to their caucuses for guidance. Whether or not the
matters before the Petitions Committee were referred to both caucuses on this occasion is
not the point. On the face of it our custom appears to be in conflict with our Standing
Orders.
I am attracted to the words of the honourable member for Henderson, who expressed
regret that the breach of privilege procedure is over-used, and can be invoked to magnify an
incident which, in essence, is of trivial consequence. If I were to base my ruling on the
custom, then I would have to say that prima facie a breach of privilege had not been made
out. But if I am to make my ruling on the basis of the Standing Orders, then it appears to me
that, on the face of it, there could have been a breach of Standing Orders. Since there is this
apparent conflict between custom and rule, I must point out to the House that I do not
consider it is my task to make the rules; it is simply to interpret them. I therefore rule that
prima facie a breach of privilege has been made out.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That the matter be referred to the
Committee of Privileges.
Motion agreed to.

New Zealand Film Commission Bill
NEW ZEALAND FILM COMMISSION BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister for the Arts): I move, That the New Zealand Film
Commission Bill be introduced. It is with real pleasure that I move to introduce the New
Zealand Film Commission Bill that will establish the New Zealand Film Commission as a
permanent statutory body. In its policy statement at the last election the Government
promised to encourage New Zealand small film producers in the production of feature films.
This can be seen as a very important aspect of our policy to develop New Zealand's cultural
identity by actively encouraging New Zealand artists, composers, playwrights, and writers to
use their talents.
Films, more than any other medium, draw upon diverse talents, right across the arts.
For this reason the establishment of a Film Commission must be seen as a major advance in
the development of the arts. I am proud to belong to a Government which, despite difficult
economic conditions, is sufficiently forward looking to establish the commission this year.
The New Zealand Film Commission, to be established under this legislation, will replace the
Interim Film Commission established in November 1977. It was estimated there were 30 to
40 independent film production companies in New Zealand making films, although few
companies could then claim to be well established. Nevertheless, this fledgling industry has
recently been responsible for four successful feature films, as well as many short films for
television and educational purposes. These have provided tangible evidence of the ability,
skill, and artistry of New Zealanders in this field. There was an urgent need to sustain the
momentum of creativity developed by New Zealand film makers. It was vital that the new
spirit in the industry should be nurtured. In its brief life span, the Interim Film Commission
achieved everything I had hoped for.
I want to thank the chairman, Mr Bill Sheat, and members of the interim commission,
particularly Mr David Gascoigne, for their assistance in the preparation of this Bill, paving
the way for the commission to get away to a flying start. The interim commission has already
invested in three feature films, and a television series is in production. A further eight
feature films and one television series are at the scripting, development, and pre-production
stages. The interim commission has provided some marketing assistance, and in the climate
that has been created by its establishment a major international film company, Twentieth
Century Fox, has offered a scholarship to provide training in Hollywood for an employee of
New Zealand's film industry. Therefore, the Bill builds on what has already been achieved to
establish a permanent commission that will continue to expand the activities of the Interim
Film Commission.
The Government has agreed to provide the administrative expenses of the Interim Film
Commission, and will continue to support the New Zealand Film Commission. The New
Zealand Lotteries Board of Control has provided funds for the commission to support film-
making projects by allocating $100,000 last year, and $500,000 this year and for the following
2 years. I want to thank the members of the Lotteries Board of Control, including the
Opposition member for Petone, for this support. I draw to the attention of the House and
the country the great contribution that the board is making to our development in so many
ways.
The New Zealand Film Commission will comprise a chairman, from three to five other
members appointed by the Minister, and the Secretary for Internal Affairs. In general, the
commission will encourage by financial and other means the making, promotion,
distribution, and exhibition of films with a significant New Zealand content. It will also
encourage and promote cohesion within the New Zealand film industry. In particular, it will
promote the exchange of information within the industry, and encourage the efficient use of
available resources. The commission will also encourage and promote the proper
maintenance of films archives.
The Bill provides for the establishment of a fully independent statutory authority with
the necessary collective knowledge and expertise to direct the course of this important new
New Zealand industry. With this encouragement, the industry will bring many benefits-
social, cultural, and economic--and it gives me great pleasure to move that the Bill be
introduced.

making-producers, directors, cameramen, and those engaged in other multifarious

Customs Tariff Classification, Luxury Goods
6. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister of Customs: Is there a customs tariff
classification for luxury goods, and, if so, what goods are included in this category?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The New Zealand customs tariff is
based on the Customs Co-operation Council nomenclature, which provides for the
systematic classification of all goods. In general, the tariff groups together all goods relating
to the same industry, and within this grouping each chapter lists all goods obtained from the
same raw material, arranging them progressively from raw material to the finished products
or articles. The classification of goods is determined according to the tariff's rules of
interpretation, which are designed to ensure that a given product is always classified in the
same tariff item. There is, therefore, no single item in the New Zealand customs tariff under
which all luxury goods can be classified.
Miss Dewe: Does the definition of the word "luxury" present any problems for tariff
classification purposes?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Very definitely yes. A number of categories of items can be
hotly contested, such as cosmetics, cameras, watches, and so on. We cannot restructure the
tariff conveniently into luxury and non-luxury classifications, even if we could agree on what
constitutes luxury.

"Frictional Unemployment"
8. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) to the Minister of Labour: What is the


## p. 2871 (#267) ###########################################

24 August
2871
Questions for Oral Answer
definition of the term "Frictional unemployment" in the New Zealand setting, and what is
the number of persons at present registered as unemployed who come into this category?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): "Frictional unemployment" usually refers
to those workers who are in the process of moving to new jobs that are available. This type of
unemployment arises as job changing is not immediate and there may be a lack of knowledge
by workers that suitable vacancies are available. "Frictional unemployment" therefore
occurs in even the best economic conditions. Statistics that measure "frictional
unemployment" are not collected as such.
Richard Walls: Is this term used in other countries, and what other sectors of the
unemployment force would be comparable?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The term is common throughout the Western World, and some
countries have tried to measure the rate. Other terminology used is "cyclical
unemployment", generally due to economic conditions; "seasonal unemployment" which
will be known to most members; and "structural unemployment", which arises from changes
in an occupational, regional, or industrial mix of vacancies.
Mr Isbey: Would the Minister confirm that the present position in New Zealand would
be called "chronic unemployment"?
Mr SPEAKER: That is seeking an opinion from the Minister.

20. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) to the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the

manpower and productive resources?

migration by occupational categories referred to in the article in the Christchurch Press are
for the net losses of permanent and long-term migrants for the year ended March 1978. I
agree that people in the skilled categories are more likely to be migrants-whether emigrants
or immigrants. The policy the Government is following is to restore the position of the New
Zealand economy in relation to the economies of other countries so that the net loss of
skilled persons will be minimised.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Does the Minister not appreciate the fact that New Zealand can
overcome its economic problems and discourage people from leaving its shores to seek work

Such people do come to New Zealand.

Government re-establish full employment regardless of skills?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: By actively encouraging overseas trade and a restoration of the
economy.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What positive action is being taken to train people without skills to
meet the shortfall of skilled tradesmen?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I cannot answer that question off the top of my head. The
Government has at least six special schemes.
Hon. W. W. Freer: How many people are involved?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I have answered the question about farm work. More than 3000

Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) said that the Labour Opposition would
wholeheartedly support any positive steps that this or any other Government might take to
rapidly expand exports. After 18 months to 2 years' prodding by the Trade Promotion
Council, the Government had announced that 1978 would be Export Year. When Export
Year had been announced, two Ministers had given two different dates for its
commencement. The Manufacturers Federation had stated that senior officials of the
Department of Trade and Industry had been caught unawares by the Government's action.
A Government official had been quoted in the New Zealand Herald of 1 April 1978 as saying
that the department had asked for a 6-months' lead-in time, but that had not been granted.
The campaign had been very expensive, with publication after publication. Although 13
seminars and forums had been held, only one active attempt had been made to increase
exports. He referred to the sales trip to America. Computer figures from the Government
Statistician had shown that when the Labour Government had been in office there had been
an annual increase of 36.6 percent in exports of manufactured goods. However, in January
1978-Export Year-exports had decreased by 13.8 percent from the previous year. In

The figures for total exports were more depressing. In March total exports had
