Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) said he was delighted that the
Labour Opposition had suddenly decided to support any positive steps taken to develop New
Zealand's export industry, especially when a few months previously the Leader of the
Opposition had said the Export Year was a farce. Basically, during Export Year it was hoped
to show the people how absolutely necessary exports were to New Zealand. In 1973-74,
76 000 c.k.d. motorcars had been imported at a cost of $99 million. In 1976, 46 000 c.k.d.
motorcars had been imported at a cost of $122 million. If the same volume of motorcars were
to be imported today, there would have to be a 76 percent increase in the volume of meat
exported. In 1973-74 New Zealand had imported 5 000 000 kg of coffee at a cost of $4
million, and in 1977-78 it had imported 3 000 000 kg of coffee at a cost of $12 million. In
1973-74 New Zealand had imported 3 000 000 kg of cocoa at a cost of $2.7 million, and in
1977-78 it had imported 3 300 000 kg of cocoa at a cost of $17 million. That meant that an
increase in meat exports of 370 percent would be needed to buy the same amount of cocoa.
That was a good reason for the Opposition to get behind Export Year.
Tremendous work had been done by people like Mr Hellaby and members of the
Export Year committee in an attempt to get the message of Export Year through to
management and the people involved in exporting. It was vital that everybody played his
part. He was delighted that at long last the Opposition was about to disown its own leader's
pronunciation that Export Year was a farce.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) said that the increase in the cost of imported items
such as coffee and cocoa had taken place between 1974 and 1976 under a Labour
Government. In those years the increase in the cost of imported items had had an effect on
the consumer price index of about 9 percent. Today that increase was only about 2 percent,
so most of the inflation now was local rather than imported. The reverse had been true under
the Labour Government.
The Government and the Minister had been unable to arrive at any decision about
export incentives. The 1976 Budget had proposed that the Government should take a careful
look at export incentives, but in that year absolutely nothing had happened. The following
year the Government had come out with two principles: that the incentives should be based
on net foreign exchange earnings, and that incentives should be applied to a firm's total
exports rather than to increased exports only. He agreed with that. This year the
Government had commissioned a report, which apparently had just been sent out to
manufacturers for consideration. The need was urgent, because tax relief of more than $100
million had been provided each year to the manufacturing industry. As taxpayers had had to
make good that loss, they were entitled to know whether the Government's incentives were
effective. Most exporters had warranted the export incentives they had received, and the
Labour Government had taken steps to increase them. In his view some manufacturers did
not warrant the incentives, because some of their exports did not add to New Zealand's
export earnings. Some exports created a drain on the country's overseas funds. He agreed
broadly with the criteria in the Government's 1977 Budget. When would the Government
implement its export incentives?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) said that the export
incentives given by the Government had been very successful, and he had been told that they
were the envy of manufacturers in Australia and other countries. The Government had
asked the manufacturers for their views on the new principles that highlighted domestic
content and net foreign exchange earnings. It did not want to change the system without first
getting the considered views of the manufacturers. It was not a delaying tactic. The Labour
Party would have moved without consulting the manufacturers. The present system had
proved its worth, but it the Government could find a better system it would be introduced. It
was up to the manufacturers to assess the two systems.
In the main, manufactured exports had increased under the National Government.

A fear had been expressed by domestic tanners of the effects of export incentives for

reducing the availability of hides for local industry. One disadvantage of export incentives
was that people who were processing for the domestic market had found they must pay the

shoe manufacturers at the expense of the New Zealand tanning industry.

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) said there had been some
considerable delay in achieving a system of incentives based on New Zealand content. Most
members would realise that it was the New Zealand content of the export that earned the
foreign exchange-the remainder of the content had already been paid for with foreign
exchange. The Government, in consultation with the manufacturers, was seeking to
establish a system that would give incentives based on the New Zealand content of the
export. Obviously, such an incentive would reward that which was earning foreign exchange.
However, there were difficulties and the matter was still being discussed with interested
groups. He expected that a new and considerably improved system would result, but he
would not discredit the present incentives, which had been effective.
Incentives had helped to divert resources into exports. Manufacturers were interested
and enthusiastic about exporting, and that had been illustrated by the fact that 110 New
Zealand companies had individual stands and about 180 exporters or producers would
display their products at the Los Angeles fair to be opened in October, the original area of
which had had to be increased by 45 percent because of the interest taken. He was aware of
the impact of incentives upon the tanning industry, and one of the side effects that had
resulted from the introduction of incentives to a processed material that could be further
processed in New Zealand. The conflict over the point at which the incentive became
effective was being investigated, and it was hoped to find a solution.
The Government had tried to encourage the building of boats in New Zealand and the
importation of boats in order to increase the capacity of the fishing industry. A case in which
a New Zealand company had sought to buy a vessel or have one built, and had called tenders
at a time when it had been virtually impossible for the New Zealand builder to comply with
the requirements, was being investigated. That case had reflected the willingness of the
purchaser to give the industry a fair go.

POINT OF ORDER PROCEDURE-STANDING ORDER 172
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I raise a point of order about
Standing Order 172 for your decision rather than for your immediate response. The Standing
Order states that a point of order takes precedence, and I refer to an incident at the closing
of last night's sitting. There is no doubt that the motion that the House do now adjourn can
be debated, but it has become the practice on the Government side that, whenever a
member on this side seeks to use that brief opportunity to bring to your attention matters
that have occurred in the House during the preceding period, a point of order will be raised,
normally on spurious grounds. It is normally designed only to deny the opportunity that is in
the Standing Orders for a member of the Opposition to speak on the motion that the House
do now adjourn.
I suggest that some reconsideration be given to Standing Order 172 to cover any point of
order arising from something that was said in a debate on the adjournment motion. I ask for
your guidance on whether it would be possible to adopt the Australian principle of giving an
immediate ruling. In the Australian House of Representatives it is quite normal for the
Speaker to interrupt a member making a point of order if the Speaker thinks that there is no
relevant point. He normally rules immediately, without hearing any long discussion from the
other members involved. I put those suggestions to you in view of what seems to be
developing an abuse of the Standing Orders of the House.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): It is curious that the member should raise
this, because he has apparently forgotten that exactly the same tactic was used by the
Opposition earlier in the session on a precisely similar occasion. I wanted to make some
comment before 10.30 p.m., at the conclusion of the business of the night, and started to do
so having moved that the House do now adjourn. It is correct, of course, that that motion is
debatable, and this gives the opportunity for the mover and for anyone else to speak in the
time that is available. On this particular night an Opposition member immediately rose to a

House do now adjourn unless I have that arrangement with the Opposition. Acting on those
instructions, that arrangement was made last night, and it was immediately broken by the
Deputy Leader of the Opposition.
This is a matter that we should deal with when we have a Standing Orders Committee
sitting in the next recess, and it is very simple to deal with. We would simply alter the
Standing Orders so that, on days when Mr Speaker comes back into the Chair within a
certain time of the 10.30 p.m. rising, he would automatically adjourn the House, and that
would be the end of the matter. The procedure is now untidy and, this year at least, has led
to some undesirable activity. We should make a Standing Order that tidies up the end of the
sittings when the Chairman at 10.25 p.m. takes steps to bring Mr Speaker back and close the
sitting. That untidy minute or two should be dispensed with, and Mr Speaker should simply
adjourn the House in terms of a new or amended Standing Order.
Last night the procedure should have been tidy, because there was an agreement
between the Whips that there would be no debate. I do not know whether the Deputy
Leader of the Opposition knew that, but he got up, and if he gets up he cannot, under our
Standing Orders, be prevented from speaking. He can be interrupted only by a point of
order.

Mr SPEAKER: I have no difficulty in ruling on the matter now. The point raised by the
Deputy Leader of the Opposition is quite correct. Standing Order 172 allows a point of order
to take precedence, and it is very right and proper that it should do so, because order is
involved. Without order in the Chamber there would be no proper debate. However, every
right a member has must be matched by a duty to use that right responsibly. Hence, as I said
last night, I deplore the habit some members have of raising spurious points of order simply
to interrupt a debate, to delay proceedings, or for some other purpose. Unfortunately,
whoever is in the chair has the difficulty of deciding whether the point of order raised is
spurious, and I cannot do that until I have heard it, because I am not in the mind of the
member raising the point of order. There must be some sort of delay when a point of order is
considered.
Standing Order 41 requires that the Chairman, not only on estimates nights, but
whenever the House is in Committee, shall leave the chair 5 minutes before the time set
down for the end of the sitting of the House. He can then report to me, the Committee
becomes the House again, and we close. The 5 minutes is to allow me to get from my office
to the House, and for the Chairman of Committees to report to me. Even if a report is
slightly longer than usual, there is time for me to put the motion to the House and go through
the formalities. Usually 3 or 4 minutes remain. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the
Minister who moves the adjournment may speak to the motion himself if he wants to, or
another member may do so. It is up to members themselves to decide to what use they will
put the remaining few minutes.
The point of order raised by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition really relates to the

USSR Incorporation of Baltic States
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is it correct that
only two countries in the world—namely, Finland and New Zealand-formally recognise the
Soviet Union's incorporation of the Baltic States, and, if so, on what basis does the New
Zealand Government continue with its recognition?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): It is true that in 1974 the
Labour Governments in New Zealand and Australia formally recognised Soviet jurisdiction
over the Baltic States in public announcements. I believe they were the first Western
countries to take that formal step, but in the Helsinki Declaration of August 1975, made by
33 European countries and also Canada and the United States, the participants undertook to
regard as inviolable all one another's frontiers as well as the frontiers of all States in Europe.
They also undertook to respect the territorial integrity of each of the participating States.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Can the Minister confirm that the Soviet Union was a participant in
the Helsinki Declaration?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes, I can.
Mr Hunt: Then can we take it that it is not correct to say that only two countries in the
world formally recognised the Soviet Union's incorporation of the Baltic States, and that in
fact all 33 countries participating in the Helsinki Declaration did so?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: That is my interpretation of the situation.
Mr Malcolm: Is the Minister not aware that by a process diplomats call expressis verbis
both Canada and the United States have expressly stated that they do not consider that the
Helsinki Declaration in fact applies to the incorporation of the Baltic States by Russia?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: There was acceptance of the territorial status quo in Europe,
without offering any vindication of the ways in which the present situation was achieved.
Mr Hunt: Then we can take it that, despite the expression expressis verbis and no matter
whether one approved or disapproved of previous actions, in fact the territorial integrity of
the 33 States concerned was recognised at the time the Helsinki Declaration was signed?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: As I have already indicated, the Helsinki Declaration stated
that all participants undertook to regard as inviolable all one another's frontiers as well as
the frontiers of all other States in Europe.

Home Budgeting Service
8. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) to the Minister of Social Welfare: When was the

it receiving from the Government?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Household Budgeting Advisory
Committee was established on 21 February 1978 under section 13 of the Department of
Social Welfare Act 1971, and a grant of $50,000 out of the revenue from the additional tax on
alcohol and tobacco has been made available to the committee. The terms of reference of the
committee are: (i) to administer such funds as may be provided from time to time by the

services was held in Wellington last month. Two points were focused on: first, the need for a
national body; and, secondly, appropriate ways of assisting existing budgetary services,
particularly with the $50,000 that has been made available from the tax on alcohol and
tobacco.

payments by about $10 million a month compared with $40 million a month during the last
few months of the Labour Government, and, therefore, is it not correct that his

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It is not correct, because when the Labour Government

Secondary School Nurses
14. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Education: On what basis are
nurses employed by secondary school boards of governors?

Cost of Living
15. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) to the Minister of Statistics: By how much
has the cost of living increased since 31 December 1975?

to the quarter ended 30 June 1978.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that the rate of increase in the cost of living under
the National Government will exceed that under the Labour Government if the present rate
of inflation continues, notwithstanding the significant reduction in import prices?

drop in the rate of increase in the consumer price index, from 16.9 percent in our first year to
14.4 percent in our second year, equivalent on the basis of the latest quarterly consumer
price index to an annual rate of increase of 10.8 percent for 1978.
Mr W. R. Austin: Can the Minister confirm that during this same period, while the cost
of living was rising by 39 percent, wages went up to a higher rate?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Wages were a factor, as were the ripple effects of increased oil
prices and a number of other factors.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that the increase in the cost of living over the past
12 months has been 12.2 percent, in spite of a reduction of 7 percent in the cost of imports?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The most acceptable measure for this is the quarterly price
index figures, and on that rate it is equivalent to a 10.8 percent increase, which represents a
marked improvement.

Baby Food Price Increases
20. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: How does
he explain the fact that under the supervision of his department the price of a 135g can of

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The price has
increased from 15c to 23c-not 24c-an increase of 53 percent over the past 3 years. The
manufacturer has been authorised to increase his price only to the extent necessary to
recover his increased costs and to obtain a reasonable profit margin. Wholesalers and
retailers are not permitted to increase their percentage margins.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What was the basis of the increased costs allowed by the
department?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I do not have the basis but I could obtain it from the
pricing authority. The honourable member knows that the pricing authority is the Secretary
of Trade and Industry. He has statutory authority and the Minister does not interfere with
his decisions. If the honourable gentleman puts down a question about the basis I will supply
the information if it is not confidential to the company.
Housing Corporation's Valuation Structure
21. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Housing: Is it correct that the Housing
Corporation has altered its valuation structure from the average square metre cost as the
value of the house, to the average of the price of houses sold in the area?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): No, the Housing Corporation's valuing
staff has not altered its valuation structure. Valuing is a subjective assessment based, among
many things, on the average square metre cost, the average price of houses sold in the area,
and the buoyancy of the market. When assessing the viability of a building proposition,
corporation valuers have always been required to assess the current market value at the time
of inspection and make a recommendation to the management on the market price, the
recommended loan, term, and other related matters. There are various tools the valuer can
use in this approach, of which average square metre cost is one, but ultimately the valuation
must be reconciled to the market worth of the property.
ADOPTION AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Adoption
Amendment Bill. I thank Mr Dave McGee and Caroline Rennie for the assistance they have

In May of this year a group of residents of Avondale made submissions to me about the
Adoption Act. I have researched the matter in great depth and talked about the legal and
social points with a number of my friends. I contacted the group and said I would ask a
question in Parliament about whether the Government would change the Adoption Act this
year, and, failing that, I was prepared to introduce a private member's Bill. I asked the
question and received a reply from the Minister on 24 May 1978.
Hon. David Thomson: On 26 May.
Mr HUNT: The Minister's reply is dated 24 May, but the reply was printed in Hansard

check it. I showed it last evening to the member for Birkenhead, as chairman of the Statutes


## p. 2905 (#301) ###########################################

25 August
2905
Adoption Amendment Bill
Revision Committee, and to the Minister of Justice.
The Bill consists of three essential clauses, and proposes to amend the Adoption Act
1955 to provide relatively limited and carefully controlled access to adoption records by a
birth parent and an adoptive parent, or an adopted person of 18 years of age or over.
Applications for such an inspection would be made through the courts, and, before
considering the case, a social worker would be required to provide a report to the court. If
the court was satisfied-and I quote from the Bill-that "having regard to all the
circumstances of the case no serious harm or injury is likely to result to any other person", it
could order that the records, or part of the records, be made available to the applicant.
The Bill is modelled on English law-and I should point out that Scotland has had a
similar law since 1930-and is intended to meet the needs of those involved in adoption,
particularly adopted people who, on reaching the age of 18—and I stress that age, as they are
then adults and entitled to vote-are for one reason or another keen to find out more about
their biological parents. The Bill has been carefully framed to make sure that such
information would be released only under very careful control, which would exclude the
possibility of frivolous or casual inquiry.
If I had to take a starting point—and I was persuaded by many of my friends and the
deputation that the need for the Bill was sound-it is perhaps the question I kept asking
myself: should a person be barred for life from knowing the truth about his origins? I think
the answer to that question, for many reasons that we do not have to go into, could well be,
while he is a child. However, the answer should surely be no once that child attains the age of
18 and assumes adulthood.
From the statistics I have examined, about 90 000 adoptees were in New Zealand in
1977. That figure takes into account the distribution curve and death rates, together with
Maori and European adoptees before 1962 and immigrant adoptees. The exact figure is not
given. According to the report released in Great Britain on the operation of the 1975 Act
from 1 January 1977 to 31 March 1978, about 1 percent of adoptees in Great Britain applied
for and received data about their origins. I should stress that in this period not one complaint
was received from any natural mother about unwanted invasion of her privacy by her
adopted offspring.
The Bill does involve an appropriation, especially under the proposed new section 23A
(10) in clause 3 in which I indicate that the fees and expenses of a barrister or solicitor shall
be paid out of the Consolidated Account; in other words, legal aid is to be provided. An
appropriation would also be involved in so far as a social worker could be asked by the court
to investigate an application. I am trying to tidy up a most unsatisfactory situation and to
provide an orderly and proper way of ensuring that those people, who, when they become
adults, are determined, no matter what, to find out about their origins if they know they are
adopted, are given a method of making some inquiries that will prevent all sorts of sudden
and unexpected emotional shocks, not just to the people they confront, but to those doing
the searching.
Since I announced my intention to introduce the Bill, about 25 people have written to
me relating their experiences when they have inquired about their natural parents. All of
them support the introduction of the Bill, and all have said that, if they could have presented
their request to a court, and the court had examined the case and perhaps recommended that
no further data be given based on the evidence available, or had been prepared to release
some information to them, that would have been much better and more logical.
The present law is so complicated that, as the Auckland District Law Society members
who recently spoke to a group of Labour MPs said, the Act means that there is some doubt
about solicitors' funds, because the society is of the opinion that, whatever the merits of
giving greater rights of disclosure of information to adopted children, the apparent intention
of the legislation is now being bypassed because, although court records may not be
examined, the contents of solicitors' records and files can, under the law, be disclosed. In
other words, two procedures are at present open: one which does not allow disclosure, and
one, which, in the opinion of the Auckland District Law Society-and I stress that it is only
its opinion-is unfair. I agree that, on that ground alone, the Act should be cleared up.
I conclude my general remarks by quoting from a very interesting recent study in 1967
by McWhinney, who did research on adult adoptees. Two sentences are worth repeating:
"Adopted children want factual information about their biological parents and about why
and how they were adopted out."; and, "Interest in their biological parents arose mainly
from the desire not to be without genetic descendants, but also, on entering into marriage.

The overriding idea behind the introduction of the Bill is to have it referred to a select

hope, for the Government next year—whichever Government it might be—to bring down
legislation that would include matters other than the one I have cited. However, I believe

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): First, may I thank the member for New
Lynn for the courtesy of giving me an early look at his Bill: he gave me a typescript of it last
night. The Government considers that any move to disturb the fundamental principles of the
Adoption Act should not be treated lightly; they have been of great concern to society for a
very long time. The central concern, particularly section 23, which the member for New
Lynn proposes to amend, is the privacy of the individual within the family.
In my opinion, and also that of the Government, that privacy must not be lightly
disturbed. As the member for New Lynn indicated, he asked on 26 May: “Will the Minister
of Justice be introducing an amendment to section 23 of the Adoption Act this year, and if
not, why not?" I replied: "The answer to the honourable member's question is that the
Government will not introduce an amendment to section 23 of the Adoption Act 1955 this
year. The question of access to adoption records is clearly contentious. The Government
therefore intends to give careful scrutiny to all points of view in the community before
determining its policy on the matter." The present law protects the privacy, not only of the
adopted child and its natural parents, but also of the adoptive parents. It is not just a case of
one person; it is a case of at least five people, because there are other members of the
adoptive family to be considered.
The Government considers the character of the family and the protection accorded to
the family by our statutory laws to be of the greatest importance to the whole of our society.
The Government considers that the family is the essence of society, and, to support and
protect it, everything that the law can do ought to be done. The law should not lightly be
disturbed. I ask the member introducing the Bill, what is the benefit of disturbing the present
provision for privacy, and to whom will the benefit go? Is it a benefit that will do mischief to
no one? The member has indicated that his Bill will empower the court to determine that to
some extent. His provisions do not go as wide as they should if the House decides to follow
the ideas he has put forward.
As a matter of importance the Government holds that all children should be brought up
within a family, having a father and a mother. For fatherless or motherless children adoption
is most desirable; indeed, that is the view of society. For married people who, unfortunately,
are unable to have children, it is generally a matter of joy for most of their acquaintances
when they are able to have a family. The law says that the privacy of those parents and the
privacy of the adopted child should be very carefully protected. I mention these points to
indicate that the proposal brought by the member for New Lynn is not one that should in any
way be taken lightly.
I quote from a recent letter from me to the Auckland District Law Society: "It is likely
that a decision will be taken next year on whether section 23 should be examined in isolation
or in the context of a general review of the Adoption Act." The Adoption Act is a statute we
inherited from the English jurisdiction, and consolidated in 1908. It has been amended a
number of times, particularly between 1936 and about 1953, and then consolidated again in
1955. It has been amended again since then, but on first sight the Act does not seem to have
so many amendments, or such confusing amendments, as to require immediate review and
consolidation. I have indicated in my response to inquiries that we are working in this
general area, and on other statutes of long standing. It is a very proper job for the Minister of
Justice and his department to update the law in keeping with changing social attitudes. How
far have the attitudes of society changed? There certainly has been some interest.
An organisation has been formed calling itself Jigsaw, a name chosen, possibly, because
of the element of identification in it-the identification of parts of the whole. I doubt that the
name was chosen because of entertainment value, or-although this could be argued—
because people wanted to disturb privacy out of curiosity. The organisation has some
support, although by no means widespread support. No doubt its members comprise many
people who are adopted, or who are parents of adopted children.
I do not propose to say more, except to summarise. The Government is very concerned
with the family and individuals within the family as the basic element of our social structure.
It is concerned that, as far as it can, the law should support and protect the individual and the

FENCING BILL
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Committee
to present the report of the committee on the Fencing Bill. The committee recommends that
the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
Because this Bill is also a consolidation of various Acts passed since 1908 there are a
number of consequential amendments by way of rewording and redrafting. There are also
other changes. One of the major changes relates to clause 2, which includes a new
description of "work” and “work on a fence" to include the cost of surveying necessary to
determine any boundary line.
Clause 3, under which the provisions apply to Crown land and refer to the Crown being
bound by any agreement, has been amended to state that, "nothing in this Act shall apply in
respect of roads, land forming part of a national park under the National Parks Act 1952,
land taken pursuant to section 45 of the Government Railway Act 1949 or the corresponding
provisions in earlier Acts in respect of land still held for railway purposes and Crown land
reserved for sale or other disposition pursuant to section 58 of the Lands Act 1948 and land
reserved pursuant to section 29 of the Counties Amendment Act 1961."
Clause 6, which deals with registered fencing covenants, has been struck out and
replaced with a provision for a court order, when and if required. The committee considered
that, instead of a covenant against the land, some responsibility should rest with the occupier
who would not be a tenant in the normal way-as, for example, a house tenant would be—
but an occupier of 10 years or more. Those are the major amendments, as well as the
consequential ones I mentioned earlier.
Motion agreed to.
SECURITIES ADVERTISING BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Securities Advertising Bill and Supplementary Order
Paper 9. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I
move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The committee tenders a report indicating the major changes recommended to the Bill.
I do not intend to discuss the Bill in any detail, but merely to indicate the major changes
recommended by the committee. First: in the form in which it was originally introduced, the
Bill made no provision for the establishment of a Securities Commission. As a result of the
select committee's subsequent consideration of Supplementary Order Paper 9, it
recommends that the concept of a Securities Commission be incorporated into the Bill.
Secondly: it was clear to the select committee that many of the detailed requirements
relating to issues contained in the original Bill-particularly those setting out the required
form of prospectuses and trust deeds--would have created substantial problems in particular
cases. The general acceptability of the proposal to establish a Securities Commission,
combined with the adaptability and flexibility of the commission concept, leads us now to
recommend that many of the detailed requirements relating to issues-particularly those
setting out the contents of and details of registration of prospectuses and deeds-be deleted
from the Bill, and that, instead, provision be made for these to be dealt with by regulations
made by the Executive Council, but only on the recommendation of the Securities
Commission, such recommendation to be made after consultation with interested bodies and


## p. 2913 (#309) ###########################################

25 August
2913
Securities Advertising Bill
after notice in the Gazette.
Thirdly: the committee recommends that the request for exemption from the provisions
of the Bill made by a number of fund-raising bodies be left to the commission, either to grant
a complete or partial exemption or to formulate whatever modest disclosure requirements it
considers appropriate in each case.
Fourthly: the committee recommends that the provisions of the Bill relating to
contributory mortgages—a previously unregulated area that has, in the past, been the cause
of some concern-be amended so that all the requirements relating to the management of
such schemes be deleted from the Bill, and that regulations, again made on the
recommendation of the Securities Commission, should prescribe the obligation of the
managers of such schemes, including the very limited number of solicitors involved in the
public solicitation of funds. The committee expects that the requirements to be laid down by
the commission for the management of such funds would closely resemble those at present
prescribed for the conduct of solicitors' nominee contributory mortgages.
Fifthly: originally the Bill contained a provision exempting bills of exchange, other than
"in house" bills, from control under the Bill. Because the bills market is undergoing rapid
development the committee recommends that it would be more appropriate for the
Securities Commission, rather than the statute, to determine whether or not an exemption
should be granted in each particular case.
Sixthly: one of the more important and difficult provisions of the Bill-clause 3-sets
out the legal tests for determining whether or not an offer of securities has been made "to the
public". The committee recommends that subclause (1) and (2) of that clause should
establish the "boundaries" within which an offer may or may not be deemed to have been
made to "the public”, and that the remainder of the clause should set out a series of “sub-
rules" to clarify that definition even further. Committee members realise that, in the form
now recommended, the clause will include a number of transactions that might otherwise be
regarded as essentially private in character; particularly offers to existing shareholders of a
company, and offers made, say, by a finance company to maturing debenture holders to
"roll over" their investments by reinvesting the funds in a newer debenture issue. However,
we envisage that in such cases the commission will be able to grant widespread exemptions
from the full disclosure requirements of the Act, thereby avoiding any unnecessary
inconvenience for both the borrower and the lender.
Seventhly: the committee recommends the removal from the Bill of the concept of
temporary custodian, which is considered to be both unnecessary for the protection of
investors and onerous on the issuers of securities.
Eighthly: we recommend a widened definition of superannuation schemes, which are
exempt from the provisions of the Bill, to cover effectively all such schemes other than those
sold to the general public.
Ninthly: the original Bill prevented the use of a prospectus for more than 6 months after
its date of issue. While the committee believes that investors are entitled to information that
is as up to date as possible, it recognises that the original requirement would have imposed a
cost and administrative burden on some issuers-particularly large trading companies—that
would not have been justified in all the circumstances. The committee, therefore,
recommends that the life of a prospectus should be extended to 9 months from the last
balance date, rather than 6 months from the date of the actual prospectus. Thus, the earlier
that a prospectus is prepared and issued after the date of the company's accounts, the longer
will be the time it can be used as the basis of the issue.
Finally, the committee spent some time considering a possible amendment to clause 40,
which in its existing form would have given rights of action against the directors and principal
officers of an issuer in respect of any loss sustained by a subsequent purchaser of securities—
for example, shares-who could show that he had relied upon the prospectus rather than,
say, upon a stock exchange quote as to the value of the shares when purchasing the
securities. The committee decided against any recommendation in respect of such a clause,
but has outlined the proposed provision in an appendix to its written report, for
consideration for possible inclusion in the Bill before it is passed.
The Bill received the closest possible scrutiny by the committee. It was introduced in
December last year and attracted 72 submissions, 32 of which were heard, and a further 22, 3
of which were heard, on the Supplementary Order Paper. Committee members believe that
the end result of this extensive public involvement—and the committee's detailed
deliberations will be legislation that ensures the availability to the investor of adequate, up-


## p. 2914 (#310) ###########################################

2914
25 August
Securities Advertising Bill
to-date, and accurate information on which to base an investment decision; but legislation
that is, at the same time, sufficiently flexible to adapt to the particular needs of the
commercial community in different types of transactions. This adaptability and flexibility
will be achieved largely by the incorporation into the structure of the Bill of the Securities
Commission-a broad-based body that has the confidence of the commercial community.
The committee has been greatly assisted in all its work, by the officials from the commercial

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 23 August 1978
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): When the House adjourned on Wednesday I was discussing clause
16, the provision that alters the definition of a de facto relationship. The member for
Henderson had expressed the view that Mr Justice Barker had gone too far in interpreting
the words "on a domestic basis”. The member for Henderson said that on this occasion he
did not agree with the learned judge. I suggest that that disagreement is the reason he
opposed the change in the law. If one accepts that the learned judge was correct in his
interpretation—and it would be quite normal to accept that a respected Supreme Court
judge is correct in his interpretation- I submit that we have no option but to change the law,
which, as interpreted at present, is clearly unsatisfactory.
The member for Henderson claimed that the judgment in the Furmage case dealt only
with the facts of the particular case. That is absolute nonsense. The judge in the Furmage
case considered a question of pure law. In the case stated the facts were set out. Although
the facts are provided in summary form in the judgment, a question of law was posed to the
judge. The question is set out in the judgment, and it is ultimately answered on page 10. I
shall quote the manner in which the question is answered. His Honour has said the question
is answered not in its exact terms, but in the following way: "The relationship contemplated
by section 63B of the Act is a relationship which need not necessarily contain all the elements
of consortium, but in which one element of consortium, that is, living under the one roof, is
stressed by the words 'on a domestic basis'." That is the ratio decidendi of the case, and the
question the judge decided. It has no reference to the specific facts of the Furmage case. The
Furmage case may well be decided in precisely the same way after the change in the law.
There is no way that any member of the House can express an opinion about that. The
amendment is brought about by the words of the learned judge, and an interpretation, which
clearly establishes that the Act does not actually state what Parliament intended it to state
when the law was enacted.
In relation to that I refer to the judgment, where on pages 9 and 10 Mr Justice Barker
states: "I cannot treat as otiose the words in section 63B 'on a domestic basis'. They may well
restrict a de facto relationship for the purpose of that section only to those de facto
relationships where the parties live under the same roof. If that is not what Parliament
intended then a statutory amendment will be needed to fulfil that intention. I am bound by
the clear wording of the section." It is perfectly clear that the judge was drawing to the
attention of Parliament the fact that it seemed to have said something it did not intend. I
believe it is quite clear that when the Labour Government brought forward this provision in
1973 it was not its intention to say that people who live under the same roof are de factos,
and that people who do not live under the same roof are not. It would lead to all sorts of
absurd relationships including those between members of the same sex being regarded as de
factos purely because they live under the same roof. It would lead also to parties who are
legally married being regarded as not having a relationship as close as a de facto relationship,
merely because they do not live under the same roof. To bring the whole question of whether
or not a couple are in a de facto relationship down to that of a material structure-a roof—is
clearly absurd. The judge himself thought it was absurd, but found himself bound to come to
that conclusion. The words proposed in the Bill are the same as those adopted by the Labour
Government in section 27 of the present Act.
The member for Henderson stressed the difference between section 27 and section 61,
and in doing so stressed the difference between the two parties. He told us that Labour had
legislated to exclude from a domestic purposes benefit a woman who was receiving support
from her partner. The National Government proposes to extend the exclusion to those who
should be receiving support from their partner. This is the nexus between the two parties--


## p. 2918 (#314) ###########################################

2918
25 August
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
the crunch issue that the House should be addressing itself to in any debate on this clause.
Should we remove the domestic purposes benefit only when the husband in a de facto
relationship is actually supporting, or when the husband in such a relationship should be
supporting? The proposed wording relates only to relationships that are "in the nature of
marriage". We are speaking about what is referred to in common parlance as a de facto
relationship. If the couple are living as man and wife, it is difficult to see why the question of
whether he should support his wife should depend entirely upon whether or not they have a
marriage certificate. I believe that my constituents would accept that their tax moneys could
properly be used to support a woman who has no partner to support her and who cannot
reasonably be expected to support herself, probably because she has children of such an age
that she would be unable to enter the work force. I do not believe that my constituents would
accept that their tax money ought to be used to support a woman whose partner does not
choose to support her, not because she is unable to be supported, but because there has been
a voluntary decision between those two parties that he will not support the woman with
whom he has a relationship in the nature of marriage. If the couple were married, the
husband would have an absolute legal obligation to support his wife. We will find ourselves
in a position whereby the taxpayers are underwriting a de facto relationship but not a legal
marriage. That is a clear disincentive for parties to enter into a legal marriage. Two persons
living together and both free to marry, with one receiving a domestic purposes benefit of
about $75 a week, could go to the Registry Office and regularise their marriage, only to find
that the Government takes that $75 away from them. Surely that would be an indication that
the Government is saying, "Don't marry. A monetary penalty will be imposed if you do."
That is not the type of situation that the House, which has so often expressed its support for
stable family units, ought to adopt.
The Labour test of, "Is the man providing financial support?", is totally inappropriate.
If the woman has the domestic purposes benefit her partner will not be supplying her with
financial support because she does not need it; she is already receiving it. The law provides a
disincentive for him not to give her financial support, and the taxpayer carries the burden.
This situation is self-perpetuating. When it is decided, after looking at the matter, that the
man is not supporting the woman, the reason is because she is receiving the benefit, and the
reason she is receiving the benefit is because he is not supporting her. If we accepted the
Labour test, that would carry on indefinitely. Once it is accepted that a de facto husband
should support his partner, there is an obligation to ensure that there are no blatant
loopholes for those seeking to abuse the system. The Furmage judgment pointed out one
obvious loophole-the requirement to maintain a separate residence. That need not be a
particularly expensive undertaking. Perhaps it could be a bedroom in a shared flat other than
where the other partner is living. That would suffice to argue that the couple were living not
under one roof, but two. It may be argued that they live under one roof most of the time, but
on the interpretation of Mr Justice Barker it was open to argument that if they were not
constantly living together under one roof and there was an occasional break, they would not
be regarded as being a de facto couple. It is nonsense to claim, as the Labour Opposition
has, that this is a "chastity belt" clause.
The Opposition also claimed that the clause was designed to promote promiscuity.
Members opposite like to have it both ways, and that is so on this occasion. They have taken
both positions: that it promotes sexual promiscuity, and that it prevents women from
indulging in any sexual activity whatever. They are ignoring the words used in the section—
"a couple in a relationship in the nature of marriage". A relationship in the nature of
marriage could scarcely be built upon a relationship that consists of nothing other than a
stable, or otherwise, sexual relationship.
Government members were taken to task for saying that the amendment was suggested
by Mr Justice Barker. Perhaps he did not say so in quite so many words, but about four
different statements in his judgment make it quite clear that he thought the law he was
interpreting was a strange law, and that something should be done about it. I refer
particularly to the foot of page 3 of his judgment where he states: "Whether the same
concept"--and he is referring to section 27-"was sought to be interpreted by this definition
as is covered by section 63, is unclear. I comment in passing that it is a pity that if the same
concept was sought to be covered, the same Act did not have consistent definitions." I think
that is about as close as a Supreme Court judge would come to inviting the Legislature to put
its House in order and adopt consistent definitions. That is precisely what the new clause 16
does. It has the same wording as that of section 27-words that were supplied by the Labour


## p. 2919 (#315) ###########################################

25 August
2919
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Government when it was in office in 1973.
The Government has an obligation to protect public funds. The domestic purposes
benefit is a good benefit, and has been in existence since 1972, when about $7 million was
provided. Today, $130 million is provided. Those figures clearly indicate that the
Government must closely peruse the legislation and its administration to ensure that it is not
being ripped off. If it is not being ripped off, those receiving the benefit who quality for it will
be entitled to retain it. There has been a clear willingness on the part of the Government not
only to retain the benefit, but also to build it up. As I said, when public funds are involved,
the Government has a clear obligation to ensure that they are properly spent. The

beneficiaries, and, indeed, other beneficiaries, allowing them to earn $25 a week without it
affecting their benefits. Under Labour they were entitled to earn only $17 a week, and they
lost three-quarters above that. In this instance they will lose only one-quarter. This is a

I refer members to the National Government's action in 1951, when it established the
special assistance fund, and to the Labour Government's action in 1975, when it established
the additional benefit scheme. I draw attention to the survey of the needs of the aged that
gave rise to the 1975 legislation. The findings of that survey can be summarised as follows.
First, there were greater hardships among age beneficiaries than among those receiving
universal superannuation, because people receiving age benefits were subject to a means
test, and in most cases those on universal superannuation had other income, so it was simply
total income that decided whether there was hardship among the elderly. Secondly,
supplementary assistance was not fulfilling the needs of those in hardship-many were
reluctant to apply for it, and the way in which it was administered, the delays, and so on, did
not always meet the case. Thirdly, the level of assistance, even with the advantage of
administration locally rather than nationally, was rarely uniform, and many anomalies
resulted from the scheme. As a result, the additional benefit was brought in.

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Industrial Awards-Delays in Printing
1. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Labour: Can he confirm that
awards registered as long ago as March have been printed and distributed by his department
only in the last 2 to 3 weeks, and can he indicate the average time lapse between the
registering and printing of awards (a) at present, and (b) last year?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. "During March 1978 the Industrial Commission registered 50 awards and collective
agreements. Within 10 days, advance copies of these documents were available in the district
offices of the Department of Labour. Final printed copies of these documents were
distributed as follows: during June 1978, 4 documents; during July 1978, 9 documents;
during August 1978, 24 documents; and not yet distributed, 13 documents. Of the 13 that
have not yet been distributed 10 are at present with the Government Printer for final print, 2
are with the Government Printer awaiting page proofs, and 1 is with my department for
proof reading. The average time lapse between the registration and the printing of awards is
currently 4 months, and last year it was 5 months."
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Are steps being taken to try to shorten the time lapse?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I believe so. Indeed, there has been an improvement of
about 11 percent on last year, and advance copies are now available within 10 days of the
registration of the awards and collective agreements.
Botulism
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Health: Has the toxic strain of
Clostridium botulinum ever been recorded in foods in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The toxic strain of Clostridium botulinum has
never been isolated in food offered for sale in New Zealand.
Electoral Rolls-Notification of Alterations
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: In view of his answer to my
question about notification of marriages, etc., by the Registrar of Births, Deaths, and
Marriages to the Chief Electoral Officer, can he say how many notices were actually sent in
each of the last 8 months?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): No detailed statistics are kept of the
number of notifications of deaths or marriages received by the Chief Electoral Officer from
registrars of births, deaths, and marriages. All notifications of death received by the Chief
Electoral Officer by 26 July have been actioned, and the appropriate entries deleted from
the main electoral rolls. Something in excess of 48 000 entries have been deleted since
January 1977. I am unable to give any accurate assessment of the number of changes of name
arising from marriages that have been actioned over the same period.

boundaries were gazetted?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Whether the 48 000 names were deleted from the rolls

activities in the regions.

State Advocacy Service
5. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: When does he propose to set up
the State advocacy service, and can he indicate (i) what service will be provided, and (ii) the
estimated cost of setting up the service?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. "The Industrial Relations Amendment Act 1976 (No.2) provided only that the
Minister of Labour may require a ballot of workers bound by an award or collective
agreement to determine whether or not they wish an unqualified preference provision to be

Education-Curriculum Development Unit
6. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Education: What is the total
number employed in the curriculum development unit, and is the manning of the unit subject
to the application of the sinking lid?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The total number employed in what was
formerly the curriculum development unit is 27. There is no separate staff ceiling for the
unit. It simply forms part of the department's total staff ceiling, which is subject to the
sinking lid.
Mr Hunt: By how much has the lid sunk from the 27 who formed the unit when it was
established?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I pointed out in my reply that there is no separate staff ceiling for
the curriculum unit, and therefore it is not in itself subject to the sinking-lid policy.
Mr Wellington: I assume that it is the director-general's prerogative to deploy staffing
resources within the department as he sees fit, and that therefore the curriculum
development unit may not necessarily be subject to any staffing reduction?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes, that is correct. It is possible for one part of the department
to have an increased staffing, provided the total staff within the whole department is subject
to the sinking-lid policy.
Mr Hunt: What is the total strength of the curriculum development unit today compared
with the number of staff in the unit at this time last year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I cannot tell the member exactly how many were employed in
the unit at this time last year, but I can tell him that at some time in the past the curriculum
unit had an establishment of 36 as against the present 27. In fact, there has been a
reorganisation within the department, so that the directorate under which the curriculum
development unit comes also covers the resources development section, the publications
branch, the National Film Library, the visual production unit, and the officers responsible
for libraries and the audio-visual media; so that there has been a spread of responsibility.
Mr Hunt: On which dictionary does the Minister base his definition of the words
"sinking lid" to mean "reorganisation"? I ask that question because the curriculum
development unit has suffered a cut of 25 percent in its staff numbers.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I thought I had explained to the member that the director-
general has the discretion of deciding where staff reductions will be made, and he makes his
decisions with a view to ensuring the most efficient service possible is rendered by the
department.

Botulism
8. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen the recent
statement by the New Zealand Alliance of Freshwater Anglers, reported in the Dominion of
21 August, in which it is alleged that there is a link between trout farming and botulism, and
can he confirm that botulism is in fact a rare type of food poisoning caused by a toxin arising
from the presence in improperly preserved foods of Clostridium botulinum, and that
therefore the origin of the trout would have much less to do with the incidence of the disease
than would the preparation of the fishmeat?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have read the report referred to. Botulism is
indeed a rare type of food poisoning and, as I said in reply to an earlier question today, has
never been isolated in food offered for sale in New Zealand. The incidence of botulism has
little to do with the origin of the trout, but depends on the manner in which the trout is
prepared for human consumption.
Mr Hunt: Is the Minister aware that the bacteria concerned are not killed by the
sterilisation process at present undertaken?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I am not aware of that. I have very little knowledge of the
technical details. If the member wants to ask a question of that nature, and believes he would
be able to understand the answer given, I suggest that he submit his question in writing.
Mr Hunt: As the recent outbreak of botulism was caused by a faulty can, can the
Minister give an assurance that the canning process in New Zealand is up to standard?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot assure the House that we will never have faulty cans in New
Zealand.
Mr Hunt: How do New Zealand statistics on death from food poisoning compare with
those of overseas countries?
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: That is not relevant to the question.
Housing Corporation Loans-Criteria
9. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Housing: Is it correct that he has asked the
Housing Corporation to use stricter criteria when granting loans for the purchase of existing
houses by disqualifying families with two children who are at present eligible to capitalise the
family benefit, and, if so, why is this being done?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Yes, I can confirm that the criteria
applying to the granting of loans to purchase existing homes have been altered to the extent
that only families with three or more children whether or not they are able to capitalise the
family benefit, now qualify. The change has been made to ensure that the Housing
Corporation is able to keep its lending to the funds available. In the same announcement to
which the honourable member refers, funds were made available for an estimated 1500 extra
purchase loans.
Mr Isbey: Will there by any variation of the rules for families with two children in cases
of extreme hardship.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The corporation regards the rules as guidelines. Clearly,
exceptional rulings will have to be made if there are exceptional circumstances. The
corporation will consider any such circumstances.
Mr Hunt: Will a person with two children who had lodged an application before the
rules were changed, receive the same consideration under the former rules, and with the
same chance of success?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: If a person has applied to the Housing Corporation and has a
family benefit capitalisation certificate that was issued before the announcement was made,
that person will receive the same consideration he or she would have received before the
announcement was made.

Steel Price Comparisons
10. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the Minister of
Trade and Industry: How does the price of New Zealand steel compare with the f.o.b. price
of Japanese, Australian, and Canadian steel of similar grades?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The current f.o.b.
prices required to answer the honourable member's question are not available, because
there are negligible imports of products within the New Zealand range of production.
Furthermore, many overseas steel companies are at present reluctant to quote in view of the
steadily rising overseas prices. However, with respect to Australia, in the long term prices
are generally comparable with those of New Zealand for a similar or equivalent product.
With respect to Japan, prices would in most cases be lower, owing, first, to the economies of
scale and, secondly, to exported steel having a separate and usually lower price than current
domestic value. No information is available on the Canadian steel industry, as that country
has never been a significant supplier on the New Zealand market.

National Superannuation Payment System
15. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth), on behalf of Mr BRILL (Kapiti), to the
Minister of Social Welfare: Will the new system of payment of national superannuation be
confined to vouchers drawn on the Post Office Savings Bank, and, if so, why has the system
not been extended to trustee and private savings banks?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The new method of payment for
national superannuitants, to be effective from 24 October 1978, is being introduced solely to
replace the present cash payment arrangements. As 90 percent of those national
superannuitants who receive payment by way of payment orders through the mail already
receive cash orders at a post office, the new system is designed to take advantage of the on-
line computer facilities of the Post Office. National superannuitants already have the
opportunity to have their national superannuation credited directly to a trading bank or
trustee savings bank account, and this service will be continued.

estimates?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Statistics): The total productivity
performance of the labour force as measured by the index of real gross domestic product per
labour force member-expressed as annual percentage changes over the previous March
years-is as follows: year ended March 1973, +3.1 percent; 1974, +3.4 percent; 1975, +1.4
percent; 1976, +0.8 percent; 1977, +0.7 percent; 1978, +2 percent; and in 1979, +0.3
percent. The last 2 years' figures are based on NZIER estimates of gross domestic products.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The department assures me that it is extremely difficult to
isolate particular reasons for the drops and rises in these figures. A large number of factors is
involved, and, as I cannot give an approximate weighting to each factor, I cannot comment
on them.

Botulism
17. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Health: In relation to recent claims
made by the New Zealand Alliance of Freshwater Anglers, reported in the Dominion of 21
August, that fish farms in Germany had been "heavily contaminated with the botulism
organism", can he confirm that the bacteria Clostridium botulinum cannot survive in the
presence of oxygen, and that, although spores may live in the soil, these will not germinate
until subjected to an anaerobic atmosphere such as is experienced in canned food, and
therefore the presence of the bacteria is of much less relevance than the canning procedure?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I can confirm that Clostridium botulinum, the
organism that causes botulism, can grow only in an environment in which oxygen is not
present, and that the spores that it forms in an unfavourable environment will not germinate
until anaerobic conditions are encountered. Canning is a food preservation technique in
which air, and consequently oxygen, is removed. Therefore it can provide an ideal
environment in which spores can germinate and multiply. However, the toxins produced by
the organism are completely killed when exposed for 15 minutes to a temperature of 100°c,
and the spores can also be destroyed by adequate heat treatment. It is, in fact, the
destruction of these spores that is the object of all canning procedures, since these
procedures acknowledge the possible presence of Clostridium botulinum and its spores.
Mr Hunt: Would the Minister be prepared to concede that that answer is an example, as
far as fish are concerned, of "long time, no see"?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I understood the question, and the answer I have given, but the
supplementary question seems to me to be meaningless.

Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) said that at a meeting in New Plymouth on 26 May
1978 the directors of the Housing Corporation had said that the demand for housing was
being restricted by the growing inability of many families to service the borrowing required.
Recent lending policies and more freely available Post Office second mortgages had eased
the position for many borrowers. Nevertheless, single-income families on the average wage
had found home ownership increasingly beyond their means. The home building industry
was in a crisis. The building industry and its ancillaries had been brought to their knees,
while home owners had found it more difficult to bridge the deposit gap. More money was
needed to finance a section and home-and it was difficult to buy an existing home.
The Government had taken the State out of housing. In its first year in office the
National Government had reduced the housing vote by almost 50 percent. The private sector
had not risen to building needs. The Government's policies and inflation had pushed interest
rates to record levels. Trustee savings bank had admitted that they could not meet the
requirements of those people who needed urgent assistance. By pushing interest rates
higher, the Government had created thousands of redundancies. In the 3 years before 1972
the National Government had purchased only 1600 building sections. Only 20 000 houses
were being built each year, although in 1971 the National Housing Commission had
recommended that 300 000 houses be built in the decade ahead. Auckland had empty State
houses. Some people could not afford a State house today.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) said that the state of the building
industry resulted from pressures put on it by the Labour Government between 1973 and
1975. In 1975 the Labour Minister of Housing had said that he had always acknowledged that
the building demand could not be sustained at the overheated level of 1973-74, and that the
Labour Government intended to avoid the stop-go difficulties that had characterised the
industry in those years, and maintain a reasonable and consistent output. Housing was not
an election issue. The people of New Zealand had not been better housed than they were
today.

had been for a long time, and also that the president of the Otago branch of the Real Estate
Institute had said that mortgage finance in the $10,000 to $15,000 range was readily
available. The Otago Savings Bank had been able to provide more housing finance than it
had for some time.
There was no shortage of housing or of good reasonably priced mortgage finance. The
number on State rental house waiting lists was low. At present fewer than 9400 people were
on the waiting list, compared with 16 500 during the term of the Labour Government.
Slightly more than 1000 people were on the urgent waiting list. Eighty-five percent of people
who borrowed from the trustee savings banks and from building societies opted to buy an
existing house.

had increased from 217 to 222, and section sales had decreased from 47 to 33, indicating that
people preferred to buy sections with houses already on them. Opposition members had said
that more houses should be built, and also that, when Labour went out of office, supply had
almost caught up with demand. If more houses were built than were wanted, the houses
would remain empty. It had been said that, out of 18 000 State rental houses in Auckland,
270 were empty. He was surprised that Opposition members had tried to make an issue out
of such an insignificant figure, after taking into account the number of tenancies that had
changed hands, the number of people who had transferred, and the number of houses that
had needed redecoration, and perhaps major improvements.
The system of calculating State house rentals was much the same today as it had been
under the Labour Government, except that now it was easier for the tenant. Under the
Labour Government, a tenant had paid a State house rental of one-sixth of his income
up to
$100 a week, and then $1 for every extra $2 that he earned. Under the National
Government, a tenant paid a State house rental of one-sixth of his income up to $100 a week,
30c in the dollar for the next $40 earned, and 40c in the dollar thereafter.
Given the choice between the house price increases under the Labour Government and
the modest interest rate increases in recent years because of the inflation that had been
encouraged by the Labour Government, he wondered what choice the average home seeker
would make. On 19 August the Taranaki Herald had reported that the Taranaki Savings
Bank was heading for a record in the amount of money it was lending in the present year for
mortgage finance on housing. Since 1 April the bank had accepted 355 mortgage
applications. Although there was still a strong demand for finance, the bank could satisfy it.
Was that the sort of statement that would be made if people could not afford to borrow?
When replying to suggestions that people were living in caravans, the Christchurch Star ħad
reported that few people were desperate for housing.
The Auckland Savings Bank had lent a record amount of $52 million, and in Taranaki it
had been reported that more money had put property deals on the way to a record. The
Palmerston North Manawatu Evening Standard had reported that the opportunities for
married couples to buy their first new home were better now than for at least the past 20
years. The Christchurch Press had reported that the banks had eased housing finance to the
extent that one insurance company no longer had a waiting list for housing mortgages.
According to the home guidance executive officer in Auckland, it had been reported that,
for the first time in many months, the supply of housing finance in Auckland was exceeding
demand. Plenty of housing finance was available.

In the quarterly report of the trustee savings banks it had been stated that in Auckland
the consistent growth of depositors' funds during the quarter had enabled the bank to accept
applications from all depositors who had met the criteria for permanent mortgage finance,

growth in depositors' funds had enabled the bank to approve most of the reasonable
applications from depositors. In the Eastern and Central area, despite the steady growth of
funds, lending had been maintained. In Otago the improved availability of funds had not
appeared to affect market prices, which had remained very much in the buyer's favour; the

beyond the corporation's control. Increased interest rates, the adverse economic situation, a
reduction in earnings, increased unemployment, and higher commitments had all been
contributing factors. It was not easy to acquire a house in New Zealand, or to repay
mortgages. The sooner the Labour Party's policy of paying one day's pay for one week's rent
or for mortgage repayments was implemented, the better. That would be a simple cure for
all housing problems.
Despite the fact that house prices had increased, over 100 000 units had been built in the
3 years of the Labour Government. The number of applications for new houses, particularly
in the south Auckland area, had declined markedly and many contracts had been phased out
because of lack of funds. Could the corporation assist Maori families wishing to get into
houses? What progress had been made with the number of applications which had been

Government was trying to settle?
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) said that 88 400 permanent private dwellings were

State houses and flats, as well as 850 pensioner units, which included 1611 units that had
become available last year.
During the term of the Labour Government waiting lists for State houses totalled
16 427, but by March 1978 that figure had decreased to 10 191. In 1975, 750 people in
Hamilton were on the waiting list for State houses, and a further 200 people were on the
urgent list. That number had been reduced to under 400 by the Government.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) said that in the past financial year a
record number of 951 pensioner flats had been built. Maoris who complied with Housing
Corporation criteria, which were virtually the same as for the Department of Maori Affairs,

Bastion Point area regarding about 32 houses in Kitemoana Street. The Housing
Corporation had the responsibility to collect overdue rents, and was making good progress in
reaching satisfactory arrangements with some tenants. The normal procedures were being
carried out. The housing shortage which had existed since the Second World War had been
overcome, and New Zealand's housing policies could be adapted to the needs of home
seekers and to making the best use of existing houses.
Progress reported.

Japanese Fishing Agreement
3. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is the report in
the Otago Daily Times of 19 August correct in stating that Japan regards the trade statement

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The New Zealand Government
has approved the fisheries agreement with Japan, and it will be signed as soon as the
Japanese Government has completed its approval procedures. Signature should take place at
the end of this week or early next week. At that time the Japanese ambassador and I will
probably make a joint statement. Under the terms of the fisheries agreement, the
Government of Japan will recognise New Zealand's right to control and manage the fisheries
resource within the New Zealand zone. The Government of Japan will also recognise New
Zealand's right to determine the total allowable catch, the portion that New Zealand
fishermen will harvest, and the surplus that will be available for allocation to other countries,
including Japan. The New Zealand Government has made it clear that in reaching decisions
on annual quotas New Zealand will regard as an important factor the level of access to the
Japanese market for our agricultural exports.

Botulism
4. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Health: Can he confirm that the
product canned need have no relevance whatsoever to the incidence of botulism, and that
occurrences in the United Kingdom have involved such foods as rabbit and pigeon broth,
vegetarian nut brawn, home-made pie, jugged hare, and macaroni cheese?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I can confirm that botulism can occur with many
foods and not just in canned foods. If the food contains Clostridium botulinum spores, and
oxygen is excluded from it, the clostridia will grow and produce toxin. If then the toxin-
bearing food is eaten, botulism food poisoning will occur. In the United Kingdom most cases
of botulism have been due to foods such as rabbit and pigeon broth, vegetarian nut brawn,
home-made pie, jugged hare, and macaroni cheese. The majority of cases of botulism have
resulted from home-preserved foods and not commercially processed products.
Mr W. R. Austin: Can the Minister confirm that botulism is anaerobic?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I can spell it, but I cannot baptise it or confirm it.
Mr Kirk: Is there any need for such questions to be asked when we do not have the
problem in New Zealand?
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: That is asking for an opinion.

Creative and Expressive Arts
8. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), to the
Minister of Education: What has been done by the National Government to encourage
education in the creative and expressive arts?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Through the Performers in Schools
Committee, a joint Department of Education - Arts Council committee, the direct funding
of individuals and groups wanting to bring the creative and expressive arts into schools and
classrooms is being maintained. The department's contribution to the fund was increased
from $20,000 to $22,000 in 1978. The writers in schools scheme-a joint scheme between the
