tutors' salaries and representation on the board of studies of the New Zealand Drama
School.
Terms of Trade
9. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) to the Minister of Finance: What are the
latest terms of trade, and do they represent an improvement on or a deterioration in the
position as at 30 November 1975; and, if so, to what extent?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The terms of trade are the ratio of
the export to the import price index, and they are published quarterly-so no figure is
available for 30 November 1975. However, the terms of trade stood at 69 at 31 December
1975, on a base of calendar year 1957 = 100. The figure for the terms of trade released by the
Government Statistician for the quarter ended 31 March 1978, which is the most recent
figure available, is provisionally put at 77-a 10 percent increase since December 1975, and
still about 40 percent below the peak in mid-1973.
Hon. Michael Connelly: As the terms of trade have improved significantly, and as the
Government has had the benefit of about $3,000 million additional export earnings, why has
the balance of payments deficit been reduced by only about $300 million?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The answer, of course, is that the Government has reduced
the deficit by about $500 million, which is about half the amount of the deficit left by the
Labour Government. It must be remembered that at the end of 1973 the terms of trade stood
at about 40 percent. The Labour Government used up the $1,000 million we had in reserves,
and then started borrowing at the rate of about $1,000 million a year. Since the Government
took office at the end of 1975 the deficit has been halved.
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Order! Too often the member asking a supplementary
question goes beyond the scope of the original question, which then lets the Minister go even
further. I would prefer members to keep within the scope of the original question, which in
this case related to the terms of trade as at 30 November 1975.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not correct that the balance of payments deficit as at the
end of March was more than $800 million, and that the forecast for the next quarter is more
than $700 million?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I think the member is confusing the balance of payments
deficit with the overseas exchange transactions deficit. Included in the balance of payments
deficit are items such as the Penrod oil rig and the Maui support ship, which appear as a
debit. In due time they sail away and come back as a credit. The overseas exchange
transactions figures leave those items out. Those figures are more accurate and are
commonly used-even by Labour Governments-in forming economic policy, as distinct
from the balance of payments figures, which have those aberrations included in them.

Noxious Animals Infestation
12. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) to the Minister of Forests: Is the level of noxious
animal infestation (principally opossum) in the Aupori, Omahuta, Puhi Puhi, Puketi,
Russell, Waipoua, and Waitangi State Forests considered to be serious, and is there any
indication that the incidence of infestation is becoming worse?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The position is that opossums are gradually
extending their range northwards. In the Russell and Puhi Puhi State Forests a moderate
opossum population exists at present and is increasing. Immediately to the north in the
Waitangi State Forest a light scattered population is present, and opossums are in similar
density in Omahuta, Puketi, and Waipoua State Forests. All these populations are
increasing, unfortunately. There are no opossums in the Aupouri State Forest, the present
limit of their range being approximately in a line from Kaitaia across to Doubtless Bay. It is
certain that opossums will eventually occupy all of the Northland peninsula.
Mr Rogers: Does the Minister intend to put any special efforts into the elimination of
opossums from the area, rather than allowing them to spread further north?
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Yes, he will put salt on their tails.

tremendous calls on the personnel and finance of the Forest Service for wild animal and
agricultural pest control. At present the personnel of the Forest Service is occupied in areas
where animal health is of concern, but I assure the member that everything practical will be
done to try to slow up the spread of opossums north, in particular. I should like to encourage
private trappers, where numbers are high enough, to use their efforts to track opossums,

14. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the Minister in

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I reply on behalf of the Minister in charge
of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation. "The Rural Bank has not fixed arbitrary
maximum loan limits for its settlement lending, but operates average guidelines. Depending

basis. Conversely, there will be others who will be required to complete their proposals with

operating are-dairy farms, $70,000; sheep and cattle farms, $95,000. For 85 percent special
settlement loans the guideline amounts are-dairy farms, $110,000; sheep and cattle farms,
$200,000."

ORAKEI BLOCK (VESTING AND USE) BILL
Introduction
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the Orakei Block (Vesting and
Use) Bill be introduced. The Bill implements a number of important agreements reached
between the Crown and the various bodies and representative groups interested in the future
use of Crown-owned land at Bastion Point, Auckland. The proposed legislation is in accord
with fully publicised and widely accepted proposals which arose after months of investigation
by an expert planning study team, representing the Government and local body agencies.
The study was overseen by a steering committee, which included Maori representatives, and
followed an invitation, widely accepted by interested parties, to put forward submissions
about future land use.
The steering committee's proposals were outlined to the Ngati Whatua elders and
supporters at a meeting in Auckland in February this year. At that meeting the elders made
it clear they accepted the recommended proposals put forward in the planning report. Mr
Justice Speight, after an exhaustive study of all aspects of this vexed question, said: "The
substituted scheme of 1978, approved by the Maori elders, and adopted by Cabinet, is a
handsome remedy of long-felt wrongs, whether they were real or imagined. The scheme
worked out by four wise men, and acceptable to the majority of tribal elders and to the
Government, appears, if I may say so, to bring peace with honour." A number of very
important land-use decisions have resulted, and the proposals will be greatly to the
advantage of the people of Auckland as a whole and to specific interest groups, including the
Orakei Maori community.
The Bill implements the Government's decisions as follows: first, to set aside an area of
12.3 ha as a recreation reserve, and a small area of 7798 sq m as a reserve for local or
community facilities, both areas to be placed under the control of the Auckland City Council


## p. 2959 (#355) ###########################################

30 August
2959
Orakei Block (Vesting and Use) Bill
for the benefit of the general public; secondly, to vest the freehold of an area of 11.6 ha in a
new Maori trust board to be known as the Ngati Whatua of Orakei Maori Trust Board-the
board is set up by the legislation and will be a board within the meaning of the Maori Trust
Boards Act 1955; thirdly, the Bill proposes to set aside an area of 4304 sq m as a reserve for
local community health purposes, and to make it available to the Youthline Trust
Organisation for a hostel site; fourthly, to add certain small areas totalling just over
1700 sq m to the existing Orakei Marae to square off boundaries and bring them into line
with the present fences and occupation; fifthly, the Bill vests an area of 1.7 ha in the Housing
Corporation for residential development.
The two main proposals covered by the legislation are the reservation of land for public
purposes and the vesting of land in the proposed Maori Trust Board. Both are important and
widely sought actions. The land for public reserve will be incorporated in the surrounding
Orakei Domain, which is already administered by the Auckland City Council on the Crown's
behalf. Incorporation of this additional land will enable the council to proceed with a
properly drafted overall management plan for the benefit of the general public.
The proposal to vest land in a Maori Trust Board on a freehold basis recognises, on the
Government's part, the asociation of the Ngati Whatua with this land, and the
appropriateness of providing them with a traditional area for administration in the interests
of future generations. The 11.6 hectares include the existing Kitemoana Street, Reihana
Street, and Watene Crescent residential settlements, together with the houses and other
improvements involved. Vacant land suitable for further residential development is also
included, together with land suitable for open space and community recreation use. A small
area is specifically included as an addition to the church and cemetery site on Okahu Bay.
While a substantial portion of the 11.6 hectares is being made available without charge
to the Maori Trust Board, the board is to pay the Crown for parts of the land, and the Bill
provides accordingly. Detailed negotiations have taken place with the elders of the Ngati
Whatua of Orakei, and full and amicable agreement was reached on the terms of the transfer
of the title to the land. The elders have extensive plans for development and administration
of the land passing to them through the proposed trust board. The Bill contains many
machinery clauses necessary to facilitate the various proposals. As Crown land is involved, I
shall move at the appropriate time that the Bill be referred to the Lands and Agriculture
Committee.

in reaching the figure of $200,000, which was the sum agreed upon in the exchange, we

a small element that might enter the meeting to disrupt the proceedings, thus denying the
obvious opportunity to resolve the grievance that had, rightly or wrongly, been felt for so

I give full credit to the officers of the Department of Lands and Survey, and particularly
the Commissioner of Crown Lands in Auckland who has had discussions for hour after hour
with all those involved—the Maori people, the elders, the protest group-trying to reconcile
the protest group with the elders, and asking for patience following the court's decision and
the Government not immediately moving to resolve the issue. The proposal in the Bill is a
generous move by the Government to resolve a land grievance that has been with us for 100
years in the heart of Auckland-New Zealand's largest city.
Whatever Opposition members may say-particularly the former Minister of Lands and
the former Acting Minister of Lands--they know in their heart of hearts that they had a
chance to resolve a difficult issue, but they looked at it, and stepped aside. This Government
has handled an issue which was made more difficult by the intrusion of people who had no
wish to have the matter resolved, who had no part in the ownership of the land, and who
sought to disrupt decisions that have resulted in the introduction of the Bill.
An opportunity will be given to the elders-and I am sure they will take it—and to the
Auckland City Council, if necessary, to make submissions to the Lands and Agriculture
Committee. We are dealing with Crown land, and the Bill must be referred to that
committee. A large part of the block will be transferred to the people of Auckland as a
whole, and another part will be transferred to the Maori people, who have historic links with
the land.
I am sure that any small amending detail required can be accommodated within the Bill
before it is passed, but the basis of the measure has resulted from the joint planning study
made by representatives of local authorities in the area, the steering committee, the Maori
people themselves, and the Crown. Instead of criticising the solution accepted by the Ngati
Whatua elders and the Government, the member for Northern Maori, in the interests of his
constituents, should welcome the Bill and help it on its way.

​8.
Housing Corporation-Land Disposal
(10/8/78)
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: (1) Since
December 1975 to date, how much land in building section equivalents has been
disposed of; 2) how many sections were sold to individuals who subsequently
built a home with Housing Corporation finance; (3) how many of these sections
were disposed of (a) at current market rates, (b) by auction or tender, (c) at
remitted value, and (d) to companies?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: (1) Since December
1975, land disposed of by the Housing Corporation amounted to 6517 building
section equivalents comprising land for school and other community purposes, the
corporation's construction and sales programmes, the needs of other Government
departments, and the sale of other raw land. (2) During the period from 1 April
1976 to 31 March 1978, 1844 sections were offered to the public for sale by the
Corporation, and during the same period 1278 individuals built homes with Housing
Corporation finance on Crown sections. (3) (a) The remitted price scheme was
discontinued in May 1976 and since then all sections have been offered at current
market rates. (b) Ten residential sections have been offered for sale by tender
between December 1976 and 31 March 1978. (c) Sales to companies include the
sale of sections to builders. Builders participate in ballots once the claims of other
priority groups are satisfied, and a separate record of those applications has not
been kept. Other sales of land to companies include, for instance, land exchanges
that provide the corporation with developed sections for immediate use, while
others include land surplus to the corporation's immediate needs.
9.
Local Telephone Calls-Charges Overseas
(10/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Postmaster-General: Could he indicate
from information available to him (a) which overseas countries, apart from
Australia, charge for all local telephone calls in addition to toll calls; (b) (i) the
amounts of the charges on local calls in Australia and any other countries about
which he has information, and (ii) any system of exemptions applied to local
calls-for example, for elderly people making calls to their medical practitioners-
that is at present in force in any of these countries?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: (a) The latest informa-
tion available to the Post Office indicates that, in addition to Australia, the
following countries charge for local telephone calls in addition to toll calls:
Afghanistan, Argentine, Austria, Bangladesh, Belgium, Brazil, Burma, Colombia,
Costa Rica, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Finland, France,
Germany, (F.R.), Ghana, Greece, Guatemala, Hungary, Indonesia, Iran, Ireland,
Israel, Italy, Ivory Coast, Japan, Kenya, Korea, Lebanon, Luxembourg, Malaysia,
Mexico, Morocco. Netherlands, Nicaragua, Norway, Pakistan, Paraguay, Peru,
Portugal, Rhodesia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Syria, Taiwan,
Tanzania, Thailand, Turkey, Uganda, United Kingdom, Uruguay, Venezuela,
Yemen. (b) (i) In Australia the charge is 10c (N.Z.) for each local call irrespec-
tive of length. In the United Kingdom the charge is 6c (N.Z.) for a standard call
of 3 minutes. Up-to-date information in respect of other countries is not available.
(ii) The Post Office has no information to indicate whether any overseas
Administration allows exemptions for local call charges for special reasons.

11.
Coal Exploration Programme, Southland
(10/8/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Was the coal
exploration programme at present being undertaken in Southland by Lime and
Marble Ltd. of Nelson the result of its being advertised and let by tender, and,
if so, how many tenders were received, how competitive were the tenders, and was
it not possible for his department to carry out this exploratory investigation on its
own behalf?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: In 1976, when the Government
decided to commence its South Island coal exploration programme in eastern
Southland, the Mines Department did not have the necessary staff to manage this
project in addition to the coal prospecting it was already undertaking in Huntly.
A management contract was therefore negotiated with Lime and Marble Ltd. of
Nelson. At the time, no other New Zealand organisation offering exploration
services had both the appropriate management experience and administrative
support to handle an exploration programme of this magnitude.
12.
Retiring Leave-Hospital Workers
(10/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of State Services: Is he aware that,
whereas employees in most areas of State funded employment receive retiring
leave as of right, hospital employees, despite the fact that they are paid in effect
by the State, receive a retiring gratuity solely at the discretion of hospital boards,
and that, furthermore, there is no obligation for the board concerned to reveal
reasons for the amount it pays; and, if so, does he intend to do anything about
this apparent anomaly?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: I understand that
the member has directed a similar question to my colleague the Minister of
Health, who has answered in respect of the hospital service. Because of the origin
of hospital board financing, the gratuity situation for hospital staff has a different
basis from the retiring leave provisions for staff in the rest of the State services.
As the Minister of Health has stated, he would expect the Hospital Boards Asso-
ciation to recommend any changes it thought necessary.

13.
Retiring Leave-Hospital Workers
(10/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Is he prepared to take
any legislative action or any other type of action to overcome cases in which a
hospital board exercises its discretionary authority in the payment of gratuities
when people retire from service so that people who have given the same years
of service receive different sums of money?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I am aware of the discretionary
powers of hospital boards in relation to retirement gratuities. On the information
available, hospital boards seldom decline to approve a gratuity, and when they do
so there are special factors. In these circumstances I would not seek to interfere
with this discretion of hospital boards unless the matter is represented to me by
hospital boards through their association. As for the qualifying periods for
gratuities, there is a standard schedule throughout the hospital service showing
what can be approved in each particular circumstance
14.
Ross Dependency and Awarua Electorate
(10/8/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Justice: What steps
could be taken to include the Ross Dependency within the Awarua electorate
boundaries?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: In principle there is
no reason why the Ross Dependency should not be included within the boundaries
of an appropriate electorate. In practice, however, it would have no effect, because
the Ross Dependency, like a number of other remote parts of New Zealand, has
no permanent population. Like the Ross Dependency, outlying islands such as
Campbell Island, the Auckland Islands, and the Kermadec Islands are not included
in any electoral district. New Zealanders living and working in those remote areas
are all on temporary assignments and, under the provisions of the Electoral Act,
they are therefore deemed to reside where they have their usual place of abode.
15.
Fractionation of Blood Plant
(10/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Health: Is he aware of the
representations made to him and other members of Parliament by the New Zealand
Haemophilia Society Inc. concerning the establishment of a fractionation plant
for blood products, and, if so, would he consider speeding up the establishment
of such a plant?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I am aware of the representa-
tions of the New Zealand Haemophilia Society Inc. concerning the establishment
of a fractionation plant for blood products in this country. As I indicated in my
reply to the honourable member for New Lynn last month, a decision has not
yet been made to establish a New Zealand fractionation plant for the preparation
of blood components. Before a decision is reached it is considered necessary to
carry out a detailed examination of the economic feasibility of this project. Work
on this investigation is at present proceeding. In the meantime, supplies of
Cryoprecipate or Purified Factor VIII Concentrate, as may be appropriate for
the individual patient, are available for the treatment of patients in New Zealand
suffering from the effects of haemophilia.

Wildlife Service-Lands and Survey Department
(11/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of State Services: With
reference to the editorial in the July 1978 issue of New Zealand Outdoor, can he
confirm that the recent move to put the wildlife service of the Department of
Internal Affairs into the Department of Lands and Survey was instigated by the
State Services Commission; will he give full consideration to any discussions before
any further moves are made; and can he give a guarantee that the democracy and
independence of acclimatisation societies will not be threatened?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: The State Services
Commission has the statutory responsibility for advising the Government on the
allocation of functions between Government departments. As part of a wide-
ranging review of the Department of Internal Affairs, the commission reviewed
the appropriate placement of the wildlife service. Some discussions were held
with acclimatisation society interests, but the Government has deferred a decision.
In the event of the Government wishing to reopen this question, full consideration
would be given to the views of all interested organisations and the independence
of the acclimatisation societies.
18.
Venison Exports-Poison Spray Danger
(11/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Agriculture: Has he seen
the editorial in the July 1978 issue of New Zealand Outdoor concerning 1080 poison,
2,4,5-T spraying, and the use of aerosol fly spray on deer carcasses, and, further,
has he made the European countries that receive those venison exports aware
of these aspects?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: I have seen the
editorial in the July 1978 issue of New Zealand Outdoor, but do not consider
there is any danger with our game exports or that the position is as implied.
There are stringent regulatory requirements covering poisoning operations and
the procurement of game, which are enforced by the New Zealand Forest Service
and my ministry, and these are well known to veterinary and health authorities
of those European countries to which New Zealand venison is exported. In fact,
West Germany, which is the biggest importer by far of New Zealand game, has
since 1975 had resident veterinary review officers stationed in New Zealand for
long periods and they have not expressed any dissatisfaction with the safeguards
being imposed to protect our game exports.
19.
Venison Exports-Quality Control
(11/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Agriculture: In view of
the reply given by the Minister of Health to a question asked on 6 July 1978 that
he "has no responsibility as to the quality of venison exported to Europe", and
that "no guarantee can be given that exported venison will not contain 1080",
can he give any guarantee about the quality of venison for export, and that export
venison has not come from a 1080-poisoned area?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Responsibility for
the quality of all venison processed for sale for human consumption in New Zea-
land, whether for the local market or export, is vested in the Ministry of Agricul-
ture and Fisheries by the Meat Act 1964 and the Game Regulations 1975. The
ministry and the New Zealand Forest Service enforce strict regulatory require-
ments related to poisoning operations and procurement of game, and I am satisfied
with the safeguards imposed to ensure that export venison does not come from
1080-poisoned areas.

20.
Wild and Scenic Rivers Protection
(11/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister for the Environment: Has he
seen the editorial in the July 1978 issue of New Zealand Outdoor, and can he give
assurances that draft wild river legislation will control the quality of river flow
as well as quantity, and embrace whole upper watersheds of rivers; and when
will the wild river legislation be introduced into the House?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment) replied: Yes, I have seen
the editorial in the New Zealand Outdoor, which mistakenly implies that legislation
has already been introduced to protect wild rivers. A good public response was
received to the discussion paper on wild and scenic river protection that I
distributed last year. A further report summarising the public submissions and
suggesting a course of action will be available in the near future. I believe that a
satisfactory river protection policy can be implemented without a special Act.
A protection policy would embrace water quality as well as quantity, and upper
watersheds of rivers could be protected under such a policy.

24.
Freezing Works-Man-days Lost
(11/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Labour: How many
man-days have been lost in each freezing works in this country in each of the
last 5 years, and what has been the total work force in each works in each of
those years?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied. The Department of Labour
does not release details of industrial stoppages or employment figures for individual
freezing works in the meat freezing industry. In 1974, the Department of Labour
provided details of stoppages in individual freezing works for the Committee of
Inquiry into the Freezing Industry. The firms involved regarded this as a breach
of confidence and threatened to withdraw their co-operation in providing the
statistics. It took some time for the department to re-establish relationships with
these firms. While the department is not strictly bound by any statute to observe
confidentiality, it is a well established principle that a data-collecting agency
should adhere to this doctrine. The Department of Statistics is bound by the
Statistics Act to preserve confidentiality. It is fatuous to suggest that the Depart-
ment of Labour should not adhere to this principle simply because it is not
legally bound to.

25.
Area Schools-Teacher Accommodation
(15/8/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Is it a
fact that in December 1976 he released funds for the building of residences and
flats for area schools, and, if so, would he advise the House of the schools for
which the building of teacher accommodation, allocated at that time, has not
yet begun?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: It is not true that I
released funds for the building of residences and flats for area schools in December
1976. What I did do was approve a special allocation of houses for four schools
that had translated to area school status earlier that year. I did not approve
funds; these were to be approved as and when finance was available and the
controlling education boards were in a position to proceed with the building
works. The four schools that were the subject of the December 1976 approval
were Wanaka, Kurow, Akaroa, and Cheviot area schools. The additional housing
has been provided at Wanaka and Kurow and is occupied. At Akaroa, purchase
of a suitable site has held up the provision of the flats. It is the Canterbury
Education Board's intention that a replacement house for the principal be built
on this new site. When the new house is completed the board intends to demolish
the old house and build the flats on that site. At Cheviot there has been consider-
able difficulty in obtaining any site for a house or the two flats. Finally, in April
1978 a house was purchased, and is now occupied by a teacher. A site for the
flats has been actively sought for some time and it now appears that a suitable
section may have been found. Once negotiations for purchase have been concluded,
the Canterbury Education Board will proceed as soon as it can with building the
two flats.

32.
War Pension Appeal Board
(16/8/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister in Charge of War
Pensions: Will he, in the interests of justice, consider adding decisions of the War
Pensions Appeal Board to those subject to scrutiny and investigation by the
ombudsmen, and, if not, will he detail his objections?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister in Charge of War Pensions) replied: No.
The War Pensions Appeal Board is an independent tribunal established to hear
appeals, on medical or service grounds, from decisions of the War Pensions
Board, another independent tribunal. The system of war pensions appeals is
designed to protect and safeguard the interests of all ex-servicemen as far as
pension entitlement is concerned. The appeal system has the support and confid-
ence of the New Zealand Returned Services Association. In any event, it is not
the function of the Ombudsman to investigate complaints against decisions of
independent tribunals and I would refer the honourable member to the provisions
of section 13 (7) of the Ombudsmen Act.

Crayfish Reserves

close existing crayfish reserves to amateur crayfishermen as well as to commercial

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: There are no "crayfish
reserves" described as such in New Zealand's fisheries law, but the taking of rock
lobsters for sale is prohibited in several areas defined in regulation 20 of the
Rock Lobster Regulations 1969. At present it is not intended to exclude amateur
rock-lobster fishermen from these areas.

Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Statistics: Will he ask his department
to calculate the overall dollar value of a 3 percent increase in the consumer price
index (being the Treasury estimate of the effect of a 10 percent tax on foreign

37.
Teaching of Reading, Porirua-Involvement of Parents (16/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: Have any
steps been taken to involve parents in the Porirua area in the teaching of reading
to their children?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: There are 29 schools
in the Porirua area, and the following actions have been taken in some or all of
them. Eight schools have assisted parents to guide their children's home reading,
through teacher-interviews and counselling. Nine schools have sent home circulars
that give background information and suggestions for helping children with
reading. Most schools issue story books for home reading, and some have
organised home-reading programmes that involve parents. Eighteen schools have
held parent meetings on reading,, addressed by staff or by reading advisers. A
large number of schools have parents helping in classrooms, where they observe
reading, and are involved in appropriate back-up support for teachers. Some
of these parents help in the school library, and with the making of large books
for shared reading in infant classes. In five schools, parents visit classrooms for
observation of programmes, including specific reading lessons. Ten schools have
issued the book On the Way to Reading, and tapes of the broadcasts have been
used as part of the parent education programme. Schools in this area are seen
to be making a sustained effort to interest and to involve parents in their
children's reading.
38.
Education Achievement Tests, Porirua
(16/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: Is there any
evidence of children in the Porirua area scoring lower than the national average
for the progressive achievement tests for comprehension, vocabulary, and listening
skills in 1973 and 1977?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Yes. The scores in
Porirua east schools show that the average child scores between 15-42 percentile.
The national norms would say that the average child in New Zealand scores
between 40-60 percentile. The levels of these reading scores correlates closely
with the level of family income. This relationship is noted in all similar standard-
ised tests administered in Western countries. PA tests favour those children from
the homes of higher economic groups. Furthermore, the PA tests are culturally
biased and therefore are an imperfect measuring tool for children from different
subcultural and non-English-speaking backgrounds. There is no real difference
between 1973 and 1977 scores.

43.
Post Office Closures, Hamilton
(16/8/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Postmaster-General: (a) How many
post offices have closed or have been placed on restricted hours in the Hamilton
postal district since 23 May 1978; (b) can he confirm that two post offices have
closed and another 12 have been placed on restricted hours, primarily in rural
parts of the postal district in question, in the period 1 January 1976 to 23 May
1978; and (c) how does he reconcile this state of affairs with National's promise
in its agricultural policy to "give greater emphasis to the maintenance and
enhancement . . . of rural life", in which “communications” and “mail delivery"
are mentioned by way of policy elaboration?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: (a) Two post offices
have been closed since 23 May 1978 and none has been placed on restricted hours.
(b) Five post offices were closed and 12 were placed on restricted hours during
the period 1 January 1976 to 23 May 1978. All were in rural areas. (c) There
has been a tendency for the rural population to shift to urban areas. This,
coupled with the greater mobility of the people left behind and their wish also to
shop at supermarkets, has resulted in the closure of country stores that operated as
post offices. Alternative post office services are offered to those still residing in
such areas, primarily by means of telephone and rural mail delivery services.
With regard to restricting the hours of attendance observed at departmental
offices, the scope and extent of services provided are examined from time to time
and adjustments made in the light of the volume of business handled. An attend-
ance is restricted only in cases in which the level of business could readily be coped
with by reduced hours.

since 1 January 1976: (i) Mangawhai Heads, (ii) Önerahi, (iii) Pipiwai, (iv)
Mitimiti, (v) Rangi Point; (c) could he indicate how it is possible to reconcile
the closure of five post offices in Whangarei, together with the placing of five
additional post offices on restricted hours, with the National Party's 1975 manifesto
promises: (i) under "Post Office" to "upgrade" and "expand" postal services,
(ii) under "Agriculture", to "ensure that the social needs of the rural communities
and rural service towns are adequately provided for", (iii) under "agriculture",
"National will give greater emphasis to the maintenance and enhancement of the
desirable social and environmental qualities of rural life. More attention will be
given to: communications, mail delivery, telephone services"?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: From the date of the
change in hours or closing of the office until 31 July 1978, the estimated savings
in expenditure were: (a) (i) Parakao, $1,118; (ii) Waimamaku, $2,043;
(iii) Waima, $2,842; (iv) Houhora, $1,125; (v) Maungaturoto Railway, $3,260;
(vi) Towai, $2,427; (b) (i) Mangawhai Heads, $307; (ii) Onerahi, $3,340;
(iii) Pipiwai, $412; (iv) Mitimiti, $580; (v) Rangi Point, $449; (c) (i) the place
of the Onerahi office was taken by the centrally situated new post office providing
full post office services in the Sherwood shopping centre. Mangawhai Heads, a
seasonal office, was closed when the agent resigned and a replacement was not
available. The remaining three offices were closed because of lack of patronage.
Residents were given upgraded telephone and rural delivery mail services: (ii) The
extension of rural delivery services and the upgrading of rural telephone exchanges
to automatic working do provide for the social needs of people in the rural areas.
The delivery of mail to farmers' gates and connection of telephones to their homes,
where before they had to travel considerable distances to a post office for these
services, are seen as an upgrading of service. Any reduction in the hours of
attendance at post offices is invariably the result of reduced business and is dis-
cussed beforehand with the local people and organisations. (iii) Improved mail
delivery and telephone services to rural areas are consistent with the Government's
stated policy.

50.
Crayfish-Closed Season
(17/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Has the Govern-
ment any plans to close the crayfish season annually from 1 March to 1 June?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: The Rock Lobster
Regulations 1969 make provision for a closed season for rock lobsters in the
waters adjacent to the Chatham Islands during the period 1 March to 30 April.
The Government has no plans to change or extend this closed season, as all avail-
able scientific data indicate that such a restriction is not necessary for conservation
of rock lobster stocks.
51.
Crayfish-Mahia Peninsular
(17/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Does he intend
to prohibit non-local fishermen from the crayfisheries around the Mahia
Peninsula area?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: I have no authority to
prohibit rock lobster fishermen from other parts of New Zealand fishing in the
rock lobster fisheries around the Mahia Peninsula area. One of the criteria to be
considered by the Fisheries Licensing Authority is the length of time that any
individual fisherman has been engaged in a particular fishery in any given area.
This would therefore tend to give preference to local fishermen in the issuing of
licences.
52.
Retail Prices Comparison with Landed Cost
(17/8/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Will he ask
his department to calculate the increase in the retail price per unit of commodity,
if the landed cost of the following items had been increased by 10 percent as at
1 April 1978: (a) sugar-per kilogram, (b) cocoa-per kilogram, (c) tea-per
kilogram, (d) coffee per kilogram, (e) petrol-per litre, (f) spare parts for motor
vehicles-per dollar value, (g) rice-per kilogram; and what were the approximate
retail prices of those commodities as at the date when they were last surveyed?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied:
A 10 percent increase in the landed cost of the commodities specified would have
resulted in the following aproximate increase in their per unit retail price as at
1 April 1978: (a) sugar-2.7c per kilogram (5.2 percent); (b) cocoa-80c per
kilogram (6.7 percent); (c) tea-32c per kilogram (7.8 percent); (d) coffee
(instant)-$1.35 per kilogram (6.1 percent); (e) petrol-1.1c per litre (3.7 per-
cent); (f) imported spare parts for motor vehicles-between 6.5c and 8.3c per
$1 value (6.5 to 8.3 percent); (g) rice-7.7c per kilogram (6.3 percent). With
the exception of motor vehicle spare parts, the commodities are generally
imported in crude form. The percentage increases in per unit retail prices are
lower than the 10 percent increase in raw material imports, because of added
value in New Zealand in the form of further processing, packaging, and trans-
portation. The general prices of these items at present are: (a) sugar-76c per
1.5 kg pack; (b) cocoa--$2.99 per 250 gm pack; (c) tea-$1.02 per 250 gm pack;
(d) coffee (instant)-$2.20 per 100 gm jar; (e) petrol-31.6c per litre; (f) N.A.;
(g) rice (Australian long grain)—55c per 454 gm pack.

Hobby Classes-South Auckland Schools
(17/8/78)
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Education: How many schools
in the south Auckland district are running after-school hobby classes?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: If the honourable
member is referring to hobby classes established under the manual and technical
regulations I can tell him that 13 secondary schools in south Auckland provide
a total in excess of 200 non-vocational evening classes for adults. On the other
hand, if he is referring to classes established under the "classes outside school
hours" regulations, then 7 primary and intermediate schools in south Auckland
offer 52 classes after school for primary pupils. In addition, two secondary schools
in the area (Aorere College and Nga Tapuwae College) have been specially
selected to establish community programmes outside school hours, and provide
after-school recreation programmes.

56.
Cook Strait Cable-Transmission Loss
(17/8/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What per-
centage of electricity transmitted to the North Island by the Cook Strait cable is
lost in transmission and conversion to AC?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: Information on this subject
was given in my answer to a similar question, No. 9 on 31 May 1978. The percent-
age losses in the transmission link between the South and North Islands vary
from year to year and depend on the loading pattern of the link in each yearly
period. Annual losses have varied from slightly less than 8 percent to about 10
percent. Over the past 10 years ended 31 March 1978, the total recorded losses
amounted to 9.2 percent of the energy transmitted from the South Island AC
system. For the year ended 31 March 1978 the losses amounted to 7.8 percent.

94.
Area School Teachers-List B Classification
(17/8/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Is it
true that under regulation 53h (1) of the Education (Assessment, Classification
and Appointment) Regulations, secondary teachers who have taught in area
schools for more than 2 years should, if the letter of the law is followed, lose
their List B classification on the teachers' register?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I assume that the
regulation to which the honourable member is referring is regulation 68 of the
Education (Assessment, Classification, and Appointment) Regulations 1976, which
provides for the lapse of classification when a teacher classified in List B has not,
within the preceding 2 years, held any appointment as a teacher in a State
secondary school. As an area school is not a secondary school, a literal application
of the regulation would result in the lapse of the List B classification of a secondary
teacher who is appointed to an area school. However, in practice a secondary
teacher classified in List B who is appointed to an area school retains the classifi-
cation whilst continuing to teach in the school.

105.
Marine Reserve, Poor Knights Island
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Has the area
around the Poor Knights Islands yet been designated as marine reserve, and,
if not, when will it be?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: The Hauriki Gulf Maritime
Park Board has applied for an Order in Council to declare the waters and sea bed
about the Poor Knights Islands a marine reserve under the Marine Reserves Act
1971. At this stage the application is being processed, and this includes the follow-
ing steps: (1) the preparation of an environmental impact report, its publication
and audit by the Commission for the Environment; (2) making a decision on the
objections received; and (3) making a recommendation for an Order in Council,
if a reserve is to be declared. An announcement cannot be made until an Order in
Council is made.

106.
Argyle Station Purchase
(18/8/78)
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Lands:
Was there any special dispensation from the Land Settlement Board in allowing
Mr F. Andrews to purchase Argyle Station in northern Southland, in view of
his owning other land, and, if so, what was the basis of dispensation and on
what date was it approved?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: There was no special dispensa-
tion from the Land Settlement Board when it consented to Mr F. Andrews
purchasing Argyle Station. The Land Settlement Board's consent, which was given
on 31 July 1978, was subject to a condition that Mr Andrews "undertake to sell the
land held by himself, the Company or his Trust by 31 March 1979”. I should
point out that this condition is not without precedent, having been used with cases
under the Land Settlement Promotion and Land Acquisition Act 1952, and also
transfers of Crown leaseholds dealt with by the Land Settlement Board in terms
of the Land Act 1948.

109.
Area Schools-Terms and Holidays Regulations (18/8/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Now
that education boards, the NZEI and the PPTA support the principle of the area
school year equating with the secondary school year (as an incentive for
staff recruitment and to allow secondary pupils to join the employment race
on an equal footing with their high school counterparts), is he prepared to
investigate the possibility of the Terms and Holidays Regulations 1977 being
amended accordingly?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I am unaware of any
agreement between the education boards, the NZEI, and the PPTA to support the
principle of the area school year equating with the secondary school year. My
department has recently received a letter from the PPTA seeking discussions on
the matter, but no representations have been received from the other parties. I
will consider the need to amend the Education (Terms and Holidays) Regulations
1977 after discussions with the interested parties.

Gleneagles Agreement-Implementation
(18/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Would
he give the names of the sporting organisations or individuals who have been
contacted by the Government specifically to remind them of New Zealand's
obligations under the Gleneagles Agreement?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: It is not the
intention of the Government to disclose the names of the sporting bodies with
whom discussions have been held in terms of the Gleneagles Agreement, because
some have requested that the approach be treated confidentially. Consequently,
we believe that we can act most effectively to ensure the implementation of the
Gleneagles Agreement if such discussions are kept confidential. I can, however,
assure the honourable member that a number of sports bodies have sought advice
from the Government on this question, and that we have been in touch with
other sporting organisations that were considering sports contacts with South
Africa to make certain they were aware of the Government's views on such
contacts.

111A
Ministerial Correspondence
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Prime Minister: What restrictions
are there on the publication of ministerial correspondence, both during and after
a Minister's term of office?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) replied: There are no restrictions,
except those that relate to classified material, on the publication of that ministerial
correspondence. When a matter of public policy is involved, publication is at the
discretion of either party. When, however, a matter concerns the private affairs of
a citizen or group of citizens, it is an established convention not to publish corres-
pondence without the consent of the affected individual or group. The same
principles should apply to the publication of ministerial correspondence after a
Minister leaves office.
112.
Development Finance Corporation-Loans Policy
(22/8/78)
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) to the Minister of Trade and
Industry: Could he list the schedule of the types of loans available through
the Development Finance Corporation, to include: (1) terms of the loans, (2)
criteria applied for loans, (3) interest rates for loans; and could he indicate
what changes have been made to each or all of the above in the last three financial
years?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied:
The Development Finance Corporation finances all types of manufacturing and
processing plant that will increase productivity and contribute to an expansion of
effective production capacity within New Zealand industry. Special attention is
given to manufacturing projects which process primary products for export;
provide direct import replacement; assist the development of technical and
engineering skills in New Zealand; service essential industries; are situated in
regional development areas. Where there are identifiable benefits to New Zealand,
DFC will provide financial assistance for overseas projects. (1) Term Loans-
(a) Loan term: terms are generally in the range of 5-15 years and are related to
the equipment's useful life and the cash flow expected to be generated. Where
overseas funds are provided DFC on-lends on terms which reflect its own borrowing
conditions. (b) Eligibility: term loans are provided for the purchase of plant and
machinery, and in special cases buildings, by companies engaged in manufacturing
and processing industries. Term loans may also be provided for companies in the
industrial sector wishing to convert existing oil-fired boilers to coal-fired, or to
install new coal-fired boilers or other energy-saving plant and equipment. Recently,
term loans have become available under certain conditions for the estabishment
of tourist accommodation. There is no fixed limit for the amount of a DFC loan.
The proportion of plant, expenditure financed is variable and depends on the
overall level of shareholders' funds in the project. (c) Interest rates: present rates
are between 11.5 and 14 percent. Rates depend on current money-market rates
and have moved up with the cost of borrowing over the last 3 years. (2) Export
Finance The corporation began its export finance scheme in late 1977. (a) Term:
the term of the advance, which is in the form of a commercial bill, is related to
the usual conversion time from raw material stage to receipt of export proceeds,
with periods of up to 180 days being considered. (b) Eligibility: export finance is


## p. 3005 (#401) ###########################################

30 August
3005
Questions and Replies
available to those companies or individuals exporting manufactured products that
qualify for the increased exports taxation incentives. (c) Interest: interest rates
vary with market conditions and are currently set at 11.25 percent. (3) Leasing
Finance—(a) Term: (i) mobile equipment-terms between 2 to 5 years; (ii) fixed
plant-terms of up to 15 years. (b) Eligibility: any company, partnership, or
individual engaged in or servicing industry and planning an approved project is
eligible. Finance is usually available for the leasing of mobile equipment such as
trucks, trailers, forklifts; fixed manufacturing and servicing machinery; specialised
buildings. (c) Cost of Lease: determined by the market rate. (4) Hire Purchase
Finance (a) Term: between 2 and 4 years. (b) Eligibility: assistance is normally
available to contractors servicing the manufacturing sectors or civil engineering
projects. (c) Finance charge: a charge calculated as a flat rate per annum is made.
It is set in accordance with the market rate and is currently 10 percent. (5) Export
Suspensory Loans (Government Scheme)-(a) Term: the term of the loan is
initially set for 5 years. If a pre-determined export target is met over 3 consecutive
years then the loan is converted to a grant at the end of the 3-year period. There
is a maximum loan of $200,000 (The maximum loan was $100,000 until early
1978.) (b) Eligibility: company or individual engaged in manufacturing and
undertaking a project which will increase New Zealand's manufacturing exports
either directly or indirectly. (c) Interest rate: interest is charged at DFC's normal
term loan rates. (6) Regional Development Suspensory Loans-(and Pacific
Island Industrial Development Suspensory Loans) (Government schemes only
partly administered by DFC). (7) Applied Technology Programme (Government
Scheme)-Three forms of incentive are available: (a) projects grants for applied
research and development. There is a maximum grant level of $10,000 per annum.
(b) commencement grants for the setting up of initial research and development
facilities. There is an annual limit of $20,000 and a maximum duration of 2 years;
and (c) investment finance for all forms of pre-commercial development, excluding
basic research. The nature and level of investment finance will be designed to
meet the needs of individual projects and to reflect the risks involved. Such finance
may include: (i) equity, (ii) contingently repayable loans (repayable out of profits,
royalties, etc.), (iii) joint venture participation, (iv) finance for trial production
runs, (v) pre-production orders. Eligibility-Assistance may be provided for any
project that involves applied research into, or development of, new or improved
industrial processes or products that have good prospects. In addition to the types
of loans described above, DFC offers other financial assistance in certain circum-
stances in the form of guarantees and equity injections. Changes over the last
3 years-Government schemes administered by DFC have been revised over the
past 12 months, and details are available from the Department of Trade and
Industry. Of DFC loans, the major change has been the commencement of the
export finance scheme to provide exporters with working capital. Interest rates
have risen in accordance with market conditions. In general, DFC interest rates
are comparable with trading bank term loan rates and first-class company
debenture rates.

Capital Equipment Credit Agreements

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Finance: What is

ended March 1978, and in the first 3 months of this financial year, and for what

Zealand dollars is given at at 30 June 1978. Drawings on capital credit agreements
during the period do not reflect these agreements, as many would reflect agree-

were not necessarily drawn on during the period specified.

120.
Women-Select Committee Recommendations
(23/8/78)
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Justice: Which of the
major recommendations of the 1975 Select Committee on the role of women in
New Zealand society have been implemented by the National Government?


## p. 3012 (#408) ###########################################

3012
30 August
Questions and Replies
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: As Minister of Justice
I cannot claim total ministerial responsibility for all women in New Zealand.
However, I do have the responsibility for the Human Rights Commission Act
1977, which incorporates the spirit of many of the recommendations contained
in the report of the select committee. In the justice field, the Government has
implemented the recommendation to provide women with equal responsibility to
men in serving as jurors. The Matrimonial Property Act 1976 replaces the 1963
legislation and is more in accord with the spirit of the report of the select com-
mittee, and the Government has been studying how the principle of the 1976 Act
relates to the position of widows. The maintenance law has been reviewed and
in the new matrimonial legislation that I will be introducing this session there will
be provision for equal rights and duties for both men and women. The Department
of Internal Affairs is responsible for the legislation that now allows New Zealand
citizenship to be transmitted through the mother. The Armed Services have
introduced a new policy for the employment of servicewomen. As far as is
practicable, equal employment and career opportunities and common conditions
of service are now offered to both sexes in the Armed Services.
The revised conditions of employment in the State services announced in 1977
also implement recommendations of the committee. These involve part-time work
and job sharing, and the convening of a joint employer/employee working party
to discuss the feasibility of career structures and permanent status for part-time
employees. The conditions of employment also remove discrimination in other
areas by applying transfer expenses equally to men and women and applying the
allocation of pool housing on the same basis for men and women. The conditions
of employment provisions also allow for paternity leave of 2 weeks leave without
pay
and the extension of maternity leave in 12 months on the basis that a woman's
job, seniority, and service rights will be protected.
121.
Chief Electoral Officer-Liaison with Registrar of
Births, Deaths, and Marriages
(23/8/78)
Mr J. L. HUNT (New Lynn) to ask the Minister of Justice: Is there some
procedure whereby the Registrar of Births Deaths and Marriages informs the
Chief Electoral Officer or the Electorate Officer concerned of deaths and mar-
riages, and could he say what action follows any notification of that.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: Section 46 of the
Electoral Act 1956 provides for the Registrar of Births and Deaths to notify the
electorate officer of the deaths of all adults registered by him. The place of
residence as recorded in the death registration determines the electorate officer
to whom advice is sent. The advice form is the electorate officer's authority to
remove the name of the deceased from the electoral roll. Section 47 of the Electoral
Act 1956 provides for a notice to be sent by the Registrar of Marriages to the
electorate officer after a notice of intended marriage has been lodged. The pro-
posed date of marriage is included in the information advice, and after a reason-
able period, the electorate officer sends a notice to the newly married woman
seeking confirmation of her marriage and of her new address as well as her new
name, if she has changed her name after marriage. Upon the bride completing
her portion of the notice, appropriate steps are taken to amend the electoral roll
if necessary. However, if the bride is residing after marriage in an electorate
other than that in which she was enrolled before marriage, she cannot be registered
in the new electorate until she has lived there 3 months. She would be informed
of her application after residing at the new address for 3 months. Section 47 (3)
provides that a married woman in this circumstance could, if need be, vote on the
roll in her maiden name if the appropriate changes had not been made before the
poll.
122.
Cancer Treatment, Auckland-TV1 Comment
(23/8/78)
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to ask the Minister of Health: Is the
statement by Mr Gordon Dryden in the TV1 programmme of Sunday, 13 August,
to the effect that Professor Wright, in his 1974 report, claimed that the success
rate for treatment of cancer cases at Auckland was only 50 percent of the rate


## p. 3013 (#409) ###########################################

30 August
3013
Questions and Replies
achieved in other parts of the world correct, and could he indicate what statements
were made by Professor Wright in his report on the quality of cancer services in
Auckland at that time and what improvements, if any, have been made since
that time?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The statement made by Mr
Gordon Dryden is incorrect. Nowhere in Professor Wright's report did he claim
that the success rate for treatment of cancer cases in Auckland was only 50 per-
cent of the rate achieved in other parts of the world. In fact, in his summary of
the section of his report referring to term of reference (1)—"The standard of
the practice of chemotherapy and immunotherapy practised at Auckland Hospital
since the first day of December 1972 in the treatment of cancer"-Professor
Wright stated, "I have found the practice of chemotherapy for cancerous con-
ditions in the haematology service at the Auckland Public Hospital to be high
by world standards". Later in his report, under term of reference (4), he stated:
"Auckland has four important hospitals concerned with cancer-the Auckland
Public Hospital, Green Lane, Middlemore and National Women's with specialist
clinics. At each of these places, there are modern units capable and interested in
care of cancer cases as their Specialties... It should be realised that in Auckland,
in each of these fields, physiological, pathological and surgical expertise has been
brought to a high level, in many instances high international level.”
Since the Wright report, the department of oncology has been restructured
clinically and administratively. The head of the department is as associate pro-
fessor with a 5/10 hospital commitment. Other additional staff include a chemo-
therapist and tutor specialist. More junior medical staff, clerks, and technicians
have also been appointed. Physical accommodation has been improved by moving
into the new block at Auckland Hospital. On the radiotherapy side, an additional
radiotherapist and a new radiation oncologist have been appointed.

128.
LPG-Price per Bottle
(23/8/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What prices
have been approved for filling each of the three 10 lb bottles of LPG labelled
NZIG, Rockgas, and Cadac; and is there any reason why filling the Cadac bottle
at some stations should cost $1.05 more than filling the other two?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The bottle-filling charges
currently allowed in the Wellington area to the two main distributors of LPG are:
Rockgas, $3.65 for a 10 lb bottle; NZIG, $4.28 for a 10 lb bottle. The prices
allowed for filling the Cadac bottles are: Rockgas $4.70 for a 10 lb bottle; NZIG,
$4.13 for a 7 lb bottle. The distribution processes associated with the Cadac
bottles are said to be less economic than those associated with the other bottles.
This is because of the nature of the inlet valve on the Cadac bottle, which is said
to restrict the flow of gas, resulting in a longer filling time and increased wastage
during filling.

130.
Fishing Vessels-Duty-free Import Scheme
(23/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: How many
fishing vessels of 21 m or more have been imported under the duty-free importa-
tion scheme by individual fishermen, how many have been imported under this
scheme by companies, and are all those vessels fishing less preferred species?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: Under the duty-free
importation of fishing vessels scheme, 14 vessels over 21 metres in length have been
imported into New Zealand, 13 by companies and 1 by an individual fisherman.
Approvals have been given for another 8 vessels, 1 of which is for an individual.
Approval was granted for the importation of these vessels on the basis that they
would fish predominantly for the less preferred species and would not interfere
unduly with the fishing operations of the existing smaller New Zealand boats.
Since July 1977 a condition of importation has been that the applicant should
continue developing underexploited fish stocks.

Fishing Nets lost from Trawlers
(23/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Fisheries: Has he seen
the article in the New Zealand Herald of 31 July 1978 on the problems with lost
and abandoned mono-filament fishing nets, and, if it is correct that trawlers are

135.
Area School Teachers-Salaries
(23/8/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Could
he explain why a part-time teacher in the secondary division of an area school
is paid at a lower hourly rate than if the school had remained a district high
school?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Secondary teachers
in district high schools are paid under the secondary teachers salary determination
E97, which provides for an hourly rate for part-time teachers of 1/855th of the
annual rate of salary. Area school teachers are paid under the area schools salary
determination E100, which provides for an hourly rate for part-time teachers of
1/1000th of the annual rate of salary (the same as for primary teachers). The
fractions are based on the number of weeks the schools are open each year.
Secondary schools are open for 38 weeks each year, while area schools are open
for 40 weeks each year, as are primary schools.

being reprinted.

136B
Rent Appeal Board
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm
that tenants seeking a rent appeal decision on any particular rent increase are
still expected to pay the new increased rent, even though an application has been
lodged with the Rent Appeal Board in their region, and can he further confirm
that, even if the rent is reduced as a result of an appeal, no compensation is made
to the tenant for the rent he has paid in the meantime over and above the fair
rent decided by the Rent Appeal Board?
Hon. F. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: In terms of the Rent
Appeal Act 1973 there is no provision that empowers a tenant not to pay an
increased rent pending the outcome of an application to a Rent Appeal Board
to assess an equitable rent. If a Rent Appeal Board fixes the equitable rent of
a tenant's premises at less than the rent he is currently paying then, in terms of
section 11 of the Act, the tenant may recover any excess rent from the date, fixed
by the Rent Appeal Board, of the commencement of the new rent.
137.
Air New Zealand-Provincial Routes
(11/8/78)
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) to the Minister of Civil Aviation and
Meteorological Services: Can he state whether the television news report that Air
New Zealand is considering disposing of some of the provincial routes, such as
Kaitaia-Auckland, to private airlines is correct, and, if so, does he support the
proposal?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services) replied: There is no proposal for Air New Zealand to dispose of any of its
provincial services. The Company is undertaking a study of the feasibility of
applying a different type of aircraft to some low traffic volume routes in the domestic
network. If this proves to be feasible the aircraft types contemplated would be such as
to sustain a level of operational efficiency and customer service consistent with or
better than those provided at present by F27 aircraft. The study will not be completed
for several months and in the event that change is contemplated local interests that
may be affected will be consulted.

144.
Practice Nurse Scheme
(10/8/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Health: What are the
conditions of the practice nurse scheme applying to nurses employed by urban
general practitioners, and how do these conditions differ from those for practice
nurses employed by rural practitioners?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The distinctions between urban and
rural practitioners for the purposes of the practice nurse schemes were removed with
effect from 1 July 1977. It may be remembered that the National Party manifesto
stated that the Government would do this. Both the 50 percent and 100 percent
schemes were made available to all general practitioners. The essential features of the
scheme are: (1) 50 percent subsidy scheme-(a) for the nurse's professional services
at the surgery, a refund of 50 percent of the nurse's salary; (b) for domiciliary visiting
by the practice nurse, the payment of a patient benefit of $1.25 for ordinary patients
and $3 for special group patients; and (c) a motor vehicle allowance at the rate of 16c
per kilometre. (2) 100 percent subsidy scheme-(a) for the nurse's professional
services, a refund of 100 percent of the nurse's salary; and (b) for domiciliary visiting,
a motor vehicle allowance of 16c per kilometre. Conditions of subsidy applying to
both schemes are that no general medical services benefit may be claimed when
services are rendered solely by the practice nurse.

short notice. The best information available on this subject is contained in the report
of the Hospital Advisory Council's committee on renal dialysis, which was recently
released to interested parties. The report states that planning should be based on a
new patient intake of 30 patients per 1 000 000 population a year. It goes on to

Pureora State Forest-Logging Policies
(10/8/78)
Mr WETERE (Western Maori) to the Minister of Forests: Has he seen the
New Zealand Herald of 4 August, in which a Mr W. Campbell claims that the selective
logging in the Pureora State Forest was causing massive damage to the trees left
standing, and that “the conditions of timber sale agreements were being seriously
breached, with excessively wide forest roads and timber haulage tracks and damage
to streams and the forest canopy", and, if so, are these allegations correct; and, if they
are, what measures is the Forest Service taking to protect the forest that is left?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply
on behalf of the Minister of Forests. "Yes, I have seen the claims by Mr W. J.
Campbell in relation to logging damage in Pureora Forest. It is possible that, because
in the general area being worked some clear felling had taken place prior to the
introduction of selection logging, the company has been the target of some unfair
criticism. The percentage of merchantable timber to be removed has been set by the
Forest Service, and the company is meeting this specification. A rubber-tyred loader
has been introduced to the operation and this has reduced the size of the loading areas
by 75 percent. Roading has been under the control of the Forest Service since June,
and width of main and secondary roads has been reduced to the minimum consistent
with safe working. Regular inspections by Pureora staff indicate that the standard of
logging is now satisfactory."

161.
Liquor Referendum
(10/8/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Justice: Has any
consideration been given to not holding a liquor referendum in conjunction with the
1978 general election, and can he indicate whether any trends in voting have been
apparent over the past 15 years in this poll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Government has not
given any consideration to amending the Licensing Act 1908 this year to abolish the
triennial liquor poll. The following trends are discernible from the last five polls.
Support for national continuance has fluctuated between 67.5 percent and 69.2
percent. Support for State purchase and control peaked at 18.3 percent in 1969 and
declined to 14.9 percent in 1975. Support for prohibition dropped to 13.3 percent in
1969, but rose 2.5 points to 15.8 percent in 1975. This quite clearly shows
overwhelming support for national continuance, a decline in support for State
purchase and control, and a minor increase in the prohibition vote.

February 1971, has a lower maximum salary than an assistant teacher in a secondary
school, and that the same is also true for F3, F2, and Fl teachers in area schools who
were in the secondary service prior to 1 February 1971; and, if so, in the event of no
action being taken by the teachers' professional organisation, what does he propose to

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): It is correct that those non-

Conditions of Employment Act 1977. The two teacher organisations concerned-the
NZEI and the PPTA-have lodged claims with the Education Service Committee,
and I am advised that the committee would expect to deal with any implications for

Planning Council
(11/8/78)
Mr LATTER (Marlborough), on behalf of Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) to the
Minister of National Development: What actions have been taken by the Planning
Council to meet the Government's requirement that it take over the work of the
Monetary and Economic Council?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of National Development): The New Zealand
Planning Council was requested by the Government to take over two tasks from the
former Monetary and Economic Council. The first was to complete a report on New
Zealand and the EEC on which the Monetary and Economic Council had already
started work. The text of this report has now been finished. More generally, the
Planning Council was asked to assume the role of monitoring economic policy and
development. To this end, an economic monitoring group has been set up. This is
fully independent, and will publish its own report. The group is chaired by a
memeber of the New Zealand Planning Council and is serviced by the Planning
Council's secretariat and the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research. The
group's first report is expected shortly. In addition to these functions that were taken
over when the Monetary and Economic Council was disbanded, the Planning
Council is continuing to study and publish reports on many aspects of economic
development as part of its own terms of reference.

178.
Overseas Students-Political Activities
(11/8/78)
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: Have there been
any cases in which political activities by overseas students studying in New Zealand
have caused embarrassment to the New Zealand Government?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Each year my department receives
a number of applications for permanent residence for overseas students. One of the
reasons put forward by those students who want to remain here is that they fear
prosecution on return to their home countries because of views they have expressed or
activities they have taken part in here. To allow students to remain in New Zealand
for that reason would undermine the aim of the student policy, which is to train
students so that they can assist in the development of their home countries. To save
any embarrassment to the Government or students, it is important from time to time
that students be made aware that they should not become involved in political
activities. The previous Government took a similar attitude in the case of the first
South African scholarship holder, when the then Minister of Immigration obtained
from the New Zealand University Students Association on 21 June 1974, a written
undertaking that stated inter alia: "We are aware of your concern regarding the
political activities of Mr Isaacs during his period in New Zealand. As we agreed
during the interview with you, the NZUSA will advise Mr Isaacs of your concern and
will not encourage him to take any active political role in this country."

votes are, and have always been, issued to overseas voters without their enrolments
being checked at the overseas post. All posts likewise have a supply of registration
cards (El) and also of the information pamphlet (E12B), and stocks are replenished
on request. Lists of streets and places in each electorate are also provided.

Television Licence Fees-Hotels/Motels
(15/8/78)
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) to the Minister of Broadcasting: What
is the justification for charging full and separate licence fees for every television set
installed in a hotel or motel room?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): Such licence-charging
provisions are based on the principle that all television receivers should be licensed at
the rates laid down and that the ordinary viewer should not be expected to subsidise
business enterprises. That principle has been adopted by successive Governments.
Since accommodation establishments tend to look upon television as a factor in
attracting custom and usually build the licence fee into their tariff structures, any
departure from the present basis into multiple licensing could, I believe, amount to a
substantial subsidy.

(15/8/78)

medical certificates covering alleged sicknesses after the events?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON Minister of Justice: I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Labour. "It is assumed that when the honourable member refers to 'sickness' he
means sickness or disability caused by accident. Neither I nor the commissioner are
aware of any widespead issuing of medical certificates referring to past incapacity. It

certificate being given for an incapacity that the doctor has not seen personally. This
has happened on a few occasions."

Farm Workers' Award
(16/8/78)
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Labour:
Has the increase in the farm workers' award led to an increase in the amount paid by
farmers to farm workers under the speical work scheme, and, if so, by how much?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Farmers employing farm workers
under the farm employment scheme are, like all other people employing labour,
legally obliged to pay at the least minimum rate specified in the appropriate award
made under the Agricultural Workers Act. If the amount previously paid was less
than the new minimum rate, the farmer is required to increase the farms worker's
pay. If the new wage payable to a farm worker employed under the farm employment
scheme falls between $120 and $150 a week there will be an increase in the subsidy
paid by the Department of Labour to the farmer.

Motor cycle Injury Statistics
(16/8/78)
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the
Minister of Labour: Will he advise the House, from the Accident Compensation
Commission's actuarial statistics of motor-cycle related injuries, what percentage is
caused by motor-cycle driver fault and what percentage is caused by other road users?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The accident compensation
scheme abolishes considertion of fault. Accordingly, the Accident Compensation
Commission does not collect statistics from which fault can be attributed to those
involved in accidents, nor would it be administratively possible to do so. Having
regard to the disputes that used to be involved in the establishment of fault, the
commission does not accept as reliable any estimates or opinions given at the present
day on percentages of blame attributable to different classes of persons or vehicles
involved in accidents.

Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act
(17/8/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Social Welfare: How many
sections of the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act 1975 still remains to be
implemented, and when will this be done; how many sections have already been
implemented; and, of that number, how many were implemented by this Government
and how many by the last Labour Government?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Disabled Persons
Community Welfare Act, which was based on the recommendations of the March
1972 Royal Commission on Social Security in New Zealand, was finally passed by the
Labour Government at approximately 3 a.m. on Friday, 10 October 1975, the day
that Parliament dissoved for the 1975 general election. The Act contains a total of 32
sections, but only one was implemented with the passing of the Act, and, because of
its defeat, Labour took no further action. Of the remaining 31 section, 30 have been
fully implemented. The remaining one, section 11, has been partially implemented by
the present National Government. The advisory council has made recommendations
concerning the full implementation of section 11, and its recommendations have been
considered, having regard to other commitments on Government expenditure. To
summarise, 31 of the 32 sections have been implemented and all 32 sections have been
acted on by the National Government.

position 3 months or more hence.
