Trade Union Amalgamation
(17/8/78)
Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Labour: To what extent have
efforts been made by the Federation of Labour, the Government, or other interested
parties to amalgamate New Zealand's plethora of unions?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Labour. "The Federation of Labour has drawn up 10 industrial groups
for affiliated unions to be organised into. I understand that these are still the subject
of discussion between the Federation of Labour and affiliated unions. It has yet to be
seen whether these discussions result in a genuine amalgamation of unions. The most
potentially fruitful means of achieving amalgamation is through the composite
agreement procedure in the Industrial Relations Act. This enables two or more
unions within an industry to join together and formulate a common set of claims. The
coming together in negotiations in this way represents a significant first step towards
eventual amalgamation. The composite agreement procedure is being increasingly
used by unions in certain industries, and I am hopeful that it will eventually be used
by the parties in the freezing industry."

Health Standards of Children, South Auckland
(17/8/78)
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Health: What action is being
taken to check health standards of children in the south and south-east Auckland
area, and what steps are being taken towards parental involvement?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): On 20 December 1977, a contract was
signed between the Department of Health and the Plunket Society whereby the
society assumed responsibility for the health surveillance of infants and pre-school
children in the south Auckland health district, allowing the department's public
health nurses to concentrate their efforts on the health of school-age children. In May
1978, a pilot scheme, using a number of schools in the south and south-east Auckland
area was implemented in order to extend school health services. The scheme involves
the public health nurse being attached to one or two primary schools with a total
school population in the region of 800, and includes the screening of all new entrants.
The nurse also carries out her usual public health duties in a small area around the
school, encompassing as far as possible the homes of those children attending school.
A further pilot scheme is in operation in two south Auckland primary schools that
share the services of a public health nurse on a full-time basis.

Inflation
(18/8/78)
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Statistics: Can he
explain why there has not been a decline of 7 percent in the New Zealand inflation
rate, in view of the answer he gave to a written question by the member for Hutt on 15
August, in which he indicated that import price rises in 1975 led eventually to an
approximate increase in the consumer price index of 9.7 percent, while the
corresponding figures for 1976 and 1977 were 2.6 percent and 2.7 percent
respectively?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Statistics): In his written reply
referred to, the Minister of Statistics provided estimates of the contribution to the
increases in the consumer price index that could be expected from rises in import
prices during each year from 1973 to 1977. There is nothing in the answer to suggest
that the consumer price index should decline, nor that the rate of increase should
decline as a result. Import prices are one of many factors that influence the consumer
price index, and, whilst import prices have risen less steeply since 1975, internal
factors have tended to enlarge their contribution to increases in the consumer price
index.

water heating is not seen as a good buy, the consumer will save less than $22 a year
with it, and it would take about 45 years to pay off a solar heater costing $1,000?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I am aware of the position taken by the
Auckland Electric Power Board. A number of views are held on the economies of solar
water heaters. Nevertheless, the investigations carried out by my ministry have
satisfied me that, provided the cost is reasonable and the system is well installed, the
savings will be worth while under today's conditions. With increased production
volumes of solar water heaters and inevitable rises in energy prices, I would expect
the economies to be even more favourable in the future.

269.
Consumer Price Index
(22/8/78)
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Statistics: Does the
consumer price index provide a statistical series roughly comparable with the similar
price indexes in the United Kingdom, Australia, the United States, Japan, and West
Germany, and, if so, can he advise the House of the most recent annual percentage for
each country, including New Zealand?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister of Statistics): Although the
consumer price indexes of New Zealand, Australia, the United Kingdom, the united
States, Japan, and West Germany are all based on the general recommendations of
the United Nations International Labour Organisation, there are differences of a
conceptual and coverage nature when the indexes are compared with each other.
They differ particluarly in respect of the statistical formulae used to calculate them,
the geographic and household coverage in the weighting pattern, and the range and
treatment of goods and services covered. Consequently, although international
comparisons can be made, these must be treated as approximations. Increases for the
latest 12-monthly periods available are as follows: Japan, 3.5 percent; West Germany,
2.1 percent for the year ended May 1978; United Kingdom, 7.4 percent; Australia,
7.9 percent; United States, 7.4 percent; New Zealand, 12.2 percent-for the year
ended June 1978. Because of the factors referred to, I would emphasise that these
comparisons have definite limitations.

272.
Bank Officers Union-Ballot
(22/8/78)
Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: Can he advise the house
how the Bank Officers Union maintains its membership roll and whether it is in a
position to conduct a ballot on the unqualified preference clause under sections 99 or
100 of the Industrial Relations Act?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I cannot advise how the Bank
Officers Union maintains its membership roll. Its rules require that a register of the
names, occupations, and addresses shall be kept. The ballot on the unqualified
preference clause, under sections 99 and 100 of the Industrial Relations Act 1973,
must be conducted by the registrar or an officer of the Department of Labour
designated by him. Section 100 requires the union to supply the registrar with a roll
containing the correct names and addresses of persons entitled to vote. The persons
who are entitled to vote are those who are bound by the unqualified preference clause.
In theory, of course, these people should be members of the union, and therefore
would be on the roll provided by the union. It is, however, common knowledge that
not every person bound by an unqualified preference clause is a member of the union.
In this respect the Bank Officers Union would not be able to supply a complete roll
from its register of members only.

Hydro Projects--Employment Opportunities
(22/8/78)
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Energy: Do small hydro
programmes offer employment opportunities in the regions in which they are located,
and can he give an indication of present and prospective job opportunities arising
from those projects?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): There are three distinct stages to small
hydro development-an initial assessment of potential schemes, detailed
investigation of the most promising sites, and actual construction. Virtually no local
labour is required for initial assessment. Detailed investigation may involve extensive
site drilling, construction of roads for access, and other engineering activities that
should involve local firms. Power station and transmission line construction would
require both unskilled and skilled labour, and civil and other types of contracts.
Construction work is controlled by the local supply authority, which decides on the
extent to which local resources are used.

changes made in the Australian Budget in so far as they affect the import of New
Zealand manufactured goods into Australia?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The
information that I have so far received suggests that the only aspect of the Australian
Budget of direct relevance to New Zealand export trade is the proposal to apply an
additional duty of 12.5 percent to certain goods subject to quantitative import
controls by Australia. Some reports in the media suggested that that move might
affect New Zealand exports. I have since stated that confirmation has been received
that the additional duty will not be applied to goods of New Zealand origin. In those
circumstances, the additional duty could prove beneficial to New Zealand exporters
in that it will improve their competitive position vis-a-vis supplies from third
countries.

Gleneagles Agreement
(23/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: How does
he know whether or not New Zealand is complying with the requirements of the
Gleneagles Agreement if, as stated on 18 August in answer to a written question, the
Government's records are not complete and it does not know what its citizens are
doing overseas?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The member for
Wanganui is implying that the Government should keep the activities overseas of its
citizens, even of an individual citizen, under surveillance. I can assure him that this
was never intended at the time of the Gleneagles Agreement, which specifically states
that it is "for each Government to determine, in accordance with its laws," the
methods by which the commitments accepted under the Gleneagles Agreement
should be carried out. The Gleneagles Agreement requires the Government to
withhold any form of support for, and take every practical step to discourage, contact
or competition by New Zealanders with sporting organisations, teams, or sportsmen
from South Africa. This the Government has done.

Maori Community Development
(23/8/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Maori Affairs: What changes
have been made in the field of Maori community development, and on what is the
emphasis being put at present?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): The main change in the
field of Maori community development has been the stronger emphasis on working
with Maori organisations in mobilising the resources of Maoridom. I refer here to
Maori committees, women's leagues, marae committees, and tribal councils. The
priority has shifted from working mostly with individuals and families requiring
welfare help to a massive effort on youth development in the fields of education and
vocational training. Programmes have been launched, such as those being
undertaken by Howard Morrison in the schools and by Maori community officers-
and a more recent programme, approved by the Government, called Tu Tangata,
which sets up task-oriented community organisations to improve Maori academic
attainment. What is already emerging are homework centres, ideas about basic skills
centres, and a gathering wave of creative ideas for community development-from
the Maori people themselves.

Windthrown Logs, Canterbury
(23/8/78)
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), to the
Minister of Forests: What volume of windthrown logs and sawn timber is still held
in stock in Canterbury, and what have been the net returns for those disposed of to
date?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Approximately 15 300 cubic metres
of logs are held in trial storage under water sprinklers at Balmoral Forest and
approximately 41 600 cubic metres of sawn timber are held in stockpile in
Christchurch. The net return to the Forest Service arising from the disposal of
salvaged roundwood on both the domestic and export markets since the recovery
operation commenced in September 1975, and including the costs of handling export
logs on behalf of private sellers, amounted to approximately $3.4 million. The
stockpiling and marketing of surplus sawn timber arising also as a consequence of the
recovery operation has been undertaken by a Government-funded company, Timber
Stockpile Ltd., the directors of which represent both the Government and the
Canterbury sawmilling industry. Now that sawlog recovery is virtually completed,
sawn timber is being drawn from the stockpile. So far, only 3500 cubic metres out of a
total of approximately 45 000 cubic metres have been sold, and it is too soon to give a
meaningful statement on the financial viability of the venture.

Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Energy: Has his department

Ohinemuri and the Waitawheta Rivers?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The possibility of using the Ohinemuri
and Waitawheta Rivers jointly to produce electricity has been investigated by the
Ministry of Works and Development acting as consultants to the electricity division of
the Ministry of energy. It was calculated that a power station in the Karangahake
Gorge might produce 15 to 20 GWh per annum with an installed capacity of 5 to 7
MW. The scheme was considered by the Thames Valley Electric Power Board, which
ultimately decided not to proceed with it because of economic and environmental
reasons.

301.
Meat Exports
(23/8/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru), on behalf of Mr BRUCE BARCLAY
(Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Agriculture: Is the statement, reported in
the Dominion of 17 August by Mr Hilgendorf, Chairman of the Meat Board, correct—
that "New Zealand would be open to accusations of subsidising meat exports if the
Government's minimum prices exceeded market prices"?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): No more so than in 1975 when
the Labour Government gave $35 million to the Meat Producers Board to lift the
price to the farmer. Any form of Government assistance to meet producers can
theoretically lay New Zealand open to accusations of subsidising meat exports. I
would not expect the action taken by the Government in the Budget to make any
significant difference. The purpose of the supplementary minimum prices is to
provide farmers with an assured and more realistic basis for forward planning than
was provided by the minimum prices set under the statutory schemes. The levels set
are not unrelated to the market prospects, and I do not believe that any substantial
supplementary payments will be necessary. I would add that in no way can the
Government's scheme be equated with export subsidies paid by other countries—for,
example the EEC-which are a consequence of high prices on tightly protected
domestic markets and the generation of surpluses that cannot be exported without
massive subsidies.

upon. At my request, as set out in the introduction to the report, many individuals
have already written to me or to the department commenting on aspects of the report.

calamity and disaster of the highest proportions. Houses were built in areas in which there
were no schools, telephones, hospitals, or motorways. Under the National Government

provide social welfare services for the young. As a result of National's policies, 6000 families
will be able to buy existing houses in areas in which there are already services. Those are
6000 reasons why the people should support the Government. It is miles ahead of the former
Labour Government in providing a decent standard of housing.
When the member for Manukau was the Minister of Housing he approved a subdivision
in my electorate. He made no provision for a school, for telephones, or for a bus service. The
Government has relocated housing so that people do not race into that type of subdivision.

facilities. About 200 people living in the subdivision I have mentioned are waiting for
telephones, and the service will be connected in October.
The Government has corrected the mess left by the Labour Government. The Labour
Government's housing policies placed a strain on young people buying their own homes.
Section prices increased by 150 percent and house prices by 100 percent. Housing prices are
now stable. There is no real increase in the price of homes. I am pleased that 6000 loans are

increase in values of the most recently built homes-homes 2 to 5 years old-which are so
hard to sell. That type of home is even harder to sell when people are not allowed to buy
existing homes with loans.
The Government has reduced the number of new homes being built, because young
people are permitted to buy empty houses with loan money. A headline in the Auckland Star
of 28 August states: "State houses empty as more people get choosy". A headline in the
Dominion of 30 August states: "State erects house-to-let signs as queues end". That is a
dramatic turnround in housing. The Minister of Housing has had homes built for people who
need them. The member for St. Kilda, who is trying to interject, allowed house prices to
double, which did nothing for young families. Opposition members want to continue that
policy.
If a Labour Government should be returned to office it would flood areas like west
Auckland with State houses. It would flood Te Atatu North with State houses instead of
doing what the National Government has done-have a New Zealand-wide competition to
design a home for that area in twenty-first century style. Under the Labour Government
housing ate up valuable building materials. It covered some of the finest farm land with
houses, but provided few amenities. I had to call the Social Development Council into my
electorate to study the social disaster created by the Labour Government.

amenities after 15 years of neglect by the National Government. The pious comments made
by the member for Waitemata do not go down well in the House.
I refer to question 243, which deals with domestic inflation. Inflation today should be

at 10 percent, is the highest in the country's history.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 25 August 1978
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): When the House rose on Friday afternoon, I was answering
certain comments that had been made by the member for Southern Maori, who had used
some colourful, if not accurate, language about the Bill and about the Minister of Social
Welfare.
It is perhaps significant that the member said nothing at all about any clause other than
that relating to de facto marriages. Hers was a complete and utter obsession, to the point
that I imagine not only the House but the country would despair as to whether the Labour
Party had any interest in any matter other than de facto relationships and the domestic
purposes benefit.
In the case referred to by the honourable member, there was no question of the
Government victimising any innocent solo mother. The simple facts are that a benefit was
stopped; an unsuccessful appeal was made to the Social Security Commission, followed by
another unsuccessful appeal to the independent Social Security Appeal Authority--both
bodies supported by the Labour Administration, and dealing with legislation passed by the
Labour Government in 1973; and, finally, on a point of law the Supreme Court was invited
by the Social Security Appeal Authority to reconsider certain aspects of law. The facts were
irrefutable, despite what the member for Southern Maori might have suggested.
The Supreme Court was invited by the appeal authority to reconsider a point of law
only, and it was at that stage, interpreting the Labour Government's law of 1973, that the
Supreme Court, in turn, told the appeal authority to reconsider its decision on the basis of
the law as expounded and interpreted by the Supreme Court, Mr Justice Barker presiding.
That is where the matter ends. The Bill merely amends the 1973 law to bring it into line with
the other definitions of "marriage" contained in the Social Security Act.
Mr Rogers: What a boring speech.
Mr McLAY: The member for Onehunga might want to make his contribution to the
debate later, but I doubt whether he or any other Labour member is prepared to get away
from his obsession with just one clause of the Bill-and perhaps that is understandable,
because the Bill contains many constructive provisions that are of benefit to the community


## p. 3065 (#461) ###########################################

30 August
3065
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
at large. Those provisions were announced in the Budget earlier this year, and it is not
surprising that Labour members of the House should refrain from discussing them in the
Chamber, because they know full well that each is a matter on which, between 1972 and
1975, the Labour Government could have acted, but failed to do so.
Clause 9 of the Bill legislates for a handicapped child's allowance of $8 a week, as
announced in the Budget, payable from 18 October 1978. The headquarters of the North
Shore branch of the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped is in my electorate. It is an
enormously effective, dedicated, and hard-working organisation, with which I am proud to
have had close contact over the past 3 years. I know that members of that organisation
welcomed the Budget announcement because the society, through both its vice-president
and as an organisation, has written to me expressing its thanks. That is hardly surprising,
because an estimated 4000 children will quality for the allowance, at an annual cost to the
Government of about $1.5 million; 4000 handicapped children—or, more correctly, their
parents-will benefit, without a means test or an income test. Small wonder that Labour
members refrain from referring to that provision.
Clause 29—another provision that Labour members have seen fit to ignore-legislates
for a new income test for beneficiaries, which was also announced in the Budget. The
purpose of the new test is to give beneficiaries a greater incentive to help themselves by
earning a supplementary income.
I came back yesterday morning bearing the views of a group of solo mothers whom I
met during the weekend-hard-working, conscientious women, anxious to look after their
families to the best of their ability, and anxious also to get out and obtain extra employment,
not just for economic reasons, but for sound social reasons as well. They said they welcomed
the new income test, and felt it was fair to them, to the taxpayers who meet the bill, and,
most important of all, to their families and particularly their children.
Members will recall that, under the former income test, income up to $17 a week for
single beneficiaries and $21 a week for widows and domestic purposes beneficiaries with
dependent children was disregarded, income over the allowable income and up to $25 a
week reduced the benefit by $1 for every $2 earned, and income over $25 a week reduced the
benefit by $3 for every $4 earned. There is no doubt-and certainly no disagreement in the
Chamber-that, particularly in the latter period over which that test has applied, there has
been substantial disincentive to beneficiaries to earn more than $21 a week.
The new income test provides for allowable income to be increased to $25 a week, but—
and this is more important-income over $25 a week and up to $40 a week will reduce the
benefit by only 40c for each dollar earned, while income over $40 a week will reduce the
benefit by 80c for each dollar earned.
The beneficiaries and the solo mothers I spoke to on Monday now know that a
beneficiary has every incentive to earn $40 a week in excess of her benefit before there is any
real penalty to her benefit. That is best illustrated by taking the example of a widow with two
children. The member for Manukau and I addressed a meeting of the Auckland branch of
the Widows and Widowers Association earlier this year, and I know from what we were told
then that this is the sort of income test and personal situation about which those people were
most concerned.
Under the previous provisions, a widow with two children, earning $40 a week over and
above her widow's benefit, would have been entitled to an abated widow's benefit of $64.03
a week; under the new income test, her entitlement will be $71.28 a week, an increase of
$7.25-more than 10 percent of her total benefit-as a result of the 1978 Budget provision
now being incorporated in the law by this legislation.
For those reasons, on behalf of the constituents I represent, and particularly on behalf
of the North Shore branch of the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped, I welcome the
special benefit of $8 a week for handicapped children. On behalf of solo parents, widows,
and widowers who will receive effectively a 10 percent increase in their cash in hand as a
result of the abatement provisions, I welcome the Social Security Amendment Bill.

interests in their employment.

working for a common employer. They are certainly organised, and by the employer. They
certainly have a common interest in their employer, and certainly have a common interest in
their employment.

I have lived through this situation. I was a doctor, and also a member of local
government, in 1951, in Denniston. What started as a lockout on the wharves became a

whether the strike should continue, and whether it was legal under their own constitution
and had been properly declared.
Quite apart from the lockout, it was in my town that the strike finally broke. I had acted

1940, under a Labour Government, there was a general wage order of 5 percent. In April
1942, still under a Labour Government, there was another general wage order of 5 percent.
No increase in social security benefits was granted between 1 April 1939 and 1 May 1942.
The first Labour Government prided itself, and dined out for years, on its supposed record
in social welfare. Two general wage orders, both of 5 percent and totalling cumulatively
more than 10 percent, were granted. After pensioners had waited for 3 years the Labour
Government granted them an increase of 15c a week. I give back to the member for Porirua
his words that the smell of starvation was in the air. Let us now turn to the record of the
second Labour Government under the leadership of the late Sir Walter Nash.

It was announced in this year's Budget that legislation would be introduced for the
payment of a non-taxable allowance of $8 a week for the parents of seriously physically or
mentally handicapped children. The Bill now before the House provides for that allowance,
which was one of the recommendations in the report of the McCarthy royal commission,
which as Minister of Social Welfare I received in March 1972. There were some 110
recommendations in that report, and the National Government implemented about 58 of
them, mostly in the monetary benefit field. The allowance for handicapped children was a
complex recommendation and we did not implement it, but we said we would provide
legislation the next year. However, we went out of office, and the Labour Government did
not implement it in its 3 years in office. I pay tribute to the Minister of Social Welfare for the

support it in a niggardly way, but it will give us no credit for it.
In its 1975 election manifesto the National Party also promised that the income test for
social security beneficiaries would be relaxed. The necessary provisions are in this Bill, and
will come into effect in October. The allowable income is increased to $1,300 a year, or $25 a
week. At present the allowable income is $21 a week for widows and domestic purposes
beneficiaries with dependent children and $17 a week for other beneficiaries.
The Bill also endorses the legislation introduced and passed in 1976, which provided for
national superannuation. That measure provided a higher pension payment level to all who

other benefit.

beneficiaries to encourage them to become more self-supporting.

entitled to an unemployment benefit if he is not employed because of a strike either by
himself or by fellow members of his union at the same place of employment." I remind
members opposite that this Government has introduced legislation under which workers can
be laid off and declared redundant through no fault of their own. That legislation, read in
conjunction with the Bill at present before the House, will mean that workers can be
declared redundant because of a strike affecting other parts of the plant or industry, and that
they will not be entitled to register for the unemployment benefit. Where is the justice in
that? People, through no fault of their own, can be declared redundant by their employers
merely because of some action taken, rightly or wrongly, in another part of the plant.
Irrespective of the rights and wrongs, or whether the employer or employee is at fault, those
affected by the strike can be laid off, and under the provisions in the Bill they will be
penalised by being denied the right to apply for the unemployment benefit. Where is the
justice in that provision? I certainly cannot find any.

rights.

the press report correctly-
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Order! I am in some difficulty when I process notices of

of motion fairly carefully, and I felt that, based on the newspaper article supplied, I could
approve it for presentation in the House. Beyond that, it becomes a debatable issue. The

of order on other grounds.
Mr MALCOLM (Eden): With respect, my point of order is not that the notice of motion

That is a shameless and irresponsible assertion, and it should be withdrawn.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): The point in the notice of motion is that deficiencies in the

Secondary School Staff Appointments
2. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Has he seen a report in the
Western Leader of 15 August in which the associate headmaster of Avondale College, Mr
Maurice Dean, and the headmaster of Kelston Boys High School, Mr Jim Paton, express

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Yes, I have seen the report referred to.
The present system of appointments for secondary teachers is embodied in the Education
(Assessment, Classification and Appointment) Regulations 1976. These regulations were
drawn up and agreed to by the Secondary School Boards Association, the Post-Primary
Teachers Association, and the Department of Education, and are subject to review from
time to time. If the appointment of senior staff is a problem for controlling authorities or for
principals in general, I would expect this to be expressed through the usual channels. If
changes in the regulations involved are deemed desirable by the three interested parties,
appropriate recommendations will then be made for new procedures.
Mr Hunt: While acknowledging the Minister's reply that there are channels to go

to have another look at the system?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The Secondary School Boards Association, the PPTA, and the
department have been reviewing the regulations. However, I remind the honourable
member that the regulations state that an applicant for a senior appointment may, if he
wishes, forward the names of not more than three referees with his application. The board of
governors then contacts the referees, and expects the answers to be back within 3 weeks.
That is a much shorter period than specified by the member in his question.

Retirement Gratuities
4. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister in Charge of

certain companies of offering lump-sum gratuities to directors upon retirement, said to be in
lieu of superannuation; and has his department taken any action when the entitlement to
such a lump sum is converted-upon the death of the director before he reaches compulsory
retirement-to a gratuity paid to the beneficiaries of his estate with the intention that it shall
not constitute part of his dutiable estate?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department): This is a complex and involved area of income tax and estate duty law, and if
the honourable member has any specific case on which he has doubts I should be happy to
have it examined. In general, any lump-sum payment made to a director upon his retirement
in recognition of his services with a company would, under present tax law, be liable to
income tax on the full amount. In regard to the second part of the question, any gratituity
paid by the company to the beneficiaries of a deceased director would normally form part of
that director's dutiable estate in terms of either sections 15 or 16 of the Estate and Gift
Duties Act 1968.

department, but there is no mention of that.

National Superannuation Rate
7. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the Minister of
Social Welfare: When the national superannuation rate reaches 80 percent of the average
weekly wage, what will happen to people receiving additional benefits?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): As I have explained on several
occasions in the past, additional benefit grants to national superannuitants are being phased
out over a period of about 5 years. From 31 August 1978—that is, from today-married
national superannuitants will receive $14.02 a week more than they would have received had
age benefits been retained. The corresponding figure for single superannuitants is $7.39 a
week. Despite the phasing out of the additional benefits, the superannuitants affected are
still significantly better off on national superannuation than they would have been had the
age benefit plus full additional benefit been retained. In addition, national superannuitants
receive a net benefit equal to or better than many in the work force who have dependent
wives and children, and to whom no additional benefits or concessions are available. There
is, therefore, no justification for the continuation of additional benefits to national
superannuitants.
Wool Export Freight Rates
8. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), on behalf of Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch
Central), to the Minister of Agriculture: Is the statement in the "Without a word of a lie"
column in the National Business Review of 9 August correct in its claim that "for the second
time in recent months, the Wool Board may have prevented the introduction of competitive
wool-export freight rates in a continued bid to preserve the profits of the Conference
Lines"?
Hon. H. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): While it is correct that the Bank Lines
have been excluded from participating in the New Zealand - European wool trade, the
statement in the National Business Review is not correct when it attributes the Wool Board's
motive to being "a continuing bid to preserve the profits of the Conference Lines". The
general objective of the Wool Board is to establish, in the interests of growers, the best
possible long-term returns for New Zealand wool. To achieve this end the board has,
amongst other things, the power to negotiate and enter into agreements relating to freight
rates and other terms and conditions for the transport of such wool. My understanding is that
it is the board's view that it is in the New Zealand wool industry's interests to maintain a
continuing shipping service for wool exports. This requirement has to be balanced against
the advantages that might at first be apparent from outside shipping lines offering reduced
freight rates. I understand that, at present, the board considers that the New Zealand wool
industry is best served by the Conference Lines in relation to wool exports to Europe and
North America. Accordingly, it has confined wool shipments to the established lines on the
trade, and this excluded the Bank Lines. As with all its policies, however, the board's
shipping policy is subject to regular review.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can I take it from the Minister's answer that, in fact, the Wool

Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No, the honourable member cannot take that, because that was

Mr Hunt: Notwithstanding the Minister's rather long initial answer, could he now just
answer the question of the member for Christchurch Central? Could he perhaps indicate
whether the statement is correct or not?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: As Minister of Agriculture I am not responsible for the freight
rates. The Wool Board is responsible under the legislation, and, as I pointed out in my
answer, the board has said that the statement in the paper is not correct.
Temporary Employment Programme
9. MARILYN WARING (Raglan), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the
Minister of State Services: Who was responsible for the decision that employment of clerical
and related staff under the temporary employment programme for longer than 1 year should
cease, what is to happen to those affected by this new ruling, and how much notice are these
people to be given?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of State
Services. "The decision was made by the State Services Commission after discussion with the
Department of Labour. Workers under the temporary employment scheme who are doing
clerical and related work are taken on by departments according to the criterion laid down
by the State Services Commission that the work is of low priority and would have been
deferred. By its very nature, work of this type is of short duration. If the job lasts for more
than 1 year then it becomes somewhat more permanent, and the person in the job should be
considered for permanent employment. The commission has advised departments that if the
person is suitable in every way, and there is a vacancy, he should be appointed to the
permanent staff. Those who cannot be appointed to a vacancy will be given 2 weeks' notice."

Samoan Overstayers
13. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Immigration: Has he received a request

Environment-Preservation
19. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister for the Environment: Will he take any
further steps to preserve the natural environment of selected streams like the Wheao
because of outstanding fishing, scenic, and wild habitat value, particularly when hydro
resources could be developed from other waterways lacking the unusual environmental
value of the Wheao?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): At my request, the Commission
for the Environment prepared, and released for public comment on 12 January this year, a
discussion paper on wild and scenic rivers protection. One hundred and ten submissions
were received. On 18 August I released an appraisal by the commissioner of the response to
the discussion paper. The main conclusion is that there is a need for a positive policy
ensuring protection of rivers, or sections of rivers, in their undeveloped state when they have
outstanding wild, scenic, or other natural characteristics. The mechanism for the
development and implementation of an appropriate policy is now being discussed by the
relevant Government departments.

AUCKLAND ELECTRIC POWER BOARD BILL
Introduction
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I move, That leave be given to introduce the
Auckland Electric Power Board Bill. This is a local Bill that I am introducing as the member
for Auckland Central. The Bill has been promoted by the Auckland Electric Power Board in
order to update, amend, and consolidate the Auckland Electric Power Board Act 1921-22.
The purposes and effect of the Bill are as follows. Under the Act the board is responsible for


## p. 3099 (#495) ###########################################

31 August
3099
Auckland Electric Power Board Bill
preparing and administering its own electoral rolls for purposes of election and polls. This
imposes a heavy and unnecessary administrative burden on the board. No similar provisions
apply to power boards constituted under the Electric Power Boards Act 1925, all of which
use the electoral rolls of the territorial authorities in their constituent districts. In practice the
board has also adopted this common-sense procedure, and the Bill brings the board's
legislation into accord with practical and economic reality.
The board's boundaries are defined by the Act by reference to the boundaries of the
territorial authorities within its district. This has meant that where a territorial authority has
altered its boundaries the board's boundaries have been also automatically altered without
reference to the boundaries of other boards. The problem has arisen in respect of an
alteration to the boundaries of the city of Papakura. To overcome it, the Bill redefines the
board's constituent districts to include the whole or any part of any territorial authority
within its district, so permitting the boundaries of territorial authorities to be altered
independently of the board's.
Alterations to the boundaries of the board's district under the Act are by a process
independent of that applying to the districts of boards constituted under the Electric Power
Boards Act 1925. Consequently, any alteration to the board's boundaries or those of a
neighbouring board may result in the two districts either overlapping or separating, so
leaving some area unserved. The Bill seeks to ensure that the boundaries of the board and its
neighbouring electric power boards remain contiguous by adopting the alteration procedure
laid down in the Electric Power Boards Act. This would permit all alterations to be made
simultaneously.
Section 12A of the Act adopts the procedure set out in section 52 of the Local Election
and Polls Act 1976 for the filling of extraordinary vacancies. However, that procedure was
repeated by the Local Government Amendment Act (No. 3) 1977. The Bill provides for a
procedure similar to that in section 51 of the Local Election and Polls Act 1976 but with
minor variation as to the power of the board to choose between the appointment and an
election, selection of appointees, and numbers required for a petition of voters. The Act
provides for a maximum tariff level which inflation has rendered obsolete. It should be noted
that the Electric Power Boards Act 1925 has never contained such a provision. The Bill
repeals this provision.
The board's Act has not been reprinted or systematically consolidated or amended since
its enactment in 1921, and in view of the major nature of some of the above amendments the
Auckland Electric Power Board considered it appropriate to utilise the Bill to this effect.
Thus a number of obsolete provisions concerning the board's takeover of electric works from
the Auckland City Council in the 1920s, loans for preliminary work, recovery of installation
costs as rates, the imprest account, and the board's contract with the Auckland City Council
contained in the schedule to the Act have been repealed. References to other legislation
have been updated and the effect of subsequent legislation noted and incorporated into the
Bill where appropriate. References to currency have been decimalised. All amendments to
the Act have been repealed and their provisions incorporated into the Bill where
appropriate. Sections have been renumbered and the Bill has been divided into parts. A
number of incidental drafting alterations and improvements have also been made.
As a general aim the Bill brings the board's legislation into line with the Electric Power
Boards Act 1925 where appropriate. Some of the amendments to this effect have been
outlined in detail above. Most of the others are minor. A number of additional minor
amendments, which have no parallel in the Electric Power Boards Act 1925, have been
made. It is my duty as member for Auckland Central to introduce the Bill and to explain it as
the power board has put it to me.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I want to raise a couple of
points on the introduction of the Bill because I do not really think that the House is justified
in accepting it. I do not know how many other members have looked carefully through the
material that was made available when the Bill was advertised to them. I assume that
members outside the Auckland area have not done so, because it was not supplied directly to
them. This power board is the largest in the country, but it operates under its own Act,
whereas all the other boards come under the general Act, the Electric Power Boards Act
1925, and its subsequent amendments.
We have heard a lot about wasting Parliament's time with unnecessary legislation, and I
think this is a glaring example. Many of the proposed changes are designed to bring the
Auckland Electric Power Board's Act into line with the provisions of the general legislation.


## p. 3100 (#496) ###########################################

3100
31 August
Auckland Electric Power Board Bill
Surely the logical thing would be simply to abolish the Auckland board's Act, and bring the
board under the same legislation as all other power boards. Instead, we have a fairly large
Bill introduced, much of it duplicating existing legislation.
As the member for Auckland Central said in his introduction, there are a few points of
difference, but I draw the member's attention to the first section of the explanatory note.
There the board admits that for practical reasons it has already abandoned the provisions of
its Act and for years has acted precisely on the lines laid down in the Electric Power Boards
Act in regard to maintaining a separate roll. Obviously in 1921 a roll was needed. The
Auckland Electric Power Board's area was a new creation. Today, however, the position is
different. The Auckland Electric Power Board's area is changed from time to time as its
constituent territorial authorities are adjusted. The member for Franklin knows that one
such occasion was a change in the area of the city of Papakura. There was no provision for
the area involved in the change to be covered by another power board. Surely the whole
matter should be taken care of under the Electric Power Boards Act. We certainly do not
want a series of separate Acts, and I suggest we are adopting an entirely wrong procedure in
accepting the Bill.
I know that the idea of coming under the general Act was canvassed, but as far as I can
make out it was rejected on only one ground-that all other boards have provision for wards
for the purposes of elections, and some members of the Auckland Electric Power Board did
not want wards in the board's area. To me that hardly seems to be a reason for taking up the
time of the House and of a lot of people associated with the House in the preparation and
passage of a Bill of this size. For years, every time there has been a change in the general Act
that change has been reflected in an amendment to the Auckland Electric Power Board Act.
If in the future the Electricity Department decides that there has to be a change in the
general Act, this new Bill, having become an Act, will again be subject to amendment.
While the House may not be prepared at this stage to consider rejecting the Bill, I suggest it
should look very closely at the possibility of its being a piece of legislation that we could well
do without.

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I propose to reply to the Leader of the
Opposition's comments about credibility, and to tell him just a few things about his
credibility and that of his party. While the Labour Government was in office, in those
disastrous 3 years from 1972 to 1975, the lack of security and confidence felt by old people
was something to be marvelled at. At that time the Labour Government introduced a
superannuation scheme, under which the first person who could obtain the full benefit had
not yet left school.
When we spoke to elderly people—those aged 60, 70, and so on-we told them about
that superannuation scheme, and they knew that the hard fact was that the first person who
would qualify for a full superannuation payment had then not even left school. Under that
scheme, people were required to pay exorbitant amounts to fulfil the whizz kid's dream
about how a socialist government could get its filthy little fingers on a lot of money sucked
out of the purses of people, who believed that the scheme would eventually be of some
benefit to them. The people saw through the scheme very easily, and the result was the
change of Government after the 1975 election.
Since then people have benefited from the type of superannuation scheme to which they
are entitled. It returns to those who have worked a lifetime for the good of the country, who
have made contributions during periods of depression and war and throughout the whole of
their lives, a benefit that allows them to live in quiet dignity. The superannuitants have been
good members of the community and now, at the end of their days, they receive a fair return
from a grateful country-not just from a grateful Government, but from a grateful country.
They welcome the Government's policies and its actions. They are very happy to have that
return, and they are very satisfied with it.
When talking about credibility we must also consider other promises made by Labour
Party members. At the 1975 election the people rejected the Labour Party, because they did
not believe it was reasonable that they should have to wait until the year 2023-until fifth
formers had reached the age of 60-before they could get the full benefit of the
superannuation scheme. At that time the beneficiaries did not have much faith in the
credibility of the Labour Government; and many other people had no faith in its credibility
in other areas. We know very well that Labour Party members made one statement before
the election in 1972 and another after being elected. I think of issues such as the Springbok
tour; and, of course, we all know something about the Matai project.

I want to discuss the present position as I see it. Since 1975 the National Party has stated
categorically that it will not introduce a means test for national superannuation. Labour
members have made clear, consistent, continuing reference to the fact that some people who
have alternative incomes are receiving national superannuation. They regularly cite Cabinet
Ministers-their pet example. If any political party in New Zealand is likely to put a means
test on superannuation, it is the Labour Party. Members opposite are backing off a little now
that the election is getting closer, but for 3 years they have constantly harped on the theme of
people in receipt of incomes also enjoying the benefit of national superannuation. We
believe that people are entitled to national superannuation at the age of 60. People in that
age group have made their contribution to New Zealand, and are as much entitled to
national superannuation as any other group. The National Government will not introduce a
means test, but I can give no such assurance for the Labour Party.
Concessions have represented a considerable area of conflict. I quote from the policy
that National went to the electors with in 1975. It states quite clearly: "Concessions:
telephone, television, and rates concessions will continue for the same categories of
beneficiaries, using the same means test and at the same rates applicable when National
assumes office." That is precisely what happened. We are quite prepared to stand on our
record of credibility, but what about the poor old Labour Party? For the last 3 years, Labour
members, spearheaded by the member for Wigram, have gone up and down the country
saying that they would return the concessions that the nasty National Government took
away. That is what Labour members have said until now, 3 months before the election, when
the brick has landed.
A speech was made in Wellington yesterday, and they had a few cheer leaders along to
try to get a bit of humour and lightness into the meeting. With the Leader of the Opposition
speaking it is usually pretty dry, so they had a bit of a sing-song. They got "Knees up Mother
Brown" going, and a bit of foot-tapping-and then the bombshell. What happened? The
Leader of the Opposition came out and announced the Labour Party's policy on transport,
telephone, and television licence concessions. He said, “Under the present system all these

a baby bonus, but their policy ignored women. What happens? With an election emerging,
they say, "We are on the side of women." Credible? Of course not. The Labour Party is not
credible and shows no signs of becoming so.
Let us consider the movements in the pensions paid by the Labour Government and by
the National Government. In 1975 the last Labour Government-not lamented, but last for
ever-authorised an age benefit of $51.26. From 31 August 1978—today—the national
superannuation payment will be $91.30, an increase of $40.04 a week, or 78 percent. It can
be fairly argued that the pension would have increased in the 3 years. Therefore, had the
Labour scheme continued, the pension today would not have been $51, but $77.28, whereas
National's payout today is $91.30-$14.02 ahead of what the Labour Party was promising.
No wonder Labour members are now saying, "We are going to give you some more. We are
not going to give you the concessions, but you might, in certain circumstances, benefit from a
tax rebate, and you might earn a little more." No wonder! If I had to contend with those
figures I would try to think up a new idea. I assume the member for Manukau has been
thinking, and probably watching the cash registers in the hotel, once again.

We are talking about credibility. In its election manifesto, National promised that
superannuation would be paid at the rate of 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly
wage. It said that it would implement that policy within 3-years, and today the scheme has
come fully into effect. Now, superannuitants are receiving a higher rate of superannuation
than ever before. All men and women over the age of 60, regardless of their class,
background, earning record, or position in society, are receiving a fair and equitable return
on the contributions they have made. That is totally in line with the policy National
presented to the electors in 1975. If Labour members want us to debate the credibility of the
National Government, we will be very happy to do so on any and every occasion.
But the National Government has not stopped only at what it promised in 1975. The
1978 Budget broke new ground and provided for new pensions. A very worth-while
concession of $8 a week is to be paid to all parents of children with multiple handicaps. The
new benefit will not in any way compensate them for all the additional costs involved, and we
do not claim that it will, but it does recognise a real need, which Labour members did not
think about during their 3 years in power. Not only is the National Government credible in
that it has done what it promised, but it is credible to the extent that it has implemented
policies that reflect its oft-stated belief in the individual rights of New Zealanders.
Government members are concerned about all sectors of the community, and that is why
they have introduced the additional benefit for those caring for children with multiple
handicaps. That very worth-while benefit has been welcomed by all in responsible positions,
and particularly by those who care for handicapped children.
The Government has also tackled the problems of the means-tested beneficiaries. A
number of beneficiaries in New Zealand are still subject to a means test, and the
Government appreciates their plight and that some of their needs, consistent with living in a
modern society, are real. It has increased from $17 to $25 a week the amount those people
can earn before their benefits are reduced. That is an indication that the Government has

estimates rather than a day later in the week. My guess is that on Friday several Bills will be
introduced. That would make it a very short day for estimates. I am not adamant about it.

Adult Population

Special Work Scheme
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Labour: When was the special work
scheme started, and when was it extended to provide work within Government departments
for unemployed clerical, technical and specialist workers?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. "The special work scheme, which had its origins in the winter work programme,
started in May 1974. The variation to this scheme, which enables the Department of Labour
to seek a wider range of employment opportunities in skilled and semi-skilled occupations in
Government departments, was introduced in June 1975. In March 1978 the scheme was
restructured as the temporary employment programme, and now covers all occupations--
whether skilled or unskilled-in Government departments, local authorities, non-
profitmaking community organisations, hospital boards, and education authorities. In
addition, four job creation programmes operating in the private sector have been introduced
to encourage employers to provide jobs for people who would otherwise be unemployed.
These are the farm employment scheme introduced in October 1977, and the skill promotion
programme, the first job programme, and the additional jobs programme in March 1978".
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Is it correct that the special work programme grew out of a
programme that began much earlier because of the seasonal unemployment in rural districts
and the freezing industry, and was extended to cover the Forest Service, for which a special
work vote was appropriated?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The winter work scheme was introduced in May 1965 to
provide productive work for seasonal workers who could not find work during the winter
months. The scheme was widened in May 1974 to provide work projects for the additional
number of persons expected to become unemployed. In June 1975 the scheme was widened
further to provide in professional, technical, executive, clerical, typing, and other related
positions, skilled work of a type that would have been done eventually, but which had been
deferred because of lack of staff, or because it was of a low priority. The purpose of the
scheme is to provide useful and productive employment in Government departments for
workers who would otherwise be unemployed, and to place those workers in positions
commensurate with their qualifications and capabilities.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Is it correct that when, and if, the unemployment position

Voting Ship Crews at Sea
5. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: What arrangements are made for
the crews of New Zealand vessels who will be at sea in November to vote at this year's
general election?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Arrangements are always made, and are
being made this year, to provide voting facilities on ships on which there are New Zealand
electors. Arrangements are being made through the shipping companies for all New Zealand
vessels that are at sea, and not calling at any port where New Zealand overseas posts exist
after nominations close and before polling day, to be provided with voting facilities. An
officer is appointed as the overseas deputy returning officer, provided with voting material,
and issued with instructions about the manner in which the poll is to be conducted. Crews
and passengers on other vessels vote as overseas special voters, as special voters, or as
ordinary voters, depending on circumstances.

Electoral Act-Special Voting
13. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: Has the Chief Electoral Officer

Government Superannuation Debt
14. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Finance: In view of the fact that the


## p. 3133 (#529) ###########################################

1 September
3133
Questions for Oral Answer
Government admitted a debt of $40 million in 1946 to be repaid with interest at 3.5 percent,
why has no statement of this liability ever been included in the report on the Government
Superannuation Fund; what are the various interest payments for each year from 1946; and
why are they not shown in the report?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The answer to this question is a little
longer than usual, but I do not think it is too long. Because of the nature of the fund it is not
the practice for the accounts to show moneys payable by the State as a liability. The scheme
is on what is termed a "partially funded" basis, in that the fund represents the contributions
of the members and the earnings of those contributions. The State's share of the costs is
determined as the benefits emerge, and is paid at that time. Because of the great variety of
factors that can influence the amount of subsidy, there is no practicable way in which future
State payments, which are, of course, guaranteed by the Government Superannuation Fund
Act itself, could be precisely determined at any given time and shown as a liability in the
accounting sense. The particular money to which the question refers relates to the
amalgamation of the then three separate State employees' funds as from 1 April 1948. At
that point it was found that for varying reasons over earlier years the accumulated funds fell
short of the value of employee contributions by $40 million. This has been adjusted by
special payments under section 95 (1) (b) of the Act, which are specifically identified each
year in the annual accounts published in the report-for example, the amount of $2 million
being shown for 1977-78. On a table basis, the interest components of the annual payments
vary from year to year, but the special payments will be completed in 1980-81 when a total of
$66,872,813 will have been paid, of which $26,872,813 will represent interest.

Electoral Rolls Special Voting
18. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Justice: In view of the wide
concern over the state of the Electoral rolls, will he outline the steps he will be taking to
ensure that every citizen entitled to a special vote will be able to cast a valid ballot?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Section 100 of the Electoral Act 1956
sets out the grounds on which "any person who is qualified to vote" may vote as a special
voter. Returning officers have been instructed, as in the past, that anyone claiming a right to
vote as a special voter is to be given such a vote. If he comes within the provisions of section
100 his vote will be counted.
Hon. Michael Connelly: When the rolls reveal substantial errors, duplications, and
irregularities so near to the election, as is the case now, does the Minister not agree that the
Government has a responsibility to take urgent action to put the matter right?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That question is so far distant from the question of special
voting and section 100 that I suggest that the member might put it down as a new question,
and with notice. However, I will say that the Government takes very seriously its
responsibility to assist the Chief Electoral Officer in his preparation for the election.
Hospital Admissions-Tobacco Use
19. Mr FENTON (Hastings) to the Minister of Health: How many hospital admissions
attributed to the use of tobacco were reported in 1976, 1977, and 1978?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): There are no figures available on the number of
hospital admissions due to the use of tobacco. Tobacco has a proven link with lung cancer,
but it is also believed to be involved with the incidence of heart disease. There are figures
available, but as yet only up to 1974, on the number of new cases of lung cancer diagnosed.
They are as follows: 1972, 939; 1973, 985; and 1974, 1075. The admission figures do not show
what proportion of these cases was attributable solely to smoking or to some other cause.
Electorate Officers and Poll Clerks-Training
20. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Justice: What steps are being
taken to ensure that all electoral officers and poll clerks are adequately trained to handle the
special votes that will be cast at the next election?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Electorate officers are responsible for
the compilation and the maintenance of electoral rolls, but have no responsibility for special
votes. I assume that the honourable member has in mind returning officers. As I told the
House yesterday, I am able to tell the honourable member that 1-day training seminars will
be arranged in late September, and other instructions are issued in circular form. Deputy
returning officers, who are in charge of polling booths, receive detailed written instructions
from the returning officer who appoints them. Poll clerks are instructed by the deputy
returning officers in charge of the polling booth to which they are appointed. All instructions
include directions about issuing special votes.

Crewe Murder Trials-DSIR Evidence
21. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Science and Technology: Bearing
in mind the fact that there have been a number of trials, appeals, and reviews relating to the
Crewe murder case and the conviction of Arthur Alan Thomas, and the fact that there have
been differing interpretations of the scientific evidence surrounding the case, is he satisfied
with the work of the DSIR in relation to this case?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): With science and
technology playing an increasing part in the fight against crime, the forensic scientist renders
a vitally important public service in giving impartial scientific evidence to the courts so that
justice may be properly served. DSIR scientists may be called out at any time of the day or
night to collect and examine scientific evidence and to undertake scientific analyses. The
work requires great skill, attention to detail, impartiality, and absolute scientific integrity.
The forensic staff of the DSIR possess all these qualities. Over a long period, the scientific
evidence in the Crewe case was the subject of much comment in the press, on radio, and on
television, and at one stage a book was written about the case. The forensic scientists of the
DSIR involved in this case-Dr D. F. Nelson and Mr R. Shanahan-felt bound not to make
a public statement in spite of being provoked in public and in private. They personally have
been subjected to abuse by some members of the public, and so, too, were their wives and
families. In spite of this, they refrained from comment because of their official positions, and
because they believed it was important for the department to remain impartial in all
circumstances. These scientists, whatever the attacks made upon them, have examined every
new hypothesis put forward in the same skilled and impartial manner that they have always
demonstrated. I am particularly satisfied with their work in the Crewe murder case.

As Deputy Speaker I have four criteria to consider to establish whether to grant the
adjournment of the House under Standing Orders 89 and 90. The first is that the statement
shall not be framed in general terms. The motion is not framed in general terms, and meets
this requirement. The second is that the matter shall deal with a particular case of recent

Yesterday I issued a press statement, pursuant to the policy I have been following, that
we will have absolutely open government for the preparation of the general election. It
would be as well if I read that press statement so that it will be in the records of the House. It
states: "All main electoral rolls have now been printed and have been or are being
distributed to post offices within electorates. Each electorate officer has distributed the rolls
within his own electorate to enable the public to inspect the roll to ensure that they are in fact
enrolled and eligible to vote at the forthcoming general election. Comment has been made
that a number of duplications appear on some electoral rolls and the Minister explained that,
because of the numbers being enrolled, it was preferable in cases of doubt for a name to be
entered twice than for an elector to be deprived of the right to vote when that elector has
fulfilled his legal obligations to enrol. Where there was clear duplication, this would be
eliminated in up-to-date printouts of rolls that would be available before election day. There
was no possibility of fraud or double voting going undetected as the computer printout copy
of the roll in the hands of electorate officers immediately prior to the poll will be an updated
copy from which obvious duplicates will have been removed. The Minister went on to
explain that, because of printing deadlines which had to be met after the main rolls were
officially closed on 26 July 1978, not all enrolments received or amendments notified were
able to be processed before the main roll computer record was closed. Since the main rolls
were prepared for printing, a further 50 000 registrations and amendments have been
processed. Computer printout listings of these persons have already been sent to each
electorate officer. The Minister stated that all persons so placed on the supplementary rolls
have been sent an advice card informing them of the enrolment and confirming that their
name would appear on the supplementary roll rather than on the main roll. Other
registration forms are still being processed, including some submitted prior to 26 July, and
these electors will also receive postal advice cards. Some electors may not find an entry
relating to them when they check the rolls presently available, although they know they have
completed an application for registration. A large number of registration applications are
currently being processed, and extra machining facilities are being made available to ensure
that these applications are processed in time to appear on the supplementary rolls. As they
are actioned, advice of registration cards will be sent to electors. If any elector still had any
doubt unresolved he should seek advice from his electorate officer or inquire through his
nearest post office, the Minister added."

the Administration. The Government is determined to see that that right is facilitated, and
that people are assisted. We have been following that in the most open way possible, and we

the preparation for the general election.
I have said before that there is a need in the first year of a new Parliament-the 1978 to
1981 Parliament-for the Electoral Act to be re-examined. With hindsight it is quite clear
that the proposals by the Labour Government's Hunt committee have turned out to do
nowhere near what that honourable member thought they would do. For example, the
requirement that people had to return electoral cards with their census forms was obviously a
mistake. Not all people returned them, and therefore enrolment was not complete. Because
many people would have thought that, having done that, it was all right and that they did not
have to do anything more about checking their position on the electoral rolls, the Chief
Electoral Officer decided, rather than scrub them entirely, to take that data as his base in the
preparation of the main rolls, and thereafter of the supplementary rolls, so he used not only
the 1975 rolls but also the cards returned with the 1976 census forms, just a few months after
the 1975 election. As a result there have been many duplications. Those are now being
purged as people, acting responsibly, as we know they will, assist in the process of cleansing
the rolls. That goes on right up to when the supplementary rolls are published on writ day
after Parliament rises. Even after that people should make quite sure, if they have not done
so before, that their names are on either the main roll or the supplementary roll. If they have
any doubt they should go to their electorate officer.
The National Government will continue to act responsibly, and to demonstrate its
concern about the serious responsibility of any Government to ensure that the process of
democracy is facilitated in every possible way. We have done that. No matter how much
criticism I receive from the Labour Party I will continue to be open. No matter how much
criticism I receive from editors, I will continue to be open. I have kept telling editors the
facts and I keep telling members of the press gallery that they are free to ask any question of
the Chief Electoral Officer. He has been instructed to answer them, and to be completely
open. If editors are not informed in any way, then they have the remedy in their own hands,
because they have representatives in the press gallery. The National Government will
continue to be responsible in this area as in others.
I have not mentioned it, but in 1975 there was great confusion over the electoral rolls
under the Labour Government. In this debate I hope that comes out. It will be seen then
what humbug has been talked this morning by Labour members. It will be seen just what
sanctimonious humbug there has been in the arguments expressed with such unction. At
least I must say to the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, who is trying to interject, that he
never sounds unctuous. He always sounds grumpy. I suppose it is one thing or the other. He
also subscribes to the idea that, no matter at what peril of confusing people, members
opposite should try to knock the Government, or the Chief Electoral Officer, who is a very
respected State servant. It does not worry Labour Party members. They will knock State
servants at every opportunity if they think it will advance the cause of the Labour Party.
I have followed carefully and consistently a policy of open information. I have answered
all the questions put to me and, if I have not been able to give the detail myself, I have told
members of the press gallery to ask the Chief Electoral Officer for the answers. I shall
continue to adopt that attitude so that people are adequately informed because, as I have
said on the many occasions the subject has been discussed in the House this session, the
preparations for an election are a partnership between the Government and the people. The
Government provides the finance and the staff, and has been assured by the Chief Electoral
Officer, who is known to members of the Labour Party, that he has the funds and the staff he
needs. However, if I believe he needs further support, he will receive it from the
Government.
Under our electoral process, people have the basic democratic right to decide who shall
represent them in Parliament, and who shall be their Government. However, with that right
goes the responsibility to see that they are registered on either the main or the
supplementary roll. The responsible attitude to this subject, which the Opposition is not
demonstrating, would be for members to encourage people, if they qualify, to check that
they are on the roll. The member for Roskill said he raised this matter more in sorrow than
in anger. I ask him, on behalf of the Government and the people, to raise it responsibly, and
to help people by clarifying the position, not by setting out deliberately to confuse what is
ordinarily a confusing situation. That is the only responsible way to go about it. I hope that
by the time the debate has ended the Opposition will have changed its attitude, and will be
ready to co-operate with people and to help them exercise their democratic right.

individuals listed on both the Western Maori and the Raglan rolls. On page 96 of the Raglan

could point out many anomalies, and that there were similar problems in every electorate.

Let us move on to Porirua. The member for Porirua has always had a lot to say on this

showing that 100 Porirua people would have to register as special voters on election day,
because they lived in Ascot Park and had found themselves on the Kapiti roll. The Porirua
electoral officer had said he was in a complete quandary over the mistake, and that they
could go over to Kapiti to vote; it was illegal, but would probably go undetected. Yet
members opposite argue this today, not the day before the election, but early in September.
We still have a great deal of time to rectify the rolls, and the Government is making available
all the manpower and money needed.
I turn now to the 1975 Christchurch Central supplementary roll. On page 110 one finds
the names of Allan and Ann Cullen, Beach Road, Waihi, and, further down Leo and
Lorraine Critchley, McCall Avenue, Pauanui Beach. The electoral officer in Christchurch
said that a lot of peculiar things had happened with the roll. Another couple who lived in
Petrie Street were advised that they had been enrolled in St. Albans, although they were
actually living in Christchurch Central. In 1975 the Christchurch Central roll was full of
people from Pauanui Beach and Waihi.
I move now to Rangiora, where the then Labour member of Parliament, Mr Kerry

relatives outside the electorate in which they last enrolled, the registrar does not know where
to send the information. When that is the case, a deceased person's name stays on the
electoral roll in whatever electorate he last voted.

It is well known that a computer will register additional information if there is a slight
difference from the information already stored. In other words, if a person is on the roll and
a card comes through giving him a different address, another name will be registered. If a
person's occupation is slightly different, or if his christian name is spelt differently-Jack
instead of John-or if, in the case of a Polynesian name, a syllable is different, the computer
will accept the information and it will be printed. That means that in some cases there will be
two names on the roll referring to one person. The reason for that is that in some cases there
could be two persons with the same name, and it would not be duplication, and nobody loses
the right to a valid vote. That is why the error is on the side of publishing extra names. I
would have thought that the New Zealand Herald would realise that, and would give some
publicity to the fact that people will not be denied their right to vote.

TUESDAY, 5 SEPTEMBER 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Deficit Before Borrowing
1. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of Finance:
What measures does the Government intend to take to finance the deficit before borrowing
following the closing of the current Government loan?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The Government has already
announced that it intends to finance its deficit to a greater extent than in the past through the
sale of Government securities to the private sector. The position will be reviewed after the
results of the current Government loan are known.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Has any preliminary examination been completed with a view to
increasing the interest rates on the next Government offering?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I would have thought that the honourable gentleman
would know that that kind of decision is taken immediately before issuing a loan.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Has the Minister already taken a decision to increase the rate of
interest to 11 percent?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The member can guess as much as he likes and he will be
wrong every time. The answer is no.
Stock Numbers-Pahiatua Electorate
2. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the Minister
of Agriculture: What are the latest recorded total stock numbers on a ewe-equivalent basis in
the Pahiatua electorate, including the Waipawa County, compared with the figures 5 years
ago and 10 years ago?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): Total sheep and dairy and beef cattle
carried in the Pahiatua electorate on a ewe-equivalent basis for the following years were:
1977-78, 8,600,000; 1972-73, 8,700,000; 1967-68, 8,100,000. These figures were derived from
sheep numbers as at 30 June of the first-mentioned years, and from cattle numbers as at 31
January from the latter-mentioned years.
Television Licence Rates
3. Mr LANGE (Mangere), on behalf of Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram), to the
Minister of Broadcasting: Is it a fact that the charges for colour and black and white
