Post Office Cheque Books
13. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Postmaster-General: When did the Post Office
transfer the printing of cheque books for Post Office accounts from the Government Printing


## p. 3165 (#561) ###########################################

5 September
3165
Questions for Oral Answer
Office to private tender, and can he confirm that new account holders, from as long ago as
February this year, are still waiting to be issued with their printed cheque books?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): The Post Office transferred the printing
of cheque forms for Post Office Savings Bank accounts from the Government Printing Office
to private tender in 1974, under the last Labour Government, when the Post Office Savings
Bank cheque accounts were computerised. The reason for this was that the cheque forms
require encoding with a special magnetic ink, and the Government Printing Office was, and
still is, unable to provide this service. The Post Office acknowledges that in some, but by no
means all cases there have been delays in the supply of personalised cheque books to new
account holders. This was due to problems being experienced in changing over to an
automatic cheque book ordering system, and to a breakdown in computer equipment used
by the printers in the production of cheque books. The problems have now been completely
overcome, and personalised books are being supplied 5 to 10 days after they are ordered. At
no time, however, have depositors been unable to operate their cheque accounts, as Post
Offices have always had ample supplies of single non-personalised cheque forms.

MISUSE OF DRUGS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the Misuse of Drugs Amendment
Bill be introduced. Medical research is continually producing new and potent drugs capable
of relieving many ailments to which the human body is prone-some previously beyond
assistance. Many people can now retain reasonable health and avoid admittance to a
hospital, thanks to modern treatment. But the array of drugs available today provides a


## p. 3168 (#564) ###########################################

3168
5 September
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
threat to those to whom they are intended to bring good. The consequences of those
developments are relevant to drug dependency and abuse in most countries of the world
today. New Zealand is no exception.
The advent of many effective and readily available remedies has conditioned society to
regard medication as a cure for all problems. Too often people tend to find solace in drugs—
a tranquilliser or a sleeping tablet. Is it any wonder that young people, conditioned to seeing
their parents acting in this way, should themselves regard drugs as an answer to their own
problems? The quantity of drugs obtained illegally, large though it is, is small compared to
those prescribed legally, and, while most prescriptions are given for sound reasons, many are
a source of supply for those who only wish to supplement a drug-induced habit. There is
strong evidence that the general public and even some doctors have begun to place undue
reliance on the use of particular drugs in the treatment of some common ailments.
This has contributed to the present widespread overreliance on the easily acquired and
easily administered remedies of our time. From this it may prove an easy step to the use of
drugs for purely pleasure or escapist purposes, and a further step on the downward path
leading to the realms of the trafficker in hard drugs. There is no doubt that the overall effect
of this demand for drugs, both in the supply of legal treatment and in the measures to combat
the activities of the illicit user and supplier, places an uncommonly heavy burden on the
public purse.
For many years there has been a strong demand for amphetamines, which are stimulant
drugs previously used for slimming. Competent medical opinion suggests that these drugs
are ineffective for that purpose, but very effective in producing dependence. Two years ago
supplies of these drugs were restricted to the treatment of only a limited number of
conditions, the main one being narcolepsy. The overall result of this move was a dramatic
drop in the use of these drugs. Similarly, for some time the demand for barbiturates caused
concern. In February last year I convened a conference of interested parties to discuss ways
in which the use of barbiturates as sedatives and hypnotics might be reduced.
One outcome of that conference was an agreement that an educational programme
should be instituted aimed first at the prescriber, and secondly at the general public. I am
pleased to announce that the results of two surveys on dispensing barbiturates in community
pharmacies indicates that there has been a 25 percent reduction in barbiturate prescriptions
and the total number of barbiturate tablets and capsules prescribed during the time of the
two surveys, between June 1977 and May 1978. The campaign will continue to be directed to
the general public.
The effects of smoking tobacco must be included in any study encompassing the overall
abuse of drugs. New evidence does not in any way detract from the conclusion that diseases
related to smoking are important causes of disability and premature deaths in developed
countries. The control of cigarette smoking could do more than any other single action in the
whole field of preventive medicine to improve health and prolong life in those countries. The
dangers are well publicised, but efforts by the Department of Health and the Advisory
Committee on Smoking and Health would seem to have been largely disregarded so far,
especially by the young, although a significant alteration in the pattern of smoking is
perceptible in the older age group.
Like most people in Western societies, many New Zealanders drink socially and
moderately. A proportion do not drink at all, but between 50 000 and 200 000 people in New
Zealand are unduly preoccupied with alcohol and are drinking at hazardous levels. In
addition there are approximately 53 000 chronic alcoholics, many receiving treatment. For
each confirmed case, it is estimated that a further 10 people are affected. That means that
more than 500 000 people in New Zealand are in direct contact with, or detrimentally
affected by, the problem known to be associated with the disruption of marriages, child
neglect, depression, suicide, road accidents, crimes against the person and property,
industrial absenteeism, inefficiency, and impaired personal relationships. That is common
knowledge to the majority of our population, yet recognition of it has not reached the point
where society will demand effective action against it.
Cannabis use, an issue often marked by emotionalism, is being examined more
thoughtfully. Much has been learnt about this drug and its personal and social consequences,
yet much remains to be understood. It is clear that cannabis is not a subject for simplistic
analysis. Sufficient is known, however, to indicate that cannabis cannot be regarded as
harmless. The concentrated active principals are extremely potent and only minute
quantities are required to produce significant alterations to perception, especially of time


## p. 3169 (#565) ###########################################

5 September
3169
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
and sound, and the impairment of reasoning. All of these significantly affect driving skills.
While evidence is put forward from time to time suggesting that the restriction of
cannabis could be relaxed, there is sufficient evidence available to support the view that the
present controls should be maintained. Three years ago, when the Misuse of Drugs Act was
enacted, provision was made in that statute to maintain the policy of providing higher
maximum penalties for offences of dealing in controlled drugs than for possession and use.
At the same time, differing maximum penalties were introduced, graded in severity, for
dealing offences in terms of the relative potential for harm of the drugs concerned. The
maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment was then thought to be sufficient to deter those
who might otherwise consider trafficking in controlled drugs to be a worth-while enterprise.
Since that time, however, it has become quite apparent that dealing in dependence-
producing drugs has become a part of organised crime.
The considerable profits to be gained have attracted an element of the underworld with
considerable resources, enabling a build-up and interchange of couriers between countries,
including New Zealand, to the extent that the quantity of drugs peddled in New Zealand has
increased considerably over the years. Rigorous measures are needed to combat this
nefarious traffic, and nearly every country in the world has devoted a great deal of time and
consideration to ways of coping with the spreading epidemic. I want to make it clear,
however, that there is no intention to restrict in any way the treatment and rehabilitation of
persons dependent on drugs who genuinely wish to receive treatment. I have agreed with my
colleague, the Minister of Justice, that the proposed new penal provisions, to be
incorporated in new separate parts of the Misuse of Drugs Act, will be administered by the
Department of Justice. The remainder of the statute will continue to be administered by the
Department of Health, as hitherto.
Now for some details of the Bill. Much thought has been given to the prevention of the
misuse of drugs and the rehabilitation of persons suffering from such misuse. Clause 2
provides that the functions of the Minister shall include the publication of reports,
information, and advice on those matters. In this regard I intend to appoint a committee to
advise me. Clause 3 increases the maximum penalties for dealing in class A drugs from 14
years' to life imprisonment, and in class B drugs from 10 years' to 14 years' imprisonment.
The maximum fines that a magistrate may impose are to be raised from $3,000 to $15,000 for
class A drugs, and from $2,000 to $10,000 for class B drugs.
The offence of conspiring to deal in controlled drugs is to be removed from the general
provisions of the Crimes Act 1961 by clause 4, and will be included in the Misuse of Drugs
Act as a specific offence carrying an increased maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment
for class A drugs, and 10 years' imprisonment for offences involving class B drugs. The
present maximum penalty is 7 years for both classes. Clause 5 proposes that the courts shall
be required to consider imposing fines as well as prison sentences for dealing offences
involving class A or class B controlled drugs.
Section 12 makes it an offence for any person knowingly to permit any premises or
vehicles to be used for the purpose of an offence. Clause 6 extends the meaning of premises
and vehicles to include vessels, aircraft, hovercraft, motor vehicles, and other modes of
conveyance.
Clause 7 provides that the prosecution will not have to prove that the quantity of the
drug was a usable quantity. Clause 8 states that the analyst's certificate of the identity of the
substance will be evidence of the fact stated in that certificate. Clause 9 exempts police
officers from any liability for anything done in the course of their official duties. Clauses 11,
12, and 13 will give additional powers to customs officers and police officers. These will allow
delivery of illegally imported controlled drugs, so that they may be followed through to their
destinations. Tracking devices may also be used by police or customs officers for similar
purposes, but the officer must, within 72 hours, send a written report on the matter to a
magistrate who, if he considers it necessary, may refer a copy of the report to the
Commissioner of Police or to the Comptroller of Customs, with his recommendations.
Clauses 14 to 28 cover the issue of warrants for listening devices. They authorise the
police to apply for a warrant to use a listening device to intercept private communications
when they have reason to believe that a person is involved in a drug-dealing offence. Several
safeguards are incorporated to prevent the possibility of abuse of this power. In the first
place, the application is to be made to a judge of the Supreme Court in writing and on oath
by a commissioned police officer. Then, full details must be given of the circumstances
making the warrant necessary, why other investigations are not appropriate, and the period


## p. 3170 (#566) ###########################################

3170
5 September
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
of time for which the warrant is needed. If the judge is satisfied in all respects, he may grant a
warrant stating the offence for which it is granted, the name, and the address of the suspect if
known, the premises where the communication may be intercepted, and the name of the
police officer who may intercept the private communications. Every interception warrant is
to be valid for a specified period not exceeding 30 days, and may be renewed on further
written application.
The safeguards do not end with the granting of a warrant. The relevant records of
information are to be destroyed as soon as it is apparent that they are unlikely to be used in
any court proceedings. Furthermore, after the warrant has expired, the police must report to
the judge on the circumstances in which the listening device was used. The judge may
request any further information as he thinks fit. Also, the Commissioner of Police shall
include in his annual report to Parliament information on use made by the police of listening
devices.
Clauses 29 to 35 cover the circumstances in which bail may be granted to a person
charged with or convicted of a drug dealing offence. Bail shall not be granted except on the
order of a judge of the Supreme Court, who may impose conditions. There will be a right of
appeal to the Court of Appeal when the judge refuses to grant bail. Provision is also to be
made for the arrest without warrant of suspected absconders or offenders who have not
complied with any conditions of bail.
Clause 37 is an important new provision that empowers a court to impose a greater fine
if it is satisfied that any money or assets owned by the offender may have been derived by
him from earlier drug-dealing offences. Clauses 38, 39, and 40 are consequential on clause
37. Clause 38 relates to power to impose greater fines. This power cannot be exercised twice.
Clause 39 provides that the inability of an offender to explain the source of his assets shall be
evidence that they were derived from previous drug-dealing offences. Clause 40 deals with
the rights of the court when assets have been disposed of. Clauses 41 to 44 relate to the
enforcement of fines. Clause 45 restricts the right to parole. The judge may, when the term
of imprisonment is 10 years or more, order that the prisoner shall not be released for a
period not exceeding 7 years as he may specify. Where the period of imprisonment is less
than 10 years, the judge may order that the offender shall not be released for up to seven-
tenths of the sentence.
Clause 46 provides that Part II of the Bill is to be administered by the Department of
Justice. Parts III to VI of the Bill, covering clauses 47 to 55, cover consequential
amendments to the Criminal Justice Act, the Penal Institutions Act, the Summary
Proceedings Act, and the Crimes Act. I should make special reference to Part VI of the Bill.
Clause 55 inserts a new part to the Crimes Act, and imposes a general prohibition on the use
of listening devices without statutory authority, a prohibition on disclosures of private
communications unlawfully intercepted, and a prohibition on offering listening devices for
sale to the public.
I have every confidence that the proposed amendments I am introducing in this Bill,
arising from international consultation, will assist in curbing the activities of the traffickers in
hard drugs, at whom they are aimed. However, so that the full ramifications of the proposal
may be studied, I propose to refer the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee for the
hearing of limited evidence and for consideration.

evidence" mean that the Minister will allow people such as the New Zealand Council for

An Hon. Member: Predictable.

Doctor Shortage
14. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen the
statement by the member for New Lynn in the Dominion of 31 August that 200 doctors have
left New Zealand in the period of the National Government, and, if so, (a) is this correct, (b)
is there a doctor shortage in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the statement by the member for
New Lynn in the Dominion of 31 August 1978. There has always been a number of doctors
leaving New Zealand for reasonably lengthy absences to gain experience and advanced
qualifications. Many return after a few years. New Zealand also recruits doctors from
overseas. The number of doctors graduating from our medical schools has increased, and, as
expected, the number travelling overseas to gain experience has also risen. However, the
number registered in New Zealand has actually increased by 300 during the term of this
Government. The net loss from migration has been only 50 during this period, and it can be
expected that the number of doctors returning will increase when they have completed their
studies. The Medical Council and the Department of Health have recently set up a joint
committee to examine medical manpower requirements in New Zealand. This committee
has not yet completed a full review of overall requirements. However, it is clear that there
are areas and specialties that could usefully have higher numbers of doctors. The increasing
number of doctors registering in New Zealand is expected to allow these areas and
specialties to be better serviced.
Mr Wellington: In his answer to part (b), is the Minister saying there is no shortage in
New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL: There is no overall shortage of doctors in New Zealand, but in some
geographical areas and in some special areas there are not as many doctors as we want. For
instance, in parts of the West Coast it is almost impossible to attract a doctor to provide the
service we would like. We are short in a number of specialties. Anaesthetists are in short
supply in Christchurch and Wellington. Psychiatrists are in short supply. It is not possible to
give a generalised answer and say there are no shortages; that could be misconstrued.
Mr Hunt: Was my statement that 200 doctors have left New Zealand since December
1975-which was quoted accurately in the Dominion on 31 August-correct?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot say that that figure is correct. Is the member talking about
net inflows and outflows?
Mr Hunt: I am talking about net inflows and outflows of people who have decided to put
on their emigration card “Departing Permanently”.
Hon. T. F. GILL: Balanced by the doctors coming in?
Mr Hunt: No, not exactly, because it cannot be.
Hon. T. F. GILL: I have not got that figure.
Mr Hunt: That is why-because I know it is more than 200.
Hon. T. F. GILL: And neither has the member got it.
Mr Hunt: I have.
Hon. T. F. GILL: The number of doctors on the register has increased by 300 during the
term of this Government. A balance between inflow and outflow of doctors has shown a net
outflow of 50.

NEW ZEALAND CREDIT AND CURRENCY BILL
Introduction
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I move, That leave be given to introduce the New Zealand
Credit and Currency Bill. This Bill provides the first step along the path of financial reform
required to allow the monetary system in this country to work for the benefit of all of the
people instead of for the benefit of a small vested minority, which at present manipulates the
system to its advantage. The Bill tackles the problem of credit creation by private trading
banks, which results in the creation of this country's money supply. The Bill does not in itself
tackle the problem of secondary credit creation by the new generation of debt merchants,
known in official journals as other financial institutions-as defined in the Reserve Bank
Bulletin of June of this year which use, as a reserves base for credit multiplication, money
initially created by the trading banks.
The problem of secondary credit creation, which is much more of a modern
phenomenon, can only be corrected once the basic reform outlined in the Bill is
implemented. The purpose of the Bill is to vest the sole right to create money in the Crown,
and exercisable only by the Reserve Bank on behalf of the Crown; to declare the monetary
policy of New Zealand to be one not of inflation, nor of deflation, but equation; to remove
the rental component from interest; to provide for a New Zealand balance sheet showing the
money supply and the value of the output of goods and services for which it exists; and to
provide for all incidental matters-all for the objective of achieving and sustaining a stable
internal price level with overall economic and social justice for all the people of New
Zealand.
The Bill proposes that there should be established a fourth branch of Government to be
known as the monetary branch, this new branch to stand beside, and be equal in status to,
the traditional three branches of the Legislature, Executive, and judiciary. The Bill
recognises that checks and balances between the existing branches of the Government are
inadequate to check the growing domination by the Executive branch under our present
system. The Bill recognises that this problem could be extended to the new monetary
branch, and for this reason includes checks and balances to ensure that the actions of the
monetary branch are continually subject to scrutiny and control by the elected
representatives of the people. Control over the monetary branch is not given to the
Executive because existing Executive domination must be reduced rather than increased.
The Bill positively denies control by the Executive over the new monetary branch of the
Government. It is intended that the monetary branch as a part of the Government has a role
comparable to the judiciary in its relationship to the Legislature. The need for another tool
of the Government is becoming daily more critical, because the deterioration of New
Zealand's economy is daily becoming more evident.
A core economic problem for New Zealand is the trading problem. The Bill contains
measures that will provide the mechanism for a start to be made on the long-term correction


## p. 3197 (#593) ###########################################

6 September
3197
New Zealand Credit and Currency Bill
needed to deal with our trading problem. Provision is made for trading credits to be
exchanged with willing partners to take up the employment and resource slack without
increasing overseas debt to an intolerable level. New Zealand's commitment to the IMF-
dominated trading system is resulting in the present serious level of unemployment and
soaring debts, the interest costs of which will be a significant part of the increase in invisible
payments to the $2 billion mark within 5 years unless an alternative is applied. The Bill
contains the alternative.
Under the present trading system unemployment would rise to approximately 250 000 if
New Zealand balanced her overseas accounts with IMF-dominated markets. The Bill
contains measures to balance the overseas account without socially disastrous
unemployment or further rundown of New Zealand's productive base. Measures are also
included for this House to take action against any international obstruction of this policy.
The Bill also provides for the credit mechanism to operate for the benefit of local
government and community development without the crippling burden of high interest
charges forcing up rates.
The Bill allows the Government to manage the economy, with the additional tool of the
monetary arm supplementing the traditional and almost exclusive use of taxation and high-
interest borrowing for Government use. In this function the policy will predominantly be one
of credit creation replacement, not addition, if inflation is to be avoided. Additional steps
will be taken later to progressively reduce the creation of high-interest private credit with at-
cost public credit. The Bill provides the tool for the restructuring of productive industry to
meet the needs of changing and new markets, and also for the social restructuring of industry
to reduce industrial conflict and unrest. A new management tool is required to halt the
serious fall in production. Over the last 4 years consumption within New Zealand has
dropped 17.25 percent, with production also continuing to decline, resulting in intensifying
social and economic problems. The latest trade export figures in terms of volume fell around
5 percent, which, when related to the overseas debt and invisible payments problem, cannot
be allowed to continue.
The new monetary branch of the Government would become the tool and the catalyst
for restructuring and rejuvenating New Zealand production, and would stop the downward
drift of living standards, which are now below those of Britain and are moving towards those
of Spain. The Bill provides the means for fairly and justly distributing production as it moves
up to the optimum level desired, with the monetary branch charged with implementing this.
The Bill contains measures to keep prices and incomes in balance so that neither inflation
nor deflation occurs to a socially damaging degree. An economic equation is contained in the
Bill that will provide the method of attack by the monetary branch in maintaining an
economic equation that is neither inflationary nor deflationary. The formula is orthodox and
is one which academic economists believe applies at present. The fact that the equation does
not presently apply, and rarely has, is a mechanical reason why a monetary arm of the
Government must be established as outlined in the Bill. The monetary arm is charged with
actually making happen what academic economists in their ivory towers mistakenly think
does happen.
The Bill contains a definition of money that aligns with reality-and I refer to the
Reserve Bank Bulletin of April 1978, at page 126--and which will cause some misgivings
amongst some, but I do not believe all, orthodox economists, because they have been busily
changing the definitions of money in recent years to try to align nasty and unpleasant facts
with their traditional beliefs. The Bill establishes the reality of what money is in the real
world, and in a properly functioning economy.
The Bill also requires the monetary arm to maintain a balance sheet showing which
institutions are using the money created solely for and on behalf of the people. This balance
sheet will be available for public scrutiny, although details of advances made to individual
trading banks will be confidential. The balance sheet will not contain details of trading bank
transactions with their customers; they will remain confidential. An exception will be the
accounts of certain public authorities that elect to use the services of trading banks, instead
of the Reserve Bank, for both loan and revenue accounts.

not provide for all of the credit coming into circulation to be brought in in a debt-free

local bodies will be in the form of low-interest loans, which will be repayable, returnable,
and cancellable.
The member for Porirua does not understand how the orthodox equation, M × V = I,
can be manipulated. He suggested that, if incomes increase, it must be because the money
supply has increased. If there are two elements in the equation, then obviously one or the
other can move. What has happened in this country for the last 20 years is that the classical
money supply has rapidly diminished and the velocity of the circulation of that supply has
rapidly increased, and the increase in incomes has reflected much more the increase in the
velocity of circulation than any increase in the money supply. In fact, the classical money
supply has shrunk.
I was particularly interested in the remarks of the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, and
I was astounded to find that he does not even know the orthodox equation, which is the
equation he was supposed to be operating for 3 years when he was Minister of Finance. No
wonder we got into such a mess! I am also astounded that the Associate Minister of Finance
does not understand the equation either because, according to the academic economists, that
is the equation he is supposed to be operating. He is not operating it, and it does not surprise

RESIDENTIAL LAND DAMAGE BILL
Introduction
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): I move, That the Residential Land Damage Bill be introduced.
In moving the introduction of the Bill, I would first like to explain to the House my reasons
for so doing. For some years I have lived in a part of New Zealand that is well known for soil
instability, especially that area which comprises Banks Peninsula and the land adjacent to it.
Over the years, there has been considerable residential development on those hills, and,
following the extreme weather conditions and substantial rainfalls in recent years, many
residents have daily lived in fear of the land upon which their homes are built, or land close
to their homes, collapsing, and creating damage or threat of damage to them. This threat is
one that creates the fear to which I allude. I can assure the House that the fear is very real
indeed to these residents.


## p. 3207 (#603) ###########################################

6 September
3207
Residential Land Damage Bill
The instability of soil is not confined to my electorate. It is also evident in such places as
Dunedin, Gisborne, the Hutt Valley, Wellington, Auckland, and parts of the Kapiti
coastline in the North Island. Also, there has been considerable threat to residential
property from sea erosion, and it is these hazards that this Bill proposes to provide for. If a
house is structurally damaged or destroyed by such an event, then the property owner is now
covered by the provisions of the Earthquake and War Damage Act, cover provided in a
proportion of his householder's insurance premium. However, the Earthquake and War
Damage Act has no provision for assistance to be granted to a householder should the
property suffer a landslip that creates no actual structural damage. Should such a landslip
take with it, in its fall, retaining walls, fences, pathways, and the like, they are not covered
by insurance, and no claim will be entertained by the Earthquake and War Damage
Commission. It seems ludicrous that a property owner who has suffered landslip or sea
erosion, which has not caused actual damage to a house but which leaves a constant threat of
further impending slips that could cause the total wreckage of a house, has nowhere to turn
for financial assistance to protect his property.
He can apply to the Housing Corporation for an additional mortgage, or, if not eligible
for a Housing Corporation mortgage, may borrow from a private source, to obtain funds to
pay for the clearance of the soil deposited by the slip, to refill erosion caused by the sea or a
river, to rebuild retaining walls, or to repair access ways to his home. I can assure members
that this can be very expensive and sometimes can be a financially crippling cost. For
example, in the Hutt, when the December 1976 flood cost was assessed, uninsured damage
alone was estimated at over $500,000. It has been said that insurance companies should be
obliged to offer insurance cover for such hazards, and I agree. The fact remains they do not;
not even fences are included in a comprehensive household insurance policy.
Because all residential development must receive prior approval from the local
authority in whose district the property is situated, this Residential Land Damage Bill
involves the local authority. It sets up machinery to enable the residents in that local
authority's area to obtain financial assistance in the event of any damage occasioned by
flood, landslip, or sea erosion. The Bill proposes that each local authority should set up a
local disaster fund by means of a levy on rates of 1c in every $100 value of rateable residential
land in its district. The moneys so levied would be paid into the National Provident Fund,
which would act as trustee. From this fund claims would be paid to 75 percent of the assessed
cost of remedial work to repair such damage. This means that residents themselves would
carry one-quarter of the risk of such damage.
The Bill is permissive; there would be no compulsion upon local authorities to establish
such a fund, but it is my hope that the residents in the areas which have suffered such harm,
or are threatened by such harm, would persuade the local authority to set up such a funding
scheme. I am sure that most local authorities who have experienced such disasters, and been
involved with residents who have been affected would be most eager to embrace such a
scheme as this Bill envisages.
I will now deal with the clauses of the Bill in greater detail. Clause 1 is the short title.
Clause 2 defines the various terminology used in the Bill, and includes the definition of the
word "damage" to mean physical damage to land. This would include retaining walls,
fences, drains, channels, pathways, reservoirs, water towers, septic tanks, and even
swimming baths. The definition of the word "flood" is any inundation of residential land by
water, however caused. The word "landslip" has been defined in great detail, in order to
remove any doubt as to what is intended. It is, in fact, the definition from the Earthquake
and War Damage Act, amended to specifically include erosion of land caused by the action
of sea water. "Residential land" is defined as rateable property that is used, or is intended to
be used, as a place of residence by any person.
I would point out that the Bill has application to residential land only, and clause 2,
subclause (3), states this very clearly. Clause 3 stipulates that the Bill will bind the Crown.
Clauses 4 and 5 set up the local disaster fund, and what would be paid into it and paid from
it. Clauses 6 and 7 define how the rate would be levied, and makes provision for a maximum
level, defined in the Bill as 0.2 percent of the total value of the residential land in any district.
Once the fund reaches that level, then a local authority may determine not to levy a special
disaster rate in a subsequent year. Clauses 8, 9 and 10 deal with actual damage, how claims
may be lodged with the local authority, and how such claims may be paid.
Clause 10 specifically states that the local authority may make good the damage by
either the payment of a specified sum, or by offering to repair the damage itself. In cases


## p. 3208 (#604) ###########################################

3208
6 September
Residential Land Damage Bill
where the local authority accepts the responsibility for the cost of repairs—that is, perhaps
by the removal of soil which has been deposited by landslip-then the resident must, of
course, refund to the local authority his 25 percent share of the cost.
Clause 11 provides, where disputes may arise, for them to be referred to an arbitrator.
Clause 12 provides for the claim reimbursement to be paid out of the fund to the local
authority, and also in subclause (2) that where insufficient funds are available in the name of
that local authority, then the local authority could apply to the Minister of Finance for
permission to borrow from the fund to enable it to discharge its liabilities to make good the
damage to residential properties within its area. Clause 13 sets out the details of applications
to borrow, made to the Minister of Finance; and clause 14 sets out how the loan repayments
shall be met.
Clause 15 provides for compensation from negligent parties and allows for the resident
to be paid for the damage to his property when it has been caused by wilful neglect on the
part of a third party. This clause also contains a provision that the Attorney-General may act
on behalf of any person to make a claim for legal liability in respect of damage caused by
negligence on behalf of a known party. Clause 16 provides for advances from the
Consolidated Revenue Account in the event of there being insufficient money in the disaster
fund to meet all the claims at once. One could envisage a situation such as the Wahine storm,
affecting large areas of the country, and in such an event, many claims could be made upon
each local fund far in excess of the total sum available. This clause gives the Minister of
Finance power to make advances from the Consolidated Revenue Account should such an
action be necessary.
There are 22 clauses in the Bill, but the latter clauses are mainly machinery. In the
opinion of many people the Bill is a necessity. It has long been felt that some facility and
protection should be afforded people in the situations this Bill envisages and, in my opinion,
it is a useful and effective extension of the provisions of the Earthquake and War Damage
Act. I do not say that the Bill is perfect, or that it is the only answer to the problem faced by
so many people, but it is a genuine and sincere attempt to place before Parliament a remedy
for people in this plight.
I know that many members represent residential areas that are not hilly, and whose
electorates contain considerable flat land, but inclement weather and extreme rainfall
damage is not confined to landslips; flooding can be extremely damaging to residents in
other areas such as the Taieri Plains. Under the Standing Orders this Bill will be referred to
the Local Bills Committee for further consideration, and I hope that very serious
consideration will be given to it by that committee. I ask all members of the House to
support this Bill.

totally committed to the expansion of the New Zealand fishing industry, and would continue
to give it the type of support it had received in the past 3 years. With that support, the fishing
industry would go from strength to strength in the 1980s.

Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) said the Opposition had been disappointed that

were out of work. In the last 2 years, 40 factories had closed in Otago, 6 of which had been
major. Inflation had been running at a record level, with record borrowing and a record level
of imports. The railcars had been scrapped, and the Rangatira had been torpedoed.
The major problem facing Otago and Southland manufacturers had been that of freight,
with a lack of freight incentives provided by the Government. When the Labour
Government had been in office 34 companies had received incentives, but now only 11
received incentives, of which 2 were getting a normal subsidy, but that was effectively cut by
half because of the freight increases over the last 2 years. The other nine companies received
incentives on a diminishing basis, which would be phased out in 2 or 3 years.
The Development Finance Corporation, which had been completely restructured by the
Labour Government, had become no more than a merchant bank and was quoting interest
rates from 11.5 percent to 14 percent, although it was supposed to be the lender of last
resort. One major manufacturer in Dunedin had said recently that he would not go near the
DFC for a loan, because his trading bank lent money at a lower rate of interest.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) said that regional development
had taken an interesting and essential new thrust since the Labour Government had been
thrown out of office. Regional development policies were now built on the essential basis of
development of the resources of the region. To that end, regional development councils had
been asked to bring together vital information for the assessment of future developments.
Confidence in Otago was stronger today than it had been 3 years previously. The
member for Dunedin North had helped to change the attitude of the people in Otago. The

reached. The Government was to proceed with hydro development for the Upper Clutha
Valley, where up to 18 000 ha of irrigation would be produced. Several manufacturers were
unable to find even semi-skilled labour to fill vacancies in industry.

The member for Porirua said-
Mr Courtney: A good member, too.
Mr N. P. H. JONES: That is a matter of opinion. This report states, "MP says social
security change could mean starving families." That is what he said about clause 11 of the
Bill. I have read clause 11 very carefully. Labour speakers have maintained that it will stop
unemployment benefits. The member for Porirua said that clause 11 will stop the
unemployment benefit for every person who is affected by a strike. Clause 11 does not state
that. The member for Porirua is quoted in the Evening Post as having said during the debate:
"If a union in which they have no say whatsoever insists on striking, they go to the Social
Welfare Department and are told they cannot get an unemployment benefit. Dr Wall said
that because one group has gone out on strike everyone else is unemployed, no one will get a
cracker, and their families will be starving."
Clause 11 distinctly states that the strike must be at the same place, involve the same
work, or be by the same group of employees. The Act already provides that the
unemployment benefit can be withheld from striking workers who have voluntarily opted to
strike for 6 weeks. Some strikes have lasted more than 6 weeks. The clause precludes
unionists who go on strike from obtaining the unemployment benefit. I shall take the mutton
butchers in a freezing works as an example. When they go on strike they will not get the
benefit. At present they get the benefit when they are on strike for more than 6 weeks.
Anyone at the freezing works who is out of work because of the mutton butchers' actions will
qualify for the benefit. The member for Porirua did not say that, and neither have other
Opposition members. They have said that people who are unemployed because of a strike
over which they have no control, and where they do not have a vote, will not receive the
benefit.
Clause 11 also states that the only employees who will not receive the benefit are those
who voluntarily go on strike. Why should they receive a benefit? In my dear old dad's days,
if one went on strike for one's principles one sacrificed one's pay. If a person accepted
anything from any other source he was considered to be a scab. The Labour Party has stated
that the State should join the scabs and pay striking unionists. For goodness sake, no one
would return to work if he could obtain the unemployment benefit. Not one person in the
country can see the justice in people voluntarily giving up $14,000 a year, or $250 a week-
and I am speaking about the freezing workers-to go on strike. Last year, 54 percent of the
strikes were politically motivated by the wage freezes and the penalties in the Industrial
Relations Act. The freezing workers expect to be paid for being on strike. Labour's policy is
to pay the striking workers. I will go to every freezing works, factory, pub, and club and say
that Labour believes in paying the unemployment benefit to guys who go on strike. National
believes in paying every person who is out of work because of a strike, but not if they have
voted to strike. That is the way I interpret clause 11.
I have no objection to workers using the strike weapon for an improvement in wages,
conditions, and safety. The Act makes provision for workers to do that. I know that many
people have another job jacked up before they go on strike. There is no such thing as a
principle of solidarity in today's unions. The union members expect and demand the
unemployment benefit. The Labour Party has fostered that attitude, and if Labour is
returned it will pay every person who is out on strike. That is my reaction, and I am sure it is
the reaction of many people.

enlightened leadership of Norman King. One of those changes was to ensure that married
students, and those living away from home, would not be means tested. I believe that the
reservations about clause 11 are justified.

The Government said that, when national superannuation reached 80 percent of the
average weekly wage-as it has done-there would be no need for the additional benefit. A
survey of the aged in 1975 concluded that, whatever the level of the basic benefit, some
elderly people would always require further financial help. Some people receiving national
superannuation had no other income, but had considerable outgoings—for instance, rents.
As the rents had gone up over recent years, their ability to make ends meet had been
constrained.
The survey of the aged authorised by Norman King was released in 1975 and showed
that, no matter what level the age benefit reached, there will always be some people who,
because of inadequacy of other income and because they have extra commitments,
particularly in housing, will not find that sufficient. I remember that the survey showed that
people who were ill sometimes thought twice about going to a doctor; there were people who
did not buy new clothes when they needed them; there were people who, when it was cold,
would not turn the heater on; and there were people who went without the occasional meal.
In reducing or restricting the availability of the additional benefit, which was created for just
that group of people, the Government is closing its eyes to the genuine need still experienced
by a small proportion of national superannuitants. The additional benefit was designed for
those people with limited income and assets. On 31 March, 40 105 national superannuitants

superannuitant will need the additional benefit, or, alternatively, if it is drawn to the
attention of the Minister that some new national superannuitants need extra financial
assistance, will the Minister consider reinstating it or making some other assistance
available?

SUPPLEMENTARY QUESTIONS SPEAKER'S RULING
Mr SPEAKER: Before I call the first honourable member to ask his question, perhaps I
could just make a comment, or give a ruling, as I promised to do yesterday, on the matter
raised by the member for Roskill. Several points of order were raised about supplementary
questions. In fact, there was a discussion about the number of supplementary questions that
should be allowed and the grounds on which I should permit them.
There was a specific request from the honourable member for Roskill to allow members
to discipline themselves—as I understood him. He suggested that I should continue to accept
supplementary questions so long as they were offering, provided they were relevant and
otherwise consistent with Standing Orders. I welcome his suggestion of self-discipline by
members, and I presume he would extend that to Ministers as well. I offer the thought that
the most productive form of self-discipline that can be taken would be for members to think
before they rise to ask a question, whether that question is in fact succinct, relevant, and in
elucidation of the original reply. Ministers' answers should be concise and confined to the
subject-matter of the question and should not contain any argument or controversial matter.
That would be a very helpful form of self-discipline not just for me, but for the House.
Experience has shown me, at any rate, that to leave to the House how many and what
supplementary questions are asked leads to chaos, with the inevitable points of order and
acrimony that seem to follow. Perhaps memories are short, but I remind members that
obviously, the system was unsatisfactory before 1972, because then the Standing Orders
Committee recommended that it should be left to the discretion of the Speaker, suggesting
that he might allow up to three supplementary questions to each question. Indeed, that
Standing Orders Committee went as far back as 1962, when new rules regarding oral
questions were introduced. It was further considered by the 1967 Standing Orders
Committee, and again by the 1972 Standing Orders Committee. The arrangement made by
the 1972 Standing Orders Committee proved to be unsatisfactory, too, because the Standing
Orders Committee of 1974 again looked at the problem and suggested more flexibility. That,
in turn, led to virtual open slather, with fewer questions being reached each day, but with a
plethora of supplementary questions, many of which bore little resemblance to the original
reply.
Since I have been in the Chair I have tried a new system; I have set priorities. The first is
that every member who has a question on the Order Paper has as much right as any other
member to have his question answered by a Minister in the House. The second is that that
member should have the first opportunity to seek elucidation of the answer by asking a
supplementary question. Thirdly, a member from the other side of the House should be able
to seek further elucidation from, perhaps, a different, but still relevant, angle. The fourth
priority is for further supplementary questions if time permits. The Standing Order provides
a maximum, not a minimum, of 40 minutes for oral questions. By and large, I try to assess
those questions that are likely to need elucidation, so that the time is fully used. Indeed, we
often exceed the 40 minutes, because I am in the habit of calling the last question even
though there may be only a few seconds left on the clock; and then we have perhaps four or
five supplementary questions thereafter. The only occasion that I can recall recently, when
we have had less than 40 minutes was the day before yesterday.
This is an important part of the function of Parliament-the constitutional right of
members to question the Executive on its policies and its administration. But it is the
opportunity for all members, not just the Opposition, and I have a responsibility to protect
that right as far as I can. My experience shows that most supplementary questions are asked
by a few members. To accede to the suggestion of the member for Roskill would tend to give
those few members an advantage over their fellows in the amount of time that is available to
them in the House. Also, if members are left to their own devices, they tend to make a
practice of asking supplementary questions for the sake of it, sometimes preventing other


## p. 3240 (#636) ###########################################

3240
7 September
Supplementary Questions-Speaker's Ruling
members from having an opportunity to ask an initial question. The honourable members
will recall that type of thing having happened.
By and large, most members have accepted, and I believe welcomed, the system that I
have been trying to operate. If fewer prime questions were asked-and I have discussed this
matter with the Whips and the people who work with the Whips putting in the questions-we
would have more time for supplementary questions, which I would certainly allow. The 40
minutes is there to be used. Yesterday, ignoring the questions withdrawn or transferred for
written reply, we had 20 questions, plus 33 supplementary questions, 23 asked by the
Opposition and 10 by the Government—a total of 53 questions. On two questions there were
four supplementary questions, and on three there were three supplementary questions. The
previous day I allowed six supplementary questions on one question.
I certainly believe question time is important to members, particularly back-bench
members, on both sides. It is important for them to be able to question Ministers. But I
believe that it should cover members as widely as possible, and I should not allow some
members to monopolise the time at the expense of others. Therefore, I propose to continue
my policy as freely as I can, and I feel sure that if members would co-operate, perhaps by
asking fewer oral questions or more written questions-if we go through the Order Paper I
am sure we could see a number that could quite properly be asked as written questions-and
by not asking supplementary questions that will be disallowed or that are trivial, then I can
allow more time and opportunity for deeper probing, which I believe is the important part of
the question period. I shall certainly do my best to follow that type of policy.

Roading Assistance, Northland
1. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and Development: Has
the special roading assistance, as introduced to Northland by a Labour Government, been
varied in any way?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): No special assistance to
Northland roading has been given by the present Government. Grants by the Government
to the National Roads Board were not tagged, as the Government respects the expertise of

Auckland Extramural Hospital—Dietitians
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa), on behalf of MARILYN WARING (Raglan), to the
Minister of Health: How many dietitians are employed by the Auckland Extramural
Hospital, what is the ratio of dietitians to patients at this hospital, and how does it compare
with the ratio of dietitians to patients in major public hospitals?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): One dietitian is employed by the Auckland
Extramural Hospital, which has 6000 patients. There is one dietitian to every 49 patients in
the Auckland Public Hospital; 1 to 60 in the Waikato Hospital; 1 to 55 in the Wellington
Hospital; and 1 to 28 in the Christchurch Hospital.

Onehunga National Party Candidate
11. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Police: Who authorised the use by the
Onehunga National Party candidate of a photograph of policemen in a propaganda leaflet,
which he has circulated throughout the Onehunga electorate?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police): No police authority was sought to
include in a political pamphlet a photograph of the Onehunga National Party candidate
talking to members of the Police. The policemen in the photograph had no knowledge that
the photograph was to be published in a political pamphlet. The attention of all the persons
involved has been drawn to section 31 of the Police Act, which provides that no member of
the Police shall take part in any election of a member of Parliament or of a local authority.
Mr Rogers: Is it correct that section 46 of the Police Regulations 1959 forbids police
officers from wearing any party emblems or otherwise manifesting political or sectarian
partisanship?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: So far as I know it does not arise.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I have difficulty in understanding how that supplementary
question can be related to the original question, which was about a photograph.
Mr Rogers: Yes-its use for political purposes.
Mr SPEAKER: I know about the supplementary question. It may be of interest, but I
cannot see how it is related to the answer that was given.
Mr Rogers: Can I explain?
Mr SPEAKER: I have allowed the member to ask his supplementary question, and the
Minister to comment on it, but I do not think we should pursue the matter further than that.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The matter raised by the member for Onehunga does not
arise, because the good-looking policemen in the photograph did not wear any emblems
other than those set down for the police uniform.
Mr Isbey: Will the Minister inform other National Party candidates about the
regulations prohibiting the use of policemen in political propaganda?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The member is wrong. The prohibition is on the police not
on members of the public. Under section 31 of the Police Act members of the Police are not
to engage in politics. It states that subject to the provisions of sections 30 and 31 no member
of the police shall, while he remains a member, take part in any election of a member of
Parliament or of a local authority. It is not a sanction on members of the public. It is on
members of the Police.
Mr Isbey: Then will the Police be taking action against the National Party candidate in
Onehunga for using the Police for party political propaganda?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No. There is no ground upon which action might be taken.
The Commissioner of Police has advised his districts, and has reminded members of the
Police of the provisions of section 31 of their Act.

Voter Identification
15. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Justice: What identification ensures
that a person claiming a vote against a name on the electoral roll is in fact that person, and,
in the event of plural voting, which vote is disallowed?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): No proof of identity is, or ever has
been, required of any voter. Our electoral system assumes the inherent honesty and integrity
of the people of New Zealand. The procedure is for an elector to attend at a polling booth,
state his name, address, and occupation, and, after the roll has been checked, be issued with
a ballot paper and licensing voting paper. When a returning officer is satisfied that plural
voting has occurred both papers are withdrawn and neither is counted.
Mr O'Brien: What is the Government's reaction to the fact that a legitimate vote has


## p. 3247 (#643) ###########################################

7 September
3247
Questions for Oral Answer
been disallowed?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Has the member got proof of that? If he does have, I ask him
to let me have it.
Mr Kirk: Is the Minister saying that if a person voted legitimately but another person
voted using the first person's name the person who voted legitimately would have his vote
discounted?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That is not plural voting. Plural voting takes place when one
person votes twice.
Mr O'Brien: How does the Department of Justice decide what is plural voting when one
person has voted twice?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: If the member wants some research into the Act for his
answer I should be glad to get it, but I shall need to be given notice. It is well known that
plural voting involves one person voting twice.

APPROPRIATION BILL-ESTIMATES
In Committee
Department of Trade and Industry
Further consideration of vote, Trade and Industry (Part Programme II, Regional
Development), $4,523,000.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) said that under the Labour Government no fewer
than 640 jobs had been created in three new industries at Dannevirke, Castlecliff, and
Foxton, and today those industries were exporting products worth $11 million. Eleven new
industries had been established on the West Coast. Under the National Government, five
companies had closed in Otago and one had moved to Christchurch; in Southland one
company formerly assisted by the Labour Government had closed; and on the West Coast
one had closed. Under previous National Governments, before 1972, there had been no
fewer than 26 inquiries, seminars, investigations, or committees examining regional
development begun by the Labour Government.
Was it correct, as stated, in the National Business Review of 6 September, that Cabinet
was considering dropping its regional development committee and allocating its functions to
the works and economics committee, and that the decision, which had been about to be
made, had been delayed to allow the Department of Trade and Industry to report? Had a
decision been made along those lines? The article had stated that the Minister had said the
Cabinet Regional Development Committee had not met for many months, and had met only
two or three times in the past 2 years. Was that a vigorous development programme? Last
year the Minister had made very fulsome comment about an upsurge in regional
development. Had the Prime Minister decided that regional development should be phased
out, or had Cabinet acquiesced because it would not buck the Prime Minister?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) said that regional development
under Labour and National Governments could be compared by the use of two words-
Matai and Kokiri. Matai had been an artifically forced project, which had continued to cause
trouble. The Government was committed to backing the regional abattoir at Kokiri with
$1 million. Matai had been an industry unsuited to the West Coast, and the Kokiri project
was resource based, built on the strength of the farm land. Members should compare the cost
to the taxpayers of Matai with the production and export earnings that would be achieved by
investment in the abattoir. About $5 million of taxpayers' money would be used to make up
for the mistakes of the Labour Minister of Regional Development. The Minister of Trade
and Industry had invited the department to analyse the consequences of the moves.
Regional development had regularly featured on the agenda of the Cabinet regional
development committee. The committee, which included six of the seven most senior
members of Cabinet, had met each week. Could regional development ask for a stronger
weighting than that? The Leader of the Opposition had requested an invitation to be the
guest speaker at a meeting of the Otago-Southland Manufacturers Association on
Tuesday, 19 September, so that he could announce the Labour Party's policy on regional
development. Otago had confidence in itself and in its future under the present regional
development policies. The member for Dunedin North, who was the chairman of the
Government caucus committee on regional development, had supported the positive future

Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) said that the Government's energy policy had been
aptly described as patchwork. The public relations exercise had gone forward in top gear,
but the policy had been found to be wanting. The Government had talked about reducing
the country's overdependence on imported energy, but energy imports still cost more than
$500 million a year. Despite the fact that in 1975 the National Party had promised a vigorous
energy policy within 12 months of becoming the Government, the goals and guidelines were
still being discussed, and the Government's only effective action had been to increase costs
to the consumer by 134 percent in 3 years, thus retarding industrial growth and employment.
Industrial use of electricity had dropped from 19.6 percent in 1975-76 to 1.5 percent in
1977-78. In 1975-76 there had been an excess capacity of 575 MW, but the excess capacity for
the current year amounted to 1443 MW, and in 1981-82 would amount to almost 2000 MW.


## p. 3255 (#651) ###########################################

7 September
3255

Most of the 134 percent increase in the consumer charges had gone to pay the interest
charges on electricity, which had increased from $59.3 million in 1975-76 to $118.8 million in
the current year. The estimate for next year was $178 million. The increase had been brought
about by the Government's policy of charging at the rate of 10 percent on all new borrowing
for power generation, and turning over all past borrowing until it reached 10 percent. The
component parts of a unit of electricity were: depreciation, 12 percent; working expenses, 38
percent; and interest charges, 50 percent. Therefore half of one's power bill was needed to
pay the interest bill. Last year there had been a shortfall of $15 million in the Electricity
Account; this year the shortfall was again $15 million. To balance its books, the Government
had borrowed $15 million from the National Development Account and charged itself 10
percent interest.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) said that the Committee should return to the
basics of energy. First, the Labour Government had not only had three separate
departments concerned with energy, but had also had three different Ministers, and more
than once there had been a conflict of interests. Electricity charges had been frozen,
regardless of the fact that oil prices had escalated five times in 1973-74. The bulk power
charge had also been frozen, with the result that the taxpayers had paid about $18 million the
first year and $13 the second year to subsidise the electricity consumers. To compound a
ridiculous situation, the same taxpayers had been asked to contribute towards the cost of a
campaign to encourage people not to use electricity.
The inclusion of the Electricity Department and the Mines Department plus the
geothermal responsibilities of the Department of Works and Development and the energy
pricing responsibilities of the Department of Trade and Industry under one Minister and one
ministry had brought a new strength and a new dynamism to energy planning. The
Government had had to cope with the consequences of the electricity bulk charge freeze,
and it was inevitable that electricity power charges should have risen, as they had, by about
100 percent in two jumps in 1976 and 1977. Despite those increases, the true cost of
electricity in real terms was less today than it had been throughout the 1960s. Using the retail
price in 1940 with 100 as a base, the average in the 1960s had been on a scale of 63.9, and in
1978-79 the real cost relative price would be 49.9—a decrease of more than 10 percent on the
average in the 1960s.
As a result of the Government's conservation policies, the cost of imported oil as a
percentage of export earnings had been effectively reduced, and, from memory, the figures
had fallen from just over 20 percent to the present figure of about 15 percent. The energy
conservation awards had been a fine idea. In August 1975, when the Labour Government
devalued the New Zealand dollar, the price of oil to the domestic market should have been
adjusted, but the Government had not increased the price, and the oil account had gone into
a great deficit. When the National Government had been elected, it had corrected the matter
within days.
Other examples of action taken by the present Government included the power plan
published in the present week, and the liquid fuels project that had been published last
week. The report of the Royal Commission on Nuclear Power Generation in New Zealand,
the liquid fuels study produced by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, and
the goals and guidelines document produced by the Ministry of Energy, also provided
evidence of what the Government had done.
The Government had shown that it was prepared to consult public opinion in the
development of a community consensus on energy policies. The Labour Government, with
its three separate departments and their feuding Ministers, had not addressed itself to
solving the problem and had managed to freeze the situation for 3 years, thus allowing no
progress for the country.

Finance Bill
FRIDAY, 8 SEPTEMBER 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON Prime Minister): The business for next week is rather
curious. Tuesday will be the last day of the main estimates. On Wednesday we will have the
Supplementary Order Paper with answers to questions, followed by legislation. The House
will rise at 6.30 p.m. on Wednesday night. Local Bills will be taken on Thursday, followed by
supplementary estimates at 7.30 p.m. The intervening period will be taken up with
legislation. It is proposed to have the next Imprest Supply Bill on Friday.
FINANCE BILL
Introduction
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Finance Bill be
introduced. This is the annual washing-up Bill relating to miscellaneous matters. Clauses 2
and 3 re-enact provisions in earlier Finance Acts that still have effect, and facilitate the
eventual repeal of those Acts. Clause 2 relates to the powers of local authorities to promote
Bills. Clause 3 deals with the terms of the Emily Johnston Scholarship.
Clause 4 validates the payment of increased fees to coroners from 15 August 1977 as the
regulations authorising that increase did not come into force until 7 April 1978. Clause 5
relates to regulation 3 of the Tertiary Bursaries Regulations 1976 Amendment No. 1, which
removed a restriction on the payment of tertiary bursaries to students who work part time.
Tertiary bursaries were paid to such students from 1 May 1977, but the regulation did not
come into force until 2 December 1977. The clause validates such payments by bringing the
regulation into force at the earlier date. Clause 6 validates the payment of a compassionate
grant by the Petone Technical Institute to the widow of a deceased employee before
regulations authorising such grants were made.
Clause 7 dissolves the Monetary and Economic Council, the functions of which have
been taken over by other bodies, and consequentially repeals the Monetary and Economic
Council Act 1961. Clause 8 repeals various spent enactments, including 12 old Finance Acts,
in their entirety.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Rutherford High School Gymnasium
7. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Is it correct that in 1975
Rutherford High School was in the second group of schools that would have a gymnasium
built in 1976, and that the National Government cancelled this scheme when it came into
office?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The Rutherford High School was placed
in a high position on the new gymnasium priority list approved by the Labour Government in
July 1975. However, it was not expected that the second gymnasium would be built in 1976,
nor is it correct that the Government has cancelled this scheme.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister confirm that in 1976 Rutherford High School was given
exactly the same priority that it had in 1975, and that the funds that were to have been made
available in 1976, were still, in the same quantity, made available in the 1976-77 Budget?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The member seems to have a false impression of the position.
Provision was made, and continues to be made, for gymnasiums in all secondary schools, and
the provision includes the wording "within the finance available each year in the education
building programme". In 1975, Rutherford High School was in a position on that list—
Mr Hunt: A very high priority.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It was nowhere near the top.
Mr Hunt: It was a high priority.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It was eighth on the list in 1975. Gymnasiums are provided at all
schools in the early stages of development. Schools without gymnasiums go on to the priority
list for building as and when finance is available within the allocation in the education
building programme.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is not one of the reasons for the delay at Rutherford High School
that some schools had not received their first gymnasium, as promised by the Labour
Government in 1975-Massey High School, which has now received its gymnasium under
the National Government, being one of them?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It is obvious that schools must take their turn on the list. That is
one reason. In any case, Rutherford High School decided that it would not have a standard
gymnasium. It wanted a special design, so a special gymnasium had to be designed, and the
school had to give an undertaking that it would find the extra money involved.
Mr Hunt: The Minister said that Rutherford High School was eighth on the list in
1975-76. Was that eighth on a list of 10, or of how many schools? Did the likelihood of the
school receiving a second gymnasium change in any way in 1976?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It changed in no way whatever in 1976. We continued to build
the gymnasiums for which funds were available-probably more than under the Labour
Government. If there has been any delay it has been brought about by the changed design
that Rutherford High School wanted. As I have said before, rolls are falling quite
dramatically and will continue to fall over the next year or two, and if they fall to a level
below which the school is entitled to a second gymnasium, then the delay resulting from the
change in design might well jeopardise the building of that gymnasium.
Mr W. R. Austin: Am I to understand that Rutherford High School already has one
gymnasium?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes, but it is a very large school and still qualifies for a second
gymnasium.

Fish Exports
13. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Fisheries: What were the
tonnage and value of fish exports for the following years: 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976, and 1977,
and has he an estimate for 1978?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): The figures requested are as follows: 1973,
14 100 tonnes with a value of $20.1 million; 1974, 12 808 tonnes valued at $20.3 million;
1975, 14 494 tonnes, with an export value of $25.7 million. It is significant to note that those
3 years are almost identical, and were the 3 years under the previous Government. In 1976
the quantity increased to 20 500 tonnes worth $37.8 million. In 1977 it increased to 26 000
tonnes worth $50.3 million. For the first 6 months of 1978 the export figure is 21 000 tonnes,
worth $33 million, and the estimate for the full 1978 year is between 35 000 and 40 000
tonnes, worth between $60 million and $65 million.
Mr Wellington: Do the Minister's figures indicate that the Government has not sold out
to overseas fishing interests, as has been alleged by the member for Nelson?
Hon. J. B. BÖLGER: The figures I gave a moment ago refute entirely and absolutely
any suggestion that the New Zealand fish resource has been sold out to overseas interests.
The figures indicate tremendous growth in the New Zealand industry, and demonstrate that
New Zealand interests are harvesting the resource at a greater rate than ever before.
Hon. M. Rata: How much of the fish for which the Minister has given the tonnage and
value has been stockpiled around the country?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: I cannot give exact details, but, as I indicated in the House 2
evenings ago, the stockpiles as a percentage of total catch are less this year than last year,
and the stockpiles in total volume in absolute figures have declined in the last 3 months.
Mr W. R. Austin: As export earnings from fish have increased four times during the
term of the present Government, can the Minister confirm that this rate of increase is likely
to continue for at least another 10 years?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: It is a little speculative to anticipate the next 10 years' growth in
the industry, but I expect that expansion at about the present rate will continue for a number
of years.
Mr Courtney: Is it a fact that half the export earnings come from rock lobsters and total
$23,000, and that no assistance is given to rock lobster fishermen?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: It is correct that the rock lobster fishery is New Zealand's most
valuable export, but I draw attention to the growth in volume exports in the last 3 years—
from 14 494 tonnes in 1975, the last year of the Labour Government, to an estimated 35 000
to 40 000 tonnes this year-which is all outside rock lobster fisheries.

Mortgage Interest Rates
13. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Finance: Can he confirm that the most
recent figures available, as presented in the Reserve Bank monthly release New Mortgage
Registrations-Interest Rates for March 1978, show that the weighted average interest rate on
all mortgages registered climbed to 10.77 percent in March 1978, and can he further confirm
that this rate represents the highest average rate ever in New Zealand's recorded history?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): According to my information, the
average mortgage rate on all mortgages registered in the month of March 1978, was 10.71
percent, not 10.77 percent as quoted by the member. It is correct to say that the figure of
10.71 percent, representing the average nominal interest rate, has not previously been
exceeded over the period that average rates have been computed. It must be remembered,
however, as I pointed out in answer to a similar question asked on 26 May 1978, that when
the nominal interest rates are compared with the rates of inflation prevailing at the time it
can readily be seen that rates of interest have been lower in relation to the rate of inflation in
recent months than at most times in the last 70 years.
Mr Rogers: From what document did the Minister get the figure of 10.71 percent?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I got it from the economic department of the Reserve Bank
of New Zealand, Wellington.
Mr Rogers: Is the Minister saying that the Reserve Bank monthly release New Mortgage
Registrations-Interest Rates for March 1978 is incorrect?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I am saying that the figure of 10.77 percent quoted by the
member is incorrect. The answer was drafted by the economic department of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand which states that the correct figure is 10.71 percent. I cannot go any
further than that. The figure the member quoted was wrong.
