RESERVE BANK OF NEW ZEALAND AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Reserve Bank
of New Zealand Amendment Bill. The Bill is a companion Bill to the New Zealand Credit
and Currency Bill. It contains some fundamental new principles of government, the most
important of which is to curb the present power of the Executive headed by the Prime
Minister, and to restore and enhance the status of the House as the effective decision-making
body.
It is important to have the capacity to curb, check, and control Executive power,
particularly in the present circumstances when the Prime Minister, as leader of the
Executive, also is able to exercise additional power in his capacity as Minister of Finance.
This very important principle is established by repealing section 8 of the Reserve Bank of
New Zealand Act, which requires the bank to carry out the monetary policy of the
Government as communicated from time to time by the Prime Minister, and by replacing
this section with a new one, which is outlined in clause 3 of the Bill. The proposed new
section clearly establishes that the bank is required to give effect to every resolution of the
House of Representatives, notwithstanding any communication from the Minister or
otherwise made by the Executive.
The proposed new section does not preclude the Minister from advising the bank to give
effect to the day-to-day policy of the Executive, as at present. That should allay the concern
and misplaced apprehension of the Associate Minister of Finance, but clearly establishes
that Executive decisions are ultimately subservient to the will of the House.
Clause 3 also establishes a new principle of government, which, as far as can be
ascertained, is both new and a first in the world, in that the growth of Executive power
through the use of regulations in financial matters is curbed by the terms this Bill, its
companion Bill, and the existing Act. The growth of Executive power through the use of
regulations concerns many people; and this has been most ably and often expressed by the
member for Hamilton West. Clause 3 establishes that the House can from time to time
make, alter, amend, or rescind by resolution any provision that enables the Minister to
exercise any power over or give any direction to the Reserve Bank. This clause also allows
the House to make, amend, or revoke regulations in addition to or in substitution of
regulations made by the Governor-General by Order in Council.
The existing section 8 enables any resolution of Parliament, as the term is used in the
present Act, to be made in relation to monetary policy. It is a right that has never been able
to be effectively exercised. It had its origin in 1950, when the Holland Government
introduced it at the behest of Sir Henry Kelliher. The need to make the House resolution
principle stick will be much more important because of the possible abuse of power by the
Executive once the provisions of the New Zealand Credit and Currency Bill apply.
The present situation is bad enough and must not be allowed to continue while the
Reserve Bank is vested with the capacity, and is the sole agency authorised, to create and
cancel New Zealand's money supply. All the proposals in clause 3 are important, and, when
carried, will represent a major advance in the necessary balancing of the powers of the
different arms of government and in lifting the status of the House so that it can truly reflect
the will and the wishes of people in a mature democracy. In another Bill I intend to apply this
principle to all regulation-making powers so that Parliament itself could make, alter, or
revoke any regulation. This Bill however, confines the new constitutional principle to
regulations under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act. The proposals contained in the
companion Credit and Currency Bill make a good starting point for the checking and
balancing by the House of any possible abuse of Executive power. Abuse of Executive
power is typical of totalitarian governments, of which communism is one form-a fact that


## p. 3274 (#670) ###########################################

3274
8 September
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Amendment Bill
should be of particular interest and, I hope, some concern to the member for Rangiora.
Clause 4 is a machinery clause requiring trading banks to furnish a special return of the
credit they have created at the time the New Zealand Credit and Currency Bill is enacted. It
is this amount of money which, at the date of commencement, will be deemed to have been
created by the Reserve Bank. Clause 5 acknowledges that the traditional system of control
over trading bank credit creation will be phased out, because after commencement of the
provisions of the Credit and Currency Bill trading banks will be able to lend only the money
advanced to them by the Reserve Bank.
Clause 6 is a tidying-up clause that provides for additional information from the trading
banks because of provisions in the New Zealand Credit and Currency Bill. The amendment
in clause 7 corrects a drafting error by changing the word "members" to "directors". Clause
8 states that if any conflict arises between the provisions of the New Zealand Credit and
Currency Act and any other Act, that Act will prevail. Clause 9 is a tidying-up clause that
brings the administration of the Acts concerned with credit and currency under the
administration of the Reserve Bank as the monetary arm of Government. Clause 10
establishes that an appropriation of public money is not required of the House of
Representatives to administer amendments to the principal Act contained within this Bill,
because these shall be a charge on the funds of the Reserve Bank.
The Bill contains two fundamental concepts, both of which are new. The financial
proposals will provide the mechanism to give New Zealand a future and the ability to
manage the economy in a way that is to the benefit and under the control of all the people of
New Zealand. This mechanism provides a way of tackling the problems of trade, social
injustices, falling living standards, inflation, and the present impasse that stands in the way
of improving the quality and environmental life of New Zealanders. The Bill contains
measures to build and strengthen democracy by allowing the House to be the paramount arm
of Government, because the House is the only branch directly answerable to the people.
The Bill contains measures that provide the first tentative steps not only towards a
better life, but also for a more involved and responsible participation in the processes of
democracy by all New Zealanders. Harry S. Truman once said that the world is not static,
and that the status quo is not sacred. May I conclude with the thought that there is no army
as powerful as an idea when its time has come.

REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT AND EXPORT INCENTIVE BILL
Introduction
Mr MacDONELL Dunedin Central): I move, That leave be given to introduce the
Regional Development and Export Incentive Bill. The Bill, consisting of four clauses, has
become necessary because the Government has failed to honour its 1975 promises. The long
title states that it is an Act to enable manufacturers and exporters to compete more
effectively on export or local markets.
Clause 2 is the interpretation clause. Clause 3 deals with a taxation deduction, and
states: "Where the Minister of Regional Development is satisfied that it would be reasonable
or desirable, he may allow manufacturers a tax deduction at 150 percent of the cost of
transport incurred for export products between the source of manufacture and the port or
airport of despatch." I believe this would assist manufacturers, particularly those in the
southern part of New Zealand, to compete more effectively on the main or export market.
Clause 4 deals with the cost of transport and states that this may be varied to assist regional


## p. 3278 (#674) ###########################################

3278
8 September
Regional Development and Export Incentive Bill
development. The clause spells out the meaning of that.
Recently, Mr Wilf Broughton, President of the Otago and Southland Manufacturers
Association, made it abundantly clear that manufacturers in the southern part of New
Zealand considered that the best type of incentive the Government could provide was a
freight incentive. He said, "The association's member companies are unanimous that the
best type of incentive for the area is a freight incentive." He went on to say, "As you all
know, the present Government has granted a continuance of the Labour Government's
freight incentive policy to very few companies and is rapidly phasing out the incentive to all
others." As manager of a large company in Dunedin he knows, as do other members of his
association, that if they are to compete on the North Island and export markets they need
this special assistance. They are not getting it under the present Government, which has
made it very clear that such assistance will be phased out if it is re-elected.
I have previously given figures for the Otago and Southland area. Very few companies
are receiving the freight incentive that applied under the Labour Government. Under the
present Government, transport has become chaotic and manufacturers, especially those in
the South Island, have to be much more efficient to compete on the North Island market.
Last year's Budget provided $4.1 million for regional development. However, because
of the Government's policy of phasing out that type of assistance, only $2.9 million, or 70
percent of the vote, was spent. The current estimates provide $4.5 million for regional
development. As inflation during the past 12 months has not been taken into account, the
vote has, in fact, been cut. If inflation is added to the amount of $4.1 million provided for in
the previous year, the amount of $4.5 million goes nowhere near the increase in costs.
The Government has tended to favour suspensory loans, but these are not
interchangeable with freight incentives. The Government fails to understand the two types
of incentive. The freight incentive is to enable companies to compete more effectively in the
north; a suspensory loan is for assistance to purchase plant and machinery and to expand a
business. There are companies in the southern part of New Zealand that are not particularly
keen or able, at present, to expand or to put in new machinery, but they do want to retain
their base industries and compete in the North Island. So they require a freight incentive, not
a suspensory loan. The two are not interchangeable, as Government members seem to think.
The member for Palmerston North has had a fair bit to say about exports. He would
claim that his Government is assisting exporters at present, but the Government is not
assisting exporters if it is not prepared to give them a chance to get their goods overseas. If
the Government continues to phase out the freight incentive that was helping exporters,
what the member for Palmerston North has said about assisting exporters is far from correct.
The Development Finance Corporation has previously assisted manufacturers. As I said
the other night, I feel that it is now nothing more than a merchant bank charging interest
rates from 11 percent to 14 percent. Manufacturers have come to me and said they no
longer have faith in the Development Finance Corporation, and that they are going to their
own banks for assistance. I also said earlier that Development Finance Corporation lending
was supposed to be a last resort to assist manufacturers. It is not providing that assistance
any more, and if the Government continues to allow that, and to cut back on funding freight
incentives, manufacturers will be in dire straits. The Bill provides for necessary assistance to
encourage manufacturers to retain their base industries in the provinces, and it will go a long
way towards cutting into the high level of unemployment. I hope the Government will
consider the Bill favourably.

MILK AMENDMENT BILL
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Committee
to present the report of the committee on the Milk Amendment Bill. The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. In doing so I want to outline a few of the major amendments. The committee
received submissions from the Milk Board and four other organisations representing
producer, processing, and vending interests. The submissions concentrated mainly on clause
4, which provided for the right of appeal against decisions of committees appointed by the
board under section 57 of the main Act to hear disputes and establish an appeal authority for
that purpose. On the evidence submitted, the committee considered that the scope of the
appeal authority should be widened and that it should hear appeals against decisions of the
board given pursuant to sections 17, 20, and 24 of the main Act. These decisions relate to the
consent of the board to the establishment of milk stations, the revocation of, or refusal to
renew, a vendor's licence, and payment of compensation to a vendor whose approval has
been revoked.
A right of appeal is already available to a magistrate's court, but there is a good deal of
support for such decisions to be subject to appeal to the proposed new appeal authority. The
Bill initially provided for a notice of intention to appeal to be lodged within 21 days, or such
longer period that the appeal authority might allow. It is now considered that 28 days would
be more appropriate, with no provision for extension. Clause 4 now incorporates an
amended section 57(c), which extends the function of the appeal authority to hear appeals
against decisions of the committees appointed by the board under section 57(3) and against
the board's decisions given pursuant to sections 17, 18, 20, and 24 of the main Act.
The committee also heard submissions on whether the board's decisions should be
implemented notwithstanding the lodging of an appeal, or suspended pending the outcome
of the appeal. There are valid arguments in favour of holding a decision, pending the
outcome of an appeal, to avoid hardship for an appellant, particularly a vendor whose
approval has been revoked. To impose a stay on all board decisions that carry a right of
appeal would, however, impede the board in its normal administrative functions. Clause 4
accordingly inserts in the principal Act a new section 57H which provides that, except for
decisions to revoke, or refuse to renew a vendor's approval under section 17, every decision
of the board or the committee of the board that is subject to a right of appeal shall have
effect until it is reversed or modified on appeal. Together with the committee, I believe that
the major changes outlined will improve the Bill.
Motion agreed to.

Transport Amendment Bill (No. 2)
TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Third Reading
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a third time.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): In addressing myself to the third reading I want to
make the point that, although there was limited debate during the second reading, because
of changed circumstances between 25 July—when the second reading was held—and the
present, the Opposition took the opportunity during the Committee stage to question the
sequence of events leading to the introduction of the legislation.
The Bill proposes to amend a section of the 1974 Transport Act, which provided for
harbour ferry service licences in a regional authority area to be dealt with by a regional
transport licensing authority. This procedure has been followed by the Auckland Regional
Authority since early 1975. However, because of a technicality, all areas within that
authority end at high-water mark, as defined in the Auckland Regional Authority Act 1963.
As I indicated during the Committee stage, the wording in the explanatory note is essential.
That part of the legislation is not disputed. However, as I said, it is essential to spell it out
again because of subsequent events. The explanatory note sets out exactly what is required
to overcome the contradiction between the 1974 Transport Act and the definition referred to
in the Auckland Regional Authority Act 1963.
The new subsection to section 120A of the principal Act will ensure that licences issued
under that Act are valid, and will remove any doubt by stating that a harbour ferry service
operated between termini, all of which are within, or in the close vicinity of, the boundaries
of a regional district, shall be deemed to be operated within that district. There is no
question about it. If the Bill is not passed, the licences that have been issued by the licensing
authority would be under question. Since the second reading of the Bill and the debate on
the short title, 'the issue has been clouded by the announcement of the resignation from the
National Party, after 41 years of service, of the Hon. Jack Scott, who gave a long period of
service to the National Party and the country.

Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: Yes, Sir.

difficult matter for members to understand-the scope for the third reading of a Bill.
The third reading is a more limited reading. Just because a matter has been referred to
in the Committee does not mean that it can be referred to during the third reading. The
amendments that have been agreed to by the Committee can be referred to during the third
reading, because they are incorporated in the Bill. Amendments considered by the
Committee, but not agreed to, can be referred to, but not discussed at great length. They can
be referred to for the purposes of recording. Amendments or propositions that were raised
by the Committee, but were ruled out of order as being irrelevant, beyond the scope of the
Bill, or whatever, cannot be referred to during the third reading although they may have
been discussed, or efforts may have been made to discuss them, during the Committee stage.

right to discuss every matter raised in the Committee, but only those that I consider to be
relevant to the principles of the Bill being discussed.

TUESDAY, 12 SEPTEMBER 1978

SITTING HOURS OF THE HOUSE

Motion agreed to.
LIQUID FUELS TRUST BILL
Introduction
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I move, That the Liquid Fuels Trust Bill be
introduced. This Bill represents a major step in the fulfilment of the Government's energy
policy, specifically with regard to a reduction in our reliance on imported oil and an
acceleration of the development of our indigenous resources. In 1977 New Zealand spent
more than $500 million on its oil imports, and of the total oil consumed in the country 67
percent was absorbed in the transport sector. Therefore, a reduction in the use of imported
fuel in this sector will contribute significantly towards a reduction in our import bill and our
external deficit. This Bill will be instrumental in achieving that aim.
New Zealand has extensive proven resources of natural gas that could substitute for a
large portion of our liquid fuels used in transport. Methanol, to be blended in various
proportions with gasoline and diesel, synthetic gasoline, LPG, and CNG are the most
important potential transport fuels that can be produced from natural gas. Alcohols for use
as fuels can also be produced synthetically by different processes from a variety of other
sources, including plant material, wood, and wastes. Hydrogen is another possible transport
fuel, and wood char, coal, and carbonised coal have been used in vehicles in New Zealand to
generate producer gas. Electrically operated vehicles, using electricity generated from
indigenous resources, and battery operated vehicles also deserve consideration.
Although the potential of these processes and fuels for achieving a replacement, or
partial replacement, of imported transport fuels by indigenous resources is recognised, the
technical feasibility, economic viability, and consequential effects such as environmental and
social aspects, require detailed investigation. The Bill establishes the Liquid Fuels Trust
Board, which will be responsible for encouraging, by providing financial assistance or
otherwise, investigatory work and tests relating to the efficient supply, processing,
distribution, and use for transport purposes of petroleum and alternative fuels derived from
indigenous resources. The board will have, as its primary function the promotion of the
reduction of the use of imported fuels for transport purposes in New Zealand.
Clause 1 relates to the short title. Clause 2 relates to the interpretation of the Bill.
Clause 3 establishes the Liquid Fuels Trust Board, and clause 4 prescribes the board's
functions. The primary function of the board is to promote, encourage, finance, undertake,
and co-operate in any activity that has as its purpose, or one of its purposes, the reduction of
the use of imported fuels for transport purposes in New Zealand. The board also has the
functions of promoting research into, and the installation of, efficient plant and equipment
for petroleum, alternative indigenous fuels, and alternative means of propulsion.
Clause 5 provides for the membership of the board. The board shall comprise the
Secretary of Energy, the Secretary to the Treasury, the Secretary of Trade and Industry, the
Director-General of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, and not more
than three persons to be approved by the Governor-General on the joint recommendation of
the Minister of Energy, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Trade and Industry.
Clause 6 relates to the term of office of members of the board. Clause 7 provides for a
deputy chairman of the board. Clause 8 provides for the appointment of deputies of
members of the board. Clause 9 prescribes procedural matters relating to meetings of the
board. Clause 10 prescribes the powers of the board and provides, among other things, that


## p. 3299 (#695) ###########################################

12 September
3299
Liquid Fuels Trust Bill
the board may, for the purposes of carrying out its functions, make grants or advances to, or
act as guarantor of, persons engaged in activities with which the board is concerned, and
acquire and develop land, buildings, plant, and equipment.
Clause 11 empowers the board to appoint advisory and technical committees. Clauses
12 to 15 relate to the appointment by the board of employees and experts. Clause 16
provides that the board shall comply with written directions given to it by the Minister, the
Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Trade and Industry. The clause provides also that
the Minister of Energy shall publish in the Gazette, and lay before Parliament, a copy of any
such direction. Clause 17 provides that the members of the board and the staff thereof shall
maintain secrecy in respect of all matters coming to their knowledge in the exercise of their
functions and powers under the Act.
Clause 18 provides that the members and staff of the board are not personally liable for
acts done in pursuance of the Act, unless done in bad faith or without reasonable care.
Clause 19 declares the board to be a statutory board within the meaning of the Fees and
Travelling Allowances Act 1951. Clause 20 prescribes how contracts made by the board are
to be signed. Clause 21 provides that the Crown may provide services for the board, and also
provides that the Crown shall be entitled to recover from the board costs incurred by the
Crown in providing administrative services for the board or administering the Act.
Clause 22 provides for the establishment of an account to be called the Liquid Fuels
Trust Account within the trust account of the Public Account. The clause also provides that
all levies paid under the Act, and all money received by the board from other sources, shall
be paid into the account, and that all grants, advances, fees, salaries, and other expenditure
payable under the Act shall be payable out of the account. Clause 23 provides for
authorisation of expenditure by the board, and also provides that in any financial year the
board may spend for purposes not authorised by the Act or any other Act any sum or sums
not amounting in the aggregate to more than $1,000. Clause 24 provides for the investment
by the board of any money available in the account in the same manner as the Treasury may
invest money according to the Public Finance Act 1977.
Clause 25 imposes a levy on all motor spirits and automotive diesel that is sold, used, or
otherwise disposed of after 1 November 1978. The levy shall be payable by wholesale
distributors of these fuels except in those instances where the fuels are sold by one wholesale
distributor to another, or the fuels are exported, or sold for export by a wholesale
distributor. The clause provides that the rate of levy shall be 0.1c per litre. It is expected that
$3.25 million will be paid into the account annually. This is based on the levy being applied
to 2 250 000 000 litres of gasoline and 1 000 000 000 litres of diesel each year.
Clause 26 provides that the Governor-General may, by Order in Council, reduce or
increase the rate of levy. The clause also provides that every such Order in Council shall
expire on a specified date unless expressly validated or confirmed by an Act of the General
Assembly. Clause 27 relates to the collection of levies payable under the Act, and applies the
collection provisions of the Motor Spirits Duty Act 1961. Clause 28 provides that all levies
paid under the Act, less an amount equal to the expenses incurred by the Collector of
Customs in collecting the levies, shall be paid into the Liquid Fuels Trust Account.
Clause 29 prescribes the effect of the imposition or alteration of the levy on agreements
for the sale of motor spirits and automotive diesel. Clause 30 provides that the board shall be
exempt from land tax, income tax, and stamp duty. Clause 31 provides that the board shall
submit a report and statement of accounts to the Minister of Energy each year, and that such
reports and accounts shall be laid before Parliament. Clause 32 empowers the Comptroller
of Customs to prescribe forms for the purposes of collection of the levy. Clause 33 relates to
repeals, consequential amendments, and transitional provisions. The clause repeals the
Kapuni Petroleum Act 1970 and provides that all money, including investments standing to
the credit of the Kapuni Petroleum Account, shall be transferred to the Liquid Fuels Trust
Account.
Having announced its commitment to reducing New Zealand's dependence upon
imported fuels and to promoting the increased utilisation of its indigenous resources, this
Government is determined to see that the precursory work necessary for achieving these
objectives is commenced as soon as possible. The Bill establishes a board that will take
responsibility for developing a work programme appropriate to the realisation of these goals.
The board will determine the alternatives that offer the greatest potential for the expedient
employment of New Zealand's resources, and will initiate the requisite work to verify the
feasibility of these options. The implementation of this Bill will be a significant step towards


## p. 3300 (#696) ###########################################

3300
12 September
Liquid Fuels Trust Bill
achieving self sufficiency in transport fuels, thus reducing New Zealand's dependence upon,
and its vulnerability to fluctuations in price and supply of, imported fuels.

anyway. Its revenue is to come from what is politely called a levy, which is a tax provided for

Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): The Bill proposes to establish a Liquid Fuels Trust
Board. To me that underlines the fact that the Government and the Minister of Energy, even
at this late stage in their term of office, have no firm policy for the development of the most
critical energy item-liquid fuels. The explanatory note on clause 4 reads: "The primary
function of the board is to promote, encourage, finance, undertake, and co-operate in any
activity that has as its purpose, or one of its purposes, the reduction of the use of imported
fuels for transport purposes in New Zealand. The board also has the functions of promoting
research into, and the installation of efficient plant and equipment for, petroleum,
alternative indigenous fuels, and alternative means of propulsion (as defined in clause 2 of
the Bill)." That is a very wide brief indeed, and it poses some very important questions on
energy, and more particularly on the liquid fuel sector-a sector that has rightly been
described as the most critical and the most sensitive aspect of any energy policy.
The Minister said that the country is paying about $500 million for imported energy, and
that the bulk of that $500 million is being spent on liquid fuels. It is amazing that, after
almost 3 years in office, the Government is now bringing in a Bill to set up a trust to advise it
and to promote a change of emphasis from imported energy to indigenous fuels. The
National Government promised a dynamic energy policy, and one would have thought that it
would have achieved much better results or indicated a liquid fuel energy policy long before
now.
The Bill provides for a levy to be imposed on petrol consumers from 1 November. That
may not appear to be of great importance, but the Minister told us that it will bring in about
$3.75 million a year, which is to be made available to the trust board for the purposes
mentioned in the Bill. Why is it necessary to impose another levy on energy users when a
significant energy levy has already been imposed? I think particularly of the energy resources
levy, which, according to the Budget, will take about $30 million a year from the consumers.
When that levy was introduced the understanding was that it would be used to promote
alternatives to imported energy. Last year the Government collected $34 million; in the first
year it collected $4 million. Therefore, about $64 million has already been collected during
the term of the present Administration. I emphasise that the Government placed that levy
on the consumers for the specific purpose for which the Bill now provides. Why was the trust
not funded from the account set up earlier? Why is it necessary to impose another penalty on
petrol users, to apply from 1 November? How much of the anticipated $3.75 million will be
spent in the first year of the trust's operations? Is $3.75 million sufficient to enable the job
envisaged to be carried out? What is the anticipated expenditure of the trust in exercising
authority over the wide-ranging field it has been asked to cover? Will the income be
sufficient to cover the outgoings of the trust? If not, will a further imposition be levied and
applied to other energy forms such as compressed natural gas, liquefied petroleum gas, or
bio-mass energy, all of which are liquid fuels used in the country?
Is it proposed to send the Bill to a select committee and to hear evidence from interested
parties? I believe that many interested people, and particularly representatives of motorist
organisations, would appreciate the opportunity of making submission on the proposals in
the Bill. I believe also that people associated with the industry-scientists and researchers—
will be vitally interested in making representations to the Minister.
The trust board is to comprise four officials to be appointed on the nomination of the
Minister, and three others. Can the Minister indicate who the three other appointees are
likely to be and which organisations they are likely to represent? Will motorist and
automobile associations throughout New Zealand be represented on the board? Will the

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I thank the Opposition spokesman on energy
for his advice that the Opposition welcomes the Bill. I remind the member that the
philosophy behind the Bill appears on page 26 of this year's Budget: "A Liquid Fuels Trust
Account is to be established to finance the development of new indigenous fuels and more
efficient distribution." It also stated that a levy of 0.1c a litre on motor spirits and automotive
diesel will be used to fund the account. The Bill follows the Budget announcement.
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition asked about finances. This will have no effect on
the price of petrol for some time, because at present the pool account is in credit. No
adjustment will be required in 1978. The trust account will begin with a credit of nearly
$500,000 through the transfer from the Kapuni Petroleum Account. Even after the pool
account is no longer in credit, the cost to the motorist will be negligible. It will amount to
about one three-hundredth part of the cost of petrol.
Clause 5, dealing with the membership of the board, requires some explanation. Quite
clearly the contribution made by the Government departments in the early stages will be
particularly significant, and that accounts for the relative balance that they will hold on the
board. The Government believes that it has a very suitable person in mind to chair the
board. I am pleased to be able to report that Dr Colin Maiden, the Chairman of the Energy
Resources and Development Committee and Vice-Chancellor of Auckland University, has
intimated that he will be available to accept the appointment, and I am sure that Opposition
members will agree that he will be eminently suitable. A number of working parties will
operate in association with the Liquid Fuels Trust Board, and the Bill provides for the
appointment of such bodies.
I have every reason to believe that the $3.25 million will be sufficient. The Bill allows for
this to be changed from time to time with the endorsement of Parliament, but we anticipate,
for the foreseeable future at least, that the levy of 0.1c a litre will be sufficient. It is not
proposed to send the Bill to a select committee. The format of the board is standard, and its
purpose was set out in the Budget. The money that comes from the energy resources levy at
present is spent on exploration for energy in its various forms, and on other research and
development work. A very considerable programme dealing with conservation measures
also requires finance. Another purpose of the energy resources levy is to deal with the
relative energy prices in relation to each other.
The member asked about secrecy. The provisions here apply only to those who might
not be public servants. Unless there was some such provision, those people would not be
required to comply with the provisions relating to the confidentiality of information that
might be made available to them. Quite clearly there will be a good deal of confidential
information that will come into the possession of those people, particularly before projects
are started. There is a requirement for the board to report to Parliament through the

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Rail Services-Availability of Alcohol
1. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Railways: Why are alcoholic
beverages not available on the Endeavour express or rail ferries on Sunday, as they are on
the Northerner and Silver Star expresses?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Railways.
"Alcoholic beverages are available on the Endeavour service on Sundays, but may be
consumed only in the dining car together with a meal purchased on the train. This is in
keeping with the generally accepted principle of confining liquor sales on a Sunday to dining
or house-bar areas. When the rail ferries were originally licensed to sell liquor the service
was provided in line with the normal trading hours of most licensed hotels. Consequently,
the liquor service on the ferries was provided only on a 6-day-a-week basis, which is the
position today."

Clutha Hydro-Electric Project
10. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Energy: What is the projected
saving in overseas funds through developing the hydro-electric potential of the Clutha as
against importing liquid fuels to produce the same energy output?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The Clutha Valley development will eventually
generate 4670 GWh from a series of stations. This development will cost approximately $240
million in overseas funds. To produce the same amount from an oil-fired plant would involve
additional overseas funds of $170 million for capital and $103 million a year for the overseas
content of the fuel at current oil prices.

Electoral Rolls
15. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: Is he aware that, on the
programme "Dateline Monday" on 4 September 1978, the Chief Electoral Officer, Mr J. L.
Wright, stated that people who are on the same electoral roll in 1978 as they were on in 1975
will receive a valid vote even if they are not on the 1978 roll, and, if this is correct, (a) does
this apply only to those few electorates in which the boundaries did not change between 1975
and 1978; or (b) does it apply to electorates in which there are substantial changes of
boundary; and (c) would a person whose name is not on the roll who lived in Avondale and
voted in Mt. Albert electorate in 1975 be given a valid vote?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I draw the honourable member's
attention to the provisions of section 99(c) of the Electoral Act 1956, which includes among
those qualified to vote "Any person who is qualified to be registered as an elector of the
district, and was at the time of the last preceding election duly registered as an elector of the
district, or where a change of boundaries has intervened, of some other district in which his
then place of residence within the first-mentioned district was then situated." In other
words, if a person was on the 1975 roll and has not changed his address, he can cast a valid
vote for whatever electorate that address is now in.
Mr Hunt: Referring to paragraph (c) of my question, can I clearly take it that a person
whose name is not on the New Lynn roll today, but who lived in Avondale and voted in the
Mt. Albert electorate in 1975, would he be given a valid vote?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I repeat-and I refer the member to the provisions of section
99(c)—that if a person was on the 1975 roll and has not changed his address he can cast a
valid vote for whatever electorate that address is now in.
Mr Hunt: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I refer you to the answer given by the Minister
and also to Speaker's ruling 119(2)(1), which states: "An answer to a question ought to be
given if it can be given consistently with the public interest." I asked the original question
and the supplementary because contradictory statements have been made by different
people about this very important matter. I think I am entitled to a yes or no answer as to
whether a person who voted in the 1975 election in an electorate, the boundaries of which
were subsequently changed, will be able to have a valid vote even though he lives at the same
address but has not been placed on the 1978 roll. As that matter concerns thousands of
people, Speaker's ruling 119(2)(1) applies.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Speaking to the point of order-
Mr SPEAKER: I need very little discussion on the point of order. The matter is really
not one for a point of order.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That was one of the points I was about to make. The other is
that the law applies to the whole of New Zealand. It does not matter whether a person
resides, or has resided all these years, in Avondale or any other non-electorate district. The
law applies wherever that address is.
Mr SPEAKER: The honourable member for New Lynn raised a point of order, which I
am sure he realises is not a point of order.
Mr Hunt: That's not right.
Mr SPEAKER: The honourable member might think it was a point of order, but it was
not, because he referred me to Speaker's ruling 119(2)(1), which states: "An answer to a
question ought to be given if it can be given consistently with the public interest." To my
understanding the Minister was giving an answer to the question. Whether that answer was
satisfactory to the honourable member is a different matter. It is not for me to say that the
answer is satisfactory or unsatisfactory. If the Minister refuses to give an answer, or if a
member who has a question down on the Order Paper refuses to ask it, I am in no position to
make either of them comply. It is a bit like the horse and the water, or vice versa.
Mr Lange: What does Speaker's ruling 119 do?
Mr SPEAKER: I am sure the honourable member has enough understanding to be able
to follow that. I am certainly not going to go into a dissertation at this stage into the

given a satisfactory answer, or words to that effect. It is not for me to say he has or has not
given a satisfactory answer. If the honourable member for New Lynn wanted further

Nuclear Power Development
19. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Energy: If the Clutha hydro
development proceeds as planned, to what extent is the necessity to develop nuclear energy
delayed or postponed?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The total output of the Clutha hydro
development will be 4670 GWh per year, with individual stations being brought in from 1987
onwards. This is equivalent to 4 to 5 years' expected growth in demand. However, the
Clutha should be seen as part of an overall programme making greatest possible use of
renewable indigenous resources, and this has allowed an indefinite deferral of nuclear
power.
Mr Prebble: Can I take it from the Minister's answer that he does not think there is any
need for nuclear energy either now or in the future?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: That is not what I said. I said "an indefinite deferral of nuclear
power". I trust that the honourable member has read the recommendations of the royal
commission chaired by Sir Thaddeus McCarthy and tabled earlier this year. If the
honourable member has read the report he will know that the commission suggests that the
earliest time for a decision on this matter will be the 1990s, with a view to coming into
production from the year 2013 onwards. However, since the royal commission heard
evidence last year we have had the opportunity of studying further the development of
power demand and alternative fuels, and we believe that the dates will be further into the
future than those proposed or suggested as possibilities by the royal commission.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is the Government's policy on nuclear power in sharp contrast with
the Labour Government's proposal of two nuclear power stations, one on the Kaipara
Harbour?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is correct that the last of the power plans of the previous
Government did provide for nuclear generation. It is also correct that this provision
continued for 1 year into this Government's first power plan, but has since been removed.
Mr Lange: Is it the Minister's thinking that nuclear power generation is a necessity,
irrespective of time?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The crystal ball that I have been equipped with is not clear enough to
see beyond about 30 years, but, within the time frame that we can reasonably plan for, we
believe there is no need for nuclear-powered electricity in New Zealand.
Mr W. R. Austin: In view of the delays resulting from this policy, is it likely that the
nuclear power that might have to be used in the future would be nuclear fusion rather than
nuclear fission?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: There is reason to hope that the product of the techniques and the
technology of nuclear fusion may well be available before New Zealand is in a position when
it has to entertain seriously the step into a nuclear technology.
Mr T. J. Young: How independent of Government direction, is the power planning
committee?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The power planning committee is not directed by the Government.
It makes recommendations to the Government, which the Government is quite able to reject
if it so wishes.

to time-if the House shall so direct a committee may report its opinions or observations
from time to time, or report the minutes of evidence only, or proceedings from time to
time." That is if the House directs the committee. When the House sends a Bill or a matter
to a committee for consideration, the House can say that it wants the committee to report
from time to time, and the committee can so report. Likewise if the chairman receives a
directive from his committee seeking leave to make a report to the House or to seek further
instructions, that may be done. There is a rather difficult ruling in Erskine May's
Parliamentary Practice that suggests that if a select committee seeks to make an interim

Mr SPEAKER: The position is really quite simple. A committee cannot come back to
the House to make an interim report unless the House has so directed. The exceptions are by
taking the leave of the House, and by a motion in the House given with notice, presumably
by the Minister associated with the committee, that the committee be empowered by the
House to make an interim report or interim reports from time to time-that motion being
debatable. The third course would be for the committee to direct the chairman to make an
interim report. It has to be done in one of those three ways: by leave, by motion, or by a
directive from the committee to the chairman. The fact that leave has been withheld today
does not prejudice the right of the committee's chairman to come back at a later date, or for
a Minister to move a motion along the lines I have given, with notice.

Ministry of Energy
Further consideration of vote, Energy, $487,810,000.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) said that in the past 12 months a new Ministry of
Energy had been created, and three separate departments-Mines, Electricity, and Energy
Resources-had departed from the scene. He was sure members on both sides of the House
joined with him in conveying thanks to the staff of the three former departments for serving
so loyally and well, and for co-operating in the creation of the new ministry.
Energy was of growing importance to Governments, Parliaments, and people, who
should be well served by a strong ministry. The new Secretary of Energy, Mr Duncan, and
his staff would serve the country well for many years to come.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) said he endorsed the comments of the Minister of Energy about
departmental officials providing New Zealanders with their energy requirements. However,
during the term of the National Government electricity prices had increased disastrously.
Consumers had received a great shock with their electricity accounts for the months of July
and August. The president of the New Zealand Clean Air Society had claimed that the
"average bloke" in Christchurch paid about a third more for electricity than his counterpart
in Auckland-and the cost to Auckland consumers was far too high. The Waitemata Electric
Power Board's consumers were charged considerably more for their electricity than were the
Auckland Electric Power Board's consumers. A further tenth of the interest charges was
being increased from 6 percent to 10 percent, and they would all be 10 percent by 1985.
In answer to a written question, the Minister had advised that Ohaki-Broadlands power
and Huntly power would cost 2.4c a kilowatt, and that Clutha power would cost between
2.1c and 2.3c a kilowatt. In 1977 terms, the current replacement cost would be at least 3c a
kilowatt-and, if inflation were taken into account, it would be very much higher.
Therefore, the price of electricity to the ordinary consumer would double at least during the
next year.
In 1975 pensioners had been assured that costs would not rise, but the cost of electricity
to the single beneficiary had increased enormously. The Labour Party's intention of reducing
the power bills of superannuitants by $1 a week would have been preferable to the policies
followed by the National Government, which had already doubled the price of electricity
and would double it again in the coming year.
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) said that during the last year of the former Labour
Government, with inflation at 16 percent, the electricity bill had been held and the taxpayer
had been forced to pay. Although the price of electricity had remained stable, the poor old
superannuitants had had to pay more tax to meet the problem. Opposition members had said
clearly that, if a Labour Government were elected, electricity charges would be doubled.

In 1975 the National Party had said that the National Airways Corporation would be
given every encouragement, and 2 years later the corporation had been done away with. Air
New Zealand had been promised modern equipment. It had been told that the Government
would support it-New Zealand's international flag carrier-but the Government had not
said that that support would be at the expense of the internal airline.
Air New Zealand had acquired some 737s and Fokker Friendships which had belonged
to NAC. Three types of planes were being investigated for use on provincial air routes. The
first was pressurised, but did not have the range to provide a service between Hokitika and
Christchurch; the second and third were not pressurised, and so could not do the trip
anyway. If any of those planes were brought into service, the Hokitika air service would be
discontinued. Other provincial towns should note that their air services were likely to be
kaput.

Ministry of Works and Development for the purchase of the ground for a new airfield at the
Chathams were well under way and should soon reach finality. Magnificent work had been
done by the Air Force to convert Andovers for the dual role of VIP flights and other work.
The annual report of the Ministry of Transport was magnificent. The highlight was the
foreword by the Minister, in which it was stated that the Government had taken several

Mr LANGE (Mangere) said that the New Zealand National Airways Corporation Act
had provided a charter for domestic services within New Zealand and a duty on the carrier to
serve areas for social purposes without necessarily having regard to whether the books would
balance or the service would make a profit. In breach of its manifesto, the National
Government had elected to transfer the services provided to Air New Zealand without a
requirement that people in the provinces-in Tauranga, Whakatane, Wanganui, Rotorua,
and Kaitaia, and in Blenheim and other towns throughout the South Island-be given an
airline service not manipulated according to economic assessment but, rather, to meet social
needs.
In the report of the Road Safety Committee it was stated that road safety continued to
cause deep concern to the Government. Notwithstanding that glorious statement, there were
fewer traffic officers on the road than there had been for a number of years. The decline in
traffic enforcement staff, which actually included parking meter officers, had been marked.
The downward trend had resulted from the 10 percent cut in the Public Service staff ceiling
imposed by the Government. In December 1976 there were 850 traffic officers; in December
1977 there were 837. In December 1975, under the former Labour Government, there had
been 938 traffic officers. That reduction indicated the measure of importance the
Government had placed on law enforcement.
Many of the remaining traffic officers were frequently engaged in non-productive
tasks-in serving notices of prosecution for minor offences that could not be served by
ordinary post, in serving summonses on witnesses to attend in courts, and in the time-
consuming trivia associated with court proceedings-none of which was an effective
deterrent for people on the roads, and all of which kept traffic officers away from the point at
which they were visible on the road.

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) said that the Government and he,

1977, 850, and in 1978, 859, with 40 more in training. Recruitment would be considered
again next year, but it was not always possible to recruit suitable persons as traffic officers.

with some of the problems.

Privilege-Speaker's Ruling
WEDNESDAY, 13 SEPTEMBER 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
PRIVILEGE SPEAKER'S RULING
Mr SPEAKER: Last evening I was asked to rule whether a prima facie breach of
privilege existed as a result of an article in the Christchurch Star of 12 September, which
appeared to give an interim report from the member for Wairarapa, as chairman of the
Committee on Violent Offending, before that report was given to the House. I had to decide
whether the article in the Christchurch Star contained any significant material that was in the
interim report that the honourable member was proposing to make to the House on behalf of
that committee. The member gave me a copy of the notes that he released to the newspaper,
and on which the article was based. I have read all three documents-the proposed interim
report, the notes, and the article.
The article accurately reflects the notes, which are headed, “Notes on interim report
from the Violent Offending Committee". Although the article states that the member for
Wairarapa was making an interim report on his committee's hearings so far this year, there is
no part of that interim report in the article, nor in the notes handed to the press. It was
submitted that the honourable member was, in any case, justified by Standing Order 368(b)
in issuing his statement as chairman of the committee. However, that does not arise, because
in his notes released to the press he said that after reading his interim report, which of course
he had not then done—and he still has not done-he was proposing to stand aside from his
role as chairman of the committee and to make some personal comments on what he had
observed during recent months on the problem of violent offending. He is quite entitled to
do that. I find there is no prima facie breach of privilege.
During the discussion of the matter of privilege, the question arose of whether the press
had committed a breach of privilege in breaking the embargo that the member for Wairarapa
told us he had put on his statement. This, I find, does not fall within our Standing Orders, or
within the practice of the House of Commons relating to privilege. It is really a matter of
journalistic ethics, and the remedy is in the hands of members themselves and of the press. I
find there is no prima facie breach of privilege there either.

Health Services Policy
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Health: Did the National
Government re-establish the Royal Commission into Hospital and Related Services, and, if
not, what has been done to formulate policy for the organisation of health services within the
community?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The National Government has not re-established
the Royal Commission into Hospital and Related Services disbanded by the Labour
Government. It has, in accordance with its 1975 manifesto, set up the Special Advisory
Committee on Health Services to consult and advise on future development. The emphasis
has been on full consultation with those involved in, or recipients of, health services. In
Northland, where a pilot scheme is being undertaken, a special advisory committee of local
people has been established as part of the consultative and policy formulation machinery. A
similar committee of local people will be established to discuss the organisation of health
services for metropolitan Wellington.
Mr Wellington: What were the basic principles adopted for the future development of
health services?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The dual system of private and public medical and health services will
continue. Voluntary agencies will be assisted to make their indispensable contributions.
Emphasis will move to community care. Hospital boards will be given increasing
responsibility and authority. Any proposals to integrate hospital boards with health districts
will be carefully considered. Hospital board members will continue to be elected. Any
proposals to appoint some members will, if made, be considered, but this Government's
policy is never to have a majority of appointed members, and for the chairman to be elected
by board members. The Government has not stated any preference for appointed members,
and discussions, consultation, and planning may indicate that all members should be elected
or that co-options may be preferable to appointments. The Government will not increase
centralisation of health administration, nor will it consider a New Zealand health authority
or any such bureaucratic machine.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I hope the Minister is coming to the end of his answer to a
supplementary question. It tends to infringe the rules on two counts: first, it is not concise,
and should be; secondly, it is tending to embark on a discussion of a policy matter that is
really beyond the scope of the question. If the Minister has just about finished, I shall allow
him to finish. Otherwise it might be as well if he ended at that.
Hon. T. F. GILL: I have nearly finished. I admit that this answer has been a little long,
but it was a difficult question to answer concisely. The Government favours maximum
decentralisation and co-ordination of public, private, and voluntary sources at the
community level.

refers, provides that when "the Electorate Officer is satisfied that the applicant is qualified

in which he is enrolled". A post office should not so receipt registration cards as to imply that
enrolment is accepted, as that can be done only after the registration card has been checked
and the electorate officer is satisfied that the application is in order and the elector is

electorate officer, who, after checking and noting the electorate name and mesh block
numbers, sends them to the electoral control office in the Chief Electoral Office in the Hutt
Valley. That was an arrangement made by the Labour Government. Because of the volume
being received, there have been delays in sending out the E2 forms which are not produced
from the computer until after a record has been made. Forty-five thousand E2 forms have
already been dispatched, and a further 40 000 should be dispatched this week when they are
received from the computer. If citizens who have applied for registration have not received
their E2 card after a reasonable length of time they should go back to the post office and tell
the post office official that they have not received the card so that a message can be sent
through to the electorate officer.

Hamilton East Post Office, or the Hamilton west one, if there is one there—for receipts to be
given, to which the Chief Electoral Officer replied no. The post office staff in the Hamilton
area are of the view that if a request is made for an acknowledgement or receipt of an
enrolment card such a request can easily be met by the staff concerned. The Chief Electoral

the clear understanding that the acknowledgement is not taken as confirmation of
enrolment.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Since numerous people who have enrolled have not received

informed if any further staff are needed, and they are to be made available.
Mr Bruce Barclay: The Minister said that if a person did not receive an

Geothermal Power Development-Cost
6. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua)to the Minister of Energy: What is the estimated capital
cost of developing New Zealand's geothermal potential?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): New Zealand's undeveloped geothermal
potential is about 2000 MW. The capital cost of developing all this potential for electricity
generation would be $1,700 million at current prices.
Mr W. R. Austin: What are the comparative costs of development of geothermal
energy, hydro-electricity, and coal?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: That is a difficult question to answer, because we are dealing with
costs that are not strictly comparable. The current cost of developing geothermal energy for
electricity generation is estimated at $850 a kilowatt. That is a capital outlay, but there is no
fuel cost and the maintenance cost can be comparatively low. It is higher than both hydro
and coal in terms of capital outlay.

been 465 applications up to 8 September this year.

their mortgages. That is one possible cause. The one suggested by the member could well be
another, but there would be many causes.

Government? Is that why the number of house sales went up to 465 by September of this
year?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The Minister of Housing assures me that the answer is no.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That is correct. They moved from 98 to 230 in 1975.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The supplementary question is irrelevant. The original
question asked how many applications for mortgagee sales were made.

Rail Passenger Services-Possible Cuts
14. Mr FENTON (Hastings) to the Minister of Railways: Is the Silver Fern service to be
withdrawn, curtailed, or modified and are any other main trunk passenger services under
consideration for withdrawal, curtailment, or modification?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Railways.
"There are no plans to change the Silver Fern railcar service in any respect, nor are there any
proposals to withdraw any other main trunk passenger services. Any changes that might be
made in the consist of trains will be made solely in response to changing passenger demand at
different times of the year."
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Assuming that the demand is the same as at present, what does
the Government propose to use for rolling stock-what plans has it to replace the existing
Silver Fern cars?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I know of no particular plans to replace the existing Silver Fern
railcar, but a comprehensive programme of updating the railway rolling stock has been
undertaken by the Government since it took office.
Labour Department-Security Vetting of Staff
15. Mr LANGE (Mangere), on behalf of Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn), to the Minister of
Labour: Can he confirm that security vetting is proposed or has taken place for employees of
the Department of Labour in the employment division, and factory inspection and weights
and measures sections, and, if so, what are the reasons?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): In the Department of Labour, security
vetting is being undertaken of certain nominated senior staff in each operating division
within head office. These include employment and vocational guidance, industrial welfare,
and weights and measures. The purpose of the vetting is to enable the permanent head to be
satisfied as to the reliability of employees required to have access to papers classified
"secret" or higher. This has been accompanied by a streamlining of procedures for the
control and safety of such material, and improved physical security. District office staff are
not involved.
Mr Lange: For what cause would an officer in the weights and measures section have
access to highly classified security information?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Highly secret papers are sometimes referred to the divisional
officers collectively. I remind the member that there is absolutely no difference in procedure
from that when the Labour Government was controlling the same division.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Does the vetting it is proposed to introduce in the Department of
Labour include, as has been suggested in the media, any unusual private habits that these
people may have?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The suggestion implicit in the question that the vetting is "being
introduced" is erroneous. It is exactly the same as when the questioner was Minister of
Labour.

Opposition members. I certainly had no intention of so doing. To put the matter beyond any
possible doubt, I am happy to record my answer. I can if need be produce the minutes of the
committee, with your leave, Mr Speaker, to confirm the fact that no Labour or National
member of the committee has formally proposed that the committee should call for
evidence. I rest on that simple proposition. I can explain other matters to the House in
greater detail if the need arises.
Mr SPEAKER: I do not know that the member is any further out of order on this
occasion than he was before, and I found him not out of order then. We have spent a great
deal of time on a procedural matter that could have been dealt with a good deal more
succinctly. However, it is not my time; it is honourable members' time.

6.
Book Publishing Committee-Recommendation
(24/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Trade and Industry:
Has the joint committee of the Printing Industries Federation, the Book Publishers
Association of New Zealand, and, when appropriate, representatives of organised
labour, recommended by the Industries Development Commission book productions
inquiry in its only recommendation, been set up; if so, has it met quarterly as
suggested; and has any progress been made towards achieving the expressed
objective of increasing the New Zealand book manufacturers' share of the New
Zealand and overseas book market without being able to offer some financial or
other incentive to those publishing or printing books?


## p. 3352 (#748) ###########################################

3352
13 September
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied:
The first of the meetings recommended by the Industries Development Commis-
sion was held on 17 May 1978 and was attended by representatives of the Printing
Industries Federation, the Book Publishers Association, and the Printing and
Related Trades Industrial Union of Workers. The meeting was chaired by an
officer of the Department of Trade and Industry. The industry representatives
indicated that they were not satisfied that the committee approach would achieve
their objectives. They are preparing further information for submission to the
department.
7.
Petroleum Group of Companies-Objectives
(24/8/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Can he give
the names of all the companies in the Government's newly formed petroleum group
of companies, the objects of each company, and the names of the directors of each?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The newly formed petroleum
group of companies consists of a holding company-Petroleum Corporation of New
Zealand Ltd.-and three subsidiary companies-Petroleum Corporation of New
Zealand (Exploration) Ltd., Offshore Mining Co. Ltd., and Natural Gas Corpora-
tion of New Zealand Ltd. The holding company's directors are Mr F. W. Orr
(chairman), Mr W. B. Barnes, Mr P. G. Hillyer, Mr C. J: Keppel, Mr B. H.
Smith, Mr W. J. P. Cook, and Mr R. J. Hogg. (This company's objectives
effectively embrace those of all three subsidiaries.) Offshore Mining's directors
are Sir Arnold Nordmeyer (chairman), Mr W. B. Barnes, Mr P. G. Hillyer, Mr
W. J. P. Cook, and Mr R. J. Hogg. (This company's task is to handle the
Government's interests in respect of Maui Development Ltd.) Natural Gas Cor-
poration's directors are Mr P. L. Laing (chairman), Mr P. J. Graham, Mr N. C.
Gardner, Mr C. J. Keppel, Professor H. J. Hopkins, Mr W. J. P. Cook, and
Mr R. J. Hogg. (This company has taken over the role of the former Natural
Gas Corporation.) Petroleum Corporation of New Zealand (Exploration) Limited's
directors are Mr F. A. Reeves (chairman), Mr P. Fels, Mr W. R. Jackson, Mr
F. W. Orr, Mr B. H. Smith, Mr W. J. P. Cook, and Mr R. J. Hogg. (This
company assumes responsibility for the on-shore and off-shore exploration involve-
ment of the Government.)
The objects of the Petrocorp group of companies cover the following broad
areas of responsibility: (1) to set up, establish, and carry on all or any of the
businesses in all or any of their respective branches of seeking, exploring for,
obtaining, acquiring, discovering, producing, treating, processing, manufacturing,
importing, exporting, storing, transporting, distributing, marketing, dealing in,
buying and selling, assessing, researching, developing, supplying, using, or con-
serving, energy, sources of energy, energy resources and all kinds of products from
energy; (2) to establish and carry on all or any of the businesses in all or any of
their respective branches of exploring, prospecting, boring and drilling for, mining,
producing, extracting, refining, distilling, treating, processing, manufacturing,
acquiring, importing, exporting, storing, piping, or otherwise transporting, dis-
tributing, marketing, dealing in, buying and selling petroleum, oil (whether
mineral, animal or vegetable), natural gas, coal, metals and other minerals and
mineral and hydro-carbon substances of every kind, and all kinds of products
and by-products derived from the foregoing or any of them; (3) to set up, estab-
lish, and carry on in all or any of its branches the business of obtaining, acquiring,
purchasing or procuring natural gas or liquefied petroleum gas from any source
and of processing or treating the same or any by-products thereof in any way
whatsoever and of transporting and delivering by pipeline or otherwise howsoever
such natural gas or liquefied petroleum gas or the products and/or by-products
thereof and of selling and promoting the sale of the same; (4) to acquire and deal
with in any way whatsoever interests in joint ventures or participating arrange-
ments of any type (including in particular but not by way of limitation with oil
explorers in respect of off-shore exploration) which the directors or shareholders
of the company may in their absolute discretion consider conducive to the attain-
ment of the above objects and the exercise of the powers of the company and to
do and perform all acts, matters, and things necessary and incidental to the
carrying out of such interests ventures or arrangements; (5) to purchase, take on
lease or exchange, or acquire by conveyance, grant, licence, lease, mineral deed,

royalty contract, concession, franchise, option or otherwise, any right, title, interest

and extract petroleum, oil, natural gas, coal, metals, minerals and other mineral

in greater detail by making arrangements with my office or by approaching the
Registrar of Companies.

Houses near Wellington Motorway
(24/8/78)
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Works and Development:
Why were the 76 National Roads Board houses in the vicinity of the Wellington
urban motorway, which are currently being let, not handed over to the Housing
Corporation rather than retained by the roads board, which has no primary
function in the administration of rental houses?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The
administration of National Roads Board property is carried out by the Ministry
of Works and Development as agent for the board. The ministry is well experienced
in this work, and its close association with the board ensures that the timing of
leases and maintenance requirements can be co-ordinated with the board's pro-
gramme of works and allocations of finance.

12.
Whangawehei Harbour Erosion Problem
(29/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Works and Development:
Will the Government assist with the construction of a concrete wall to contain
further erosion at the Whangawehei Harbour?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: Financial
assistance from the Government for erosion control is provided through the National
Water and Soil Conservation Authority to catchment authorities, and if an erosion
problem exists at Whangawehi it should be discussed with the appropriate local
authority. Such assistance is confined to the protection of land and general com-
munity assets in accordance with well established policy. Problems affecting
navigational or harbour facilities do not come within this policy and would
need to be discussed with the Ministry of Transport.
13.

(29/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Works and Development:
Will the Government assist with the clearing of the sandbar at the entrance to
the Whangawehei Harbour?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: Whether
the clearance of a sandbar at Whangawehi can be justified or not, and whether
there should be any Government assistance, is a matter for my colleague the
Minister of Transport. I am informed that officers of the Ministry of Transport
have been discussing navigational problems and anchorage facilities at Whangawehi
with the parties concerned with a view to bringing these under proper control.
14.
Marshall Report-Penal Sections
(29/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: How far do the
penal sections of the Marshall report reflect efforts by the Department of Education
to overcome the teacher shortage by hiring people who may not be suitable as
classroom teachers?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I assume that in
referring to the "penal sections of the Marshall report" the honourable member
for New Lynn means chapter 8, which deals with the disciplining of teachers.
The Marshall committee's terms of reference were: "To review present arrange-
ments for the certification, registration (including de-registration) and discipline of
teachers, to inform itself of the statutory arrangements for other professions in
this country, and to make recommendations." The committee was, therefore,
required to study and make recommendations on the disciplining of teachers, and
the report in no way reflects any effort by the Department of Education to over-
come the teacher shortage by hiring potentially unsuitable teachers. All professions
have disciplinary codes, and, in accordance with its terms of reference, the


## p. 3356 (#752) ###########################################

3356
13 September
Questions and Replies
Marshall committee informed itself of the statutory arrangements for six other
professions. The committee was concerned to establish a single common disciplinary
system that would apply to all teachers. There are two disciplinary systems at
present for teachers in state schools-one for secondary and technical institute
teachers, and another for all other teachers employed in the State education
service.

16.
Argyle Station-Purchase by Mr F. Andrews
(30/8/78)
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Lands:
Will he list the cases under the Land Settlement Promotion and Land Acquisition
Act 1952 and the Land Act 1948 that are similar to the purchase of Argyle Station
by Mr F. Andrews?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: For the year ended 31 March
1978 the Land Settlement Board dealt with 1620 applications for consent to
transfer and sublease, while for the same period, under the Land Settlement
Promotion and Land Acquisition Act 1952, the Land Valuation Tribunal dealt
with 5307 applications, the vast majority being under Part II of the Act relating
to the undue aggregation of farm land. It will be appreciated that with such a
large number of applications it would be a mammoth undertaking to extract
details of those cases for which approval has been granted subject to the condition
that a purchaser dispose of existing property and/or properties in those cases in
which the purchase of the additional land constitutes undue aggregation. However,
the percentage to which the condition is imposed is small in relation to the
number of transactions approved and I should point out that the transfers are
not registered until the condition has been complied with.
17.
Research Experiments on Animals
(30/8/78)
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) to the Minister of Agriculture: Can
he name the various places in New Zealand where experiments are carried out
on animals for (1) medical research, and (2) commercial reasons, and will he
list the types of animals used and indicate whether researchers in both areas are
licensed by his department?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: No licensing procedure
is operated by my ministry, and the places in New Zealand where experiments
are carried out for (1) medical research and (2) commercial reasons are not
known to me. As far as agriculture research is concerned, experiments are carried
out with animals (sheep, cattle, and small animals) at the ministry's Whatawhata
Animal Research Station, Ruakura Animal Research Station, Wallaceville Animal
Research Centre, and Invermay Agricultural Research Centre. At each of these
centres there is an ethics committee, one of whose members is a veterinarian.
These committees are responsible for approving all projects and for ensuring that
the welfare of the animals is safeguarded. They were set up to meet the require-
ments of the National Laboratory Small Animals Committee established in
1973. In addition, the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research applied
biochemistry division experiments with cows and sheep and some small animals
at Palmerston North. These experiments are also done in aid of agricultural
research.
