18.
Tomatoes and Bacterial Wilt Disease
(30/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Agriculture: Is the statement
in the Auckland Star of 11 August that "Auckland tomato growers say that
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries officials could be endangering tomato crops
throughout the country by their attitude"-to the outbreak of bacterial wilt
in a tomato crop in Whangarei-correct, and what measures are being taken to
ensure that the infection is contained?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: (1) The Ministry of
Agriculture and Fisheries has maintained a close liaison with the grower of this
tomato crop since bacterial wilt disease was diagnosed on 19 July 1978. (2) The
disease flourishes on a number of crops in the tropics and the organism has pre-
viously been found here on potatoes. An immediate national check survey has
established that it was present only in the nutrient film technique glasshouse
complex of this grower. It was concluded that the conditions associated with this
technique would be necessary for this disease to cause serious economic damage
to solanaceous crops in New Zealand. (3) At the time of identification the grower
had been marketing his tomato crop at Whangarei, Palmerston North, and
possibly Auckland. Marketing was subsequently directed to Wellington where
sale for consumption in mid-winter was considered to present no risk to glass-
house production. Some 4000 cartons had been sold before identification, and
2000 have been sold since. There will be 200 cases left to market over the next
10 days, then harvesting will cease. (4) The affected vines, which are the main
source of residual bacteria, are being removed from the houses and stockpiled
on the property in readiness for burning when the weather permits. (5) The
ministry has given advice to the grower on the steps needed to clean up the
property before any further solanaceous cropping could be undertaken. In its
opinion the grower should move from the property and make a fresh start if he
is to continue in tomato production. (6) A follow-up investigation into the source
of the infection is underway. (7) The ministry recognises that this disease can
have serious commercial consequences in a glasshouse where conditions are
optimal for the bacteria. There are only a few glasshouse systems similar to this
in New Zealand and elementary hygiene standards make the chance of any
bacteria from the affected property entering these houses a very remote possibility.
The risk of establishment in outdoor potato and tomato crops is also considered
very low because of the tropical nature of the bacteria. Notwithstanding this,
the ministry is ensuring that all the infected plant material will be destroyed,
and, should the grower decide to close down his complex, close supervision will
be maintained to ensure that any possible contaminated plant and equipment
are treated to destroy residual bacteria before leaving the property. (8) The
grower has indicated that he proposes to change to a non-host crop cucumbers-
and the move will not be opposed. He has been made aware of the procedures he
should follow if he does this. (9) In conclusion, the ministry is treating this out-
break as an unusual one. It is taking every reasonable step to ensure that other
growers of solanaceous crops are not placed at risk.

ately sets out registered unemployment and temporary employment programme

internationally accepted definition, unemployment and unemployment rates refer

be counted among the unemployed. The registered unemployed and temporary
employment programme workers have been expressed as percentages of the total
estimated labour force, as this includes all industries. The surveyed labour force
is an inappropriate measure of total labour force since it excludes the industries of

Wage Adjustment Regulation 1974-Exemptions
(30/8/78)
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Can he list each of
the decisions, changes, or new regulations passed that have resulted in exceptions
being made or exemptions being created from the requirements of the Wage
Adjustment Regulations 1974, Amendment No. 13 (S.R. 1977/204), which
required rates of remuneration fixed by instrument to remain in force for 12
months?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: No list is kept of the
decisions that make exceptions to the requirement of the Wage Adjustment
Regulations 1974 Amendment No. 13 (S.R. 1977/204) that rates of remunera-
tion fixed by an instrument must remain in force for 12 months. All such decisions
must, in any case, be made in terms of the relevant legislation. The following legis-
lation enacted since Amendment No. 13 has resulted in exceptions to the 12-month
rule being created or re-enacted: section 19 of the Higher Salaries Commission
Act 1977; section 6 of the State Services Conditions of Employment Act 1977;
section 5 of the General Wage Orders Act 1977; regulation 3 of the Wage Adjust-
ment Regulations 1974, Amendment No. 16.

31.
National Provident Fund Subcommittee Membership
(31/8/78)
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Finance: Who are the
members of the subcommittee of the National Provident Fund Board investment
committee on the local authority loan market, what are the duties of the committee,
and when were the members appointed?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The committee on
the local authority loan market is not a subcommittee of the National Provident
Fund Board. It is an informal ad hoc committee with no powers of any kind. It was
set up in 1967 to disseminate information and consider ways and means of increasing
the availability of finance for local authorities. It organised the programme of local
authority public issues to remove the difficulties for both borrowers and lenders that
existed under the previous disorganised system. By agreement amongst the various
interested parties, the committee is chaired by the superintendent of the National
Provident Fund and has two members representing the Life Offices Association and
two representing underwriters of local authority loans. Because of the informality of
the committee and the infrequent meetings, members can change from meeting to
meeting, but it is customary for the life offices to be represented by officers from
the two life offices investing most in local authority loans, and the underwriters by
partners from the two Wellington stockbroking firms most active in the local
authority field.

Massaging of Sports Representatives—Restrictions
(31/8/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen an article
in the Sunday Times of 13 August 1978 by Alex Veysey, which says that "the man
who massaged Rebecca Perrott to the Commonwealth Games and a bagful of medals
is being legislated out of existence", and, if so, is the report accurate?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: I have seen the
article referred to. The Massage Parlours Act permits persons to massage anyone


## p. 3364 (#760) ###########################################

3364
13 September
Questions and Replies
referred to them by a sports body or to massage any member of a sporting team
on being engaged to do so, without coming within the meaning of masseur or
masseuse in the Act. However, the Massage Parlours Act prohibits therapeutic
massage designed to cure or alleviate any abnormal condition of the body by a
masseur licensed under the Act. This is to ensure that no one who is licensed under
that Act can contravene the provisions of the Physiotherapy Act 1949, which
prohibit a person who is not entitled to do so from holding himself out as a
masseur or physiotherapist. It is the Physiotherapy Act, and not the Massage
Parlours Act, that prevents Mr Smith from holding himself out as a masseur.
I have been advised that the chairman of the Statutes Revision Committee has
discussed the matter with Mr Smith, who now accepts the fact that his concern
about the provisions of the massage parlours legislation is unfounded.
33.
United Kingdom Pensions Affecting Adjustments
to National Superannuation
(31/8/78)
Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Is it
correct that United Kingdom pensions and allowances payable in New Zealand
are now to be made direct to pensioners and that national superannuation is
reduced by the amount of the British pension payable; and what effect will this
have on the tax paid by superannuitants who are affected by this decision?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Payment of United
Kingdom national insurance pensions is the responsibility of the United Kingdom
Department of Health and Social Security, and that department has decided to
pay its contributory pensions to pensioners residing in New Zealand by direct
payment from the United Kingdom. The reciprocal agreement with the United
Kingdom provides that, when a United Kingdom pension is payable, the New
Zealand benefit shall be reduced by the amount of the overseas pension. The
purpose of this provision is to ensure that people who receive an overseas pension
are not placed in a more advantageous position than a long-term New Zealand
resident who is entitled to only one New Zealand benefit. Accordingly, in cases in
which a United Kingdom contributory pension is payable, the corresponding New
Zealand benefit or pension is reduced by the amount of the United Kingdom
pension. It should be noted that this provision has applied for many years in New
Zealand, and pensioners affected by the decision of the United Kingdom auth-
orities to pay pensions direct to them will not suffer a reduction in their total
pension income. United Kingdom retirement pensions are not subject to United
Kingdom income tax, but are regarded as taxable income in New Zealand. Those
people whose United Kingdom pensions are being supplemented by national super-
annuation are having sufficient tax deducted to meet their tax liability on their
national superannuation. However, the amount of tax deducted will not be
sufficient to meet their full tax liability on the aggregate amount of national
superannuation plus United Kingdom retirement pension. Pensioners have been
informed of this situation by the Department of Social Welfare and advised that,
if they wish, they can obtain a special tax code to have sufficient tax deducted
from their national superannuation to meet their total liability.

37.
Fish Quota-Russia and South Korea
(1/9/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What
benefits does New Zealand derive from allowing Russian and South Korean fishing
vessels to fish in its 200-mile zone?


## p. 3366 (#762) ###########################################

3366
13 September
Questions and Replies
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: Before I reply,
could I make it quite clear that New Zealand is obliged at international law to
allocate to foreign fishing vessels the fish it cannot harvest itself, up to the level
of the sustainable catch. It is for New Zealand alone, however, to determine each
foreign fishing country's quota, although consideration must be given inter alia to
each country's record of fishing in our waters. The 200-mile zone came into force
on 1 April 1978. New Zealand derives or may expect to derive financial, scientific,
and broader trade benefits from giving the Soviet Union and South Korea access
to the zone. Fees are payable to the New Zealand Government by licensed foreign
fishing craft for all fish caught within the zone. In a full year the total amount
received from the two countries named above should amount to several millions
of dollars. The fisheries agreements that this Government has negotiated with
the Soviet Union and the Republic of Korea require those governments to provide
full catch data as well as statistical and biological information about our fisheries
resources. Provision has also been made in the agreements for close co-operation
in the conservation and utilisation of the living resources of the sea. This applies
not only to those stocks found within our 200-mile zone, but also to those species
whose habitat straddles the zone boundary and those in 'antarctic and sub-
antarctic waters. Fishing vessels belonging to the Soviet Union and Korea are
also required to respect all New Zealand law relating to fishing and also our law
regarding the protection of marine mammals. I would also expect and these
expectations have been spelt out to Korea and the Soviet Union-that the degree
of access we have granted these countries to the fisheries resource in our zone will
be taken into account by Korea and the Soviet Union in their broader trade
dealings with New Zealand. New Zealand for its part has left no doubt that it
will regard the level of access to the markets of these countries as an important
factor in reaching decisions on the annual quotas of fish to be allotted to them.

had further considered the matter. At present those ballots for which warrants
have been issued are continuing, but no other warrants have as yet been issued.
The major recommendations on industrial policy from the Industrial Relations
Council since 1 January 1976 are: 11 August 1976-(a) "That a subcommittee of
this council be set up immediately to formulate ways and means for a return to
negotiations in accord with provisions of the Industrial Relations Act 1973."

43.
Geothermal Investigations Programme
(1/9/78)
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Energy: What progress has
been made by the National Government with geothermal investigation?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: In the 1977 Budget the
Government announced an accelerated geothermal investigations programme.
This programme provides, in a full year, for 14 to 16 investigation wells to be
drilled by the Ministry of Works and Development and for associated scientific
work to be done by DSIR. The estimated annual expenditure is $7.5 million.
Substantial progress has already been made in implementing the full programme.
Specifically: (a) a second drilling rig has been commissioned; (b) arrangements
are in train for the purchase of two new drilling rigs next year; (c) existing
facilities at Wairakei are being upgraded; (d) drilling is continuing at Broad-
lands, with four wells due for completion by Christmas, which will define the
productive area more precisely; (e) a major injection trial of waste well water
is going on at Broadlands and a pilot condenser is nearing completion-these
are concerned with key aspects of the proposed geothermal power station; (f)
two further wells are scheduled for completion at Kawerau this financial year,
and an interim report shows that steam capable of generating 80 MW has been
discovered so far, about half of which is committed to the Tasman Pulp and Paper
Co. mill; (g) at Ngawha in Northland two wells have been completed under the
present programme and further drilling is currently under way-low rock permi-
abilities have been encountered but temperatures have been good; (h) a light
rig will drill some shallow wells at Mokai, north-west of Lake Tapuo later this
year; (i) pre-investigation work, including the collection of information for an
environmental assessment and the obtaining of water rights, is to be undertaken
at Ruahine Springs just south of Lake Rotoiti; (j) planning continues for the
supply of geothermal energy for industrial use; (k) much work on the modelling
of geothermal fields, to provide further insights into the behaviour of these fields
particularly under exploitation, has been done by DSIR and through research
contracts funded by the New Zealand Energy Research and Development Com-
mittee.
44.
Marshall Report-Medical Safeguards for Teachers (5/9/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Does the Marshall
report mean that authorities must institute permanent medical safeguards against
teachers "cracking up" under the strain of teaching in a system with very high
class-contact hours, and, if not, why not?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The report the member
is quoting is that of an independent committee, which is at present under study.
My reading of the report does not suggest that authorities must institute
permanent medical safeguards to determine whether a teacher's physical or mental
health has deteriorated to the point at which it is a cause for concern. Paragraphs
7.3 and 7.8 of the Marshall report indicate that the Committee on the Registration
and Discipline of Teachers envisaged complaints against teachers as being a
possible way in which these cases would come to notice. I believe that cases
involving physical or mental deterioration in teachers are few in relation to the
size of the teaching service and that the committee was simply seeking to provide
a procedure for employing authorities to take some action if standard guidance
and counselling of teachers has failed to produce a desirable solution. The
Marshall report proposes a sympathetic and humane approach to a difficult
human problem. The Marshall committee's approach attempts to strike a proper
balance between the needs of the employing authorities, the teachers, and parents,
and the students. The procedure recommended by the Marshall committee for
the handling of these cases provides very adequate safeguards for the teacher-for
example, the right to obtain a second medical opinion, the right to leave on full

result.
45.
Bastion Point Prosecutions
(5/9/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Police: In view of
the time and cost involved in continuing the hearings, did the Commissioner of
Police suggest to the Solicitor-General that some action be taken to deal with the
Bastion Point prosecutions?
Hon. D. S. THOMSON (Acting Minister of Police) replied: Yes, the Commis-
sioner of Police did discuss the Bastion Point prosecutions with the Solicitor-
General. Concern had been expressed to the commissioner by the officer in charge
of the Auckland police district that the prosecutions were taking up valuable
manpower resources in time spent at court as witnesses, and coping with demon-
strations outside the court. This concern was shared by officers of the court, who
could see the business of the Auckland court being disrupted for many months
whilst processing trespass charges.
46.
Automatic Telephone Exchange, Waipukurau
(6/9/78)
Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) to the Postmaster-General: What progress is
there with the Waipukurau automatic telephone exchange, and what is the expected
date of operation?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: All the exchange
equipment has been received and is now being installed. Recabling of the urban
area of Waipukurau has been completed, and cabling of the rural area will begin
shortly when ground conditions improve. Laying of a junction cable between
Waipawa and Waipukurau is about to commence. Where necessary, rewiring
of homes is proceeding and the replacement of telephone instruments is expected
to commence early next year. It is expected that the exchange will cut over
about the middle of 1979.

49.
School Leavers-Projected Destinations
(6/9/78)
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Education: From his projection
of the number of school leavers at the end of this year, how many are estinated to
be going on to tertiary education, how many will be applying for apprenticeships,
and how many will be trying to get other jobs?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The Department of
Education conducts a school leaver survey as at 30 September each year, the
results of which are usually available in November. On figures now available
it is estimated that the total number of school leavers will be between 59 000
and 62 000. Of these, if past patterns continue, between 11 800 and 12 400 will
go on to full-time tertiary education. A survey of probable destinations showed
that about 15 percent of all school leavers (a proportion that has been stable
for the past 5 years) indicated an intention to seek apprenticeships. Of these,
the ratio of males and females is about 9:1. For at least a decade the propor-
tion of males entering apprenticeships has been fairly steady at about 1 in 4
of all male school leavers. It can be assumed on past trends that about 15 percent
of all school leavers at the end of this year will indicate an intention to seek
apprenticeships. This would give a figure of between 8800 and 9300, or about
the same as for 1977. The balance of leavers for the whole school year-between
38 400 and 40 300-will presumably be seeking other jobs. Of this number, up
to half may have left school during the year before 30 September 1978 to go
into jobs. I emphasise that until the results of the school leaver survey are
known, however, these figures can be treated only as approximations.

Mail Misdirected
(6/9/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Postmaster-General: Has he
seen the article in the New Zealand Herald dated 5 August about a letter sent to
a Mr Dixon, which apparently was printed in the New Zealand Truth before it
was delivered to Mr Dixon by the New Zealand Police, and, if so, can he explain
why a letter addressed to Mr Dixon should in fact be delivered by the New Zealand
Police and published in the New Zealand Truth?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: I have seen the article
referred to. The article refers to Mr Dickinson, not Mr Dixon. It also states
that the letter was printed in the New Zealand Truth a few days after it was
delivered to Mr Dickinson, not before, as stated in the honourable member's
question. I understand that the letter was found in the street by a member
of the public and was not in an envelope. It was handed to the Police, who
delivered it. I have no knowledge of how the letter came to appear in the
Truth newspaper, beyond what is in the article. No official complaint about
the incident has been made to the Post Office by Mr Dickinson and there are
no indications to suggest that there has been any malpractice or mishandling
by the Post Office.

61.
Abortion Supervisory Committee Adequacy of Data (6/9/78)
MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Justice: Is he satisfied
that the Abortion Supervisory Committee can determine from the forms it has
issued whether those women who obtained certificates: (a) obtained abortions,
and by whom and where; (b) were not provided with the services of an operating
doctor; (c) spontaneously aborted; (d) decided to continue with the pregnancy;
(e) obtained abortions elsewhere (e.g., Sydney illegally, under the guise of a
D. and C.)?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: (a) For every abortion
performed, information is available as to the name of the operating surgeon and
the licensed institution at which the abortion took place. (b) In terms of the
amended legislation this situation should no longer occur. Whenever a certificate
has been issued by two certifying consultants it has already been ascertained that
the services of an operating surgeon, who is satisfied that lawful grounds exist
and is willing to perform the abortion, are available. Before the amending legis-
lation came into force the Abortion Supervisory Committee had no means of
determining from the forms it had issued whether or not the services of an
operating surgeon had been obtained. It was kept well informed by other means,
however, of those cases in which an operating surgeon was not available. (c) The
report form to be completed by a certifying consultant does not specifically provide
for the notification of spontaneous abortion. Certifying consultants often indicate
if this has occurred. (d) The report form does not specifically provide for this
information, but certifying consultants often indicate if this is the case. (e) Here
again, there is no provision for this information to be given, but sometimes
certifying consultants indicate informally if this is so. The number of cases in
which a certificate was issued but an abortion not performed could, after a period
of time, be ascertained from matching reports of certifying consultants and reports
of medical practitioners performing the abortion. In these cases all the circum-
stances from (c) to (e) could have occurred.

abortions performed in New Zealand in terms of the Crimes Act and the Contra-

Abortions-List of Operating Surgeons
(6/9/78)
MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Justice: Will the
Abortion Supervisory Committee be providing a list of names of operating
surgeons to general practitioners throughout the country?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: There is no provision
for the Abortion Supervisory Committee to license or approve surgeons willing to
perform operations. Consequently, it does not have, and indeed has no means of
obtaining, a list of names of such surgeons. Procedures will follow normal medical
practice, as in any situation in which the services of an operating surgeon are
required, and the names of surgeons available to perform abortions will doubtless
be known within the medical profession.
64.
Abortions-Finding an Operating Surgeon
(6/9/78)
MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Justice: Is the onus
to find an operating surgeon for a termination operation on (a) the woman,
(b) her general practitioner, (c) one or both of the certifying consultants?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: Section 32 of the
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act places the onus of finding an
operating surgeon on the first doctor consulted by the woman (referred to in the
Act as the woman's own doctor). The first doctor will, in the majority of cases,
be the woman's general practitioner, but may be a certifying consultant, or, in a
few instances, the operating surgeon.

67.
Electoral Rolls
(24/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the
Prime Minister's statement in the Evening Post of 15 August that "if electoral rolls
were not prepared in time for the general election, then those who were eligible would
still be able to vote", and can he say if the preparation of the rolls is so far delayed
that this could happen, and, if so, what proposals has he under consideration to
ensure that such voters will actually be able to cast valid votes?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen the reported
statement referred to. The Prime Minister correctly pointed out that the availability
or even the accuracy of the printed rolls does not affect eligibility to vote, which is
dependent on the fact of registration. However, this question should not arise. The
main rolls will be published on 1 September, as stated previously. That means that
there is no delay. The supplementary rolls will close, as usual, on the day of the issue
of the writs for the election and will be published before the election. Both sets of rolls
will be available for use at the general election.

Accident Compensation Commission-District Offices (24/8/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Labour: Are there any plans
to give greater autonomy to some of the district offices of the Accident Compensation
Commission, as has been done in Dunedin, and, if so, is the Hamilton office under
consideration for such a move?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Accident Compensation
Commission advises me that, as a matter of policy, it has been almost continuously
delegating to its regional and district offices, including Hamilton, more and more
functions formerly exercised in head office. The commission states that the creation of
branch offices, such as Dunedin, with full claims-handling facilities, involves
important questions of the commission's relationship with its agent, the State
Insurance Office, and of staffing, training, accommodation, and cost. The question of
whether any further branch offices will be established is being fully considered by the
commission at present, but no decision has yet been made.

71.
Allied Farmers Co-operative-Export Licence
(24/8/78)
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Agriculture: Why was
the application of Allied Farmers Co-operative for an export licence for the
Whangarei abattoir declined, and is it possible to have the earlier decision reviewed?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): While the decision to approve
an abattoir for export lies with the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries,
applications are referred to the Meat Industry Authority for its investigation and
recommendation. In this case a public hearing was held in Whangarei last
November. The authority recommended against approval, as it was of the opinion
that export facilities in Northland were adequate for the needs of farmers and
additional export facilities would have an adverse effect on other works in the area.
The matter has in fact already been reviewed. When the authority's views became
known, the applicant approached me with additional evidence, which I asked the
authority to investigate before a formal decision was made. The authority in due
course reaffirmed its earlier views, and the director-general agreed that the
application be declined. I can see no advantage in any further consideration of the
matter.
72.
Customs Tariff Classification, Luxury Goods
(24/8/78)
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister of Customs: Is there a customs tariff
classification for luxury goods, and, if so, what goods are included in this category?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The New Zealand customs
tariff is based on the Customs Co-operation Council nomenclature, which provides
for the systematic classification of all goods. In general, the tariff groups together with
all goods relating to the same industry, and within this grouping each chapter lists all
goods obtained from the same raw material, arranging them progressively from raw
material to the finished products or articles. The classification of goods is determined
according to the tariff's rules of interpretation, which are designed to ensure that a
given product is always classified in the same tariff item. There is, therefore, no single
item in the New Zealand customs tariff under which all luxury goods can be
classified.

74.
"Frictional Unemployment"
(24/8/78)
RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) to the Minister of Labour: What is the
definition of the term "frictional unemployment" in the New Zealand setting, and
what is the number of persons at present registered as unemployed who come into this
category?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): "Frictional unemployment"
usually refers to those workers who are in the process of moving to new jobs that are
available. This type of unemployment arises as job changing is not immediate and
there may be a lack of knowledge by workers that suitable vacancies are available.
"Frictional unemployment" therefore occurs in even the best economic conditions.
Statistics that measure "frictional unemployment" are not collected as such.

correct that only two countries in the world-namely, Finland and New Zealand—

108.
Housing Corporation's Valuation Structure
(25/8/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Housing: Is it correct that the
Housing Corporation has altered its valuation structure from the average square
metre cost as the value of the house, to the average of the price of houses sold in the
area?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): No, the Housing
Corporation's valuing staff has not altered its valuation structure. Valuing is a
subjective assessment based, among many things, on the average square metre cost,
the average price of houses sold in the area, and the buoyancy of the market. When
assessing the viability of a building proposition, corporat ion valuers have always
been required to assess the current market value at the time of inspection and make a
recommendation to the management on the market price, the recommended loan,
term, and other related matters. There are various tools the valuer can use in this
approach, of which average square metre cost is one, but ultimately the valuation
must be reconciled to the market worth of the property.

been a significant supplier on the New Zealand market.

125.
Botulism
(29/8/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Health: In relation to recent
claims made by the New Zealand Alliance of Freshwater Anglers, reported in the
Dominion of 21 August, that fish farms in Germany had been "heavily containin ated
with the botulism organism", can he confirm that the bacteria Clostridium botulinum
cannot survive in the presence of oxygen, and that, although spores may live in the
soil, these will not germinate until subjected to an anaerobic atmosphere such as is
experienced in canned food, and therefore the presence of the bacteria is of much less
relevance than the canning procedure?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I can confirm that Clostridium botulinum,


## p. 3392 (#788) ###########################################

3392
13 September
Questions and Replies
the organism that causes botulism, can grow only in an environment in which oxygen
is not present, and that the spores that it forms in an unfavourable environment will
not germinate until anaerobic conditions are encountered. Canning is a food
preservation technique in which air, and consequently oxygen, is removed. Therefore
it can provide an ideal environment in which spores can germinate and multiply.
However, the toxins produced by the organism are completely killed when exposed
for 15 minutes to a temperature of 100°c, and the spores can also be destroyed by
adequate heat treatment. It is, in fact, the destruction of these spores that is the object
of all canning procedures, since these procedures acknowledge the possible presence
of Clostridium botulinum and its spores.

Japanese Fishing Agreement
(30/8/78)

Zealand farm products into Japan, a point that the Prime Minister has consistently
held to be a co-requisite for the signing of any fishing agreement?
Rt. Hon. B. É. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The New Zealand
Government has approved the fisheries agreement with Japan, and it will be signed as
soon as the Japanese Government has completed its approval procedures. Signature

quotas New Zealand will regard as an important factor ine level of access to the
Japanese market for our agricultural exports.

Botulism
(30/8/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Health: Can he confirm
that the product canned need have no relevance whatsoever to the incidence of
botulism, and that occurrences in the United Kingdom have involved such foods as
rabbit and pigeon broth, vegetarian nut brawn, home-made pie, jugged hare, and
macaroni cheese?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health); I can confirm that botulism can occur


## p. 3393 (#789) ###########################################

13 September
3393
Questions and Replies
with many foods and not just in canned foods. If the food contains Clostridium
botulinum spores, and oxygen is excluded from it, the clostridia will grow and produce
toxin. If then the toxin-bearing food is eaten, botulism food poisoning will occur. In
the United Kingdom most cases of botulism have been due to foods such as rabbit
and pigeon broth, vegetarian nut brawn, home-made pie, jugged hare, and macaroni
cheese. The majority of cases of botulism have resulted from home-preserved foods
and not commercially processed products.

Noxious Animals Infestation
(30/8/78)
Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) to the Minister of Forests: Is the level of noxious
animal infestation (principally opossum) in the Aupori, Omahuta, Puhi Puhi, Puketi,
Russell, Waipoua, and Waitangi State Forests considered to be serious, and is there
any indication that the incidence of infestation is becoming worse?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The position is that opossums are
gradually extending their range northwards. In the Russell and Puhi Puhi State
forests a moderate opossum population exists at present and is increasing.
Immediately to the north in the Waitangi State Forest a light scattered population is
present, and opossums are in similar density in Omahuta, Puketi, and Waipoua State
Forests. All these populations are increasing, unfortunately. There are no opossums
in the Aupouri State Forest, the present limit of their range being approximately in a
line from Kaitaia across to Doubtless Bay. It is certain that opossums will eventually
occupy all of the Northland peninsula.

Retirement Gratuities
(31/8/78)
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister in
Charge of the Inland Revenue Department: Has his department given recognition
to the practice of certain companies of offering lump-sum gratuities to directors upon
retirement, said to be in lieu of superannuation; and has his department taken any
action when the entitlement to such a lump sum is converted-upon the death of the
director before he reaches compulsory retirement-to a gratuity paid to the
beneficiaries of his estate with the intention that it shall not constitute part of his
dutiable estate?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Acting Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department): This is a complex and involved area of income tax and estate duty law,
and if the honourable member has any specific case on which he has doubts I should
be happy to have it examined. In general, any lump-sum payment made to a director
upon his retirement in recognition of his services with a company would, under
present tax law, be liable to income tax on the full amount. In regard to the second
part of the question any gratituity paid by the company to the beneficiaries of a
deceased director would normally form part of that director's dutiable estate in terms
of either sections 15 or 16 of the Estate and Gift Duties Act 1968.

week. This means that at any time a social worker has a case load of about 60 cases,
on average.

National Superannuation Rate
(31/8/78)
Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the
Minister of Social Welfare: When the national superannuation rate reaches 80
percent of the average weekly wage, what will happen to people receiving additional
benefits?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): As I have explained on
several occasions in the past, additional benefit grants to national superannuitants
are being phased out over a period of about 5 years. From 31 August 1978—that is,
from today-married national superannuitants will receive $14.02 a week more than
they would have received had age benefits been retained. The corresponding figure
for single superannuitants is $7.39 a week. Despite the phasing out of the additional
benefits, the superannuitants affected are still significantly better off on national
superannuation than they would have been had the age benefit plus full additional
benefit been retained. In addition, national superannuitants receive a net benefit
equal to or better than many in the work force who have dependent wives and
children, and to whom no additional benefits or concessions are available. There is,
therefore, no justification for the continuation of additional benefits to national
superannuitants.

Wool Export Freight Rates
(31/8/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), on behalf of Mr BRUCE BARCLAY
(Christchurch Central), to the Minister of Agriculture: Is the statement in the


## p. 3397 (#793) ###########################################

13 September
3397
Questions and Replies
"Without a word of a lie" column in the National Business Review of 9 August correct in
its claim that "for the second time in recent months, the Wool Board may have
prevented the introduction of competitive wool-export freight rates in a continued bid
to preserve the profits of the Conference Lines"?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): While it is correct that the
Bank Lines have been excluded from participating in the New Zealand-European
wool trade, the statement in the National Business Review is not correct when it
attributes the Wool Board's motive to being "a continuing bid to preserve the profits
of the Conference Lines". The general objective of the Wool Board is to establish, in
the interests of growers, the best possible long-term returns for New Zealand wool. To
achieve this end the board has, amongst other things, the power to negotiate and
enter into agreements relating to freight rates and other terms and conditions for the
transport of such wool. My understanding is that it is the board's view that it is in the
New Zealand wool industry's interests to maintain a contin uing shipping service for
wool exports. This requirement has to be balanced against the advantages that might
at first be apparent from outside shipping lines offering reduced freight rates. I
understand that, at present, the board considers that the New Zealand wool industry
is best served by the Conference Lines in relation to wool exports to Europe and
North America. Accordingly, it has confined wool shipments to the established lines
on the trade, and this excluded the Bank Lines. As with all its policies, however, the
board's shipping policy is subject to regular review.

Temporary Employment Programme
(31/8/78)
MARILYN WARING (Raglan), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East)
to the Minister of State Services: Who was responsible for the decision that
employment of clerical and related staff under the temporary employment
programme for longer than 1 year should cease, what is to happen to those affected by
this new ruling, and how much notice are these people to be given?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of State Services. “The decision was made by the State Services Commission
after discussion with the Department of Labour. Workers under the temporary
employment scheme who are doing clerical and related work are taken on by
departments according to the criterion laid down by the State Services Commission
that the work is of low priority and would have been deferred. By its very nature,
work of this type is of short duration. If the job lasts for more than 1 year then it
becomes somewhat more permanent, and the person in the job should be considered
for permanent employment. The commission has advised departments that if the
person is suitable in every way, and there is a vacancy, he should be appointed to the
permanent staff. Those who cannot be appointed to a vacancy will be given 2 weeks'
notice."

(31/8/78)

environmental value of the Wheao?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): At my request, the
Commission for the Environment prepared, and released for public comment on
12 January this year, a discussion paper on wild and scenic rivers protection. One
hundred and ten submissions were received. On 18 August I released an appraisal by
the commissioner of the response to the discussion paper. The main conclusion is that
there is a need for a positive policy ensuring protection of rivers, or sections of rivers,
in their undeveloped state when they have outstanding wild, scenic, or other natural
characteristics. The mechanism for the development and implementation of an
appropriate policy is now being discussed by the relevant Government departments.

Special Work Scheme
(1/9/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Labour: When was the
special work scheme started, and when was it extended to provide work within
Government departments for unemployed clerical, technical and specialist workers?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Labour. “The special work scheme, which had its origins in the winter
work programme, started in May 1974. The variation to this scheme, which enables
the Department of Labour to seek a wider range of employment opportunities in
skilled and semi-skilled occupations in Government departments, was introduced in
June 1975. In March 1978 the scheme was restructured as the temporary
employment programme, and now covers all occupations-whether skilled or
unskilled in Government departments, local authorities, non-profitmaking
community organisations, hospital boards, and education authorities. In addition,
four job creation programmes operating in the private sector have been introduced to
encourage employers to provide jobs for people who would otherwise be unemployed.
These are the farm employment scheme introduced in October 1977, and the skill
promotion programme, the first job programme, and the addi ional jobs programme
in March 1978".

Government Superannuation Fund; what are the various interest payments for each
year from 1946; and why are they not shown in the report?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The answer to this question
is a little longer than usual, but I do not think it is too long. Because of the nature of
the fund it is not the practice for the accounts to show moneys payable by the State as
a liability. The scheme is on what is termed a "partially funded" basis, in that the
fund represents the contributions of the members and the earnings of those
contributions. The State's share of the costs is determined as the benefits emerge, and
is paid at that time. Because of the great variety of factors that can influence the
amount of subsidy, there is no practicable way in which future State payments, which
are, of course, guaranteed by the Government Superannuation Fund Act itself, could
be precisely determined at any given time and shown as a liability in the accounting
sense. The particular money to which the question refers relates to the amalgamation
of the then three seperate State employees' funds as from 1 April 1948. At that point it
was found that for varying reasons over earlier years the accumulated funds fell short
of the value of employee contributions by $40 million. This has been adjusted by
special payments under section 95(1)(b) of the Act, which are specifically identified
each year in the annual accounts published in the report--for example, the amount of
$2 million being shown for 1977-78. On a table basis, the interest components of the


## p. 3404 (#800) ###########################################

3404
13 September
Questions and Replies
annual payments vary from year to year, but the special payments will be completed
in 1980-81 when a total of $66,872,813 will have been paid, of which $26,872,813 will
represent interest.

Crewe Murder Trials-DSIR Evidence
(1/9/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Science and Technology:
Bearing in mind the fact that there have been a number of trials, appeals, and reviews
relating to the Crewe murder case and the conviction of Arthur Alan Thomas, and
the fact that there have been differing interpretations of the scientific evidence
surrounding the case, is he satisfied with the work of the DSIR in relation to this case?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): With science and
technology playing an increasing part in the fight against crime, the forensic scientist
renders a vitally important public service in giving impartial scientific evidence to the
courts so that justice may be properly served. DSIR scientists may be called out at
any time of the day or night to collect and examine scientific evidence and to
undertake scientific analyses. The work requires great skill, attention to detail,
impartiality, and absolute scientific integrity. The forensic staff of the DSIR possess
all these qualities. Over a long period, the scientific evidence in the Crewe case was
the subject of much comment in the press, on radio, and on television, and, at one
stage, a book was written about the case. The forensic scientists of the DSIR involved
in this case-Dr D. F. Nelson and Mr. R. Shanahan-felt bound not to make a public
statement in spite of being provoked in public and in private. They personally have
been subjected to abuse by some members of the public, and so, too, were their wives
and families. In spite of this, they refrained from comment because of their official
positions, and because they believed it was important for the department to remain
impartial in all circumstances. These scientists, whatever the attacks made upon
them, have examined every new hypothesis put forward in the same skilled and
impartial manner that they have always demonstrated. I am particularly satisfied
with their work in the Crewe murder case.

the Post Office Savings Bank cheque accounts were computerised. The reason for this

222.
Doctor Shortage
(6/9/78)
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen the
statement by the member for New Lynn in the Dominion of 31 August that 200 doctors
have left New Zealand in the period of the National Government, and, if so, (a) is this
correct, (b) is there a doctor shortage in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the statement by the member
for New Lynn in the Dominion of 31 August 1978. There has always been a number of
doctors leaving New Zealand for reasonably lengthy absences to gain experience and
advanced qualifications. Many return after a few years. New Zealand also recruits
doctors from overseas. The number of doctors graduating from our medical schools
has increased, and, as expected, the number travelling overseas to gain experience
has also risen. However, the number registered in New Zealand has actually
increased by 300 during the term of this Government. The net loss from migration has


## p. 3412 (#808) ###########################################

3412
13 September
Questions and Replies
been only 50 during this period, and it can be expected that the number of doctors
returning will increase when they have completed their studies. The Medical Council
and the Department of Health have recently set up a joint committee to examine
medical manpower requirements in New Zealand. This committee has not yet
completed a full review of overall requirements. However, it is clear that there are
areas and specialties that could usefully have higher numbers of doctors. The
increasing number of doctors registering in New Zealand is expected to allow these
areas and specialties to be better serviced.

Teachers' Retiring Leave
(6/9/78)
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei), on behalf of Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay), to the
Minister of Education: Is it true that New Zealand school teachers are in the only
teaching profession in the Western World not already receiving retirement leave, as
stated by NZEI President, John Davenport, in a report in the Evening Post of 22 April
1978, and, if so, what plans has the Government to rectify this situation and bring the
profession in New Zealand into line with the profession in other countries?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I am not aware of the retiring
leave provisions enjoyed by teachers in other Western countries, or the circumstances
under which these provisions were granted. The employment conditions of teachers
in New Zealand have been negotiated with the teachers' service organisation, and
reflect the internal circumstances within this country. The question of granting
retiring leave to teachers has been raised by employee organisations in the past, but
no firm proposals are under consideration at present.

Consumer Price Reductions, Tauranga

Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Can he

reduction of freight rates from Hamilton to Tauranga of the following commodities;

National Superannuitants, Additional Benefits
(6/9/78)
Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the
Minister of Social Welfare: What criteria will be used in determining whether a
national superannuitant will be able to receive additional benefits, and what levels
will they be paid at?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Social Security
Amendment Bill 1978, at present before the House, precludes new grants of
additional benefit to national superannuitants after 31 August 1978. Existing grants
are being progressively withdrawn over a period of about 5 years. From 31 August, all
national superannuitants received substantial increases in the rate of the national
superannuation. Married couples are now receiving $14.02 a week more by way of
national superannuation than they would have been receiving by way of age benefit
had that benefit been retained. The corresponding figure for single superannuitants is
$7.39 a week. These increases have removed any need for new grants of additional
benefit unless there are exceptional circumstances, in which case special
consideration will be given to a grant of additional benefit under section 61G of the
Social Securrity Act.

Mr LANGE (Mangere): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to questions, I

The Labour Party believes in the role of the courts as forums where differences arising
between citizen and State may be settled. The Labour Party believes it is abhorrent for a
member of the Executive, even the Attorney-General, to interfere politically in a judicial
process. This party believes that the present Attorney-General is incompetent and inept
when he does so intervene. His intervention in the Bastion Point prosecutions was as inept as
his intervention in the Ford Motor Co. case. The member for Hastings will remember that
in the case he is so keen to talk about, the Attorney-General and the Labour Government
acted honourably, and gave the fiat.
Mr Fenton: Pre-empting the court.
Mr LANGE: The Attorney-General and the Labour Government put the matter into
the hands of the court; there was no question of pre-empting the court. What a stupid

member for Hastings and other back-benchers to find out where this country is with the rule
of law. What happened in the Bastion Point cases was simple: the Attorney-General moved
too late to stop prosecutions. Had he been a competent Attorney-General he would have
known, from the time of the first prosecution, that there would be convictions and
discharges.
It is not the function of the court to punish people more heavily for having exercised
their right to plead not guilty. In any event, a defended case came before the court fairly
promptly, and that person was convicted and discharged. The die was cast then, but the
Attorney-General waited until some 50 persons had been convicted before he interfered
politically in the process. He did no service at all to the police, because when those
prosecutions were launched the assistant commissioner in Auckland said emphatically that
there would be no withdrawals. The moral of the story is simple: get yourself into a mess, or
into a situation with a lot of other people, then change your name by deed poll to Zechariah,
and under this Government you will be free of trouble because you will be down the list; you
will be safe because you will not be among those called.
I want to know what principle that is in terms of the administration of justice. Some
people still want to go to the court and say, "I do not believe I was properly charged", so
that, if possible, they can be acquitted. The Attorney-General has denied those people that
recourse, but, more importantly, he has moved so ineptly that, if we believe the
commentator in the Auckland Star, Bruce Christopher, who admired the action, all those
people were guilty. People who take that view have a most extraordinary prejudice, and are
prejudging the issue that is before the court. The fact is that the Attorney-General mucked it
up, and he was far too late. He has caused many people to wonder where the Government
stands on the question of political interference in judicial matters.
I remember a back-bencher from the South Island-the deep south-who loudly said
that he would resign if certain prosecutions were stopped. Where does he stand on the issue
of Bastion Point? Has his voice been heard clearly? The member for Invercargill has been
absolutely silent, a rare event, because justice is different when one looks at it from the
different end of the telescope. This Government is unfitted to interfere politically. It is inept,
and its ineptitude is evidenced by the Prime Minister asking Federated Farmers to get him

from the Government the pressure of actually being an informant in court proceedings?

wanted to get a Bill through the House, and did not want to have political or social pressures
at that time. If the Government says it took the action to relieve the pressure on the court, it
should give the police and the courts the resources to deal with matters at issue between
citizens and the State. It should not be said that murder trials cannot be dealt with because
there are a lot of murderers around.

Mr MALCOLM (Eden): The member for Mangere has been recorded as saying that he
is better at law than he is at politics. With respect, after his last speech I think he is not good
at either; and, when he mixes the two, it becomes even more confusing.
I refer to questions 149, 204, and 225, which deal with national superannuation. Elderly
people in New Zealand, as a generation, tend to be an honest and trusting group because
they were brought up in an era when honour and trust were values that were respected.
Those are values that they apply to their own behaviour, and they expect other people to
apply them to their behaviour. Hence, the elderly people in New Zealand over the age of 55
or 60 tend to be a particularly honourable and trusting section of our population. I feel
sickened and ashamed when I think of the way in which, in the last 3 or 4 years, Labour
politicians have betrayed the trust shown by people over 60, because the modern
opportunists of the Labour Party-not the old-fashioned Labour Party members whom
many people voted for in the 1930s, but those who threw principles out the window in favour
of opportunist politics-have consistently misled the elderly people as to the truth and the
reality about superannuation.
In 1975 we fought an election on the superannuation policy. The National Party's policy
was clear and straightforward, and it gave people over 60 some dignity. The Labour Party's
policy was to give nothing to people over the age of 60. Now it is all finished, and we are
introducing the last stage of national superannuation; we have implemented the National
Party's policy in full. Under national superannuation, married couples are now getting $105
a week before tax and $91 a week after tax. Had the Labour Government remained in office,
those people would have been getting $77. The difference is $14 a week between what they
are getting now under National and what they would have got if Labour's policies had
succeeded. That is an increase of 78 percent for national superannuitants since 1975, at a
time when the cost of living has increased by 44 percent. That is justice under the National
Administration. It is not what was promised by the Labour Government.
The final irony comes with the telephone and television concessions, about which the
Labour Party made so much fuss. What is the Labour Party's policy? It is to change nothing,
not even the concessions. The elderly people, who value honesty and trust, believed
something different of Labour because of their experiences back in the 1930s. It is clear that
the Labour Party of the late 1970s is comprised of men who do not share the basic principles
of justice and social equality held by the old-time Labour people. The present members of
the Labour Party are opportunists, the worst sort of political opportunists, who simply seek
to gain as individuals, and who will lead elderly people up the garden path again and again,
as they have done in the last 4 years.
In spite of what Labour members have said in all their bleatings about concern for the
elderly, the fact of the matter is that under National, before tax, a married couple are getting
$105; under Labour, if all its policies had continued as promised, those people would have
been getting $77. Even when one allows for tax, the difference is that between $91 after tax
under National and $77 under Labour. In spite of all the noise they have made in the House,
the Labour members are not going to reinstate the concessions.

ELECTIONS AND POLLS BILL
Introduction
Dr WALL (Porirua): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Elections and Polls
Bill. In doing so I express regret that such a measure is necessary, because the people have
now lost confidence in the rolls as a means of entitling them to a valid vote in the next
election. They have had every reason to lose that confidence. Accurate reports of people
who have carried out the necessary enrolment procedures, but have been told they are not
on the roll, are coming in from all over the country. They have had no assurance that their
application has been received by the electoral officer in time or in such a way as to enable
them to be on the roll.
That difficulty would have been overcome by the previous legislation I attempted to
introduce, because a voter's entitlement to vote would have been based on his entitlement to
be on the roll, not on the fact of his being enrolled. As the Government thought it proper not
to allow the Bill to be introduced and adequately discussed, it is now necessary for those of
us who are concerned about the preservation of the democratic process to ensure that
measures should be put before the House to allow voters to go to the polling booth and,
despite any errors, omissions, negligence, or failings on the part of the Minister's staff
responsible for enrolments, be able to cast a valid vote.
I expect the Minister to say that everyone will be allowed to cast a vote. That is true.
Under existing conditions, no one will be denied a vote at the polling booth. However,
neither the Minister nor anyone else can say that anyone who casts a vote will have that vote
counted. The requirements of secrecy under the Electoral Act will mean that only the
scrutineers and the polling staff will know which votes will not be counted. Therefore, those
people appointed by the Government to conduct polls will secretly rule out many thousands
of votes cast in the next election unless, by some miracle, the Government can restore public
confidence in the rolls and bring them to a state of perfection that will justify confidence.
There is no indication of any such miracle at present.
I recommend the Bill because it provides that there should be no cessation of enrolment
after the issue of the writs, and that people may legally enrol at the time they cast their votes.
There is considerable legal opinion about the accuracy of the statement made by the Chief
Electoral Officer that the enrolment cards constitute the roll. The Bill will ensure that that
has a legal foundation, and that every vote cast by a person who is already on the published
roll or any other roll, or who legally and correctly fills in an enrolment card at the time of
voting, will be able to cast a vote that will be counted. Unless a procedure such as the one I
am proposing is adopted, no Minister or person will be able to say with certainty that that
situation will prevail in the polling booths at this year's election.


## p. 3424 (#820) ###########################################

3424
13 September
Elections and Polls Bill
I have extended the provisions for the formation of rolls, and have limited and
circumscribed the rights and duties of scrutineers. The Bill defines the relationships between
the scrutineers and the returning officers. This is a matter of considerable urgency, because,
with the lack of confidence in the Government's ability to produce democratic provisions for
voting or enrolment at the next election, differences of opinion between the scrutineers, who
are there to safeguard the democratic process, and the returning officers, whose primary
responsibility is to get the job done, will inevitably recur. At present their relationship is
mainly defined at departmental level, with very little true legal backing to justify the
decisions under which they work. The sensitive matter of the counting of votes should be
regularised in a way that will ensure that the rights and responsibilities of the returning
officers are maintained by satisfactory statutory backing. The scrutineer's duty to act as an
official witness is circumscribed by the Bill to allow that duty to be more efficiently carried
out. Sufficient rights are given to scrutineers to ensure that they will not be unduly restricted
in the proceedings they officially observe.
I have also made provision in the Bill to protect those people who, because they have
not to date been on the roll, are fearful that their attempts to enrol would bring them to the
notice of the authorities, and possible prosecution. Their fears are ill founded, and statutory
assurance that that will not happen should be given to them.
I have made provision for transfers of registration under the Electoral Act 1956 for
people who, for one reason or another, have been wrongly enrolled. They will be able to do
so right up until the time of voting. Otherwise, the great number of people whose names
have been entered on wrong rolls-and to date we have had no satisfactory assurance that
their names will be on the right rolls-will be disfranchised, because of the actions of the
electoral officer's staff, who have wrongly-and I am not saying negligently, but
accidentally-placed those people's names on the wrong rolls. When they go to a polling
booth at which they expect to be able to cast a vote, they will find that their names are not on
the roll, and that they will not be able to cast a vote at all, because they will not know which
roll they are on. In many cases it will be the roll of an electorate in which the elector has no
interest or concern. For these reasons I suggest that the matter be considered seriously by
the House.
The Bill is well drafted. I think it will achieve what I say it will achieve, but should there
be any minor inaccuracies in drafting, or matters that have been overlooked, the Bill should
be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee. I do not think that it will be necessary to call
witnesses, but it will give an opportunity to correct any minor deficiencies, and for the
committee to review it to ensure that it will produce the effect that I desire. I ask the House
to support the Bill, because unless this, or some other Act of similar intent, is brought into
the House before the end of the session, voters cannot be assured of a vote. The Minister's
assurances about the electoral rolls and the Chief Electoral Officer, who is under his
direction, have not been borne out; and there are numerous examples of this. So, any
assurances now given on the basis of public experience cannot be taken as watertight. There
is no reason to suppose that the Minister's promises now will be any better than they have
been in the past.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Government will oppose the Bill's
proceeding any further. I am not a fiercely ambitious man, but I have developed an ambition
this year, and that is to see the day when the Labour members of Parliament will stop
messing about with the electoral law. I hope that when we have a look at the Electoral Act
next year, the member for Porirua will bring his proposals forward so that they can be given
proper study in a select committee. The proper time for them to be brought forward is the
beginning of a session, not the end of one.
The Bill looks like a last-minute panic measure by the member for Porirua. He
described it to the Evening Post of 8 September, as "a Wall attempt to clear up the electoral
roll mess". I thought it desirable to comment on this description, so I sent out a press
statement recording my regret at the introduction of the Bill and deploring the fact that it
showed the readiness of the Opposition to sacrifice important electoral principles for
political expediency. In his description of the Bill, as published by the Evening Post, he did
not refer to a fundamental provision of our electoral process that is set out in clause 9 of the
Bill, which would breach the secrecy of the poll. This is thoroughly bad in principle, and the
Government is totally opposed to that provision in the member's Bill.
I will repeat, for the record, my statement to the public in reply to the member for
Porirua's comment in the Evening Post. I described his Bill as simply a rehash of his earlier
Voting Rights Protection Bill, and included the member for Wigram's earlier Bill, both of


## p. 3425 (#821) ###########################################

13 September
3425
Elections and Polls Bill
which Parliament rightly saw as a device to avoid and reject pre-registration. That type of
scheme could have led to electoral frauds that no honest Government would have accepted.
A similar proposal was tried and found wanting by the Labour Government in 1975, and the
National Government lost no time in repealing the infamous section 99(f), which would have
allowed anybody at all to walk into a polling booth, declare that he had done all the things
required of him, and have his vote counted, whether or not he was lying.
The same provision now reappears with the proposal to remove the limitations on
registering as an elector after writ day, and again to have enrolments in polling booths on
election day. Why should anybody in New Zealand bother to enrol earlier than polling day if
he could do it then? Pre-registration would be largely a waste of time and money. The
concept of compulsory registration as a prerequisite to voting, which has served us very well
since 1925, conceives a partnership between the State and the individual; and I believe it is
good to have responsibility on both sides. Registration is still relied upon today, as it was in
the past, to enable a person's eligibility to vote to be checked before voting on polling day,
and, more importantly, to safeguard the integrity of the poll. Moreover, registration at
polling booths is quite impracticable on any large scale, as anyone familiar with the electoral
process would know, including Labour members.
One of the important principles of the electoral law is that the polls are conducted by
impartial persons, and I find abhorrent the idea that a person's eligibility to vote should be
dependent on the say-so of a member of any political party, yet that, according to the
member for Porirua's statement in the Evening Post, is what the Bill suggests. I am appalled
at the readiness of the Labour Opposition to sacrifice important electoral principles for
political expediency. As I have said time after time, every person who has properly
completed an electoral registration card will be able to vote at the coming poll. If people fill
in their voting papers correctly, their votes will of course be valid, and they will be allowed.
Since then I have had time to study in some detail the clauses of the Bill--and I am
obliged to the member for an advance typescript of the Bill. I find that clause 2 contains a
number of wordy and difficult-to-follow definitions, many of which were contained in the
member's Voting Rights Protection Bill. What, for instance, does a regular election mean?
There are three definitions of "roll" that appear to encompass a much greater variety of
listings than is intended. The member refers to main rolls, current rolls, and supplementary
rolls, without indicating what he means. Clause 3 is taken from the Voting Rights Protection
Bill, and purports to override, without amending, the various Acts. As a drafting technique
it is of doubtful validity.
Clause 4 is an important clause. It repeals the restriction on registration after writ day,
to which extent it seeks to achieve the same result as clause 6 of the Voting Rights Protection
Bill. I suspect that the member thinks that the mere repeal of the restriction will have
ramifications similar to his earlier provision. Certainly the Evening Post quoted the member
as wanting deputy returning officers to have the power to enrol someone on the spot if they
believed the person to be 18 years of age of over and living in the electorate. The Bill will not
allow that, and the Electoral Act, changed by the Labour Government in 1975, required, in
section 7A, that all electoral officers should be postal officials.
The purpose of clause 5 is not clear. It confuses two different steps in the post-election
process: the scrutiny of the rolls, which is directed to ensuring that polls are carried out
without fraud and has little or nothing to do with the actual counting of the votes; and the
official count, which leads to the declaration of the result of the election. Apart from this, it
is virtually a restatement of what is already in our electoral laws, and to that extent it is
unnecessary.
Subclause (3) is much wider than the present provision. Scrutineers are entitled to be
present at the scrutiny and the official count. The effect of the member's subclause would be
that they could accompany the returning officer, and presumably the police, when they were
investigating offences under the Act. I refer to paragraphs (b) and (c) to paragraph (n).
These would enable scrutineers to be present when the electorate officer performs his duty;
and that refers to paragraphs (j) and (k). In my view these rights are inconsistent with the
proper function of scrutineers. We must not have them breaching the secrecy of the poll.
Clause 6 seems to be unnecessary; its purpose is not clear. Adequate provision now
exists for the appointment of scrutineers; and I know of no obstacle to political parties
appointing scrutineers. Whether or not they are chief scrutineers seems to me to be a matter
of internal organisation within the parties.
Clause 7 extends the functions of scrutineers. For example, paragraphs (f) to (i) apart,
the clause is a restatement of their rights. Paragraphs (d) and (e) require further

Elections and Polls Bill
consideration, and I am concerned that the extended powers could unduly delay the official
count, which would not be good. Again, the proposals go beyond the present functions of
the scrutineers, and the member might tell us what evil it is hoped this will cure. It is not
apparent.
Referring to clause 8, under the present law a recount means simply that. A magistrate
checks each vote. It does not involve a further scrutiny of the rolls, and I see no reason why a
mechanical task of that nature should need reviewing-similarly with the investigation of
offences and other matters incidental to the conduct of the poll.
Clause 9, which is thoroughly bad in principle, is in direct conflict with perhaps the most
important principle of the Electoral Act-the secrecy of the poll. Under the clause, a query
could be ansered only if it was known where the vote was cast, after which it would be
necessary to take the electoral roll number, find the counterfoil with that number, and then
search the ballot papers to find the appropriate paper. The polling staff would know
immediately how that person had voted. Is that what the member for Porirua wants? Does
he want the secrecy of the poll blown apart? That is what his Bill provides for.
Subclause (2) is in direct contrast to section 132(2) of the Electoral Act. I do not have
any comment on clause 10; and as to clause 11, as no person has been prosecuted for failing
to enrol the need for this clause is quite unclear. Clause 12 was clause 10 in the member's
earlier Bill, except that paragraph (b) of subclause (1) and subclause (2) have been deleted.
That clause enables a Maori voter to change electoral rolls at any time before the close of the
poll if he discovers that, contrary to his intention, he is not on the roll on which he intended
to be registered when lodging his application. In effect, that allows a Maori elector to switch
rolls at any time up to the close of the poll. The political implications of any widespread roll
switching of this nature are significant. This proposal comes from the Labour Party, which
brought in that extraordinary measure in 1975 to gerrymander the elections.

Labour Opposition members have had a strange change of heart within the past 2 years.
They tend to base their arguments on the rolls, but the availability or even the accuracy of
the printed rolls does not affect eligibility to vote, as the Minister of Justice has said in the
House on many occasions; it is dependent on the fact of registration. Section 100 of the
Electoral Act 1956 sets out the grounds upon which any person qualified to vote may do so as
a special voter. Returning officers have been instructed this year, as they have been
instructed in the past, that anyone claiming the right to vote as a special voter will be given
such a vote; and if he or she comes within the definition of section 100 of the Act, the vote
will be counted.
This is the third attempt this year to introduce legislation altering the polling
procedures. The second Bill was introduced by the member for Porirua and the earlier one
was introduced by the member for Wigram. Parliament rightly saw both measures as a
device to avoid pre-registration and threw them out; it rejected them. As the Minister of
Justice has said, that sort of scheme could lead to electoral frauds that no Government could
accept. The proposal to remove the limitations on registering as an elector after the closing
of the writs and to allow enrolments at polling booths on election day was submitted to the
former Labour Government in 1975. It was tossed out then as being totally impracticable,
and the demand was made that the election results be made available as quickly as possible.
If we were all able to enrol and vote on election day, I for one would not waste my time,
effort, or money pre-registering. Why should I bother? If I were able to turn up at the polling
booth on election day, register, and vote, I would not waste my time registering beforehand.
Today we must still rely on registration, as we have done in the past, to enable a person's
eligibility to be checked before election day-not afterwards-and so that we do not go 2
weeks or more without a Government. I can hear the member for Onehunga trying to
interject. In 1975 his own Government said that that was most important. The idea of
registering at polling booths is quite impractical, particularly on a large scale, as anyone who
is familiar with the voting procedure will know.
