CO-OPERATIVE FORESTRY COMPANIES BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Co-operative Forestry
Companies Bill be introduced. In doing so I want to inform the House that it is the
Government's proposal to refer the Bill to the Lands and Agriculture Committee for study.
The Bill provides for the registration of co-operative forestry companies. Its object is to
provide, through such companies, the management and services necessary for the utilisation
of forest produce of small-forest growers in New Zealand, including about 2000 such growers
who have already established small forests and woodlots pursuant to various Government
incentive schemes. For the proposes of the Bill a co-operative forestry company is a
company that has adopted certain provisions in its articles of association and has, for its
principal business, all or any of the following objects: the establishment of forests for its
shareholders; the protection and management of forests for its shareholders; or the
utilisation of marketing of forest produce for its shareholders.
The Bill provides for the compulsory and voluntary surrender of shares to enable a co-
operative forestry company to ensure that the majority of the persons who are its
shareholders are persons who are growing forest produce. That is in line with other co-
operative companies' legislation, and is, of course, consistent with the concept of a co-
operative company-that it is owned by and operated for the benefit of those using its
services. The approval of the Minister of Justice is a prerequisite to the registration of a co-
operative forestry company. The Bill permits the Minister of Justice to specify conditions in
respect of certain matters relating to registered co-operative forestry companies such as
areas of operation, the minimum number of members, the minimum area of forestry land to
be held by qualifying shareholders, and amalgamation. Before exercising any of these
powers the Minister of Justice is to obtain the advice of the Minister of Forests. These
powers are considered necessary by both the Government and the co-operative forestry
movement, because forest produce is a long-term crop of about 25 years, and thus co-
operative forestry companies have to be set up as long-term ventures. That these powers are
to be exercisable by the Minister of Justice should not be regarded as definitive, and the
question whether such powers should be exercisable by a tribunal could be considered
further by the select committee to which I propose to refer the Bill for study.
The Bill permits a registered co-operative forestry company to enter into supply
contracts whereby the company has the exclusive right to harvest, purchase, or sell the forest
produce owned by the other party to the contract. Where the owner or occupier of land to
which a supply contract relates enters into the contract, it may be registered against the title
of that land and thus bind successors in title. The registration of supply contracts will allow a
co-operative forestry company to enter into long-term commitments, based on assured
future supply of forest produce.
Although the Bill stands in my name as Minister of Justice, I wish to acknowledge that
the Bill is the result of the work of an informal committee set up by the Minister of Forests,


## p. 3436 (#832) ###########################################

3436
14 September
Co-operative Forestry Companies Bill
comprising representatives of the New Zealand Forest Service, the New Zealand Farm
Forestry Association (Inc.), and the Federated Farmers of New Zealand (Inc.). The
enactment of the Bill will bring to four the number of co-operative companies Acts on the
statute book, all with many similar provisions. In fact, I am sure members are familiar with
the dairy industry scheme, which has great similarities. Having regard to my comments
about activity-based legislation in the context of the Securities Bill at present before the
House, I consider that the next development in co-operative companies legislation will be to
have one Co-operative Companies Act, consolidating all those similar provisions and
containing those special provisions relating to a particular type of co-operative company.
The Bill represents an important step in the development of the small-forest sector of
the wood industry in New Zealand, to assist landholders to diversify their produce, improve
land use, and to provide greater employment opportunities in the rural sector. I commend
the Bill to the House.

Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The Bill provides that the owners of any land
who are qualified—the qualification being that they have 4 ha or more of forestry land—can
become members of a forestry co-operative. We do not want legislation that specifically
mentions or deals with Maori landholdings. Obviously they are included. There is nothing in
the Bill to exclude such co-operative bodies. In the model articles of association for a
forestry company certain restrictions are placed on voting rights. Those articles comprise a
large part of the Bill, and are in the first schedule. They describe the type of administrative
structure that the Minister of Justice would require for the establishment of a forestry co-
operative. I envisage that a number of owners of Maori land will have interest in this
measure, because it brings together for the purposes of silviculture, management, or
processing and marketing a wide range of individual owners, particularly those who may not
be in a position of strength because they have only small holdings. If this happens they can
then engage staff qualified in silviculture, forest management, and other activities.
Two years ago in Scotland and in Sweden I had a look at this structure, where I saw its
great advantage to individual forest owners. As the Minister of Justice has said, it is
interesting to note there are about 2000 individual forest owners in New Zealand. The total
planted area is about 50 000 ha. Through the Government's forestry encouragement and
grants scheme, an additional 50 000 ha has been approved for planting. In total size that
represents a forest equal to in size to Golden Downs, or half the size of the Kaiangaroa
Forest. The time is opportune for this type of legislation. After all, the first plantings under
the forestry encouragement schemes are now about 13 years old, which means that they are
ready for preparation for logging thinnings and for other purposes to prepare the trees for
ultimate sale. Much of the produce from those privately owned forests will, because of their
geographical distribution, probably be in the form of logs and sawn timber. If it is managed
properly, silviculturally much of it is well suited for the export market. It is of advantage at
this stage, with forests 13 years old or younger, to ensure that the greatest degree of
silviculture is incorporated into the management of those forests, thus ensuring that high
quality logs are available to the market.
I pay a tribute to the officers of the Forest Service, who have worked most of this year,
after several years of consultation with the Farm Forestry Association and Federated
Farmers, for the work they have done to bring this Bill before the House. The measure has
been prepared after full consultation with the Farm Forestry Association and Federated
Farmers. I hope it helps to break down the feeling of antagonism towards forestry that we
sometimes find in the farming community. I hope it will build up an appreciation among
landowners that they can plant certain areas of their farms with trees. There is a minimum of

TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 3)
Introduction
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Transport
Amendment Bill (No. 3) be introduced. The main intention of the Bill is to implement certain
recommendations of the parliamentary select committee on road safety, set out in its annual
report recently tabled in Parliament. This is to be done by a series of amendments to the
Transport Act 1962. Two major matters dealt with by the select committee are included in
this Bill.
The first concerns the blood-alcohol provisions of the Transport Act, and the second
concerns the provisions relating to limited drivers' licences. The Government has long been
concerned about the danger that alcohol-impaired drivers present to other road users and to
society in general. Publicity campaigns, such as the recent nationwide blitz on drinking and
driving, may produce a downturn in the incidence of drunken driving, but unfortunately this
is only temporary. To ensure a continuation of the deterrent effect of enforcement, a
permanent increase in the risk of apprehension is needed—that is, a person must realise that
it is more than likely that he will be apprehended if he drives after drinking. The select
committee on road safety has recognised this, and has acknowledged the need for urgent
action.
In June this year the committee released an interim report that recommended a number
of changes. It is the intention of the Government in this Bill to take positive steps to deal
more effectively with the drunken driver. At present the minimum time needed by the
Ministry of Transport to process a driver suspected of excessive blood alcohol levels is about
2 hours. This necessarily imposes limits on the efficiency of enforcement. To increase this
efficiency or apprehension rate, the committee proposes to introduce evidential breath tests.
In the committee's view, these breath tests should substantially replace blood testing. It
1


## p. 3445 (#841) ###########################################

14 September
3445
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 3)
would mean that the courts must accept the result of an evidential breath test, showing a
breath alcohol proportion of more than 500 micrograms per litre of expired air, as evidence
of an offence when the test is preceded by a positive alcotest R80, or similar screening test,
which is the usual roadside breath test used at present. The Government has adopted the
committee's recommendations.
A new offence of driving with excess breath alcohol is provided for in the Bill, based on
the breath-alcohol proportion recommended by the committee. The existing screening
breath test is to be retained. If this test and the evidential breath test prove to be positive, the
suspect is advised that if he does not, within 10 minutes, express a wish to take a blood test,
the results of the evidential breath test will be taken as proof of the level of alcohol for the
purpose of a prosecution. The Government has further decided to reduce the present blood-
alcohol level from 100 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood to 80 mg. Hospital blood sampling
provisions are simplified, and provision is made for all samples taken to be analysed. The
select committee pointed out that, although breath tests may never rival the blood test for
analytical accuracy, they are relevant to the fitness of a person to be in charge of a vehicle.
The immediate determinant of alcohol impairment is the concentration of alcohol in the
blood in the capillaries of the brain at the time of driving. The Government therefore
considers that a breath test is at least as relevant as blood for the assessment of alcohol
impairment.
As an adjunct to the proposals to strengthen the blood alcohol provisions, the
Government believes that it is necessary to tighten the provisions relating to limited licences.
The Act restricts the criteria for obtaining a limited licence to extreme hardship to the
applicant or undue hardship to any other person. No person who has been convicted of a
second offence of dangerous driving, excess alcohol, or similar offences within 5 years of the
first offence will be able to obtain a limited licence. Furthermore, no order granting a limited
licence can take effect until 1 month after it is made.
Many people consider that a further problem with the current blood- and breath-
alcohol legislation lies in inadequate penalties. In 1974-75 the Road Safety Committee had
before it a Ministry of Transport survey showing that 36 percent of the community favoured
more severe penalties while only 7 percent did not. În 1977 the question of increased
penalties was raised again. In its 1978 interim report the committee recognised increased
public disgust at drunken drivers and recommended increased penalties. In particular, the
maximum fine for causing injury or death by dangerous driving, or when driving under the
influence of alcohol, has been increased from $2,000 to $4,000. The maximum fine for
causing injury or death by dangerous driving has been increased from $1,000 to $3,000. The
maximum fine that may be imposed for a blood-alcohol offence is increased from $400 to
$1,500. The Government believes that the measures I have outlined will act as a major
deterrent to those people who are foolish enough to think that they can drive when they are
under the influence of alcohol. The drunken driver has no place in our society.
The opportunity has also been taken to increase the maximum fine that may be imposed
for an offence against the transport licensing provisions of the Transport Act. The maximum
fine is increased from $200 to $2,000 for breaking the 150-km limit that is built into link
transport. Such offences have a serious effect on the economy. The increase in the maximum
level of fines for licensing offences therefore reflects the economic importance of these
offences and is seen to be timely. The only deterrent available to deal with a transport
licensing offence is a substantial fine.
I hope the Bill will go some way to being a deterrent to those who drive when they are
under the influence of alcohol. After all, 90 percent of New Zealanders like a drink or two,
but I believe the Bill will bring about a change of life-style, and that people will think, and
change their actions, so that they do not commit these offences. This will be in their own
interests, and in the interests of others who use the roads.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I welcome the introduction of the Bill, which
implements some of the recommendations in the interim report of the Road Safety
Committee that was presented to Parliament earlier in the session. Why were other
recommendations made by the select committee not included in the Bill? Would the Minister

Fuel Conservation-Water-car Inventor, Archie Blue
5. Mr BRUCE BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Energy: What steps has he
taken, or does he intend to take, to investigate fuel-saving claims made by the "water car"
inventor, Archie Blue, who is reported in 8 O'clock of 26 August 1978, as planning to sell
patent rights to overseas oil companies, when there is an urgent need to reduce overseas oil
imports into New Zealand?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Energy. "The claims made for Mr Blue's water-powered vehicle have been investigated by
the Ministry of Energy. The ministry believes that the in-vehicle conversion of water to
hydrogen and oxygen for vehicle propulsion is unlikely to become a practical proposition.
largely because the process could not produce mechanical energy in excess of the electrical
energy required by the electrolysis. For this reason the ministry has no plans for investigating
this invention further at this stage. The member may not be aware that the member for
Hamilton East asked an oral question in the House on 10 November 1977 on this very
subject. The member may also not be aware that as Minister of Energy I receive many
proposals regarding exciting new developments in the energy scene. Some are scientifically
sound, and, when possible, advice and encouragement are extended to their authors. There
are some, however, that are not so practical, and on average I receive one proposition a
month on a new form of perpetual motion."
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Perhaps I could invite the Minister of Education to draw it to the
attention of the Minister of Energy that replies to questions must be concise and related to
the subject-matter of the question.
Mr Beetham: I found the answer interesting and helpful. However, could the Minister
say whether it is true that the overseas oil companies have shown an interest in this, and, if
so, does that not suggest that the ministry's appreciation of the usefulness of the invention
might be somewhat astray?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I am unaware of what the overseas oil companies might do. I can
only repeat that the total mechanical energy available from the process will be no greater
than the amount required to electrolyse water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Electoral Rolls-Mobile Voters
6. Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of Justice: Can
a prospective elector who reaches the age of 18 years in the period between the issue of the
writs and the day before the election, and who has left home to take up an apprenticeship or
a job in another electorate 2 months before the election, enrol as an elector and cast a valid
vote, and, if so, in which electorate?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I refer the right honourable gentleman
to section 50 of the Electoral Act 1956, which provides for registrations to close at 6 p.m. on
writ day, but further provides "that this section shall not apply to any applicant who satisfies
the electorate officer that he has become qualified as an elector of the district not earlier than
1 month before writ day". Section 99(b) of the Electoral Act makes such a person a qualified
voter as long as he has applied for registration before polling day. In the case mentioned by
the right honourable gentleman, the person would appear to be qualified to enrol for the
electorate in which his home address was situated, because that is where he would have last
lived for 3 months. If he was not in that electorate on polling day he would cast a special
vote.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: The Minister was very definite in his answer in relation to
sections 50 and 99(b), but in the latter part of his answer about the electorate in which a
person lived, the Minister said the elector would "appear to be qualified". Why is the
Minister hesitant about making an unqualified indication as to which electorate this person is
in?

Perch-Fishing Potential, Lake Rotoroa, Hamilton
7. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East), to
the Minister of Fisheries: Has any assessment been made of the potential for perch fishing in
Hamilton's Lake Rotoroa, what stocks are believed to be extant, and has current angling
pressure had any effect on these stocks?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Fisheries. "Over the past 2 years the fisheries research division and the Auckland
Acclimatisation Society have undertaken detailed studies into the fishing potential and
biology of perch in Hamilton Lake. The lake contains an abundant stock of perch, and

effect on the perch stocks."

Zealand—and it has done it quite knowingly, in the hope that it can put it across and hang on
to a few votes in order to remain the Government.
I have quite a bit to say about the deficit before borrowing. At the level proposed, give
or take $100 million, it is still the largest that has ever been proposed. It is 57 percent higher
than the figure budgeted for at supplementary estimates time in 1975, and yet the Minister of

We are on sound ground when we criticise the Government for failing utterly to come to

that charges would be made for individual phone calls, and that rail charges would increase

Opposition members cannot criticise-although they are lamely trying to do so-the
deficit in the estimates and the budgeted deficit. Frankly, they are on weak ground. They
know it, and it is about time they admitted the fact, got down to the Committee stage, dealt
with the estimates in detail, and got it over with. We are here to discuss the supplementary
estimates. We are in fact discussing, predictably, the deficit of about $1,300 million, which
amounts to 8.3 percent of the gross national product, which the Labour Opposition finds so
objectionable.
I remind Opposition members once again—and I doubt if they could be reminded often
enough, as they have very convenient memories-that in 1975-76 the deficit as a percentage
of GNP was 9.2 and that had the Labour Government remained in office it would have been
11 percent of the GNP. It got down to only 9.2 percent because of the actions taken by this
Government when it took office. Let us lay that on the line once and for all. It is time their
memories were refreshed and they accounted for the fact and admitted that they were
negligent in the extreme in regard to that deficit. This deficit is planned. [Interruption.] I
notice a roar of laughter from the Opposition members. They do not understand the
meaning of the word "planned". They do not understand how an economic deficit can be
planned.
Opposition members often ask in committees that matters be expressed in 1975
monetary terms. I shall express this in monetary terms of 1975 for their edification and
information. The deficit is about $990 million, expressed in their favourite 1975 terms of
dollars and cents. There are some differences between this Budget deficit and the 1975-76
deficit. I have mentioned that this is a planned deficit, unlike their unplanned one.
Another difference is the amount that is included in the supplementary estimates and
the amount that was provided for supplementary estimates in the Budget. The 1978-79
Budget included $250 million for supplementary estimates. We have before us tonight
provision for $603 million, $250 million of which was included in the Budget, so we are down

but in essence that is where we are. It is a real rate, my guess is, of the order of 2 percent.
That is to say, those unemployed, those on relief work, and those who are out of
employment but who would be in employment if there were jobs-namely housewives,
people like that." At that time the registered unemployed and relief workers numbered
8600. The figure now is about 50 000, or five and a half times as much, if we take the Prime
Minister's calculations, which I concede are a more accurate assessment. Five and a half
times 2 percent is 11 percent, and that is probably a more accurate calculation of the
unemployed rate today compared with the rates of our trading partners, which are a little
higher, but of course they count the unemployed differently.
I remind Government members that, when the National Government came into office,
it said it was faced with four problems and we look to these last supplementary estimates for
the final positive response to the problems the Government itself has described. The first
was inflation. Let us remember, for the benefit of Government members, that domestic
inflation has risen. After these supplementary estimates are passed it will probably rise
further. The Government has no credibility on inflation, although it keeps trying to say, to
prove that it has been successful, that things are different from what they really are. The
Government has not controlled domestic inflation. Any reduction in inflation has had
nothing to do with the Government. Imported inflation has fallen drastically.
The second problem was the Budget deficit. These estimates may result in its exceeding
a $1,400 million deficit, the highest level ever. The 1976 cuts in Government spending came
too much too soon. The October 1977 mini-Budget was too little too late, and the Budget
deficit resulting from these measures is too much too late. The Government has no
credibility in the Budget deficit.
When the Government came into office it said the third problem was the balance of
payments. These measures, and a Government tax scheme that gives more to those who
have more, will result in a further widening of the balance of payments deficit, which the
experts have already said will rise. In the last 6 months of the Labour Government, when
things were not particularly easy, Labour reduced the deficit by about $270 million. The
Government has taken more than 2 years, with the biggest export boom in New Zealand's
history and the worst unemployment since the great depression, to reduce it by a similar
amount. The Government has no credibility in the balance of payments.
The fourth major problem claimed by the National Government was unemployment.
The official figure released today puts the total unemployed and people on special relief at
just on 50 000—almost 5 times as bad as the highest figure ever reached under the Labour
Government. The National Government has demolished full employment. It has shown it
believes in using the taxpayers' money to pay people for doing nothing. By further
undermining business confidence, the supplementary estimates will result in a further

worsening of unemployment.
In addition to being unable to solve the four economic problems stated in 1975, the
National Government has created others that did not exist-record interest rates; record net
outflow of permanent and long-term migrants, with a consequent loss of considerable
important skills, often developed at the taxpayers' expense; falling investment; falling
production and productivity; and a considerable change in the real gross national product
per head. The National Government said it would restore New Zealand's shattered
economy. The supplementary estimates show that a more accurate statement would be that
it has shattered New Zealand's restored economy.

Mr SPEAKER: I am sorry that the honourable member asked a question that I did not

adequately. It is not a matter of the Leader of the House stopping broadcasting hours on
Thursday. We are still on Thursday's sitting. Does the member not understand that? The
Standing Order states that the proceedings of the House shall be broadcast during certain
hours of sitting-7.30 p.m. to 10.30 p.m., for example, on Thursday. The hours can be
varied by the House taking urgency. But the Standing Order also says that the proceedings
of Parliament shall be broadcast during all hours of sitting prescribed by Standing Order 39.
The hours for a Thursday in Standing Order 39 are 7.30 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. The broadcast
ceases at 10.30 p.m. unless the Leader of the House, at his discretion, extends it. The
broadcast does not commence again until 9 a.m. on Friday morning's sitting. The Standing
Orders are clear about the hours of sitting prescribed. I hope that makes it clear to the
honourable member.

getting a little impatient, I must say.

Mr SPEAKER: I am sorry to tell the honourable member that Standing Order 39 refers

Opposition, knowing that Friday is a day when many members have commitments in their
electorates and that their families also have to be considered? Does the Deputy Prime
Minister intend to use such a parliamentary weapon to bludgeon the Opposition? If that is
his intention, he is not going to be successful, and he might as well forget about his motion. I
put it to him that he should withdraw it. We have a light legislative programme. Let us
debate the matter sensibly and intelligently on Tuesday. We are prepared to debate the
matter then, and we will do so as befits our democratic traditions, and as people expect us to
debate.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): This Standing Order, although it is not used
very often, is obviously there so the House may use it when it is necessary to proceed in an
orderly fashion with its business. I suggest that it would not have been necessary for the
Government to move this motion today had the Opposition sought to follow the traditions of
the House last night.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I cannot permit reference to what occurred in the House last
night. Last night's debate or the items on the Order Paper that could be put up for debate
today are irrelevant to the discussion about whether the House should sit during the hours
proposed by the Deputy Prime Minister.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: There is, however, one reference to last night that I believe, Mr
Speaker, you would permit. I understand that, when the Minister of Trade and Industry was
Acting Leader of the House, he was asked when the House would go back on the air, and my
colleague said it would go back on the air when we returned to the Friday programme. We
have not yet reached the Friday programme. The resolution before the House was moved
because of a desire to resume a Friday programme. Obviously, the sooner we dispose of this
debate, the sooner that can take place. The member for Auckland Central also asked how
long the sitting would last if urgency were taken. That inevitably depends upon the
Opposition. Opposition members can talk at length about a subject, as they have evidenced
for the last 24 hours, or they can come to the point and concern themselves with the more
essential features of the business before the House. The member for Auckland Central, who
rose in protest, was seeking to do two things. I suppose he deserves credit from his
colleagues for both. First, he was giving his leader time to collect his thoughts.
Mr Prebble: What's wrong with that?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Nothing is wrong with that, but obviously the member for Auckland
Central had not had time to collect his thoughts before he opposed the motion. It is not an
unreasonable request in the circumstances. The other feature of his immediate rising,
conspicuously alone on the matter, is obviously the lead he is taking in the succession stakes
in the Labour Party.
The member for Auckland Central said that he is anxious that the House shall have an
opportunity to talk about certain matters before it in a sensible way. I am sure that is the
wish of every member, and it will be possible if we can put aside the consequences of some of
the bickering that has taken place and the time delays that occurred last night. I commend
the motion to the House.
Mr SPEAKER: I do not want to hear any further references to bickering, time delays, or
whatever occurred last night. What happened last night is irrelevant to the question before
the House, which is simply whether or not the House is to agree with the motion put forward
by the Deputy Prime Minister about the proposed sitting hours for today.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I should have expected a little
better from the Minister of Energy than his comments about the member for Auckland

precipitated the motion I was out of the House, and the Opposition Whip properly, and

Miss Dewe: And whose fault is that?

business the Deputy Prime Minister wants to pursue during the proposed session from

The second point that requires answering relates to the broadcasting of the proceedings
of the House. The Minister of Energy said that when we get into a Friday situation,
broadcasting of the debate can resume, but if the House agreed to the motion and resumed
at 12.30 p.m. one would assume that broadcasting would cease at 1 o'clock. Is that to be the

urgency motion on the resumption of the sitting of the House at 12.30 p.m. That also is

12.30 p.m. until 2 p.m. is just a certain amount of humbug and has no actual meaning in

therefore no excuse for driving members beyond reasonable bounds. If the Deputy Prime
Minister can give an assurance that any debates that take place this afternoon will be
confined to the hours mentioned in the motion he proposed, there may be a rather more
amenable approach to it from this side of the House than can be the case at the moment.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): When I was asked
earlier this morning, I said as my colleague the Minister of Energy has said, that we would
start broadcasting when we started Friday. At the moment we are still in Thursday. My
understanding of Standing Orders 49 and 39 is that it would be proper for us to broadcast for
the time mentioned in the motion, the motion that would bring us back to the House at 12.30
and continue until 2 p.m. I believe that is the correct position in terms of the Standing Order.
The business is as set down for today, and the Government considers we should proceed with
that business.
Mr Prebble: Any urgency?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: We always have urgency. That is the position. I
sensed during the week that the Opposition was keen to get on to the imprest debate. I am
sure that it is keen to get on to the imprest debate now.
Mr Prebble: But you cannot start on the imprest on the air.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Imprest is the business for Friday. I cannot
understand the member's interjection.
Mr Prebble: What about questions, notices of motion, and reports of select committees?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: My understanding is that we will move on to the
imprest debate and the Opposition will have a period on the air until 2 p.m. arrives. My
understanding is that under the Standing Orders it can be done; it will be done; and it should
be done. If the Opposition wants to get on with the debate and I suppose there are some
issues they want to bring up in an imprest supply debate-this motion will enable it to do so
on the day that members opposite expected they would be doing so, namely, on Friday of
this week.

He has given us an assurance about broadcasting hours, and it was carefully framed. He

Imprest Supply Bill.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: You are being difficult.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: It has nothing to do with being difficult. It is a question of the

business and the Government honours its promise to the member for Rangitikei, we will not

Paper does appear until after 2 p.m. when, according to the Minister of Trade and Industry,
we will be off the air. The business of the House for the last day—although actually it has
been 2 days-went back to the actions of the Government when it introduced a Bill today. If
the situation is getting complex I refer you to one of your own rulings during the debate.
Mr SPEAKER: Perhaps I can remind the honourable member of another one. We are
not debating the introduction of a Bill so his comment is not relevant.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: But how shall we know when it is Sunday? Everybody outside the
House knows it is Friday, but the unfortunate inhabitants or inmates of this building are told
it is Thursday. There is a provision that the House shall adjourn at midnight on Saturday,
and the Chairman is supposed to be aware of the fact at 5 minutes to midnight that Sunday is
coming up. The calendar tells him it is Friday. Does he have a 23 hour 55 minute hiatus or
aberration when he jumps from the clock he sees before him to a calendar that says it is
Friday, and realises that after all it is Saturday and, in the words of Mr Speaker Algie,

Hon. L. R. Adams-Schneider: Is the honourable member going to Church or to golf on

Hon. R. J. TIZARD: I am going to Nuie if I can get to the bank to get some money. Of

ridiculous and is of the Government's making because of its wasteful discussion on a Bill that
was not contested. We should proceed with the supplementary estimates, dispose of them,
and forget the Imprest Supply Bill until Tuesday.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): Members know that normal sitting hours for Friday are from

Hon. A. J. Faulkner: With a normal Government, yes.
Mr BIRCH: With a normal Opposition debating the supplementary estimates, Friday's

intends to debate an Imprest Supply Bill on Friday, and the Opposition knows it is normal
